Hold Steady, Hold Steady

by thetalee

Summary

After Eddie's bombshell announcement on Christmas, Buck runs away and finds himself back on his first day on the job.

A time-travel fix-it fic of sorts, ft. a stranger that totally just wants to help, honest.

The Past is Prologue

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Buck wasn’t certain what brought him so far outside of the city. Or, no, that wasn’t quite right. He knew how he’d ended up outside of Los Angeles. He knew exactly what had driven him out of the city. He just wasn’t certain how he’d ended up here, precisely: on the side of a deserted crossroads, miles and miles and miles from home.

Twelve hours ago, during Bobby and Athena’s impromptu Christmas party for everyone from the red-tagged apartment building, Eddie had gathered them all up and announced that he was leaving. Twelve hours ago, Buck had dropped his Santa hat to the ground, turned, and got into his jeep. Twelve hours ago, he had started driving without a destination in mind, no thoughts beyond “no” and “leaving” and “why.”

His phone had been ringing constantly the first few hours, taunting him from its spot in the passenger seat, where he’d thrown it before starting the engine. Taylor, Bobby, Hen, Ravi, and of course Eddie. He never answered, didn’t even bother to reach over and deny the calls, and eventually his phone suffered the same fate as his Christmas spirit. His jeep had died too, eventually. It turns out that unlike him, it couldn’t continue running on anxiety alone.

So, there Evan Buckley was: stranded on the side of the road, a long walk away from a gas station, in the middle of the night on Christmas. 

Alone.

Or, as the case may be, not alone.

He’d gotten out to start the trek for gas when he spotted the other man. He was tall and skinny and looming, with a wide brim hat and a long black coat. The light of the waning moon was enough to see how the man smiled pleasantly at him from across the intersection, to see how thin his face was. His eyes were set deep into their sockets, and his cheekbones jutted out. Buck couldn’t help but think of skulls.

“Howdy, stranger,” the stranger said, walking across the pavement. His footsteps made no sound in the near silence. “What's got you out here at this hour?”

“My, uh, my jeep died,” Buck answered, awkwardly gesturing at it over his shoulder. “It’s out of gas.”

“Well I can see that,” he said. “But why are you here?”

“Just out for a drive, I guess. I wasn’t paying attention.”

“You were just out for a drive? Alone? On Christmas?”

“My friend’s leaving,” Buck told him, and even just speaking the words out loud sent a pang of loss through his heart. “My sister and her boyfriend left with my niece months ago, and now my best friend is leaving, and I- I just wanted to clear my head.”

“Did you? Clear your head, I mean.”

“No. I just got myself stuck.” He let out a humorless laugh. “Eddie told us he was leaving the station and I just couldn’t stand to be there anymore. I wasn’t thinking ahead. I never think ahead.”

“The station?”

“I’m a firefighter, in LA. And I know leaving the station isn’t the same as leaving me, but- Why am I telling you this?”

“Sounds like you needed a friendly ear,” the stranger said, holding out his hand. “Name’s Ichabod.”

“Uh, Buck,” he answered, shaking it awkwardly, uncomfortable about giving his name to a total stranger in the middle of nowhere in the middle of the night. “Listen, uh, can I borrow your phone?”

“Don't have one on me,” Ichabod told him. “Tell me, what is it that you want?”

“What?”

“What do you want, Buck?” he repeated, the words carrying an almost physical weight.

“I- I don’t- To fix things,” Buck blurted out, the words clawing their way out of his throat of their own volition. “I want to fix whatever broke my family but I don’t even know what that was. I don’t even know when it was.”

“Well, I guess I can work with that,” the man said, smiling broadly. He had never let go of Buck’s hand, fingers keeping it in an iron grip.

Had his eyes always been black?

Buck woke up in his bed with a headache worse than the time he tried to outdrink a Russian tourist in Peru. It didn’t help that Felix was in the kitchen blasting Britney Spears at top volume while he cooked. Normally that would be okay - top volume was the only acceptable volume for listening to Toxic, after all - but not when his brain was doing its best impression of a conga-line in his skull. There was nausea to go with it, too, and all of this would be perfectly normal for a hangover if he’d been drinking at all the night before.

He hadn’t. Been drinking, that was. It was his first day as a probationary firefighter, after months and months of going through the academy, and Buck needed-

Wait.

What?

He blinked his eyes open, took in his surroundings with pained confusion.

“What the fuck?” It was whispered, but it was still akin to poking his own eye with an icepick. 

The problem wasn’t that he didn’t know where he was, oh no. He recognized his room in the apartment he had shared with the guys he’d followed from Peru.  The apartment he hadn’t lived in since Abby. The apartment he hasn’t stepped foot in for literal years now.

Why was he suffering the worst hangover ever in his old room?

Why did he wake up thinking it was his first day at the station?

Why did it sound like Felix was strangling a cat as he sang along to the music?

There were two options here. Option one: he got really, really, really drunk after Eddie’s bombshell of an announcement and for some reason texted Felix or one of the others, who then brought him back and laid him out in his old room. Or option two: the last four years or so of his life were nothing but an extremely vivid, detailed, and realistic dream. For some reason, Buck was simultaneously relieved and disappointed when he checked his phone for the date to find that it was, indeed, 2017.

The second option, then.

What the hell, brain.

He couldn’t shake the utter feeling of loss that settled over him, though. Some of the things his subconscious had come up with had been awful - his leg, the tsunami, the well, the sniper - but he’d had a family. Even if it was splintering at the end. Chimney and Hen and Ravi and Eddie and Chris, they probably didn’t even exist outside of his imagination. Maddie was - hopefully - perfectly safe in Hershey. And Bobby was probably nothing at all like the real Captain Nash.

Was it normal, to grieve over a life that was never even real? He’d have to ask Dr. Copeland when- No. She wasn’t real, either. Shoot.

The alarm on his phone chose that moment to start blaring as a warning that he needed to be getting up. He hurried to dress and grab his work bag and rush out the door, dry swallowing a couple of ibuprofen and waving awkwardly to Felix as he went. He could not wait to start his actual first day, he could not wait to tell Maddie all about it in the next postcard.

Buck paused as he got out of his jeep, because… The outside looked the same. It looked exactly the same. But that was to be expected, he’d driven by it once, just so he knew where it was and how to get there. His subconscious must have grabbed onto that memory and milked it for all it was worth.

What wasn’t to be expected was how the inside wasn’t any different from his dream, either. What wasn’t to be expected was how he followed the smell of Bobby’s familiar cooking up the stairs to a loft he knew like the back of his hand. What wasn’t to be expected was to find Hen and Chimney and Bobby sitting there eating, exactly like that first day. Hen and Chimney and Bobby, all of them perfectly real and not a dream.

“Hi, uh- Evan Buckley, new recruit,” Buck said, while on the inside he was screaming. “I was- I was told to report to uh, Captain Nash?”

He watched as they all feigned confusion and looked at each other, as Bobby asked them if they knew Captain Nash, and Buck-

Buck had no clue what was going on, anymore.

Not option one.

Not option two.

What the fuck was option three, then?

Chapter End Notes

Begin Again

The first time around, Buck spent his first day settling in with the others and getting to know his way around the station. He had been excited and ecstatic and could not wait to get out there and help save the day. Sitting down at the table to eat with the others after he’d introduced himself had felt every bit like coming home, not that he had ever really known what that was like before that moment.

This second time around? He spent it an anxious mess. They all probably thought he was weirder than they had before - or would? Whatever. He nearly started crying at the sight of Chimney, back in the station, and then had to keep himself from flinching away whenever the man got into his space. He knew that Hen had noticed it, because she sent him concerned glances at every aborted jerk of his body.

He definitely started crying when his eyes automatically went to find Eddie, only to remember that the man wasn’t even in the state yet. Luckily, he managed to keep the tears at bay long enough to run to the bathroom with a hasty excuse. It didn’t even dawn on him until he was wiping his face that he hadn’t even pretended to ask where the bathroom was first.

This wasn’t okay. Whatever the hell was happening, or had happened, it was not okay and neither was he. But he had spent his entire life pretending to be fine even as he desperately wanted to scream until his throat bled. So he would ignore how much it hurt to see his family and have them not see him. He would ignore how much it ached to turn around and not have Eddie there to joke with.

He would ignore the agony of knowing that Maddie was back in Hershey with Doug, trapped in a cycle of abuse he could do nothing about.

In the bathroom, he met the eyes of his reflection and painstakingly rebuilt that cocky mask he hadn’t used in so very long. He had to remember that he was a stranger to these people that he had - would - call family. He had to remember that he wasn’t supposed to know anything about them, that he couldn’t ask this Hen about Denny and Karen, that he couldn’t ask this Chimney about the brother he didn’t even talk to yet. He had to remember that he hadn’t even met Athena yet, that she and Bobby weren’t anywhere near being a couple

He had to remember, no matter how much it pained him, that this Bobby was still mourning the loss of one family and was yet to be convinced that he deserved a new one.

And he still didn’t know what was going on.

Somehow, Buck managed to get through the shift without convincing everyone he was insane, and without actually going insane. When he casually mentioned his bisexuality during a conversation with Hen, it managed to goad her into telling him about Karen and Denny. He had never straight up admitted it Before - as he was referring to it in his head - but Buck 1.0 had never hidden the pronouns of his casual partners before Abby, so it wasn’t like it was ever a secret.

In hindsight, he wasn’t certain if Eddie had ever known, because it wasn’t like he was going around bragging by the time the man was with them.

It was easier, so much easier, to begin reforging what he once had with Hen than the others. Bobby was actively working against forging bonds at this point, still tallying up lives saved versus lives taken until he could justify carrying out the most mortal of sins. And everything with Chimney was overshadowed by the feeling of a fist smashing into his eye and angry words of “I am not okay.” It was still a tangled mess of pain and sorrow caused by being left behind again, by his sister running off and Chimney running after her with his niece.

It was easier, so much easier, with Hen. Except it was also harder, because she wasn’t an idiot. Because unlike Chimney, who could be painfully oblivious at times, and Bobby, who wasn’t willing to look, she was perfectly able to see that something was going on. By the time he left the station at the end of his second first day, he could tell that she had a list of questions to ambush him with as soon as she deemed him comfortable enough for it. She probably had theories about his flinching from Chimney, about the way he teared up when Bobby asked if he could cook, that could never be anywhere near the truth, but which he wouldn’t be able to correct. Because what could he say to her if she asked? That he dreamed up an entire future with them in it?

She would never believe it. He still had trouble believing it.

After his shift, he had to remind himself to turn in the right direction, muscle memory threatening to take him towards the loft. And how did he even have that muscle memory, anyway? It was a procedural memory, gained by doing something so many times that the neurons of the brain are permanently bound to that path. That would imply that he physically traveled back in time, but his leg was scar free. He had checked it when he dressed before leaving the apartment, just to reassure himself that everything had been a dream.

The last thing he remembered, before waking up in his bed, was meeting Ichabod at the crossroads. And boy, if that phrase didn’t send a shiver down his spine. He was tempted, almost, to drive back there and see if he reappeared, so he could demand answers. Except that he had been, in essence, utterly lost when his jeep ran out of gas that night. The drive had been aimless, and he wasn’t even certain of which turns he had taken or how far outside of Los Angeles he’d ended up.

Finding those crossroads again, finding Ichabod, would have to wait until he had the time for it.

Buck stumbled into the apartment, waving at Felix and the others in the shared living room as he passed, and collapsed into his too small bed. He wasn’t sure if he could live like this again, tripping over people in a too-cramped living space. It had been okay the first time around, when he hadn’t known anything better and was still chasing the vague idea of family. But now? Now he missed his giant king sized bed. Hell, he missed Eddie’s couch.

He missed Eddie.

He was lonely. Lonelier than he had been after his leg, when he was stuck hobbling around his loft. He was lonelier than he had been during and after the lawsuit, when he was briefly the pariah at the station. At least then, even if they were pissed at him, everyone was still themselves.

The day had been spent working beside people he cared for that weren’t the people he knew. Years of history had been torn away, and he was the only one to remember, and it left him adrift and alone. Just thinking about it had tears gathering in his eyes again. It had only just been a day, but Buck already missed them. He missed Bobby and Hen and Chimney, even if he had just seen them, because they hadn’t been them. They hadn’t been the people he spent four and a half years running through fire with.

He missed Maddie, which came with a wave of powerless despair, and he missed Jee-Yun, who wasn’t even born yet and might never be. He missed Athena and he missed Ravi and he missed Albert. He missed Taylor, who had reported on the traffic as he drove, the surprise of her voice nearly sending him off the road.

He missed Chris, and Carla.

He missed Eddie.

It was a terrible time to realize that he was in love with someone, when he had already lost them and yet also hadn’t even met them yet.

Tomorrow, he’ll figure out what he was doing. He’ll start looking at apartments, because he could not stand the idea of living with these near strangers a moment longer. He’ll send that postcard to Maddie, and try to entice her to run away from Doug earlier. He’ll sit down and write out everything he remembered, because Ichabod had asked him what he wanted and he said it was to fix whatever had gone wrong.

Tomorrow, he’ll figure out what he was doing with this second chance.

Tonight, he was going to lie here and wallow in his loneliness.

Chasing Waterfalls

Dear Maddie,

California is amazing and I know you would love it here. I had my first day as a probationary firefighter yesterday. Station 118 is where I’m meant to be. I know it is.

I plan on looking for an apartment of my own, one with enough room for you. If you ever want to visit, I mean.

You’ll always have a safe place with me.

P.S.: There were three other Evans in my class at the fire academy, so everyone calls me Buck now.

One of the most difficult things about this second chance was knowing about Maddie’s circumstances, and not being able to do anything about it. Sure, yes, he could get on a plane to Pennsylvania and play the white knight, but what would that accomplish? Maddie hadn’t gone with him before, he couldn’t go and try to drag her out now, not without spooking her. Not without possibly sending her burrowing further into Doug’s clutches. Buck had to wait for her to make the choice to leave the situation on her own terms. Again.

There was nothing he could do, except make sure she knew the option was there.

Life at the station was an adjustment. Gradually, as days became weeks became months, he stopped seeing the ghosts of a future yet to be around every corner. He got used to not having Eddie at his side, and he got used to being the probie again instead of Ravi. He stopped flinching every time Chimney was suddenly in his space or reached for him out of the corner of his eye.

Hen, exactly as predicted, cornered him one day about a month into his probationary period. She brought with her pamphlets with resources for abuse victims and the open offer to listen if he ever wanted to talk about it. He thanked her, and then silently swore to never take her up on it. What would he say, anyways?

“I keep flinching whenever Chimney makes sudden movements because four and a half years from now, he punched me for not telling him about my sister and their daughter. Oh yeah and also I somehow traveled backwards in time. PS: Don’t sleep with Eva.”

Yeah, no, that was never going to happen. Psych evals were a thing, and the department didn’t let crazy people work for them.

The first few months, Buck didn’t really make an effort to change anything. There were changes, because he was a much different person than he was the first time around, but he didn’t actively try for them. Mostly, he just didn’t sleep around like the original Buck 1.0 did. His ill-fated relationship with Abby, and the subsequent therapy with Dr. Copeland, helped him realize that what he had thought was a sex addiction was just him desperately seeking scraps of positive attention and affection wherever he could get it.

Buck still went to the Springsteen concert with Bobby. The first time around, he had just been desperate to bond with a father figure, any father figure. This time around, he just desperately wanted to have Bobby back in his life in the way he had been before. Or, the way he would be. Was going to be?

Keeping the tenses straight gave him a tension headache.

Working on calls that he had already lived through was interesting, to say the least. Some of them, he only vaguely recalled, and those were the easiest because he didn’t have to pretend. Some of them he remembered well, and he caught the others staring at him oddly whenever he anticipated their needs.

“Are you psychic?” Chimney eventually demanded one day between calls, cornering him in the station kitchen. “What are my lucky lottery numbers?”

“I’m not psychic,” Buck said, silently mourning the fact that he hadn’t paid attention to the lottery the first time around. That would make apartment hunting so much easier.

“That’s bullshit, you have to be. There’s no way you can just guess what’s going to be needed ahead of time. And you went straight for the room with the woman in it, at that last house fire.”

“I… Heard her shouting?”

“Was that a question or an answer?” Hen asked, smirking at him from where she was sitting.

“Either I heard her shouting, or I’m psychic. Which is more believable?”

Hen shrugged.

“That’s fair.”

It didn’t help his case any when the day finally came with the baby in the wall and he carried the saw in with them, ”just in case.” Chimney and Hen both sent him odd looks when it turned out to be exactly the right tool to get the baby safely extracted.

Coming face-to-face with Athena Grant for the first time since waking up years in the past was something he had been looking forward to, only he hadn't thought about how they had met. She hadn’t been impressed with the way he shouted at her, that first time. She was probably going to be even less impressed this time.

“Is that the mother? No,” he told her, when she started loading the mother onto the ambulance. “Look what she did!”

“She’s bleeding out!” Athena retorted.

“They can’t ride in the same bus together,” he told her, swallowing as she directed the full force of her glare at him. Five years later, he could finally make this argument without his emotions getting the better of him. But five years was hardly enough experience to make weathering Athena Grant’s displeasure an easy task. “It’s against protocol. This baby is the victim of a crime she committed. One of them needs another ride.”

Bobby and the others arrived in the middle of it, as they did last time. And like last time, he was overridden and had to bite his tongue as the mother was taken onto the ambulance with them. When they got to the hospital, he didn’t need Bobby to explain where their obligations ended, even though that became less and less true as the years went by. It was still difficult, though, to watch them wheel the nameless baby through the doors and not follow.

“Hey!” Athena shouted, stomping her way to him. “You do not get to choose who lives and- I am talking to you! Who are you calling?”

“Child Protective Services,” Buck explained. “We’re mandatory reporters, sergeant, and she flushed her newborn down the toilet.”

It was possible, maybe, that this second first encounter with Athena went worse than the first one. Just maybe. And he couldn’t tell if Bobby and the others were impressed by his ballsiness, or if their opinion of him dropped several notches. The latter wouldn’t be so bad, though, because their opinions of Buck 1.0 had been much lower on the first go.

There were positives and negatives with not having hookups while on the job. Positive: He wasn’t fired, even if only briefly. Not that Bobby actually had the authority to fire him - that was entirely up to the fire chief - but that was just semantics. Negative: He wasn’t fired. Yes, not being fired was both a positive and a negative. Because, with the benefit of hindsight, he knew that having been left at the station to clean out his locker instead of going on that call with the others was what allowed him to aid Athena with the break-in call. It allowed him to be there so he could keep that last burglar from shooting her.

The others looked at him oddly, when he requested to be the man behind. But it worked, because he was free to take the other truck out at Hen’s request. Nevermind that this was probably doing nothing to convince them that he wasn’t psychic. Maybe he should just lean into it.

And he still didn’t know what Athena meant by “don’t go chasing waterfalls.”

See the Sun Again

Hearing Abby’s voice again had been the oddest of experiences, because it hadn’t hurt. Buck had spent the entire time leading up to the call with Athena dreading to hear the dispatcher’s voice again, and he hadn’t really felt much of anything. Once upon a time, he had been certain that he loved her. Now, having realized the full breadth of his feelings for Eddie in the man’s absence, he knew that whatever he had felt for her was nothing compared to that all-consuming fire. But he had felt something for her, once. Something more than he ever felt for Taylor, even as they stumbled through awkward “I love you”s.

(He didn’t love Taylor. He was aware of that even before he met Ichabod and rewound time. How could he, when his heart had been so devoted to another, even if he hadn’t known it?)

With the benefits of hindsight and therapy and many years between now and then, Buck realized how ill-fated his relationship with the older woman had been. He had listened to Bobby’s advice, had delved into the mess with her, except that hadn’t been what she had wanted or needed. She had just been looking for something to distract her from her ailing mother. He had seen something serious, where she had seen a distraction, and that disconnect caused more pain in the end than her leaving ever did.

But it was through Abby that he had met Carla, and the home health aide had been such a godsend for Eddie and Chris. If nothing else, the pain that Abby caused him was worth it just for that. She was a matter for later, though.  She wasn’t going to reach out to him until after the rollercoaster.

After Devon.

The first time around, they had come from the wrong angle with the truck, the ladder unable to reach where the young man was hanging. Buck had had to climb up and get the harness onto him. Buck had reached his hand out, and the other man had simply… Let go.

To say that the sight of him falling and hitting the ground had stuck with him was an understatement.

This time around, Buck casually suggested that they take the truck to the other side of the ride. Bobby had looked at him, contemplating and examining, but he let him drive them where he wanted. The ladder was able to reach where everyone was stuck this time, and Buck was able to go straight for them.

Devon still didn’t take his hand.

Devon still fell.

The news interviews that followed, the fact that he was famous for failing (again) to save a man, did not help matters at all. Even with years of experience now under his belt, it wasn’t any easier. His relationship with Taylor did come in handy in this, however: he wasn’t fumbling through his answers in front of the camera like he had the first time.

Abby getting his number from the burglary report and using it to call him after seeing one of those interviews was not as… Endearing, as it had been before. Not when he was no longer that brash kid he had been, starved for affection.

At least this time around, he managed to avoid worrying Bobby enough to be sent to Welles. The thought of her made his skin crawl and nausea bubble in his throat, and he knew exactly why that was. But as long as he didn’t say it out loud, it wasn’t what happened. He hadn’t said yes, but he hadn’t said no, and so it couldn’t have been that. That was not what it was, that was not what happened. Not to him. And it wasn’t going to happen.

If he made an anonymous complaint of therapist misconduct all the same, it still wasn’t an act of admission. It was just… Unprofessional.  She’d said so herself, when she ran him out of her office.

(That she was investigated and then quietly sent packing did not make him feel any better.)

It was an odd tightrope he had to walk, when Abby called him again. Buck didn’t want to date her again, didn’t even want a fling with her, but he needed something with her. He needed to meet Carla, so he could introduce her to Eddie when his abuela broke her hip. Hopefully, just being friends with Abby would achieve the same end result. And it had been really nice to talk to someone outside of the station again that wasn’t his pseudo-Frat roommates.

It wasn’t just Abby’s phantom haunting him, either. It was at some point between the rollercoaster fiasco and him meeting the dispatcher face-to-face that he knew May had her suicide attempt. Except he wasn’t even supposed to know anything about Athena’s family yet, so he couldn’t just cryptically tell her to throw out her pills. He was leaning a bit more into the psychic joke, including a whole “the universe tells me…” routine that he made sure to get hilariously wrong every time, but the sergeant was about as superstitious as Eddie was. Which is to say, she’d likely shoot him for stalking her children if he came to her with concerns about May.

And it wasn’t just May, either.

When Chimney came into work in a mood while he and Hen ran over virtual people in a virtual firetruck, Buck knew exactly what day it was. He watched, a horrible feeling of dread coiling in his guts, as Bobby dressed down the paramedic for all the flaws in his relationship with his girlfriend, Tatiana. It was made worse as Chimney grew angrier and angrier, which had all of Buck’s nerves alight with fight-or-flight.

“Y’know what? I feel bad for your wife, I really do,” Chimney sneered. Buck couldn’t hold back his gasp of shock, because this time he knew exactly what kind of hit that was, even while the paramedics didn’t. “It must be tough, living with someone who thinks they’re right all the time.”

“Chim-” Hen started to say as he walked off.

“No, I’m getting some air.”

“Chimney, don’t go driving while you’re angry,” Buck tried. “Please-”

“Oh stuff it, Uri Geller,” Chimney sneered, before stomping down the stairs.

“Who’s Uri Geller?” Buck asked, not really caring about the answer.

Finding a friend and coworker with a piece of rebar through his head was just as harrowing as it had been the first time. Waiting for word about the surgery had him climbing the walls, and he knew that everything was going to be okay in the end. How did he get through this last time, without that reassurance?

The call with the Mexican migrants in the truck was a welcome distraction this time as it was the last. He could even offer more than fractured Spanish to them this time, offering them a bridge in the confusing and traumatic moment. When Hen and Bobby both looked at him weirdly, he simply mentioned living in Peru for a bit.

(At one point, after Hen football tackled the driver of the truck the migrants had been in, Abby called him. He didn’t answer, because he was working and because he wasn’t that desperate for connection anymore.

He called her when they were back in the station, because he still wanted to be her friend and he still wanted to meet Carla again.)

He eventually found an apartment at the beginning of February, not far from where Eddie had- or rather, would live. The loft wasn’t available yet, and honestly he didn’t want to get somewhere with stairs again. At one point, he saw that Eddie’s place was available, but he couldn’t bear to even do a walkthrough of it. It would just be an empty husk of what had once been a second home, and it would just kill him to see Christopher’s room so empty.

He still drove by it, though. Because apparently he was a bit of a masochist, but that wasn’t anything new.

His new apartment was only a couple streets away, a two-bedroom with a large kitchen. Felix and the others helped him move what little belongings he had in this time, and afterwards the place was still mostly empty. But there was room for him, and for Maddie when she finally came, and for Eddie and Chimney when the world began to end again, and for Albert when it was his turn.

He sent a new postcard to Maddie, the day he had everything moved in. It had his new address, and where he was going to keep the spare key, “just in case you ever drop by and I’m not home.”

After the plane crash, there weren’t many things that Buck could change, not that he didn’t try. He couldn’t keep Bobby from going on that bender, despite doing his best to invite himself over so he wasn’t alone. He couldn’t keep Hen from entangling herself once again with Eva, because that would require that she open up to him about her ex. He did manage to keep from earning a new tracheotomy scar, if only by virtue of fully friendzoning Abby and therefore not going on a date that Valentine’s Day.

It wasn’t until the day was over and done with that he realized he had missed that bonding moment with Bobby, learning how to tie a tie. He wasn’t sure how he felt about that, because he still remembered it. But this Bobby would never have that moment with him.

Reliving the full moon shift, with the yoga babies and the tapeworm, was frustrating. Just like last time, neither Bobby nor Abby believed him about the effects the moon could have on people. Last time, their skepticism was easy to brush off, but that was before he met Ichabod. After encountering a black-eyed stranger in the middle of nowhere who can send people back in time, the moon’s ability to affect people and animals was the least implausible part of his existence.

Wait, shit, did that mean a ghost really did call 9-1-1 that one time?

In March, there was the blood drive and the man-eating tiger, and the flooded elevator, which was not kind to his post-tsunami PTSD. Then there was the hoarder call, which was funny to tell later, but god if it wasn’t nerve wracking at the time. He managed to avoid the bowling ball to the face, though. Afterwards, when Patricia died, he helped Abby with everything, just as he did before. They might not have been together romantically this time, but she was still his friend. 

And then, Buck saw them.

It was on his way to work, when he drove down South Bedford on a whim and past their house. He saw them both, together, for the first time in months and also ever. It was the glint of sunlight on crutches that first caught his eye, and he had to pull over before he became a statistic on the hazards of distracted driving. They didn’t even look at his jeep, didn’t even recognize it, because of course they didn’t. They’d never seen it before.

But it was them, it was Eddie and Chris. In LA, finally.

Not even being accosted by a complete stranger accusing him of ghosting her was enough to shatter his mood.

(At least this time it was easier to get the others to believe him.)

Always for the First Time

When the day came, Buck woke up with a smile. For weeks, ever since that chance moment in March, he had been counting down the days. Now, finally, the day was the day. He was practically dancing through the apartment as he got ready for work, placing the spare key on top of the doorframe where he told Maddie it would be, and more-or-less skipped out of the building to his jeep.

He didn’t drive down Bedford. He wanted to, but decided against it. Besides, Eddie was probably dropping off Christopher at that ill-equipped public school he started out at. The A/C was on full blast, as was the radio, and Buck sang along at the top of his lungs, even as he got to the station and walked in to start the day.

“Whatta man, whatta man, whatta man, whatta mighty good man!”

“Okay seriously, what is up with you both?” Hen asked, pointing between him and Bobby. “You have both been annoyingly happy recently.”

“Can’t we just be happy, Henrietta?” Buck asked, grinning at her.

“Don’t call me that,” she scolded. “And sure you could, but this happy? At the same-”

She stopped mid-sentence, narrowed her eyes, and glanced between them. It took Buck a moment, because there was no way she could honestly think that, but what else could that look be about? She’d directed that look at him and Eddie enough times, and hopefully she would again.

“God no, Hen!” he shouted, recoiling. “That’s not- That is just- No. Just no.”

“What’s wrong?” Chimney asked, joining them.

“Hen. Hen is what’s wrong,” he told him. To her, he said, “If you really must know, I’m at my goal weight for the Hot Days, Smoldering Nights: Men of the LAFD wall calendar.”

It was an utter lie - he knew they’d go with Chimney, after all - but the mention of the calendar competition distracted her from the frankly horrifying line of thought she’d gone on.

“Do you really need to use that whole title?” she asked. “You could just say, ‘that idiotic, reductive, sexist calendar that insults the dignity of this organization and furthers the myth that all firefighters are male.’”

“Mine was less of a mouthful.”

“Hen, come on, it’s for charity.”

“No. Bobby, you, too?” And honestly, Buck had forgotten how disappointed she had sounded that he was joining in.

“Why not?” Bobby asked. “They say a man is at his sexiest when he reaches fifty.”

“No offense, cap,” Buck said, “But I never want to think of you in terms of ‘sexiest’ ever again.”

“You’re both wrong,” Chimney interrupted. “Alright? Y’see, I think sorority houses all across this great nation are ready for a new male Asian sex symbol.”

“Pretty sure they already have Daniel Wu for that,” he said. “But I think it’s great you’re both going up for it.”

“Because you don’t think we have a chance,” Bobby accused.

“Did I say that? I mean, they are only picking one candidate from each station-”

“Okay that,” Chimney cut him off, “is a beautiful man.”

“Where’s the lie?” Hen asked, following his gaze to the locker room behind Buck. “And I like girls.”

Shit, shit, shit, this was the moment. Okay, Buck had to act casual. He couldn’t just run in there and start badgering him about Chris. Eddie didn’t know him yet, he’d just get punched for it and then Eddie would never let him close. He turned to the lockers, and immediately cursed and thanked whoever decided to make the locker room walls out of glass, because he got to see Eddie half-dressed and pulling on his shirt.

(Was he actually doing it in slow motion, or was that just in Buck’s head?)

But he had to act casual. He couldn’t act like he was seeing the long-lost love of his life, or like a pet dog finally seeing their owner after too long of a separation. He had to act casual, like Eddie was the total stranger he was supposed to be. He had to act casual.

“Who the hell is that?” Shit! He was overcorrecting! “I uh, I mean-”

“Eddie Diaz, new recruit,” Bobby told them, and both he and Hen were smirking at his reaction, though probably for different reasons. Buck only half-listened as their captain sang Eddie’s praises.”Graduated top of his class last week. The guys at Station Six were dying to have him, but I convinced him to join us. Multiple tours in Afghanistan as an Army medic, got a silver star.”

It took every bit of strength Buck had not to jump in and tell them to not bring up that silver star. Because he wasn’t supposed to know the how or the why of it. Eddie was supposed to be a brand new coworker that he never met before. He wasn’t supposed to be tearing up at the sight of him like this.

“C’mon, I’ll introduce you,” the captain said, leading them to the lockers. “He likes to be called Eight Pack.”

God, Buck had missed him so much and he was so in love, and this was going to be so much harder than he ever could have imagined it would be.

(“I’m leaving the One-Eighteen…")

So much harder.

“So, Silver Star, huh?” Chimney asked. They were in the truck on the way to the auto-repair shop with the poor guy pumped full of air. Having Eddie there with them settled something deep within Buck. He was a step closer to having his family back together again, and this time he was not going to let any of them slip away.

“Yeah.” Eddie glanced at them and then quickly back out the window, clearly uncomfortable with the paramedic’s curiosity, and Buck felt like such a dick for not noticing it the first time

“You save a-?”

Buck elbowed him into silence, shaking his head when Chimney looked at him in confusion. Hen, bless her, took his cue and changed topics.

“Eddie, you heard about the hot firefighter calendar?”

“Sorry, the what?”

“It’s for charity,” she explained, shooting a mocking grin at Buck.

“Is your full name ‘Eduardo’?” Buck asked, nudging Eddie’s foot with his own and ignoring Hen’s attempt to tease him about the calendar.

“No.”

“People ever call you ‘Diaz’?” He was following the old script, because he had missed teasing him like this.

“Not if they want me to respond,” Eddie answered, which had Buck frowning, because he had responded to Lena when she did it.

“Well something’s got to give. We’ve got Cap, Hen, Chimney, Buck,” he explained, pointing at each in turn. “We can’t just call you ‘Eddie.’ What about Eight Pack? Cap said you liked being called that.”

“I can’t tell if he’s being serious or not.”

“I like to always operate under the assumption that nothing he says is serious,” Chimney told him. “Unless he’s having one of his psychic moments, then it’s very serious.”

“Psychic moments?”

They didn’t get a chance to fill Eddie in on their assumption of Buck’s psychic ability, as the truck was pulling into the auto-repair place. They got to work, Eddie slotting easily if hesitantly into place with them. As Before, they had trouble getting the oxygen into him. This time, when Bobby told him to take the angiocath to the man’s chest, Buck waved him off.

“Eddie should do it,” he said, handing the needle over to him and tearing the patient’s shirt open for ease of access. The others were all staring at him in confusion. “What? He was an army medic, that means he has more medical experience than me.”

“I’ve treated guys with collapsed lungs in combat before,” Eddie confirmed, jabbing the catheter in.

“See?” Buck said, waving his hand at where the patient was now deflating. “I know when to let someone else handle it.”

Getting home after shift, he stood in front of his door for a moment, fingers crossed and hoping. There was no guarantee that Maddie would be inside, just like there had been no guarantee that Eddie was going to be at the station. There was still every bit the possibility that something was going to go horribly off the rails. 

But it wasn’t going off the rails yet, because he opened the door to the sound of the shower running.

Seeing Maddie again was perhaps the easiest out of everyone, because he didn’t have to act like they were strangers, and he could act like he hadn’t seen her in forever. He set his work bag by the door, along with his shoes, and started fixing dinner for them. Last time, she’d been impressed by his ability to scramble eggs. This time, she was going to get a proper dinner.

“I like this place,” Maddie told him when she came out, still toweling her hair. “And- What is that smell? Are you cooking food? Actual food?”

“It has been a few years, Mads.” He had to swallow back the emotions threatening to overwhelm him, but he didn’t stop himself from grabbing her in his arms and spinning her around. “I have missed you!”

“Okay, okay! Let me down, you oaf!” she laughed, slapping at his shoulders until he did as was told. “As your big sister, I should tell you how dangerous it was just having your spare key where it was. You didn’t even check to see who was in your shower.”

“Eh, I knew it’d be fine,” he told her, not bothering to tell her how the key had only been there for that one day. “C’mon, sit down, we can talk while we eat.”

Explosive

The call with the grenade in the collector’s leg was the start of their friendship the first time around, and Buck honestly could not wait for it to get here again. He ached for that easy camaraderie they developed afterwards, that quick bond they formed. They were getting along, since Buck wasn’t being an insecure asshole this time, but that was more along the lines of friendly coworkers. And he didn’t want Friendly Coworker Eddie, he wanted Best Friend Eddie, and for that they needed to bond over an antique explosive.

When the call finally came, it was almost underwhelming. Buck and Bobby got the guy out of his house, and then loaded into the ambulance. The captain still wanted him and Eddie to go together, though this time with less of an emphasis on playing nicely.

“I guess you’ve seen a lot of shrapnel wounds,” he said, distracting himself from his nerves by using the old script to bug Eddie. He was almost certain that this would go the same way as it did last time, but there was always room for his anxieties to take root. The other week he did a deep-dive into Chaos Theory and the Butterfly Effect, and so that conviction was not absolute. It would be just his luck, that not being a dick somehow led to the grenade exploding prematurely.

(Sure, it wasn’t rational, but there was absolutely nothing rational about his life right now.)

“My share,” Eddie replied, barely looking at him, which was just rude.

“You ever seen a guy with a length of rebar stuck through his skull?” he asked, grabbing fresh bandages to redress Charlie’s leg, as the old ones were soaking through. And really, what was the significance of this guy having the same name as the Munchausen-by-Proxy kid? The one from the call that indirectly led to Eddie being shot. Was it entirely incidental, or was it the Universe Itself having a little laugh at everyone’s expense?

“What are we measuring here, Buck?”

“Nothing fun, or else you’d definitely lose,” he replied. “Hey, how do you know if it’s a practice round?”

“The color of the cap. Practice rounds are blue.”

“Interesting.” He pointed down at the grenade. “What does gold mean?”

Buck already knew the answer, but Eddie going pale and banging on the ambulance cab with a demand for them to pull over would have told him everything he needed to know, regardless. The discussion that followed, at a safe distance from the ambulance and the grenade, went the same as before. The bomb squad wasn’t willing to handle it themselves, the military was an hour away, and Charlie couldn’t afford to wait. Eddie volunteered to extract the grenade, and Buck (obviously) volunteered to assist. 

If he looked closely enough, he could probably watch Bobby’s new gray hair come in.

“Listen, Buck,” Bobby said, grabbing his shoulder when he went to follow Eddie. “You don’t have to do this.”

“I’m not going to let the new guy have all the fun. Besides, it’ll be a bonding experience. We could end up real close.”

“Buck…”

“We’ll be fine, Cap,” he said, doing his best to seem unworried, despite his nerves. “Trust me.”

Extracting the grenade went much the same as it had the last time Buck lived through the moment. It was also still hell on his nerves, despite knowing how it would end. There was just something about handling a small metal orb of death and dismemberment that made him anxious. But they got it in the box, and they got Charlie (less one explosive ordinance) out of the ambulance. 

“You’re a badass under pressure, brother,” Eddie said as they crossed the parking lot to where Bobby and the others were waiting.

“Me?” Buck knew he sounded breathless, but he couldn’t help it. The first time he heard those words, and the words that followed, had felt like being accepted and being seen and being appreciated. No one had ever accepted or seen or appreciated him like Eddie had, and he doubted anyone ever would.

(How did it take him so long to realize he was in love with the man?)

“Hell yeah. You can have my back any day.”

“Or you could have mine,” he said, when what he really meant was, Please don’t leave this time. Please, I’ll do anything, just don’t leave me again.

“Deal,” and Buck wished it was Eddie agreeing to the words unspoken and not just the words he heard.

“Nice work, fellas,” Bobby said, coming in like a proud father, watching his kid make a new friend. “I’m glad you both made it out of there.”

“The guy’s a professional,” Buck said. “And I told you we’d be fine.”

The ambulance exploded then, right on cue. The suddenness of it still made him flinch, but he didn’t automatically duck for cover like the captain did, which earned him a curious glance from Eddie.

“You guys hungry?” the former army medic asked, entirely unfazed by the burning wreckage behind him.

“I could go for something,” Buck said. “What about you, Cap?”

“Sure,” Bobby agreed, sounding dazed. Under his breath, he said, “oh God, there’s two of them.”

They ended up at a diner across the street, eating overly salted fries with greasy burgers, but not before Buck took a selfie in front of the remains of the ambulance. He sent it to Maddie, and received a bunch of concerned punctuations in reply.

“Okay, there’s something that’s been bugging me,” Eddie said, batting away his hand when he attempted to steal a fry.

“Shoot,” he said, and then immediately regretted the word choice.

“Psychic moments?”

“Oh, uh.” No one had actually straight up asked him before, it had just been Chimney’s superstition and a running joke at the station. What to say, what to say… “I have really good instincts, I guess? And Chimney accused me of being psychic, once, and it kinda became a joke from there.”

“Really good instincts?”

“At one structure fire, he bypassed five closed doors to get to a woman that was trapped,” Bobby said, between bites of his salad. “She was the only person in the building.”

“Like I said then, I heard her shouting.”

“She was unconscious when you found her, Buck,”

“You don’t actually believe you’re psychic though, right?” Eddie asked, and Buck frantically shook his head.

“I know I’m not,” he told him, finally snagging a handful of fries from him and stuffing them into his mouth. It earned him a grumpy scowl from Eddie and a ketchup packet to the head.

“Buck, eat your own food,” Bobby scolded, sounding every bit the put-upon father. “Eddie, don’t throw things.”

“Yes, Cap,” they chorused, and then grinned at each other at the tired sigh he gave.

After the grenade was the call with the guy’s head cemented into a microwave, which was still incredibly stupid. Then there was the reveal of Chimney being Mr. April, which was still confusing, but who was Buck to judge the tastes of others. And then when Athena came by to reveal her relationship with Bobby by making out in front of them - which, ew, those two were practically his parents - Hen was a bit put-out, because this time she didn’t make money off it.

(“I didn’t keep Chimney from taking the bet, Hen.”

“No, but when you refused to get in on it, so did he. I could be forty dollars richer right now if it wasn’t for that.”)

Coming back to the apartment to find Maddie’s bags all packed was just as disheartening as it had been the first time, perhaps even more so now. No, it definitely hurt worse this time. Buck definitely needed to get talking to Dr. Copeland, just as soon as he could explain everything in a way that wouldn’t get him locked up in a padded cell.

“Leaving already?” he asked, throwing his keys on the table by the door.

“Road ahead awaits,” Maddie said, trying to smile. She was sitting on his second-hand couch, looking stiff and uncomfortable.

“I’m more concerned about the road behind you,” he told her. “Are you going to tell me why you’re running from Doug?”

“No, I’m not gonna bring my little brother into this.”

“I am always willing to stand between you and the world.”  Buck sat down beside her. “Is this why you didn’t leave Hershey with me?”

“I should have. I regretted it every day after, but I was so worried that he’d-” She cut herself off, wiping at her eyes. “Everything Mom and Dad hated about him, the things you noticed as a teenager, it got so much worse. When I threatened to leave, he threatened to kill me. And he meant it.”

Buck wrapped an arm around her, pulling her in close.

“You got away from him, though, and I am so proud of you for that,” he said. “But now is not the time to be alone. You should stay here, I want you to stay here. It’s why I got a place with two bedrooms.”

He held up his hand, pinky out.

“United front, you and me,” he said.

“United front,” she echoed, wrapping her pinky around his.

Mi Mundo

Five minutes before the earthquake hit, Buck made sure to send a text to his sister, reassuring her that he’d be fine. Maddie had been so worried last time, he knew, and hopefully this would do something to assuage her nerves. It probably wouldn’t, but hopefully. His phone chimed with her reply, but he ignored it. There was the temptation, briefly, to shout at everyone to get outside where it was safe. But there was always the risk of them not believing him, or of someone getting injured from falling debris because he tried to get them out of the incoming danger. When he lived through this before, no one at the station had been seriously injured, and he refused to mess with that outcome.

(That thought was probably going to become his mantra, by the end of everything.)

Driving through the streets in the truck afterward, it was still a bit awe-inspiring to see the destruction that the earthquake had caused. It was far more widespread, compared to the tsunami, and as they went past the damage he mentally superimposed his memories of what the healed scars would look like over the gaping wounds that were currently there.

Eddie was focused on his phone, thumbs flying along the screen, and Buck’s first instinct - as always - was to offer comfort.

“Is everything okay?” he asked, knowing full well the other man was trying to reach someone in regards to his son.

“Yeah. There’s no service,” Eddie said, shaking his head in frustration. “Texts won’t even go through.”

“Who are you trying to get a hold of?”

Eddie glanced at him, and Buck could see the hesitation then as he had before. It stung a bit, but he reminded himself that this Eddie was not yet the one who trusted him with his world. That would come, eventually. Hopefully. If a butterfly didn’t flap its wings and wreck everything.

“My son,” he finally answered. ”I’m trying to reach my son.”

“You have a kid?”

“Christopher.” Eddie pulled up a photo on his phone and showed it to him. “He’s seven.”

“He’s adorable,” Buck told him. “I- I love kids.”

I love Christopher, he didn’t say. I love him so much and I ache to be a part of your family again. 

I love Christopher, he didn’t say. I love him so much and I miss him so much and I miss you even though you’re sitting right there.

“I love this one. I’m all he’s got,” Eddie said. Buck almost didn’t let him take his phone back, so desperate was he to see Chris again. “His mother’s not in the picture.”

And that’s right, Shannon was still alive. It wasn’t until shortly before the bombing that she was hit by the car. Perhaps, this time he could- No, that was a thought for later. Right now he had Worried Father Eddie to soothe, and then a tilted building to climb.

Priorities.

“He’s at school?”

“Yeah.”

“Hey,” he nudged Eddie’s foot with his own, until the man met his eyes. “He is fine. Trust me.”

He didn’t, not with this, not yet, but Buck tried not to take it personally.

Seeing a high-rise building cosplaying as the Leaning Tower of Pisa was still one of the most awe-inspiring sights he had ever seen. It was beaten only by the absolute pants-shitting majesty of the entire ocean rising up to murder everyone.

(He was not looking forward to repeating that day.)

They met Hen and Chimney on site, and gathered around as Chief Williams rattled off the current specifics of the situation. Bobby gave them their marching orders, Chimney made a half-hearted attempt at convincing Hen to stay outside, and the officer came to show them the guy pinned to the window. The guy that had fallen to his death before, and could very well again.

Honestly, Buck wasn’t sure how to prevent that one. Perhaps that was a situation where Bobby’s advice - “You don’t worry about the things you can’t do anything about.” - came into play.

Climbing through the tilted halls wasn’t any easier just because he’d done it before. It was less nerve wracking, though, when he knew that the building actually could hold up through the aftershocks that were coming. Still, by the time they got to the room they needed to be in, he was feeling a bit jealous of mountain goats and their ability to go up and down sheer cliffs.

Seeing Ali again was… Well, it wasn’t much of anything, really. Buck didn’t feel anything when he saw her, not like he had when he saw Abby again, and definitely not like he had when he saw Eddie. She was just a familiar face, just someone he had once known.

Just yet another person who left him and didn’t look back.

(Okay, maybe he did feel something.)

“Well that sucks,” Buck said, as he and Eddie looked at the tree that had fallen behind the latter’s truck. They had returned to the station from the hotel, after getting Ali down and rescuing Hen, hours after their shift had ended, and everyone was ready to go home. Especially Eddie, who Buck knew was anxious to get to Chris.

“How am I supposed to-” Eddie cut himself off with a frustrated huff, running a hand through his hair. “I need to go get Christopher.”

“I can drive you,” Buck offered, trying not to sound too eager about it.

“I can’t ask-”

“When did you ask? I was offering,” he said, taking him by the shoulder to guide him to the jeep. “Just tell me where to go.”

The drive to Chris’ school was slow and winding, filled with detours to avoid a broken overpass or scenes of accidents. Eddie spent the car ride bouncing his leg and cursing every roadblock - literal or metaphorical - they came across. Taking off his seatbelt before they even came to a stop at the front entrance, he just about tripped over himself getting out. And Buck wanted so badly to run to his little boy like Eddie did, but he was a total stranger to the kid.

But not for much longer.

“H-Hi!” Christopher chirped when Eddie carried him over, holding him tight to his side. Buck watched from the driver’s seat as he buckled the boy into his booster, which they’d transferred over from his truck. “Daddy said you’re his friend from work.”

“I am! My name’s Buck.”

“Th-that’s a funny name.”

“Oh yeah? What’s so funny about Buck Buckley?” he asked, just to hear the kid laugh.

“Thanks for doing this, man,” Eddie said, when he climbed back into the passenger seat.

“Because I was totally going to leave you and my new best friend stranded,” Buck said, rolling his eyes and pulling away from the curb. “Where are we headed?”

“South Bedford.”

“Convenient. I don’t live that far from there.”

“H-hey Buck?”

“Yeah,  Christopher?”

“Do you think dogs know they’re dogs?” he asked.

“They do actually!” Buck said, grinning at him through the rearview mirror. “They did a whole test on it a few years ago. They know they’re dogs, and they know a fish isn’t a dog, and they know people aren’t dogs.”

“R-really?”

“Yup!”

In the passenger seat, Eddie was smiling warmly at them both, and it was that smile. The smile he had ever only directed at him and Christopher, before. The smile that made everything, redoing years of his life and maybe damning himself in the process, worth it. Buck would go through hell and highwater for that smile, for Christopher’s laugh.

Whatever it took, he was not letting either of them slip away from him this time.

“Everything’s going to be fine, don’t worry?”

Maddie ambushed him pretty much the moment he closed the door to his apartment, sitting on his couch with a glass of wine in hand and the muted TV playing the news. She did not look particularly pleased with him, and it almost made him want to turn around and go running to Eddie.

“Hello Mads, I had a wonderful day, thank you for asking.”

“You told me everything was going to be fine and not to worry, then you didn’t respond when I texted back, and then!” She stood, so she was better able to jab him in the chest. “Then! There was an earthquake and you went climbing that deathtrap of a building.”

“But was I wrong?” he asked, moving to put the couch between them. “I mean, everything turned out fine. Like I said.”

“Uh-huh. And how did you even know to send that text, before the earthquake?”

“Well, uh…” He wet his lips. “The truth is, I’m actually from the future. I met this creepy guy with black eyes named Ichabod at some crossroads, and he sent me back in time to-”

“Yeah, yeah, try again.”

“I had a dream?”

“Okay, Dr. King.” Maddie rolled her eyes and downed her wine. “If you didn’t want to tell me, you could just say so.”

“No I couldn’t, you wouldn’t listen to me if I did.”

“I still wouldn't, but I’ve had a really stressful day, so I’m letting it go.”

“Truly, you are a saint.”

“I know.” She sat down on the couch and refilled her wine. “And one day, you might even deserve me.”

It Takes a Village

Buck wasn’t sure which still confused him more: that someone’s idea of flirting with a girl was to dare her to stick her head in his truck’s oversized tailpipe, or that said girl was willing to do so. And it wasn’t even a kinky euphemism, because she actually stuck her actual head into the actual tailpipe of an actual truck. Sure, there was alcohol involved, but Buck would have to be too drunk to manage it before he would even contemplate such a thing. And that would have been at his most desperate.

People could be so weird.

They could also be very thirsty.

“Just type in your number,” one of the patient’s lady friends told Buck, shoving her phone at him. “And I’ll text you so you have mine.”

“Thanks, but I actually, uh-” Shit, he didn’t have Abby to use as a talisman to ward off these carrion eaters. What to say, what to say, what to- He glanced at Eddie, kneeling down to help with Tailpipe Lady. “I actually have a boyfriend.”

The others all looked up at him in surprise. Well, not Hen, she just smiled and shook her head in amusement while continuing to help with the patient. For a brief moment, he was confused as to why they were surprised, and then he remembered. This time around, there hadn’t been a Buck 1.0 with his many and varied and very non-discriminate hook-ups, and so neither Bobby nor Chimney had any inkling about his sexuality like they had the first time around.

There were worse ways to come out, he supposed. And at least it sent the vulture slinking away in defeat and disappointment.

Poor Eddie, though. He wasn’t so lucky in warding them off.

“Hi, do you have snapchat?” another vulture asked, swooping in on him.

“No. And uh, I don’t think I’m what you’re looking for,” Eddie told her, looking very uncomfortable under her attention. “I have a son.”

And that was a rookie mistake. A hot firefighter was one thing, but a hot firefighter with a kid? Practically catnip to these beasts. Buck should know, seeing him with Christopher was half the reason he fell in love.

“That’s great!” said the vulture, her feathers utterly unruffled. “So do I.”

“I think I’m gonna puke,” Tailpipe Lady cried, distracting her vulture friends from their hapless prey. Which was very lucky, because the more discomfort Eddie showed, the more tempted Buck was to start throwing hands. And considering he was currently holding a power saw, it would not end well for anyone.

“You better not,” one of them said. “These fire guys are totally hot.”

“All right, what say we move the peanut gallery a few steps over this way,” Chimney said, finally shooing them away. “Thank you. Everybody back a little bit, thank you.”

Getting the lady - Jennifer, that’s what her name was. Getting Jennifer out of the tailpipe was actually very easy. The power saw cut through the metal like butter, and Buck got to witness the minor glory that was the devastation on Truck Guy’s face as his obviously-compensating-for-something customization was sliced off.  With the use of some lube provided by one of the vultures - someone came to the bar prepared for a happy ending - they managed to get the remnants of the tail pipe off her head.

“You need a better excuse to give them,” Buck told Eddie as they left Jennifer and her friends to Bobby’s paternal concern. “The next time you get hit on, I mean.”

“It’s the truth, though. That and they weren’t my type,”  Eddie replied. “But it’s complicated when you have a kid.’

“It’s a weak excuse. Admitting to being a DILF is only going to make the vultures thirstier.”

“You lied about having a boyfriend, and you’re telling me about weak excuses?”

“I mean, I could have a boyfriend,” he said. “That wouldn’t bother you, right? If I did?”

“What? No!” was Eddie’s quick response. “Of course it wouldn’t! Not when-”

He cut himself off to dig into the pocket of his turnout pants for his phone, and Buck wanted to strangle someone. Not when- What? What was the rest of that sentence going to be? Because he was quickly realizing that he had never actually broached the topic of his sexuality with Eddie in the Before, having spent so long with it being an open secret that didn’t need to be spelled out. So how was that sentence going to end?

Urgh, couldn’t Abuela’s hip have held up for five more minutes?

After a quick word with Bobby, the two of them took the ambulance to the hospital. It was faster than using an uber or waiting until they got back to the station for one of their own vehicles. Tia Pepa was standing in the waiting room when they rushed in, Buck a bit more leisurely than Eddie.

“Tia, ¿qué pasó?” Eddie huffed, coming to a stop in front of her. “Is Christopher okay?”

“You mean Prince Charming? He’s peachy.” She nodded over to where the boy was holding court with a pair of nurses, enchanting them as he did everyone. “It’s your abuela. She broke her hip.”

“What? How?”

“She was out back on the steps, calling him to come inside,” Pepa explained. “She lost her balance, and Christopher called nine-one-one.  They got there really quick.”

“I want to see her.”

“No, she’s sleeping now,” she told him, and then turned on Buck. “And who is this?”

“This is Buck, we work together.”

“And I thought you just dressed alike.” There was that Diaz sass he so adored.

“This is my Aunt Josefina,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes. “Pepa.”

“Hi.” Buck smiled and waved awkwardly.

“You can’t keep doing this, Eddie,” Pepa said, right back to business. “You cannot keep leaving him with her, she’s not up to it.”

That sounded a bit unfair, to Buck’s ears. From how it sounded, her hip was going to break whether Chris was with her or not. A lot of times with patients of a certain age, the broken bone led to the fall, not the other way around. Actually, Chris being with her was probably better than if it happened when she was alone, because God only knew how long it would have taken for help to arrive then.

“I know, and I’m sorry,” Eddie told her. “I’m trying to find some permanent help, its just… Too many forms to fill out. It’s worse than the V.A.”

And if that wasn’t the perfect opening, Buck would eat his shoe.

“I know someone who could help,” he said, cutting in before she could start insulting Shannon. He might not have the most positive of opinions when it came to what she did, but it would be hypocritical of him to judge another for running away. After all, it was what Buckleys did best. “A friend of mine, she’s a home health care aid. My sister once told me that the only people who can really navigate a bureaucracy are the people who work inside it.”

They stared at him for a minute, in utter silence, before Pepa turned to her nephew.

“I like this one,” she said, and Buck just about wiggled in joy. “I’ll keep Christopher for tonight, but you need to get this figured out.”

“Daddy!” Chris called, drawing Eddie away from them and across the room.

“It’s been rough, hasn’t it?” Buck asked, already knowing the answer.

“Raising any child alone is rough,” Pepa told him.

“He’s not alone.” The correction was automatic, out of his mouth before he could think better of it, and he hurried to backpedal. “I- I mean, he has you and his abuela. And hopefully Carla, soon. And- And there’s everyone at the station, so-”

“You have a big heart,” she interrupted, laying her hand on his arm. “I’m glad Eddie has a friend like you, now. My nephew is a saint, but I pray for him anyway.”

Afterwards, as before, he called Bobby who in-turn cleared it with the chief, and Christopher spent the day at the station with them. There were certain moments in the future he did not want to live through again. But this moment, this day? Buck would relive it again and again, without complaint, and be thankful for the opportunity.

“I wish there was more I could do to help,” Buck told Maddie later that day, while he fixed dinner for the both of them. “Christopher’s a great kid. He’s smart and adorable and funny. He just needs a little extra help.”

“Cerebral palsy, right?”

“Yeah, his Tia Pepa said he got stuck in the birth canal. There were complications, and then…” He trailed off, letting her fill the gaps.

“Did Pepa explain what’s happening with the child care situation?” Maddie asked. “Because there are programs.”

“Eddie’s working on it. He’s being foiled by the bureaucracy, but I have a friend I’m planning on calling,” he told her, plating food for the both of them. “She’s a health aid, helped with Abby’s mom before she passed.”

“Well, the only people who can navigate a bureaucracy are the ones who work in it,” Maddie said, unknowingly quoting him quoting her.

“It shouldn’t be that way, though,” Buck said, the frustration getting to him as he made his way to the couch with his plate. “With Eddie always trying to figure out how to care for Chris, and Chris feeling like a burden to his dad.”

“Eddie doesn’t feel that way, right?” Maddie asked, following with her own plate in one hand, a glass of wine in the other.

“No! Not even a little.” And perhaps that answer was a bit too passionate, because she was clearly taken aback by it. “He loves that kid like crazy. He’s a wonderful father.”

“Someone has a boy crush,” she teased.

“That’s cute,” he said, rolling his eyes. If only she knew. “What’s the difference between a boy crush and a regular crush?”

“I… I don’t actually know,” Maddie admitted, before waving it off. “Anyways, I have news. I’ve found an apartment.”

Ah, fuck.

Flying High

Taylor Kelly was less pleasant than he remembered. Or maybe he was just less able to ignore it now. Eddie’s announcement of his departure - without even talking to Buck first, who was supposed to be his friend, god damn it - had shaken him from his delusion of contentment. His entire relationship with her had been based on the fact that she had stayed, while everyone else left. It was based on the fact that Taylor had chosen him, while for everyone else - Abby and Ali and even Eddie - he kept being the second choice, or the third, if even that. He had convinced himself that everything was worth it, that it was okay to settle for someone he did not love, because she was there and hadn’t left.

It wasn’t, though.

It was towards the end of day two with her doing a story on them and the station, trying to use her momentary fifteen minutes of fame from the helicopter crash as a stepping stone to something more. Buck had every intention of intercepting the brownies this time around, to throw them out before anyone got their grubby hands on the things. But, he’d been so busy avoiding his… future ex-girlfriend? His ex-future-girlfriend? The mistake he made that he didn’t yet make? Whatever, he’d been busy avoiding Taylor - and therefore making her just as suspicious of him as she was of Bobby - that when he swung by the table with the baked goods, Eddie and Hen were already wiping chocolate crumbs from their mouths.

“Don’t eat that!” he snapped at Chimney, slapping the last brownie out of his hand. It landed on the floor, while everyone’s eyes landed on him.

“What did the innocent brownie do to you?” the paramedic asked. “It was fudge. With nuts. I love fudge with nuts. Why Buck, why?”

“Just- They were bad. It was a bad batch. Like that cartoon.” Wait, was that cartoon even out yet? Whatever.

“A bad batch?” Chimney stared at him. “How would you even know? Are you having a psychic moment?”

“Or just a loco moment,” Eddie said.

“Psychic?” Taylor asked, her narrowed eyes reminding him far too much of a cat spotting a defenseless bird. “What does he mean by-?”

The alarm cut her off, adding credence to the possibility that a merciful god existed and had not yet abandoned him. It was only as they were pulling away from the station, sirens wailing, that he remembered that Bobby was being left in her merciless, ambitious clutches. Buck felt moderately bad about that, but it was like the captain himself said: he couldn’t worry about the things he couldn’t do anything about.

Eddie and Hen started feeling the brownies on the ride to the beauty pageant, and it was a lot more amusing on this end. Did it make him an awful friend, that he was contemplating using his phone to record what was to come? Just to torment him, somewhere down the line.

“Man, my allergies are going crazy today,” Eddie said, squinting around the cab of the truck.

“Allergies, huh?” Buck asked, smirking at him. “I don’t think that’s it, bud. The pollen count wasn’t even that high this morning.”

“You’re not feeling this?” Eddie asked, scowling down at his hands. He looked so adorably confused.

“No, no we’re not,” Chimney said, glancing between him and Buck.

“I can see the pollen,” Eddie announced, looking out the window in wonder, and yeah. Today was going to be delightful.

When they got to the pageant, he didn’t follow Chimney straight to the lady with the shoe in her face. Insead, he stopped beside Eddie, who was staring in silent terror at the child beauty queens. Hen, meanwhile, was playing the role of Narcissus with the nearest reflective surface.

“You okay, Eds?” he asked, trying not to giggle too much.

“They’re so small,” the former army medic whimpered. “I- I don’t want to step on them. Did I grow? Am I giant? Buck, are we giants?”

“Can someone please bring me the rest of my gear!” Chimney shouted.

“I think he means you guys,” Athena told them, overseeing the perp walk of the crazed beauty pageant mother.

“Yeah, about that,” Buck said. “We have a tiny problem. Teeny-tiny, really.”

“So tiny,” Eddie whispered, eyes fixed on the little girls. He sounded so horrified, it was taking everything Buck had to not burst out laughing.

“What kind of problem?” she asked.

“Oh, ‘Thena, you smell of love,” Hen said, coming over to sniff the air around them.

“That kind of problem,” he answered. “What does love even smell like?”

She was too busy breathing it in to answer him.

“Chimney! We need you over here!” Athena called, before requesting another RA for backup.

“What’s going on?” the paramedic asked, rushing over. “Where’s my lido…?” He trailed off, perplexed by the sight of his partner swaying in place with her eyes closed.

“They’re tripping balls, Chim,” Buck told him.

“What? Okay, look at me guys, do you know where you are?”

“We’re everywhere, man,” Eddie said, poking his head through a bundle of balloons, and that was the limit of Buck’s self-control. He burst out laughing, doubling over and clutching his stomach.

“They’re on drugs,” Athena said, stating the obvious.

“Oh my god, it was the brownies,” Chimney realized, and then whirled on a still laughing Buck. “It was the brownies! You slapped the last one out of my hand, how did you know!?”

But he was too busy laughing to do much more than feebly wave the question away.

“Brownies?” Athena asked.

“We’ve been getting a lot of baked goods donated to the station recently, especially since the earthquake,” Chimney told her, staring down Buck still.

“You guys eat that stuff? We just throw that away.”

“But everybody loves firefighters,” Chimney protested.

Things weren’t quite so funny when Athena’s backup arrived and they put Hen and Eddie both in handcuffs. Buck understood why, of course. They were all fully capable of carrying a full-grown adult, and no one wanted things to turn ugly if their trip took a turn. But just because it made things easier, didn’t mean it was easy.

“What’s going on?” Eddie whined, tearing up and stomping his foot. It was startlingly similar to Christopher, when he was exceptionally tired and on the verge of a tantrum.“I don’t like this.”

“Easy, Eds,” Buck soothed, rubbing a hand down his arm. “Just breathe. Everything’s gonna be okay.”

“We just don’t want you to hurt yourself or anyone else,” Athena told him and Hen.

“Yeah, I don’t want that,” Eddie said, scrunching his eyes closed. It was a pathetic sight, and kinda heartbreaking.

“‘Thena.” Hen was grinning and pointing at the officer. “Your head is beating like your heart.”

And Buck lost it again.

“You’re so bright. And sunny and sparkly,” Eddie said, and Buck had to dodge his finger as it came close to poking out his eye. It was not easy, guiding a six-foot tall firefighter through a room when he kept getting distracted by sights that only he could see. With the station taken off-line, and the lady with the shoe in her face carted off to the ER, Buck had volunteered to babysit Eddie at his apartment until he came down. It was a decision that came with the added benefit of dodging Chimney and his inevitable questions.

Carla and Pepa had thought the situation hilarious, when he called them to sort out Christopher. 

“Okay, let’s sit down and find something to watch on Netflix, yeah?” Buck offered, gently pushing his friend onto the couch. “Something bright and cheery.”

“You’re bright,” Eddie repeated, gaze still caught on him.

“And sparkly, so you’ve said.”

“Everything’s sparkly.”

“Yeah, okay,” Buck laughed, picking up the remote and turning on the television. Immediately, the other man’s attention was focused on the screen, eyes wide in concern.

“Buck! Buck, there are people trapped in the box!” he cried, tugging on his arm. “Buck, we need to get them out!”

“Okay, so not Netflix,” Buck said, turning it off. Eddie stopped pulling on him, gazing in confusion at the black screen.

“Where did they go?”

“They’re free now, Eds.” He sat down next to him with a sigh. “I set them free from the box with this magic wand.”

“Oh, good.” Eddie leaned against him. “You smell like sparkles. But sad sparkles.”

“What do sad sparkles smell like?”

“Blue.”

“Oh, of course, that makes perfect sense.”

“I miss Christopher,” Eddie whined, pressing his head into Buck’s shoulder.

“You’ll see him tomorrow, man. He’s with your tia.”

“Promise?”

“I promise, Eds,” Buck said, stretching his legs out in front of him and settling in for the long haul. “Now close your eyes and take a nap, so tomorrow will get here faster.”

“Okay,” he mumbled, already sounding half asleep. “You’ll stay, right?”

“Of course I’ll stay,” he said, and then, quieter, “I’m not the one who left.”

“What?”

“Nothing man, don’t worry about it.”

That Time A Ghost Called 9-1-1

The spooky season was always fun, in Buck’s opinion. The creepiness of ghost stories, the costumes people got to wear, the candy and the pumpkins and the decorations, it was all fun. Halloween had always been a favorite holiday of his, second only to Christmas, and that was especially true when it became The Day That Eddie Forgave Him in his head and on his calendar. Although, Christmas might have lost its place of prominence, after… Well, after.

Spooky Season 2018, Take Two, was perhaps going to be more full of stress than it was filled with creepy fun.

It started when they rescued the gravedigger who had been buried alive, thanks to the earthquake shifting everything beneath the surface and turning it all into “eggshells and bubble wrap,” in Chimney’s words. Like last time, Hen reached her limit and jumped into the backhoe to dig him out. And like last time, Buck praised her for how badass it was.

“You literally pulled a man from a grave,” he said.

“We did,” she corrected. “I just hope they understand.”

And Buck didn’t need to ask who she meant, his stomach dropping to his knees like the backhoe dropped into the sinkhole behind them.

It continued when they rescued the hiker with the broken leg, the one who hadn’t called 9-1-1 because they’d lost their phone on the way down. It continued with them finding the remains of the hiker from seven years previous, the one whose call for help that Maddie received far too late to make a difference for him but just in time for it to help another.

The original Buck of 2018 had thought it was neat. That Buck was young and innocent and stupid, because there was nothing neat about it now. This Buck, the one who had gotten lost and met a black-eyed stranger, was not taking chances. He delved into the deepest reaches of the internet, ordering trinkets and crystals and anything else that could potentially keep the possibly-all-too-real spirits at bay.
