He even bought a bundle of sage from a local shop, which set off the smoke detectors in his apartment when he burnt it.

And sure, okay, maybe he’d gotten through this once without any ghosts haunting him, as far as he knew, but last time he’d been living at Abby’s and had moved out shortly after. There was always the possibility that they had followed him, but he’d managed to lose them there. There was always the possibility that the spirits Hen had been worried about upsetting followed him to his own apartment this time.

Of course, nobody believed him about the ghosts, not even Maddie when she came over with Chinese takeout and told him about the “glitch” the dispatch center’s IT guy had presented to her and Athena.

“So it was a ghost,” he gloated to her.

“Why are you whispering, and what did I just say?”

“That it was a ghost, and that I was right.”

“No, I said there was a glitch and a bunch of the calls had weird static.” She rolled her eyes at him.

“You said it was the exact same call, with the same voice and everything.”

“I said it sounded the same, but a lot of them do.”

“Denial is such a Buckley trait,” he told her, and she threw a piece of chicken at him.

“I keep thinking about the wedding ring,” Maddie said, moving on and therefore conceding that he was right. “I mean, you saw it, right? How many nights someone was just waiting for news…”

“A person can be legally declared dead after they’ve been gone for seven years. You have to sign a petition, though.”

“God, that’s so awful, having to admit that you’ve lost hope.”

“You probably lose hope long before you hit the seven year mark, Mads,” he told her. “It’s finicky, y’know. The thing with feathers that perches on the soul and sings the tune without words.”

“Did you just quote Emily Dickinson?” she asked, getting up to enter the adjoined kitchen and refill her wine glass from the bottle by the sink.

“I might have,” he admitted. Christopher’s school had sent him home with a project on famous poets, and when Buck helped with it, Dickinson’s poems had stuck with him. “I’m a complicated guy these days, I contain multitudes.”

“You contain something-” She stopped mid-sentence, head tilted as she stared at the window above the sink. More specifically, at the bottom of the window. “Buck, why is there a line of salt on the windowsill?”

“Well, uh, y’see-”

“Oh my god.” She cast her eyes around, spotting the dreamcatcher hanging from the ceiling of the living room, the horseshoe he’d nailed to the wall above the front door, and the chunks of quartz strategically placed in the corners of the room. “Oh my god, is this because of the ghost?”

“Aha!” he cried, pointing at her with his chopsticks. “So you admit that there is a ghost!”

“Oh my god.”

The first time around, he spent the day after Halloween talking to Carla and writing that final letter to Abby. He’d been blissfully ignorant of Eddie reconnecting with Shannon, too busy accepting that it was time to move on from his own failed relationship. This time there had been no relationship with Abby and no need for Carla’s advice. This time he wasn’t the ghost in someone else’s apartment.

This time there was no blissful ignorance.

Buck tried to convince himself it was okay. He tried so fucking hard. They weren’t going to stay together, he knew that. Even if she hadn’t died, she had asked for a divorce. This was only going to be temporary. So surely, he could stomach the knowledge that very soon, it would be her in Eddie’s life and in Eddie’s home and in Eddie’s bed. He managed it the first time around, he managed it with Ana. So why was it so difficult this time?

He knew why. It was because this time, he knew exactly how he felt for Eddie. It was because this time, when he thought of the two of them together, white-hot jealousy seared through his bones.

Driving always cleared his head, and so it wasn’t much of a decision to get in his jeep and go. He wasn’t running from anything, this time. He wasn’t fleeing the possibility of being left behind. He was just lost in his head, with no destination in mind and paying no heed to where he was driving.

Pretty soon, it wasn’t just in his head that he was lost.

He took a turn, and suddenly he didn’t quite recognize his surroundings. He took a turn, and a cloudy sky became a field of stars. He took a turn, and his jeep came to a rolling stop at a crossroads that he could never forget.

Ichabod was waiting for him, standing in the middle where the four roads came together. He was unmoving, seemingly content to watch from under his wide-brimmed hat as Buck cautiously climbed out and made his way towards him.

“Howdy, Buck,” the man greeted him when he came to a halt a few feet away. “Your jeep out of gas again?”

“No, it uh… It just stopped,” Buck said, shifting his feet. “How did I get here?”

“Pretty sure you drove.”

“Funny.”

“Well, you ask a stupid question…”

“I looked for this place on my days off after you did whatever it was you did,” he told him. “I looked and I looked, but I could never find it.”

“Because you have to be well and truly lost to end up here,” Ichabod explained. “Were you feeling lost today, Buck?”

“Yes,” he blurted out, when he’d intended to say no. “Wait, that wasn’t what I meant to say. I- How did you do that?”

“It’s a neat trick. What’s got you feeling so lost?”

“Eddie’s with Shannon and- Stop doing that!” The act of cutting off his own words was not dissimilar to trying to swim against the current during the tsunami. “What are you? Are you a demon? Did I sell my soul for a second chance?”

“Sell your- What?” Ichabod looked baffled. “Why would I want your soul? What would I even do with it?”

“I dunno, eat it? Torment me for eternity? You’re the demon, you tell me.”

“I’m not a demon, Buck.”

“Black eyes, creepy outfit, crossroads,” he listed, counting the points off with his fingers. “I might not have gotten on that particular bandwagon, but if it looks like a duck and sounds like a duck…”

“I’m also not a duck.”

“Then what are you!?”

“I am very old,” Ichabod told him. “And very bored.”

“Bored,” Buck repeated dully. “You’re bored.”

“To death. Well, if I could die. Being trapped in a place that can only be found by those who are as lost as you is murder on the social life.”

“Wait, hold on.” He dragged a hand down his face, feeling very tired and very done with everything. “Is that why you did this to me? Because you were bored?”

“It benefitted you, didn’t it?”

“Well, yes, but-” He cut himself off with a sigh. “What even is my life?”

“High quality entertainment.”

“Thanks,” Buck drawled. “Listen, you’re great company and all, but how do I get out of here? Are you just going to zap me back to last year, again?”

“You leave the same way you got here,” Ichabod told him. “In your jeep.”

“But my jeep is-” He was cut off as it rumbled to life behind him, the headlights illuminating them. Buck could see the shadow the other man cast, and it seemed to blur and wiggle along the ground, even as Ichabod stood unmoving. “Thanks.”

“You’re very welcome,” he said. “And I can’t wait to see how it goes with Eddie. I’m rootin’ for you two love birds.”

Buck gave him a dry look before turning and getting back in the jeep. Ichabod stayed standing in the middle of the road, so he opted to take his words literally and turn back the way he came. Eventually, the crossroads were lost from the rearview mirror and the stars were lost behind clouds, and he could see the lights of the Los Angeles skyline in the distance.

Sent back in time because something man-shaped was bored and needed entertainment.

What even was his life, anymore?

To Be Seen

There was a woman on the side of an overpass, demanding to be seen. Her name was Lola and there was a hand-painted sign stuck to the concrete behind her, a message for her husband, Norman. Traffic was held up for miles, officers were cordoning off the area, Chimney was overseeing the inflation of the air cushion. Above her, Eddie was helping Buck get the safety harness on. Below her, Athena was on the bullhorn with Bobby at her side.

There was a woman on the side of an overpass, demanding to be seen. She was just wearing a bathrobe, and there was a gun in the pocket, although only she and Buck knew that at the beginning. Everyone else found out shortly after he climbed down to join her, when she shot the air cushion and then pointed the gun at him.

“Lola, listen to me very carefully. You now have every firearm in the Greater Los Angeles area pointed at you,” Athena announced over the bullhorn. “If you continue to threaten that man, they will fire. Do you understand?”

“I don’t want to hurt anybody!” she shouted back down, lowering the gun. “I just can’t handle being ignored anymore.”

“I know exactly what you mean,” Buck told her, checking to make sure his radio was off. He glanced up at Eddie, who was watching and holding the safety line, and prayed for the man to be suddenly struck deaf.

“Oh yeah, I’m sure you get ignored all the time.”

“You have a Norman, and I had a-” He glanced up at Eddie again. “I had someone, too. You think everything’s going wonderfully, right? You have his back, he has yours. It’s the two of you against anything and everything the world can throw at you. You think everything’s fine, that everything’s going to keep being fine, until one day reality hits you and forces you to admit that nothing is fine.

“The distance between you gets bigger and bigger, no matter what you do. Sure, he’s still there, but he’s also not, y’know? You still see each other almost every day, you’re still talking and joking and working side-by-side, but he’s not telling you anything. You have to find out from someone else, a complete stranger, that he’s having panic attacks. And then, on Christmas, he tells you that he’s leaving. Because his kid is scared of losing his father. And you understand why he’s doing it, because you love that kid like he’s your own and you would do anything for that kid, but he doesn’t talk to you about it first. He doesn’t even give you the courtesy of telling you before telling the others. You just get gutted in the middle of what's supposed to be the season of love and joy and togetherness, and you’re left to deal with it along with everyone else.

“He tells you like he tells everyone else, because to him, you’re just like everyone else. You’re no different anymore from his other friends. And you have no clue how or when that happened, because-” Because once Eddie had trusted him with Christopher, where he hadn’t trusted anyone else. “Because once upon a time he trusted you with his entire world. But now? Now he won’t even trust you with his thoughts or his fears or his future. And he tells you that he’s leaving, just like everyone else leaves, and you realize that you’re going to end up all alone. Again. Just like before, just like always.”

“Lola? Lola, honey, it’s me.” Norman’s voice over the bullhorn ended Buck’s emotional word vomit, much to his relief. A glance up to check on Eddie revealed that he hadn’t been rendered miraculously deaf, because he was looking down at him with his brown eyes filled with concern and worry. Buck focused back on the relationship drama going on in front of him, because he just could not deal with his own right then. Not that his own actually existed, really. “I’m here and I see you. Just like the sign says.”

“Liar!” Lola shouted down at him. “You look right through me! You don’t even notice me! I-I’m just… I’m just like everyone else to you!”

“Lola, honey. Listen to me. I’m here, and I see you, and I need you to put the gun down, okay? Put down the gun and let them bring you to me,” Norman said. “And then we can spend the rest of our lives together, and I can show you how much I love you.”

“I don’t believe you, Norman! You don’t even know who I am anymore! I mean, I don’t even know.”

Visibly confused, Norman briefly consulted with Athena. He looked back to them and raised the microphone to his mouth again, but Lola steamrolled on. She had been given a pulpit, and she wasn’t letting the opportunity pass.

“I’ve been a mother for eighteen years! And now that Zack’s gone, I don’t remember who I was before that! Back when you used to look at me!” Lola shook her head in disappointment when, instead of answering, her husband pulled out his phone and started scrolling through it. “Maybe you’re right. Maybe I’m alone, too.”

She took a step towards the edge, but Buck quickly grabbed at her,

“Hey, no,” he said, pulling her back. “If you were alone, really alone, he wouldn’t be here right now, doing this.”

And then, to prove his point, music started playing over the bullhorn.

It was easy, getting Lola down to the street below after that, as everyone in the crowd clapped and cheered. She and Norman reunited, and then Athena arrested her, because life rarely had romantic endings.

“What’d you say to her?” Bobby asked him, as everyone else cleared the scene.

“Oh, y’know. That everything was going to be okay,” he lied.

Avoiding Eddie was easy, at first. Buck stayed on the street below, while Eddie stayed on the overpass, putting away the equipment up there. And then Buck rode the firetruck back to the station, while Eddie drove the ambulance. When they got to the station, though, avoidance wasn’t quite so easy.

“So, those things you told Lola,” Eddie started, when it was just the two of them in the locker room. “How much of that-?”

“No.” Buck slammed the door of his locker shut, the metal clanging loudly. “I don’t want to talk about it. I really, really do not want to talk about it. Not with-” You. “-anyone.”

“Okay, I won’t ask then,” Eddie said, and that capitulation hurt, in a way. Because his Eddie- Well, his Eddie probably wouldn’t have pressed, either, at the end.

“Thank you,” Buck said, breathing out a sigh of relief, and brushed past him to the gym.

“Do you guys know anything about Buck’s exes?” Eddie asked the others, when he joined them in the loft. Buck was downstairs, going to town on the punching bag. “Like, did he have any really bad break-ups on Christmas?”

“Buck hasn’t dated anyone since he started here,” Bobby told him.

“What about before?”

“According to Maddie, there hasn’t been anyone serious, ever,” Chimney said.

“You talk to Buck’s sister?” Hen asked. “About Buck?”

“Well, yeah. I mean, we’ve been hanging out since I helped her move.”

“You mean when Buck and I helped her move while you fiddled with gadgets,” Eddie retorted.

“Why did you ask?” Bobby cut in, interrupting the developing family squabble.

“I’m just concerned, that's all. Because of some of the things he said to that crazy lady.” That, and one of the things he remembered Buck saying while Eddie was high off his ass.

“A lot of things about Buck before he got here is concerning,” Hen chimed in. “He used to flinch around Chimney a lot, at the beginning. Like when he made sudden moves towards him.”

“He eventually stopped,” Bobby said. “But we’ve never been able to figure out why he was acting that way to begin with.”

Judging from the face Hen made at that statement, Eddie figured she had some idea, or at least a theory.

“What did he say?” Chimney asked, always curious. “To Lola?”

“Nothing I’m going to tell you. I just don’t think he should be alone.”

“I’ll have Maddie drag him out to the karaoke bar with us tonight.” The shorter paramedic was utterly oblivious to the looks this garnered from the others, too busy being pleased with himself over this solution.

Playing third wheel to a Not Date between his sister and his coworker was not an experience Buck had intended on repeating. But Maddie had called and invited him along, concerned with him being alone - he sometimes forgot how Eddie could be just as gossipy as everyone else - and he could never truly say no to his sister. It was a skill he really needed to gain, because it had caused problems before and would probably again, but he hadn’t really found the motivation to learn it.

He arrived at the karaoke bar before she did, meaning he was left alone with Chimney while they waited on her.

“So, Buck-”

“I didn’t want to talk about it with Eddie, I don’t want to talk about it with you.”

“You don’t even know what I was going to say.”

“So you weren’t going to ask me what I talked to Lola about?”

“No,” Chimney lied. “I was going to ask, uh… About the brownies!”

“About the brownies.”

“Yeah! Like, I’ve been wanting to ask, but how did you know they were drugged?” he asked. “Because either you baked them yourself, or you really are psychic. And Athena and Bobby found the lady who gave us those brownies, so…”

“Listen, Chim,” Buck started, and then stopped as he was hit by inspiration. For weeks now, he’d been trying to figure out what to do about Doug. His first and so far only idea had been to find a picture to show everyone, so that they all knew what he looked like, but that wasn’t working out. All of his social media was private, Maddie’s social media was nonexistent, and his staff page at the hospital didn’t have a photo. So he’d been growing increasingly frustrated with his inability to appropriately warn Chimney of what was to come.

This, though. This could work.

“You know what, yes, you’re right. You’ve been right this whole time. I am psychic,” he said. “But the others will never believe you if you tell them.”

“Prove it.”

“Which part, that I’m psychic, or-?”

“That you’re psychic. Dumb ass.”

“What, the brownies weren’t enough?” Buck asked. “Fine. Your mother’s name was Jee-Yun, and you have a younger half-brother that lives with your father in Korea.”

Chimney stared at him in slack-jawed silence for several moments, long enough that Buck was mildly concerned that he had broken the man.

“What are my lucky lottery-”

“Chimney,” Buck cut him off. “What I am about to tell is very important. Remember how I told you not to drive fast while angry? Before the rebar?”

The other man nodded frantically.

“Okay, so listen to me, Chim. If you run into someone named Jason Bailey, do not trust him. No matter how nice he seems, or how much he wants to be your friend,” Buck said, reaching across to grab the other man’s forearm. “Do not trust him, Chimney. And tell me the moment you meet him.”

“Don’t trust Jason Bailey, got it,” Chimney said. “But what about-”

“Sorry I’m late,” Maddie said, interrupting them. “I don’t know why I get on the freeway, I always regret it.”

“Because you’re an eternal optimist, that’s why,” Chimney told her, and Buck was once again relegated to spectator for the weird Not Date that was to follow. Eventually the two abandoned him to go sing some old love song together, but no, they totally weren’t dating yet. He needed a drink.

Of course, it was when the bartender gave him a bourbon, because “the lady said real heroes don’t drink pale ale,” that he remembered that Taylor Kelly was still a thing. He saw her across the bar, trying to smile coyly at him, and he just… Couldn’t do it. He left the full glass of whiskey on the bar and headed for the exit.

But God forbid she let something go.

“So, Buck, I see Chimney’s got a girlfriend,” she said when she intercepted his escape.

“What do you want, Taylor Kelly? What are you doing here?”

“Stalking you,” she tried to joke. “I’m kidding, the station is right around the corner, and I like to keep my ear to the ground.”

“Well, that’s nice, but I’m leaving now.”

“Buck, c’mon, I just want to talk.”

“But I don’t want to talk to you,” he said. “Especially when I know you’re just fishing for a story. I haven’t forgotten what you tried to do to Bobby.”

“Okay, fine, you’ve got me,” Taylor admitted. “It’s about what Chimney said, when everyone else was eating the special brownies. He asked if you were having one of your psychic moments?”

“You want to do a story on me? On that?”

“I’m just curious. A psychic firefighter? There’s a goldmine, right there.”

“Fine, y’know what? I’ll do a free reading, just for you,” he spat, finally having enough. The entire time she spoke, he just kept hearing all the times she talked down to and about him, belittled him, called him needy and self-centered. “Your mother died and your father went to jail for it, and he’s been denying his guilt ever since. You say that’s why you’re so obsessed with telling everyone else’s truth. You use your childhood to justify trying to ruin a good man’s life. But it’s all just an excuse, because you’re really just a loathsome bitch trying to make herself feel better by capitalizing on everyone else’s worst day.”

Taylor was shocked into silence, lips parted and eyes shining with gathering tears.

“You’re not pretty enough to hide that much ugly for long,” Buck told her, before turning on his heel and marching out.

He was definitely going to feel awful later for all of that. Much later.

Silent Night

Buck tried to enjoy the festive season, he did. The first Christmas back, when half his family hadn’t even come back into his life yet, had been difficult. But there had been a mercy to that, because he hadn’t really needed to pretend. He’d posed for a picture at the station and sent it off as postcard to Maddie, and then went back to the overcrowded party apartment he’d been living at the time.

He had thought, briefly, that the second Christmas would be easier. Surely, after a year and change had passed, it wouldn’t be such a sore wound. Right?

Wrong.

He saw Eddie surrounded by Christmas, and all he heard was, “I’m leaving the One-Eighteen.”

He did a good job pretending despite it, he thought.

It definitely wasn’t made better when Shannon came storming into the station in the middle of their annual toy drive. He had such conflicting feelings about her. One the one hand, she gave the world Christopher, which was an act deserving of Sainthood. On the other, she abandoned Christopher, which was an act demanding eternal damnation. Not that he didn’t sympathize with her need to escape a daunting situation. There was also the fact that she currently had what he never would, so, y’know. Contradictory feelings there.

“Shannon, what are you doing here?” Eddie demanded, looking every bit the deer caught in headlights. Buck was trying not to eavesdrop too obviously, and Chimney was clearly doing the same next to him.

“You won’t answer my texts or return my calls,” she answered, and a small irrational part of Buck felt stupidly smug, because Eddie always answered his texts and returned his calls.

“This is not the place.”

“Maybe it’s the perfect place,” she retorted. “We can actually have a conversation that doesn’t end up with us in bed.”

There was no pretending not to be listening after that. Eddie didn’t even glance their way before he led her to the locker rooms, leaving them behind.

“If you keep scowling like that, your face will get stuck,” Chimney said.

“Shut up,” Buck said, watching through the glass as the two Diazes argued..

“What are they talking about in there?” the paramedic asked. “I mean, you know, right?”

“It’s none of our business.”

“But you know.”

“Of course I know,” he ground out. “That’s why I know it’s none of our business.”

“Where did this negativity come from?” Chimney asked. “Because just a few minutes ago, you were all full of holiday cheer with the kids and with Eddie. And then…” He trailed off, glancing between the locker room and Buck. “Oh, god.”

“Don’t.”

“You like him.”

“Chimney…”

“You like him and you just had to hear his wife talking about-”

“Chimney!” He snapped, shutting the man up. “Please, can we just…Not?”

“Of course, of course,” he said, holding up his hands. “I’m sorry, I won’t say a thing, uh… What should I get your sister? For Christmas?”

“I dunno,” Buck shrugged, tracing lines with his finger along the surface of the refreshments table. “Yourself?”

“Wait, really?”

“Yeah, she… She’s in less of a festive mood than I am this year, so just… Keep it small. Small tree, small celebration.” It was easier to throw out a small tree, after all, if she reacted to it the same way she did the large one they got her, the first time around. “Don’t be surprised if she doesn’t react well to the tree at first, though.”

“Okay, thank you,” he said, nodding. “Hey, just uh… Hypothetically speaking. If your sister and I ever- I mean, if she decides to-”

“You mean if your Not Dates become actual dates?”

“Yeah, exactly. If that happens… Would you be okay with that?”

“You make her happy,” Buck said, shrugging. “Why would I not be okay with it?”

“Thanks, Buck, that means a lot to me,” Chimney said. And then, because he never could help himself, “so, you and Eddie…”

“Chimney, please.”

“Thanks for coming with us,” Eddie said as they settled on the edge of the fountain pool, to wait for Christopher’s turn to meet Santa. “I wasn’t sure if you would want to, since…”

“Are you kidding? I wouldn’t miss this for the world,” Buck told him.

“Okay, good, I just wanted to make sure,” he said. “That it wouldn’t make you uncomfortable or, I dunno, bring up bad memories? Because the guy you told Lola about, you said he had a kid and he left on Christmas, and I just…”

It took strength not to laugh at the absurdity of his situation. Because here Eddie was, concerned that he was making Buck uncomfortable by reminding him of Eddie and Chris, not knowing that they were who he’d been talking about. But Buck also really, truly, desperately did not want to talk about Eddie with Eddie. Less even than he wanted to talk about Shannon, and he knew that conversation was coming up. It didn’t require knowledge of future events to know that his best friend was chomping at the bit to talk to someone about it, no matter how much he’d claim otherwise.

“We’re well past worrying about bad memories, Eds,” he told him.

“Okay, good. I just wanted to make sure.”

“And that’s kind of you.”

“If you ever wanted to talk about it though-”

“I won’t.”

“But if you do, I’m always willing to-”

“Oh look, Christopher is close to the front.”

The distraction worked, because Eddie was soon letting the topic go in favor of desperately digging out his phone to take pictures of his son.

“I offered to wait in line with him,” he said, “But he said it was private.”

“I love how he always wants to do things on his own.”

“Yeah,” Eddie agreed. “So uh, you’re not going to say anything?”

“About what?” Buck asked.

“You know what.” He did.

“If you mean what Shannon said, I figured it was none of my business.”

“Good, because it’s not.”

“That’s what I said.”

“It just kind of happened,” Eddie told him, making it Buck’s business, however much he wished he wouldn’t. “It’s not like I planned on it when I reached out to her for help with Chris’ new school. We just… Ended up in bed.”

“I’m confused, were you both naked for some reason and tripped, or…?”

“What?”

“Well, I’m just trying to figure out how you accidentally sleep with someone,” Buck told him. “Like, whenever I’ve ended up in bed with someone - or a car, or a bathroom stall - I’ve always meant to end up there.”

“Well- It’s none of your business.”

“That’s what I’ve been saying.”

“I just can’t believe I’m sneaking behind my kid’s back with his mother,” Eddie said, and Buck was really confused here. He spent two months knocking boots with his wife of almost a decade, and he’s all in knots about letting her even near their son. But he’s in a relationship with Ana Flores for barely a month, and he’s jumping the gun to reintroduce her to Christopher as his girlfriend. Sometimes, Eddie’s contradictions gave him a migraine. “The other day, I made her sneak out so he wouldn’t see her there.”

“You’re just trying to protect your kid from getting hurt again. I mean, she ran out on him. Right?” He tried not to sound bitter about that, and from the quick look that Eddie sent him, he wasn’t too successful.

“I ran out first, on both of them,” Eddie told him. “When Chris was first diagnosed, I was in Afghanistan, at the end of my tour. I reenlisted and told myself it was to pay for the bills.”

“But you were running, too.”

“Yeah, and got to pretend it was for a noble cause. But when Shannon did it, she just got called evil.”

“At least she kept in contact with you and Christopher, right?”

“Well…”

“And she continued to help with the bills and his medical needs, right?”

“No, she didn’t-”

“And she definitely made a point of saying goodbye to the both of you and telling you that she’d be back.”

“Well, she left a note, but- What are you getting at, Buck?”

“I’m just saying that if what you did was running away, then it was in a… Productive way? Like, raising a kid is tough and expensive, but add special needs? That’s the kind of desperation that recruiters prey on, y’know? And I know for a fact that you called home whenever you could, because you’re too good of a father not to have,” Buck said. “But it sounds like when Shannnon ran, she burnt all her bridges and didn’t look back. Which is…Not okay, but not completely awful when it’s just a partner or a spouse. But to do it to your own kid…”

“You don’t like Shannon at all, do you?”

“I haven’t even met her, not really. All I really know is that she left and now she wants back in Chris’ life,” Buck said. “So why don’t you let her, when it seems like she’s already back in yours?”

“That’s where I get confused, because, would I be doing it for Christopher or for me?”

“Well, what did Carla say?”

“That a boy needs his mother.”

“That’s horribly heteronormative sounding, and I am very disappointed in her.”

“What, you don’t agree?” Eddie asked, and Buck snorted out laughter.

“My mother is at least a quarter of the reason I need therapy,” he said. “Besides, I think you keep asking the wrong person for their opinion.”

“Oh yeah? Who should I be asking, then?”

Buck didn’t answer out loud, instead nudging him and pointing over to where Chris was being guided towards them by one of the helper elves. Sometimes, the universe really did have excellent timing.

“How’d it go, pal?” Eddie asked, crouching down to eye level with the boy.

“It went great.”

“So what’d you ask for?”

“Can’t tell, Santa said he’d work on it.”

“Oh man, okay,” Eddie said, sighing, and swept Chris up in his arms. “Let’s go!”

“You two have an adorable son,” the helper elf told Buck, as they watched father and son walk away. Once, hearing those words had filled him with confused wonder, that someone would ever think that a kid as wonderful as Chris could have been his. Now, hearing it just felt proper, because damn right was their son adorable.

“Thank you,” he told her, and followed after them.

On Christmas, he begged off the invitation to celebrate with Bobby and Athena, claiming that he didn’t want to intrude on their family time. They had countered that Hen and Karen were going to be there, and that anyway, he was invited, so he wasn’t going to be intruding on anything. Buck had countered that he just wasn’t feeling the Christmas spirit, and he knew from the look they shared that Eddie had obviously expressed to them his concerns about Buck’s past experience with the holiday.

It was to his advantage, though.

Chimney had told him a few days before, about running into Jason Bailey while shopping for a Christmas tree and while getting a movie at the video store. He had asked, concerned, for what to do. Buck had advised that if he saw him again to avoid him where he could, to not talk to him if he couldn’t, until he hopefully took the hint and went away.

Pretty soon, he was going to go away, regardless.

A few hours before midnight, while everyone else were celebrating with their respective families, he took an uber to a street corner a few blocks away from Maddie’s. He walked the rest of the way, pulling on nitrile gloves and a baseball cap to cover his hair. Concealer and shadows covered his birthmark, while long sleeves covered his tattoos.

Parked across the street from his sister’s apartment was a car that he recognized far too well, the image of it ingrained from that day in Big Bear. Seeing it filled him with as much relief as it did dread. There had been the chance, of course, that he wouldn’t be there. But then, the man thought Maddie was his to use and abuse, so of course he wouldn’t be far, of course he'd be spying on her being happy with someone else. Pulling out a syringe from his pocket and uncapping it, he calmly strode to the driver’s side window, which was rolled down. Doug looked up from the wallet he was going through to see who was bothering him.

“What do you- Evan.”

“Hi, Doug,” Buck said, stabbing the needle into his neck, pressing down on the syringe’s plunger. Grabbing the sedative while doing inventory had been impulsive but also thought-out, in the way all of his best and worst decisions out in the field were. He caught Doug’s head before it could fall onto the steering wheel and set off the horn. It was not a difficult task to move him into the passenger seat after that, not for a man who regularly carried adults out of burning buildings.

This hadn’t always been the plan. Originally, after giving Chimney his warning, he had intended on waiting for him to do something, anything, that would give him an excuse to sic Athena on him. He had even thought, very briefly, of hinting to the paramedic that maybe Maddie should start checking for strange cars hanging around her place. It was only a brief thought, though. He hadn’t wanted his sister to live her life anymore terrified than she already was.

Not to mention that she would probably run again, if she knew Doug had followed her. And Buck could not keep her safe if she did that.

Then Chimney had told him about how the man was trying to ingratiate his way into the paramedic’s life again, and he just couldn’t stand to sit by and wait any longer. Not when he knew what Doug was going to do, to Chimney and Maddie both. Not when he knew what Maddie was going to have to do, just to survive. He just could not wait for Doug to do something that could get him arrested, to have the opportunity to do something even worse than before.

Warning Chimney about him had been the flap of a butterfly’s wing, impulsive and well-meaning as it had been, and for all he knew the storm it caused would be Doug resorting to violence even sooner out of frustration with being stonewalled. It wasn’t a risk Buck was willing to take.

With the right motivation, he was quickly learning, anyone could be pressed into doing awful things.

Out, Damned Spot

It was the end of March. Three months since Christmas. Nearly one hundred nights of uneasy and interrupted sleep, of waking from memories turned nightmares. Nearly one hundred days of getting dressed, going to work, and acting as if he hadn’t done what he did. Days that were spent smiling at everyone around him, as if there wasn’t a monster crawling under his skin.

They could all tell that something was wrong, he knew. Each new sleepless night made the bags beneath his eyes a little darker, a little bigger. He was fighting not to lose weight, forcing himself to eat Bobby’s meals at the station and trying his best to keep it down, even as bile clawed at his throat. He couldn’t even look himself in the eye anymore, avoiding the sight of his own reflection whenever he could.

“If you ever want to talk about what’s bothering you,” Bobby had said, midway through February, sitting across from him with paternal concern, “I’m here, I’ll listen.”

But Buck couldn’t. Telling Bobby, confessing to Bobby, was one of the last things he could let himself do. He’d be horrified and tell Athena, or worse, he’d keep the secret and make himself an accessory after the fact. Telling Bobby would destroy something precious, one way or another. It would destroy Bobby, hearing what he had done, and choosing between Buck and his fiance would destroy him even more, no matter the choice he made.

So no, he couldn’t tell the man he wished was his father, even if he wanted to.

There was blood in the nightmares. Blood all over the car, all over his clothes, all over his hands. He’d wake up and vomit into the toilet, and then stand in front of his sink scrubbing at his skin until everything was red and raw. There hadn’t been any blood when it actually happened. Everything had been clean, or as clean as a death ever was.

It was just an empty syringe, filled with nothing but air.

Doug hadn’t even been awake to struggle.

The worst part of it all was the relief he had felt, when it was done. Relief that Maddie and Chimney were safe. Relief that he had managed to spare them yet another trauma. Relief that it wasn’t Maddie who was burdened with the costs of simply surviving.

Perhaps it was that which truly fuelled the guilt, because it definitely wasn’t regret. Because Buck didn’t regret doing it. He would do it again, he knew, if it meant keeping his family safe. He would walk through fire and swim against the ocean, throw himself in front of a hundred bullets and do a hundred awful things, if it kept his family safe.

That wasn’t helping him sleep at night, though.

Maddie let herself into his apartment, the day after her date with Chimney. The date she didn’t get to go on before. The date she got to go on because of what he did. She looked stressed and harried, entirely unlike what he expected her to look after a romantic night spent with her boyfriend. She came in and then just stopped, staring at his coffee table in confused concern.

“Is everything okay?” Buck eventually asked, after several moments of her just standing there. The TV was on, some ridiculously cheesy Hallmark movie playing, and there were maybe one too many empty beer cans on the table she was staring at.

“I should be asking you that. Are those all from today?”

“No,” he answered truthfully, because some of them were from last night.

“Good, because there’s a lot of those there, and it’s barely five, and-”

“Maddie, what did you come over for?”

“Doug’s missing.”

Buck drained the can in his hand and set it down to join its brethren.

“Well shit,” he said. Buck hadn’t… The last time around, as far as he knew, no one had reached out to Maddie to update her on Doug’s whereabouts. He had already been in Los Angeles for months, deciding to strike when Chimney told him about the date with Maddie, after she sent off the-

The divorce papers, of course. They went to serve them, he wasn’t there, they told Maddie. During the first time around, did they try to serve them before he took her? Or did she tell them it was a moot point, after everything was said and done? Buck wasn’t certain, couldn’t remember. That night and the days that followed was a blur of fear and prayer and then relief that he hadn’t lost any pieces of his family.

Buck hadn’t taken into account the divorce papers, even though he should have. Even though he knew filing for divorce was Maddie’s last step for making her Not Dates with Chimney into actual dates. How could he be so stupid?

“They don’t know where he is at all?” Buck asked, trying to sound casual as he stood up.

“No, they said that the process server made a few attempts to give him the divorce papers,” Maddie said. “That his neighbors hadn’t seen him in months, that he got put on leave from his work after he got physical with my old boss.”

“Oh shit, is she okay?”

“She’s fine, security ran him off. But that was months ago, Buck. He’s been missing for months, he could be anywhere,” Maddie said, chewing at her nails. “He could be in the city, watching me, and I-”

“Hey, hey, calm down,” Buck said, stepping closer and gently taking her fingers away from her mouth. “He doesn’t know where you are, remember? If he had followed you, if he knew where you were, he would’ve done something already, right?”

“Right, you’re right,” she agreed, taking calming breaths. “It’s just the thought of it, of him being out there…”

“You’re safe from him, Mads,” he told her.

“But I wanted to be free.”

“You are,” he said, thinking of the bottom of the cliffs in Palos Verdes, where he already knew someone could go years without being found. “You’re safe and you’re free.”

“Okay Buck, seriously, what’s been going on?”

It was four days after Maddie had told him about Doug, and he’d just gotten off shift. Eddie had asked him to come over to his, and Buck had gone willingly. He had expected an easy night watching stupid television, maybe play some video games, hopefully spend a bit of time with Christopher. But apparently that wasn’t in the cards, because the boy was spending the night with Shannon.

It was just him and Eddie and the things that he could never tell Eddie.

“Nothing’s going on,” Buck said, plopping down on the couch. Eddie didn’t take his usual seat on the other end, instead staying standing, his arms crossed and his brow furrowed in concern.

“Yeah, I don’t believe you.” Rude.

“Well, that sounds like a you problem, honestly.”

“Buck…”

“What? Nothing’s been going on, everything’s fine.”

“According to Chimney, Maddie found you with a coffee table full of empty beer cans.”

“Is this an intervention?” he asked. “It’s kinda short-staffed, if it is.”

“This isn’t an intervention,” Eddie said. “Do you think you need one?”

“I was joking, Eds.”

“I’m not,” he said, plopping himself down on the coffee table, so he was right in front of Buck.

“I don’t have a drinking problem, Eddie. I just… I’ve had trouble sleeping lately and it helps.”

“That sounds like a problem to me. Something’s been wrong since Christmas, we’ve all noticed. We know that you know we’ve noticed. Bobby said you wouldn’t tell him-”

“So, what? You got elected to go next? How does it feel to be the second choice?”

“Buck.” It was the dad voice, the I’m-Serious-Now-Listen voice, which always worked on him just as well as it did on Christopher and the people they were rescuing. “Did something happen on Christmas?”

“N-No,” he stuttered out, and cursed himself for how weak it sounded. “No, Eds, nothing happened.”

“You can tell me if-”

“No I can’t!” Buck snapped. “No. I- I can’t…”

“Did… Buck, did someone do something to you?”

“No, Eds,” Buck said, letting out a bitter laugh. “No one did anything to me.”

“Then what is it?” Eddie begged. “You can tell me. We’re all worried about you. You’re drinking too much, you’re not sleeping enough, you’re hardly eating. Whatever it is, it’s eating away at you.”

“I can’t,” he repeated. “If I tell you, then you… Then you…”

“I won’t think any less of you.”

Buck let out a wet, broken laugh. At some point he had started crying, and he hadn’t even noticed.

“Yes you will. Hell, I think less of me.”

“Buck, you promised to have my back,” Eddie said, gripping his shoulder, thumb pressing into his collarbone. “Let me have yours.”

“Fine,” he whispered, and then louder. “Fine. I- You know how they said Doug was missing?”

“Yeah.”

“He’s not.”

“He’s not?”

“He’s not,” he repeated, shaking his head.

“And you… You know where he is.”

“I do.”

“But what about Maddie?”

“Maddie’s safe.” He met Eddie’s eyes, trying to get the meaning across without saying the words. “She’s safe.”

“Buck, what did you- Oh, Buck.”

“He was in front of her house. He was sitting there in his car and…” He trailed off, burying his face in his hands. Eddie was still gripping his shoulder, though it was looser. When he let go, Buck thought that was it, that he had ruined their friendship beyond repair. He wasn’t expecting the other man’s arms to wrap around him, pulling him into a hug.

“It’s okay, I get it,” the other man whispered. “I’ve got sisters. I get it.”

“Eds…”

“You’re gonna stay the night here, okay?”

Buck did, because he was a weak man for the offer at the best of times. And when Eddie found him in the bathroom in the middle of the night, scrubbing at his hands, he didn’t say anything. He just gently guided him back to the couch and stayed until he fell back asleep.

That Time They Were Framed For a Bank Heist

The morning after Eddie sat him down and cared at him until he crumbled like a sand castle against the tide, they both went back to Buck’s apartment. There he helped clean the apartment of cans and bottles, both empty and unopened, even going so far as to help clean the entire place, under the guise of making sure Buck didn’t have anything stashed away. It was while watching him pour out one beer into the kitchen sink followed by another and then another - the entire time dreading the night to come, because how the hell was he going to get any sleep now? - that Buck started to admit to himself that perhaps he did have a problem. At least he hadn’t gone into work drunk yet, but judging by the amount of empty beers waiting for the recycling bin, that day probably hadn’t been too far away.

“Thanks for doing this, man,” Buck said as Eddie tied the last bag closed. “You didn’t have to waste your day off cleaning my mess, I’m sure you want to spend it with Christopher.”

“Hey, this isn’t a waste,” the other man corrected him. “And we’re both going to see Chris after this.”

“Both? Me? Y-You want me to-? But Eddie, I-”

“You did what I would have done, if it was my sister,” he said. “I told you, I don’t think any less of you. Did you forget that I fought in a warzone?”

“That’s different, though.”

“Is it?” Eddie asked. “Now c’mon, I told Shannon we’d meet them at the park.”

Spending time with Shannon was not something he wanted to do much off. Spending time with Shannon as part of their little family unit was something he wanted to do even less. The first time around, he managed to avoid it, his time with the Diazes a well-balanced act that always coincided with her working or her having just left. It hadn’t even been intentional, just a side-effect of Eddie’s initial reluctance to mix the two parts of his life. Hell, he wasn’t even sure if the man had ever realized he was doing it.

What did it mean, that the man had been so reluctant to allow Shannon in fully, even as he was trying to work things out? What did it mean, that he was willingly bringing Shannon and Buck into full contact now?

They took Eddie’s truck to the park, presumably because even this early into the friendship, the man had realized that Buck was a flight risk when anxious. Shannon was already sitting at a picnic table when they arrived, watching Christopher trundle along the playground equipment. She stood and met them when they approached, and he had to look away while she and her husband exchanged hugs and kisses in greeting.

“Shannon, this is Buck,” Eddie introduced, stepping aside.

“Ah, this is the infamous Buck,” she said, smiling up at him. She was a pretty woman, he had to admit, with a friendlier and warmer smile than Ana Flores ever had. “These two talk about you all the time.”

“Th-they do?” Buck stuttered out. “Good things, right?”

“Eh,” Eddie said, and Shannon smacked him for it.

“Only good things,” she assured him. “It’s almost enough to make a woman jealous.”

“Oh, I- I didn’t-” Buck scrambled for how to respond to that. “Chris talks about you just as much.”

“Chris does, huh?” She shot a glance at Eddie, and Buck couldn’t figure out what it meant. “That’s something, at least.”

“Shan…”

There was a tension now between Eddie and Shannon, and it was making Buck uncomfortable. He had no clue what that look had been about. Was it something he said? Didn’t say? It was a very welcome distraction when Chris came running up, shouting his name.

“Buck!” He threw himself at his leg, Buck bending down to hug him tight.

“Hey Superman, you’ve been having fun with your mom?’

“Yes!” the boy cried. “Can you come push me on the swings?”

“Well, uh,” he glanced over his shoulder, to where Eddie and Shannon were both watching, the former with a warm smile and the latter with a frown. She kept glancing from them to Eddie, chewing at her lip the entire time. “Yeah, of course, lead the way.”

He wasn’t sure what the hell was going on with the two of them, but he had no desire to stick around and suffer through it.

If anyone asked, not that they ever would, but if anyone ever asked, Buck would blame forgetting about the time they were framed for a bank heist on the months of poor sleep and the various traumas he’d lived through since. He’d been sleeping better since that day with Eddie. The man had insisted he call him, any time of night, if he couldn’t get to sleep on his own. And more nights post-shift than not were spent on Eddie’s couch, the man calmly coaxing him back to sleep whenever he found him awake and scrubbing his hands raw again.

It still meant that, when the end of April came, the overly-complicated scheme to rob a bank snuck up on him and caught him unawares.

Being questioned in a police interrogation room was not something he particularly wanted to relive. Especially not when he was actually guilty of a crime much worse than theft. His anxiety was just not handling it well.

“You seem nervous, Mr. Buckley,” the lady detective, Mercer, noted.

“Because I’m being questioned for a crime I didn’t commit.”

“If you didn’t do it, then you have no reason to be nervous,” the male detective, Wash, told him.

“Actually, according to the annual report released by the National Registry of Exonerations, there’s anywhere between two and ten percent of innocent people in prison that were wrongfully convicted. And there’s been more than three-hundred convicts found innocent because of DNA testing since Nineteen-Eighty Nine. And there’s a large statistic of confessions that turned out to be false and were coerced or made under duress, and…” He trailed off as he finally took in the blank stares from the two detectives sitting across from him. “I- I read when I can’t sleep. So I’m just… I’m nervous, and I have cause to be nervous.”

He licked his lips, and did what he should have done from the beginning.

“Shouldn’t I have a lawyer with me?” he asked. “I think… I think I would be less nervous if I had a lawyer with me.”

“You’re asking for an attorney to be present?” Wash clarified.

“Yes. Yes I am. I am asking for an attorney to be present before you ask me any more questions.”

Buck tried not to take too much petty pleasure in how much this simple statement visibly annoyed them. He still didn’t quite understand what they thought happened, when they finally explained their theory of events to him and the attorney that had been summoned, a lovely bronze-skinned woman named Attica Rose. Her smile had been all teeth as she faced down the detectives and passive-aggressively criticized them for trying to start with the questions before she’d been called.

“I’m sorry, I am still so confused,” he told them.

“We’ve gone over this twice now, Mr. Buckley,” Mercer said.

“And I still don’t get what you think happened. Are you saying that we somehow got these two people sick on purpose so we could rob the armored truck? Or are you saying that we came up with the plan on the fly while Hen was stuck in the vault and we were trying to get her out?”

“Just to be clear,” Attica said. “You have no actual evidence that my client here has done any wrong doing at all? You’re just assuming he had something to do with it, despite your own photographic evidence showing him busy doing his job the entire time?”

“At least one of them, maybe more, conspired with whoever this firefighter in the photo is to rob the armored truck,” Wash said.

“But do you have any proof, any whatsoever, that it was my client?” Attica asked. The two detectives stayed silent, glaring at her mutinously, and it was enough of an answer for the attorney. “We’re done here. My client and I will be leaving now. Have a good day, detectives.”

She stood and didn’t glance back at them as she marched out of the room, Buck at her heels. When the door closed shut, he had to resist throwing himself at her like the overgrown puppy people liked to joke he was.

“Thank you so much, ma’am.”

“It wasn’t a problem. It is literally what I went to school to do,” she told him, reaching into the side pocket of her purse and pulling out a card. She handed it to him. “If they give you any more trouble, and they probably will, give me a call.”

“Thank you again,” he said, gripping the business card tight. She waved it off, and he hurried down the halls and out the station doors. He’d been the last to be questioned, and that had been hours ago, so he expected everyone else to be long gone. Apparently not though, because in the parking lot was Eddie, casually leaning against his truck.

“About time,” he said, straightening up. “I’ve had time to get a ride to the station and come back.”

“Yeah, sorry, I kinda annoyed them and asked for a lawyer,” Buck said, hurrying over. “So they had to wait on that, and then I made them explain what they thought happened, like, twice? And I still don’t understand it.”

“You asked for a lawyer?” Eddie got into the truck and waited for Buck to hurry around and get in also. “Why didn’t I think to do that?”

“Because people are always, ‘I’m innocent so I don’t need a lawyer,’ but I’ve read too many statistics to trust that.” Not even taking into account the thing, which neither of them had actually spoken about directly since the day Eddie helped clean his apartment.

“Well, hopefully they’ll stop bothering us and find the actual guy who did it,” Eddie said, pulling out and heading in the direction of both their places. It was probably going to be another night spent on Eddie’s couch, not that Buck would ever complain about it.

“Yeah, hopefully,” he said, remembering the sight of officers rummaging through his jeep as he sat off to the side, throwing his things out like worthless trash. “I doubt it though…”

Even though Buck had known it was coming, Bobby’s suspension was still a kick in the ass. It meant he had little time left to keep Shannon from being hit by the car. It meant the ladder truck explosion was fast approaching. And it also meant that he was about to suffer through the first iteration of Interim Captain Han, again.

Getting his leg crushed had been less painful.

In Which Buck Damn Well Can Choose Who Lives

Interim Captain Han was an acquired taste. With hindsight, Buck could see that it was clearly fueled by insecurity, but it didn’t make it any easier to have the man treat them like they were all idiot probies. An explanation, not an excuse, that’s what Copeland had said before. She’d been talking about his parents' treatment of him in the context of the revelation about Daniel, but it was equally applicable to this, even if the situation was nowhere near as severe.

At least after nearly seven years of experience on the job - technically, if one factored in the time travel - Buck was far more comfortable pushing back when it came to it. Like when Chimney tried to get him to wash his car, or insisted on following Bobby’s example by cooking dinner.

“What the hell are you doing, Chimney?” Buck asked, nudging the man away from the stove.

“I’m cooking for the team, Buckley,” the man snapped.

“Have you taken cooking lessons in the past couple of weeks and didn’t tell anyone?” Buck asked, taking the skillet from him. “What were you trying to make, anyways?”

“Shaking beef. Hence the shaking.”

“The meat’s not even cubed, Chim.”

“Was it supposed to be?”

Perhaps this was how the other Bobby had felt, during their earliest cooking lessons.

“Get out,” Buck ordered, trying to figure out how to salvage the meal with what he had available to him.

“Hey, I’m the captain. The captain cooks, so-”

“Bobby cooks because he can cook, Interim Captain,” he corrected, stressing the title. “You can’t.”

“Fine!” Chimney said, throwing up his hands and walking away. “But don’t think this gets you out of washing my car!”

“Wash your own car!” Buck called after him. Maybe he should just order everyone pizza…

The first time around, he’d been one of the first people to go complaining to Bobby, if not the very first person. He managed to last a little bit longer this time around. When the door opened after he knocked, the suspended captain looked very unsurprised to see Buck darkening the doorstep. Harry was also inside, sitting at a table covered with Bobby’s wedding planning.

“Are you here to complain about Chimney, too?” Bobby asked.

“Is that what he’s doing here?” Buck asked, pointing at Harry. “I didn’t realize Interim Captain Han’s reign of terror had reached that far.”

“No, Harry is here because- Wait, have you two properly met?” Shit, had they? Buck wanted to say yes, but he hadn’t gone to the Christmas dinner where he would have actually met Athena’s kids. “Harry, this is Buck. Buck, this is Harry, Athena’s son.”

“Nice to meet you, kid,” Buck said, plopping himself down next to him at the table.

“You’re the guy that mom was angry at, something to do with a baby,” Harry said, staring up at him. “But then you helped her with something else, so she didn’t hate you any more.”

“Harry here has a girl he wants to ask to a dance, but he’s not sure if he should.”

“Oh, you should totally ask her,” he encouraged.

“What if she laughs at me?”

“What if she doesn’t?” Bobby countered, taking the seat across from them. “You think I wasn’t nervous to ask your mother out?”

“Yeah, but you have a fire truck,” Harry pointed out.

“I do, or I did.”

“You will again,” Buck told him, and then to Harry, “If she laughs, then she laughs, and you’ll know she wasn’t worth it. Take it from someone who knows, you’ll regret not asking her out far more than if you do and she says no.”

“How do you know? Hen says you haven’t had a girlfriend or a boyfriend.”

“Just how often do I get mentioned at your house, kid?” Buck asked, leaning in closer. “Y’know what, I’m gonna give you my number, so you can tell me whenever you hear them gossiping.”

“You are not turning Athena’s son into your informant, Buck,” Bobby protested, shaking his head. “Didn’t you come here to also complain about Chimney?”

“You mean to tell you how he’s utterly insecure in his new position and that it’s manifesting as a severe power trip?” Buck asked, channeling Dr. Copeland for a moment. Bobby blinked in surprise. “I’m not an idiot.”

“I never said you were, kid.” Never mind that the other Bobby actually had, once. Though to be fair, he’d been an idiot. “But at least you understand where he’s coming from.”

“Yeah, but that doesn’t make it better,” he retorted. “He’s so focused on proving his worth or whatever, but it all comes out like he thinks he’s better than us. He doesn’t even ride on the truck with us, Cap. He takes the battalion chief’s. And he keeps trying to make me wash his car.”

“Seriously?” Harry scrunched his nose up at that.

“And! And! I had to stop him from cooking.”

“What!?” That seemed to shock Bobby out of his placidity. “Did he ruin any of my-?”

“No, no, I stopped him in time,” Buck reassured him, and watched with some amusement as the man literally sank in seat with relief. “But seriously, Cap, you need to talk to him or something.”

“I thought having Chimney in charge would be easier on all of you. He’s your friend.”

“Chimney is my friend. Interim Captain Han is doing his best to make sure he doesn’t have any friends.”

It did nothing to help the situation that Buck “confirming” to Chimney that he was psychic some months ago was coming back to bite him in the ass. When they were on a scene, the interim captain would give an order and then glance at Buck, as if expecting him to slap another brownie out of his mouth. A metaphorical brownie, of course. He was second guessing everything he did or told the others to do, and was using his belief in Buck's supposed psychic ability as a crutch to reassure himself that he wasn’t screwing things up. Except all that was doing was stressing Buck out, because there was a reason he wasn’t the guy in charge.

If it wasn’t obvious to the others what he was doing before, it definitely was after the call to the chocolate factory.

“We tried pulling him out, but he was struggling so much that he sank even deeper,” the factory worker explained as she led them across the catwalks to the vat their victim was in. “Our chocolate is the richest in the country, but unfortunately that also makes it the heaviest.”

“Sir?” Chimney kneeled by the vat’s edge. “Sir, how are you feeling in there?"

“W-warm,” the man stuttered out, just barely keeping his face above the surface of the melted chocolate.

“We had to leave the heat on,” the factory worker told them. “My foreman was afraid that if we didn’t then the whole batch would just harden up.”

“Then we’d be chiseling him out,” Chimney concluded. “All right, let’s get to work!”

Buck and Eddie laid a ladder across the mouth of the vat, both of them climbing onto it and reaching down to pull the man out of his Willy Wonka nightmare. Except the harder they pulled, the harder the chocolate pulled back, until Buck lost his grip and nearly fell in with him.

“What’s happening here?” Eddie demanded to know.

“Physics!” Hen answered. “Physics is happening here. You’re creating a low-pressure pocket when you pull him up, and then that pocket is pulling him right back down.”

“So it’s chocolate quicksand,” Buck said.

“Okay, everybody just stop for a second,” Chimney ordered. “Hen, take out an O2 tank, rip off the mask, create an air tube. It’ll buy us some time if he goes under.”

“Time for what?” she asked.

“For me to think,” he said. “Uh, Buck?”

“What?” Buck snapped, trying to get a better grip on the guy.

“What do I do?” Chimney hissed under his breath.

“Seriously?” Hell, Buck didn’t remember every detail of every call they’d been on. This one had been overshadowed by Shannon’s death and everything else that followed. It hadn’t exactly been notable enough to make it to the highlight reels of his memory, not like the well or the tsunami or the shootings, or even the call with the baby in the wall. “You’re the captain, why are you asking me?”

“You know why, Buck! C’mon!”

“Okay, fine, uh,” he glanced up, meeting Eddie’s eyes, who was clearly wondering what the hell he was bearing witness to. What did they do last time? He remembered something being poured into the vat, and Hen helping to stir, and- “Cocoa butter! Get the cocoa butter, pour it in.”

“What?”

“It’ll uh, temper the chocolate? Decrease the viscosity,” Buck said, praying that he was remembering right. And then when Chimney didn’t move, snapped out, “Cocoa butter! Get going, cap!”

“What the hell was that?” Eddie asked them while Chimney ran off.

“I think Chim phoned Miss Cleo,” Hen said, rolling her eyes.

“Who?” Buck asked, but didn’t get an answer before Chimney was back.

Buck had requested the day off months ago, and had gotten it approved months ago. No one had asked what he needed the day off for, and he didn’t offer an explanation. What would he have said? That he couldn’t work that day so that he was available to save a woman whom he hadn’t even met yet when he requested it? Again, psych evals were a thing.

This should be relatively easy, right? Just go, keep Shannon from stepping off the sidewalk, save her life. Piece of cake.

“Oh, hey Shannon, fancy seeing you here!” Buck greeted her when she stepped out of the store, as if he hadn’t been loitering around the corner.

“Buck, hi,” she returned. “I wasn’t expecting to see you. Isn’t… Aren’t you working today? I mean, Eddie is.”

“Nah, I have today off,” he told her, following along as she made her way to the crosswalk. “So, uh, how was your dinner last night?”

“Eddie didn’t tell you?”

“I haven’t spoken to him today,” he told her. The truth was, Eddie had told him, months from now and years ago, after the lawsuit and the fight club. But this Eddie hadn’t yet, and it was a good excuse to keep Shannon on the sidewalk, talking to him. “Did it… Did it not go well?”

“We’re getting a divorce.”

“Oh, I’m sorry to hear that, I thought you two-”

“Are you, though?” she asked, stopping just short of the crosswalk and cutting him off. “Sorry to hear that?”

“What do you mean, Shannon?” Buck asked, unsure where the hell this conversation was going.

“I’m not blind, Buck. I saw the way you looked at him, that day at the park. I know you love him,” Shannon said, the words taking him by surprise. “And the way he talks about you, looks at you, I-”

The sound of brakes screeching and the soft thumps of people hitting pavement and then metal slamming into metal interrupted her, and he was simultaneously relieved and frustrated. He had managed to keep Shannon on the sidewalk, had managed to keep her alive and well. But what the hell was she going to say? It was like the day Abuela broke her hip all over again, the universe going out of its way to interrupt conversations he was desperately curious to hear.

“Oh my god,” she said, hand covering her mouth.

“Stay here, call nine-one-one,” he ordered, hurrying over to check on the driver of the red car.  It was a woman, and she looked petrified. “Ma’am, can you hear me?”

“I tried to stop but I didn’t see any of them,” she said, voice trembling. “Are they okay?”

“Don’t worry about them right now,” Buck told her. “What about you? Are you okay?”

“M-my neck hurts…” She turned her head to face him and he immediately reached out to stop her, placing his hand on either side of her face to keep her still.

“Okay, don’t move your head,” he told her. A glance over at Shannon showed she was still on the phone, the sound of sirens growing in the distance. “Help is on the way…”

The 118 arrived not long after, Chimney jumping out and handing out orders. Eddie and Hen hurried over to the red car, surprised to see Buck already there.

“Isn’t this your day off, Buckaroo?” Hen asked him.

“Right place, right time,” he told her, and never was a truer statement said. “She has a possible neck injury. She also said something about not seeing anyone when she tried to stop?”

“Something visual then.”

“Okay ma’am, I’m gonna put this on you as a precaution, until the doctor can check you out,” Eddie said, reaching in with a c-collar to put around her neck.

“I should probably tell you that Shannon is here,” Buck said, pointing over at the sidewalk.

“What?” Eddie’s head shot up, nearly hitting the roof of the car. He craned his neck over to look, and then quickly ducked back down. “Crap.”

“Yeah, we uh… We were talking when this happened.”

“Talking?” His voice sounded strangled. “To each other?”

“No, I was talking with the sidewalk and she was holding a riveting conversation with the tree over there,” Buck said, rolling his eyes. “Yes, to each other.”

“So you know then.”

“Yeah, I know.”

“Okay as interesting as this chat is,” Hen interrupted, glaring at them from the other side of the car. “Eddie has a job to do. You two can have your little girl talk later.”

Buck raised his hands and backed away, unwilling to evoke her wrath any further.

“I’ll leave this to you two and uh, be over there,” he said, heading for the sidewalk. He’d meant to waylay Shannon and ask her what she was going to say before the crash, but the woman was already across the street and hurrying away. Which was disappointing, but at least she was capable of walking away from there.

Once upon another time, Athena had told him that he didn’t get to choose who lived or who died. Except that wasn’t true, was it? Buck had chosen. He just hoped that it stuck.

The Crushing Weight of What's to Come

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The worst part of reliving the bomb scare plaguing the city was how many of the details Buck either never learned or didn’t remember. He knew the kid’s name was Freddie, and that he’d been gunning for Bobby. He knew that there had been other bombs before the truck, but he hadn’t truthfully paid much attention to them at first. They’d been called to the first one shortly after the chocolate factory, before Shannon’s death, but it had just been another call with a victim in need of help at the time, so it wasn’t like her name or address had stuck in his mind. And they hadn’t been called to any other bombings, so he hadn’t paid much attention to the news about it beyond ‘wow that’s fucked up.’

The only one that really stuck out was the one mailed to Athena’s house, which was also the only one he didn’t have to worry about, because she had Michael well trained.

Buck hadn’t bothered to commit the details to memory, and then the ladder truck happened, and he mentally recoiled from everything that surrounded it. The videos of it, the coverage of the trial, he avoided it all like a vampire avoiding sunlight and garlic. Most of that night had been stuffed into a box and thrown into the back of a closet, never to be touched. His mind had just taken as much of the trauma that it could and stuffed it down, so he could go on healing. He remembered it in fragments, disjointed and clouded by pain.

He remembered Freddie appearing out of the smoke, calling him new and demanding to see the captain.

He remembered Bobby calmly strolling towards them, and the absolute certainty he had that everything was going to be okay now because his captain was there.

He remembered a crowd of people coming to lift the truck off him, each and every one of them an utter stranger who had no idea who he was and were willing to help all the same.

He remembered someone holding his hand the entire ambulance ride, only letting go when they rushed his gurney into the ER.

But not a single one of those details could help him now. If Athena or Bobby were as superstitious as Chimney, he could warn them about someone named Freddie much as he had given the paramedic the warning about Jason. But they weren’t, so he couldn’t. If he tried, Athena would probably look at him in that fond exasperation of hers and ask if he knew how many people in Los Angeles went by that name.

The night after he managed to keep Shannon from her untimely end, Buck sat down to watch as the news reported on the second of the explosive packages, and didn’t feel much like celebrating.

He had honestly forgotten about the false alarm at the school until they were rolling up to it again. Buck was disappointed in himself for that, because honestly? Calls with kids that weren’t hurt or in mortal danger were the best calls. Kids were just the best, period.

“Alright everyone, as close and as tight to the truck as you can be,” he instructed, herding students and teachers alike into place along the far side of the trucks from the suspicious backpack, Chimney doing the same with his own group. The kids weren’t frightened, not that they really had cause to be. They just thought it was an exciting excuse to get out of class.

“Teacher spotted it out there after recess,” Athena told them as they gathered around. “Nobody claimed it.”

“Yeah, but it’s not a package,” Buck pointed out. “This guy sends his bombs through the mail.”

“The guy could have branched out,” Eddie offered. He hadn’t been there for it originally, Buck remembered. He’d had the day off for Shannon’s funeral. A funeral that didn’t happen this time, and hopefully would continue to not happen for many years to come.

“Or inspired some other crazy,”  Athena countered.

They watched from afar as the bomb squad guy stomped over to the innocent-looking backpack, decked out in what honestly looked like a green spacesuit. He waved a handheld camera over it, and Buck could hear them debating what to do over their comms. Then, he watched the man gingerly lower something - the controlled charge, he guessed - onto the bag, and haul ass to safety.

The first time around, the lack of a proper explosion had been a disappointment as much as a relief. This time around, it was neither, because Buck knew better. The controlled explosive sent gray goo flying into the distance, splattering against trees and walls. The bomb guy made his way to one of the trees and leaned in close to inspect.

“Substance appears to be some kind of…  Grayish paste,” he reported over the comms.

“It’s tuna fish,” a little girl said, and everyone turned to stare at her.

“Emily,” her teacher said. “Was that your lunch?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you say something?” Athena asked, in the same scolding tone she used on all her children, Buck included.

“I don’t like tuna fish,” the little girl answered, as if it was the most obvious of things and it was everyone else’s fault for not understanding such a simple fact. “Am I under arrest?”

Buck caught Hen’s eye, and then Eddie’s, and he knew both of them were as close to breaking into laughter as he was. God he loved kids.

“Hey, I meant to ask earlier, but uh… How’s things with Shannon?” he asked Eddie as they packed away what little bit of gear they’d dragged out.

“Things are… Well, they just are,” he answered. “We sat Chris down the other night to explain to him what was going on.”

“Together? How did he take it?”

“Uh, okay? I’m not really sure if he understood that anything was changing,” he said, closing the compartment door and heading for the truck cab.

“Speaking of Chris, have you talked about custody agreements yet?” Buck asked, following him.

“No, why? Do you think I should?”

“Yes!” Buck said. “She left, she came back, now she’s divorcing you. There is literally no guarantee that she won’t decide to move to New York and try to take Chris with her.”

“That is a good point,” Eddie said, sounding uneasy as he climbed in. “I hadn’t thought of that.”

“That’s what you have me for.” Buck climbed in after him and slammed the door shut.

“To think the worst of Shannon? Because I have my parents for that.”

“No! Maybe? No.”

It was weird, comparing this life to the last. At this point in time during the first go around, he was apartment hunting with Ali while Eddie was mourning Shannon and fending off his parents' attempts to lure him and Christopher back to Texas. This time, Buck already had his own apartment and was very single, while Eddie was finalizing his divorce and probably still fending off his parents. There was also Maddie and Chimney, who weren’t on a brief, trauma-induced break-up. And speaking of Maddie…

“The judge finally agreed to a default divorce,” she told him when she was over for one of their regular dinner get-togethers. “Since it’s been a couple months and they still can’t find him to serve the papers.”

“That’s good, right?” Buck asked, trying not to dwell on why they couldn’t find him, and where they would if they knew where to look. “What does, uh, what does that mean? Exactly?”

Maddie rolled her eyes.

“It means there won’t be any legal fees or hearings. It means I don’t have to fight about who gets what, which honestly, I wasn’t going to anyway. It means that by the time Doug does show his face anywhere, I’ll be Maddie Buckley again.”

“It means you’ll be free.”

“Yeah,” she agreed, smiling at him over the table.

“So then, you and Chim?”

“Are perfectly happy as is, thank you,” she said, throwing a pea at him. “What about you and Eddie?”

“Uh, what?”

“You and Eddie. Now that he’s getting a divorce, are you two-?”

“Woah, woah, woah, what makes you think there’s a me and him to talk about?”

“Well, Chimney told me that your boy crush was an actual crush.” At some point, the temptation to sew that man’s mouth shut will grow too great to ignore. “So I figured, now that he’s available, the two of you can actually be a thing instead of just dancing around it.”

“We’re not- He’s- There’s-” Buck was stammering for an answer. “Mads, he doesn’t like me in the same way I like him.”

“How do you know?”

“Well, firstly, he doesn’t even like guys,” he said. “And secondly…  I just do.”

Because there were three and a half years of another life that told him so. Because if Eddie was even a little bit bicurious, it would have come up at some point during their friendship in the other life. Because if Eddie ever had more than platonic feelings for him, he would have said something during the year and a half that they were both single. Because if Eddie had ever seen him as anything more than a friend and a fallback plan for Chris, he would have talked to him before deciding to leave the 118, even if it was just to say, “this is what I need to do, please support me.”

(And Buck would have. He would have! If only Eddie had talked to him, like they were the friends and partners he had thought they were. But Eddie had dropped the bombshell on them, and Buck had panicked and ran and by the time he was done running and panicking, it was already too late to do anything more than regret and start anew.)

But he could never tell Maddie any of that, so he just sat there and ate his food, trying to ignore the pity he saw in her eyes.

It was with dread and trepidation that Buck walked into the station on The Day. He had barely gotten any sleep the night before, spending the hours tossing and turning. There had been the thought to call Eddie, let him try to talk him into a few hours of sleep as he had promised to do in those situations, but it had been a transient urge. Fleeting. There and gone again. And the few stolen moments of slumber he had gotten were interrupted by vague memories turned hazy dreams of the bombing.

When he walked in to start his shift, it was undoubtedly obvious to everyone that he’d had a rough night.

“You should have called,” was literally the first thing out of Eddie’s mouth when he saw him. “I told you, any time of night.”

“Yeah, sorry, I- Sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry, just remember it next time,” Eddie said.

“You going to be good for the day, Buckaroo?” Hen asked when they joined her up in the loft.

“Of course,” he reassured her, heading straight for the coffee.

The day was spent much like any other day. They did chores, they joked, they went on calls. And at every moment of free time, and every time they came back to the station, Buck went over the truck with increasing nerves. Every hour that passed without anything suspicious showing up, the shakier his hands got. He had no idea when Freddie had planted the bomb, or where it would be. He could make a guess, based on how the truck had flipped and landed, so he mostly checked the left side.

But what if the bomb had never been on the truck? What if it had been on the road, waiting for them to pass over it? Or what if Freddie had stuck it on the engine this time? What if-

“Buck, is everything okay?” Chimney asked after the ninth time he got on the rolling board to check the underside of the ladder truck. He sounded suspicious and worried, nerves creeping into his tone.

“Yeah, everything’s perfectly fine.” He doubted his words were convincing, his voice shaking more as the night set in and the clock ticked closer to boom time. “Just, y’know, checking the truck.”

“Yeah, I can see that,” the interim captain said. “You keep checking the truck, so I have to ask, is there something I need to be worried about?”

“No, no, there’s noth-” Buck stopped, because right over his face was the bomb. It was smaller than he’d been expecting, disturbingly so, considering it nearly ended and ruined his life. Freddie must have snuck in while they were busy, or stuck it on when they’d gone out on a call. It was right under the gas tank, held in place by layers of duct tape. Hardly daring to breathe, he carefully rolled back out, and met Chimney’s worried eyes with his own. “Call Athena.”

It didn’t take long after that, for everyone to be evacuated from the building and the bomb squad to arrive. Athena and Bobby had already been on their way, having somehow realized the station was the next target just a few scant moments before. Huddled in the parking lot, squeezed in between Eddie and Hen, he wrapped his arms around himself as the bomb squad’s robot carefully extracted the device.

“How did you know?” Eddie asked him. “How did you know to look?”

“Just… A feeling. Instincts,” he lied. “Bad vibes…”

Phantom pains made his leg ache, a reminder of what was and what could have been.

Under the nearby streetlight, a large blue butterfly was dancing in the air, and he could not bring himself to look away.

Chapter End Notes
