*Anakin Skywalker voice* This is where the fun begins >:)
(My fun. I make no promises about yours.)

Cause and Butterfly Effects

The first sign that things were not quite rainbows just because Buck prevented the truck bombing became apparent within days. Originally, Bobby had been reinstated to his captaincy almost immediately after Freddie’s bit of morbid, terroristic pageantry. This time, however, he was still sitting in his apartment, planning out his and Athena’s wedding. A wedding that was supposed to have been disregarded in favor of a courthouse elopement.

It was an intolerable development, Bobby’s continued suspension. Chimney had gotten marginally better, but only in that he was no longer overcompensating with superiority. He hadn’t tried to make someone else wash his car for weeks now, for instance, and he had stopped his demonstrations of how to properly roll up the hoses. But it still wasn’t the same, and he was still depending on Buck’s “psychic abilities” to assuage his uncertainties.

“So why haven’t they put you back in your spot?” Buck asked when he swung by to see him. The dining table they were both sitting at was still covered in planning resources, but there was something that looked half-hearted about it now. Like he didn’t have the energy to truly care about the details of it any longer. “Are they still investigating? Is the inquiry still ongoing?”

“No, no, they… They’re finished with that.” Bobby told him, and busied himself going through the pile of detritus on the table.

“Then when are you coming back?”

“I’m not coming back, Buck.”

“What?” Surely he’d misheard, there was no way he hadn’t. Bobby came back. He was supposed to come back. There was panic crawling under his skin, now. “What do you mean, you’re not coming back?”

“Exactly what I said,” Bobby told him, sighing wearily. “I was asked to resign, effective immediately.”

“Well, say no.”

“Then they’ll just terminate me. This is… Less of a mess, for me, for them. For Athena.”

“Well, what about the union? Can’t they-”

“Buck, this was the best the union could get me.”

“I- I don’t…” He didn’t understand. This wasn’t right. What was going on?  “Why?”

“They felt that my… That what happened in Minnesota would…” Bobby dug through the wedding resources aimlessly, refusing to meet Buck’s eyes. “If they had known what happened, they would never have hired me. And there’s that reporter, Taylor Kelly, too.”

“Taylor Kelly? Wh- What does she have to do with it?”

“She heard about my suspension, apparently. Went poking around,” he said. “She wanted to do a story on it. On me. On what I did.”

“But- But the department’s lawyers kept her from-”

“From using the footage of when we were all dosed, but that was before the brass found out about Minnesota. Now?” Bobby shrugged and finally looked up. He tried for a smile, but it looked too broken to be convincing. “Now there’s a story to be made about an alcoholic, drug addicted fire captain who burnt down an apartment building, killing his family and one-hundred forty-five others. And then fled the state.”

“But…That wasn’t how it happened. It was an accident.”

“It still happened, Buck.”

“So… What?” he asked, getting up to start pacing. “They’re firing you, and in exchange the news execs kill the story?”

“No.” Bobby shook his head. “They asked me to resign to save face for when the story comes out.”

“The story that Taylor Kelly is doing?”

“Yes.”

Buck barely made it to the kitchen sink before his lunch was making a reappearance.

“It’s all my fault.”

Buck and Eddie were out hiking, enjoying the sunshine and the warm weather. Or at least, they were trying to. Buck was carrying his own personal cloud cover everywhere he went, so it wasn’t a truthfully successful endeavor. Not even the fact that his leg was whole and pain free, that he could climb over rocks and tree roots without a care, could distract him from the overbearing guilt he felt.

“How is it your fault?” Eddie asked, stopping to lean on the rock wall and take a drink from his water bottle. The trail they had decided on was one of the more difficult ones, hugging the edges of cliffs and going up deep inclines. Christopher was with his mother, and so it had been easy to convince Eddie to go with him. “You didn’t burn down that building, you didn’t tell Bobby to lie to the brass. You didn’t get him fired.”

“But I did, I think,” he said. “They’re forcing him to resign because of Taylor Kelly.”

“So then it’s her fault.”

“You don’t- Before Christmas, after Lola? When Chimney dragged me out to the karaoke bar with Maddie?” He waited for Eddie to nod. “I ran into Taylor there. And I… Wasn’t nice.”

“What do you mean, not nice?”

“The phrase ‘loathsome bitch’ might have been used,” Buck said, turning away from him to look over the tree line below. The sun was starting to set, the sky turning the tiniest bit orange and pink in preparation. There was a tree, a maple, old and tall and wide-reaching, defying fate by growing right on the edge. “And- I didn’t call her ugly, but I might have implied that she was an ugly person.”

“Dios, Buck,” Eddie said, sounding impressed. “I wish I’d been there to see it.”

“Yeah, but I’m pretty sure she took it personally, because now she’s ruining Bobby’s life.”

“That’s a bit self-centered of you, Buck,” the older man said. “You’re assuming this has anything to do with you, when it’s clearly because she’s just a loathsome bitch trying to profit off the misfortune of others.”

“But would she have gone after Bobby if I hadn’t insulted her?”

“If she had heard about it? Probably.”

“Okay, but what if-”

“Buck, stop. You can’t dwell on ‘what if’s, not when there’s nothing you can do about them.” And that statement was just so absurdly untrue that if he wasn’t so busy tying himself in knots over his misstep, Buck would laugh. As it was, he huffed in amusement and leaned against the tree.

“I can’t help myself, Ed-”

The tree gave.

The ground gave.

The tree fell, and Buck fell with it.

Eddie screamed his name.

He scrambled for rocks, for roots, for anything he could grab.

He bounced off one outcropping, and felt something break. He bounced his head off another.

He fell through the limbs of trees below, the impacts barely slowing his fall as he slammed into the ground.

The maple he had leaned on, which he somehow managed to outpace in the descent, landed on him.

On his leg.

His left leg.

Buck screamed, or at least he thought he screamed. Or maybe he’d been screaming the entire time. His throat was raw, and his right eye was blinded with blood pouring out of a cut near his scalp. Everything hurt, and when he tried to get up, he felt the bones of his leg grinding together beneath the weight of the maple tree pinning it down.

Something bounced off his head. A pebble.

He looked up, and he saw a boulder - part of one of the rocky outcroppings he had tried to grab hold of - getting closer and closer and-

Buck opened his eyes when no impact came, having closed them in the face of inevitability. What had once been the warm summer sun had turned into a cool night sky. Beneath him, instead of leaf-littered earth, there was dusty pavement. There was no blood in his eye, and no tree on his leg. He stood to his feet and didn’t feel the grinding of broken bones.

“I’m not dead.”

“Now.” Ichabod’s voice startled him. He jumped and swirled around, coming face to face with the black-eyed entity. “It was a bit rocky there for a moment.”

“Did… Did you just make a pun?” Buck asked. “About my death?”

“Do I strike you as the type to make light of such a grave occurrence?”

“You just did it again!” he cried, pointing accusingly at the entity.

Ichabod shrugged, appearing entirely unconcerned with his sins.

“Okay, so how did I get here this time?” he asked the entity.

“You died.”

“Yeah, I get that, but- Oh God, is this hell?”

“Sometimes, I do wonder,” Ichabod snarked. “But no, and also, still not a demon. Do you remember the first time we met? What your answer was when I asked what you wanted?”

“I said I wanted to fix things, to fix what broke my family,” Buck answered. “What does that have to do with me dying but not being dead?”

“Did things seem fixed to you, before your pretty little head was smashed like a watermelon?” the entity asked. “Do you believe your death at that moment fixed anything?”

“No.” He felt that it should have been an achievement, admitting that his death hadn’t fixed anything. It was something that Dr. Copeland would have been equal parts proud of and concerned about, that it was to be considered an achievement at all. “But what does that mean?”

“It means try, try, try again.”

“Are you… I can go back?”

“You can go back,” Ichabod said. “I can send you back again.”

“How far back? Are you going to send me all the way back?” Buck didn’t think he could handle that, having to live through those two years again. To have to go another year without Eddie and Chris and Maddie, to have to remake his family from scratch again.

Ichabod hummed in thought.

“No, not this time,” the entity said. “Maybe if it was ever amusing enough.”

“This time? What do you-”

Buck opened his eyes again and scrambled out of bed. There was no Felix singing along to Britney Spears in the kitchen, he wasn’t back in that overcrowded apartment. He also wasn’t in his loft, like a small naïve part of him had hoped. It was his apartment, the two bedroomer, and checking his phone told him a date and time that did not surprise him one bit.

It was the morning of the ladder truck bombing. Again.

There was a routine that developed after that, a never ending cycle of sorts. Buck would go in, get through the day of calls, and then check the undercarriage of the ladder truck as evening fell. Every time, he would find the bomb duct taped to the gas tank. Every time, he would have Chimney call Athena and the bomb squad. Every time, he would watch the blue butterfly dancing beneath the streetlight.

Every time, Bobby would tell him that he was being forced to resign.

And every time, he would die and end up back at the crossroads with Ichabod.

Once, his leg was pinned to the bed of a river by a truck, and he drowned watching Eddie struggle to get him free.

Once, he fell through a floor during a three alarm fire, a piece of furniture landing on his leg. The flames started licking at his face before the smoke finally strangled him.

Once, through some Rube Goldberg machination, he lost his entire leg and bled out in the ambulance.

Each and every time, it was his leg.

“Why!?” Buck finally shouted at Ichabod, after the seventh time he woke up there. “Why do you keep doing this to me!?”

“Bold of you to assume any of this is my doing.”

“Really? Bold of me? You’re the one that keeps sending me back!”

“Would you prefer to stay dead?” Ichabod asked.

“Well, no. But I’d also prefer not to die at all.” Buck ran his hands through his hair, stomping his foot in frustration. “I just… I don’t get it. I didn’t die last time. Obviously. My leg was crushed, it healed, I limped on for another few years before running into you. I don’t get it.”

“Maybe, perhaps, you changed something that shouldn’t be changed?” Ichabod asked, tilting his head to look up into the starry sky.

“What are you looking at?” Buck asked, following his gaze. He peered into the sky, straining to see whatever had the entity’s attention. And the longer he looked, the more he could make out… Something. It was like a river, winding through and around the stars above, branching out into infinite directions, and each of those in turn splitting off into branches of their own, and so on. The longer he looked, the more he could see, until he could almost make out images of-

He blinked and lost it.

“What was that?”

“Time,” Ichabod said, turning his black-eyed stare back on him. “Perhaps you keep dying because you keep changing something that should not have been changed?”

“You said that already, but what?” Buck asked, but truthfully, he thought he already knew the answer. “I’ve changed other things. Shannon’s alive, Doug didn’t take Maddie or stab Chimney. Why is it this one thing that has the universe lashing out at me?”

“Perhaps it doesn’t like you, in particular?” Ichabod joked. “Or perhaps this thing is carved into stone, while the others were simply written in ink, and is thus not so easily altered?”

“I don’t understand.”

“There are certain things that are fundamentally unalterable,” the entity said. “However much you try to change or prevent them, they happen all the same. One way or another. And often that other way turns out… Well, you’ve discovered how they turn out. And the best part is, you never know what those moments are until you try to change ‘em!”

“And my leg is one of these?”

“Your leg, or the truck bombing. Or both.” Ichabod shrugged. “It was a big night, was it not? Your captain even got his job back because of it.”

“My captain?” Buck had not even made the connection before, but… “You mean, Bobby would have his job back if I let my leg get crushed?”

“Seems unfair, doesn’t it?” Ichabod’s smile was not kind. “Everyone else on the truck was back to work in a matter of weeks, were they not? And Nash was back in uniform within days.”

“But… Taylor’s story. They might fire him anyway.”

“Or they might not,” the entity said. “It will be a gamble, yes? You let the truck bombing happen and crush your leg, Nash keeps his job, and you keep living. Or, you crush your leg and Nash loses his job regardless, and you still keep living.”

It wasn’t really much of a choice.

This time, when he woke up in his bed, Buck rolled over and screamed into his pillow. He screamed and he screamed and he screamed, because it wasn’t fair. Nothing about this was fair.

But then, nothing about his life to this point had been fair.

When he went into work that day, everyone could tell there was something bothering him. He told them everything was fine, though, and he kept telling them that. Right up until the ladder truck exploded beneath him and landed on his leg, and then he didn’t have to keep pretending any more.

A Leg to Stand On

Somehow, Buck was still surprised when he woke up in his hospital bed to find Carla at his side. He wasn’t sure why that was the case. Perhaps it was the distance that had grown in the other time, as the pandemic had meant their circles were tightened and separated. Perhaps it was that Buck had been half-expecting to wake up at the crossroads again, with Ichabod making another pun in poor taste at his expense. Or perhaps it was simply that he was always going to be surprised to have someone waiting at his bedside, a carry over from spending so many years alone.

“Hey,” he said, his voice sounding hoarse even to his own ears. “You’re here…”

“Of course I’m here,” she said, like it was stupid of him to even think otherwise. And maybe it was. “If I see my friend on the news being crushed by a fire truck, where else would I be?”

Mention of what he had gone through - again - drew his attention to his leg. It was casted up to the knee and in traction, a pillow placed beneath it. It looked the same as it had, when last he suffered this injury, but what if it only looked the same? What if something he had done had changed the severity of the break? The placement? What if the truck had landed on it differently? What if a different doctor had been on call? What if-

“Okay, okay, Buckaroo, it’s gonna be okay,” Carla said, trying to soothe him through his building panic. “It’s gonna be okay.”

“I know,” he said, and tried to believe it. “What, uh, what did the doctor say? Did you talk to him?”

“You’re now the proud owner of a titanium rod and four beautifully cobalt-chromed screws,” she told him. Something must have passed over his face at the mention of the screws, because she asked, “You were hoping for something more?”

“No, no, this was… Pretty much what I was expecting,” he admitted. “The doctor said he was pretty confident I was going to walk again. It was… Everything else, he wasn’t so sure about.”

“I’m not gonna lie to you and tell you that it’s gonna be alright,” she told him. “But let’s not go borrowing trouble, not yet. Let’s just take this moment to be glad that you’re alive.”

And that was just so ridiculous, he had to laugh.

“Someone’s in good spirits,” Maddie said, walking in with coffee for herself and Carla. It was just her, this time. No Ali, because she hadn’t reentered his life after the earthquake, but also no Eddie. And he wasn’t sure why he had expected the man to come in with his sister, because it wasn’t like anything had changed to suggest that he would. A small part of him had still hoped, foolish and baseless as it was.

Eddie was at work, or should be. Without him. Again.

At least this time, he could plan ahead to avoid letting Bobby put him in the same position as before. Assuming Bobby was captain again by that time.

Eddie did, however, show up to escort him from the hospital to his apartment. Buck had honestly been expecting Maddie, or Carla, or even a guilt-ridden Bobby. But no, it was Eddie. Of course it was Eddie. The car ride had been spent arguing with the man that, no, he shouldn’t stay at Eddie’s place until his leg healed. Why? Because he had a perfectly usable bed within hobbling distance of the kitchen at his apartment, and there was no way he was spending every night on the other man’s couch.

“Well of course not,” Eddie had argued. “You’d be in the bed, I’d take the couch.”

“Your old man back can’t handle the couch every night,” Buck countered.

Eddie had acquiesced by the time they pulled onto his street, although Buck wasn’t certain it wasn’t going to come back up later. Last time around, there hadn’t been any arguing about if he was going to stay at the loft or not, though perhaps they had all thought Ali would be there helping him. It was different, to have Eddie so insistent on having him where he could help. Nice, even.

“They reinstated Bobby,” Eddie informed him as he held the door to the apartment open. “And they’ve replaced the truck already.”

“Well that’s… Something.” Buck tried not to feel bitter about that. Getting his leg crushed had almost ended his career, but it was what let Bobby keep his? Who then did his best to keep him away, regardless of his reasons? It was just… There wasn’t a word he could think of, to describe the unfairness of it. 

Apparently some of that bitterness had made it into his tone, because Eddie was frowning.

“I- I’m sorry, do you not want to talk about work?” he asked, sounding guilty. “Because I can talk about something else…”

“No, no, it’s fine,” Buck said, using his crutches to hop his way to the junk drawer in the kitchen. “Hey, your shield ceremony is coming up, right?”

“Yeah, it is,” he said. “My family’s coming up.”

“You don’t sound excited about that.”

“My parents and Shannon in one place?” he asked. “What’s to be excited about?”

“The fireworks,” Buck answered, grinning at him. He dug through the drawer, letting out a small whoop of victory when he found what he was looking for. He held it out for Eddie to take. “Here.”

“A key?” he asked, coming over to take it from him.

“It’s one of the spares, from when I moved in,” Buck explained. That was a lie, of course. He’d had that key made specifically to give to him.  “Maddie has the other. I figured, it’d be easier for you to have one, so I don’t have to struggle to the door every time you come over.”

“Do you mind if I make Carla a copy?”

“Go ahead.” Buck could almost see the plot forming in the little furrow of his brow.  “Now help me get settled on the couch, and then you can tell me what to expect to see happen between your parents and Shannon at the ceremony.”

“At the- Buck, you don’t have to be there, not with your leg like this.”

“Of course I have to be there.” He rolled his eyes. “My best friend’s probation period is ending. Why the hell would I not be there?”

“Best friend?” Eddie asked, grinning. “I thought that was Chris?”

“Chris is my Best Friend Forever,” Buck corrected. “Get it right, Diaz.”

“Of course, my mistake,” Eddie said, sounding impossibly fond.

Buck loved his sister, he did. It was just that, sometimes, he had to repeatedly remind himself of that fact, or else he’d do something rash like scream at her. To be fair, with his leg constantly aching even through the pain meds - which he may or may not have been taking as often as he was supposed to - he was constantly on the verge of screaming at people.

Watching Maddie lose her patience with the leg of the uniform pants she’d been cutting through and instead tear it off was one of those times.

“Come on, be careful,” he told her.

“Were you gonna sew these two pieces back together?” she asked. “I don’t think so.”

“You still didn’t have to rip them.” He watched as she held the pants up to look at them, and they both grimaced. “It looks terrible.”

“It’ll be fine, we’ll just tuck it into the top of your cast,” she assured him. “Although I don’t even know why I’m taking you. You shouldn’t be on your feet, you need to be healing.”

“This is more important,” Buck insisted, even though he wasn’t sure why he bothered. “If I break anything else, they can just fix that too, with the other stuff.”

“What other stuff?”

“They want me to do another surgery, after seeing the x-rays,” he explained. “The doctor wants to go back in and replace the rod, do some bone grafts.”

“Is it just a delayed union or a nonunion?” she asked, forgetting about the pants. “If it’s just healing slower than expected, you can just wait a few weeks.”

“I’m not gonna wait. The sooner the surgery, the sooner I’m back at work with the others.”

“The doctor wants you to wait, doesn’t he?” Maddie asked, though it wasn’t really a question. “You should listen to him. We’re talking about your health, your ability to walk. We’re talking about the rest of your life.”

“Exactly!” Buck snapped at her. “My health. My leg. My life. My choice.”

“Buck…”

“No, Maddie. I’ve already made my choice,” he told her. “You can either accept and support that or… Or don’t.”

He didn’t ask her to like it, because he knew she wouldn’t. Maddie would just never be able to understand how important being a firefighter was to him, how much running into fires and saving idiots from microwaves cemented to their heads and yes, even rescuing cats stuck in trees, completed him. She would never understand that while she could switch careers and be happy, he couldn’t. Not after spending so many years searching for a place to belong and finding it at the station.

So Buck wasn’t expecting her to like his choices, not when he already knew she wouldn’t, not when she had never expected him to like hers. But he did expect her to accept it.

Shields

Seeing Shannon and her former in-laws together was an experience that Buck felt kinda bad for enjoying. It was like watching one of those trashy reality programs, or maybe an episode of Eddie’s telenovelas. Buck’s parents were big on the passive-aggressive, subtly cutting to the quick with back-handed compliments and a well-placed disinterested hum. Eddie’s parents were… Not quite like that. He remembered what Eddie had once told him about the argument that sealed the deal on him leaving Texas, the way they accused him of dragging Chris down with him. There was an argument to be made there that they cared, but what they cared about and how left much to be desired.

So it was only moderately surprising when Shannon sat down across from him with a huff after everyone - Buck included - had lined up to congratulate Eddie.

“Is everything okay?” Buck asked, raising his eyebrows as he exchanged quick glances with Maddie.

“No!” she said, stuffing a bite of cake into her mouth. “Well, this cake is. It’s Eddie’s parents. If I have to listen to one more comment from Helena, I will stab her with this plastic fork.”

“Have they been that bad?” Maddie asked.

“You have no idea,” Shannon told her. “They hate me.”

“Well, you did kinda run away and leave Eddie and Christopher behind,” Buck pointed out, and then yelped when his sister smacked him. But the comment had Shannon laughing, albeit somewhat bitter sounding.

“No, that was probably the best thing I ever did in their eyes,” she said, rolling her own. “It let them be the do-over helicopter parents they’d always wanted to be.”

“Is she complaining about them again?” Eddie asked, suddenly appearing behind Buck, causing him to jump.

“I complain about them behind their back, they complain about me to my face, it’s a never ending cycle,” Shannon told him. “They tried telling Carla that Chris needed a sippy cup. That Helena had just happened to bring along.”

“And Carla gently shot that down, I’m guessing?” Buck asked.

“She is a godsend,” she told him, voice solemn. “If she wasn’t married, and a woman, I would have proposed at that very moment. Actually, with the way she handles his parents, the gender bit might be negotiable.”

“Our divorce isn’t even finalized,” Eddie pointed out, sounding amused.

“I said propose, not elope,” Shannon said.

“My divorce is,” Maddie said, grinning widely. “The paperwork went through for everything, finally. I’m a Buckley again.”

“I dunno, maybe instead of changing it back, you should have gone with something else,” Buck said, ignoring the worried glance Eddie sent him with the new topic change. “Maddie Mackenzie has a nice ring to it.”

“And what, go around calling myself Eminem?” she asked, giggling.

“So him you know?” Chimney, sitting on her otherside, threw up his hands. “You didn’t know Mission: Impossible, but you know Eminem?”

“What’s Mission: Impossible?” Buck asked, just to watch the look of anguish pass over the paramedic’s face.

“Were the two of you raised Amish?” he asked, sounding pained.

“I mean, it was Pennsylvania,” Maddie said.

“Eddie.” Helena’s voice had Shannon’s face souring, and she stuffed the last piece of cake into her mouth. Eddie’s parents had come up as they were talking, and a quick glance around showed that Chris was busy with Abuela and Carla. “Your father and I just wanted to tell you again how proud we are that you’ve made it this far.”

Something about the wording had Buck’s hackle rising, but he wasn’t sure what it was.

“Hello Mrs. Diaz, Mr. Diaz,” he interrupted, grinning at them and sticking out his hand. “I’d stand but your son is blocking my crutches.”

“Mom, dad, this is Buck,” Eddie explained while they shook Buck’s hand in turn. “He’s the one who introduced me to Carla.”

“Well, that was very kind of you,” Helena said, smiling wanly at him. “Eddie, your father and I were thinking, now that your probationary period is over…”

“What about it?” Eddie asked, already glaring.

“Well, there’s no need for you to stay in Los Angeles any longer, is there?” Ramon said. “You can transfer to a station in Texas, be closer to family.”

“Isn’t Isabel your mother? And Pepa your sister?” Buck asked, blinking up at him. 

“We can help you with him,” Helena said, ignoring him. “We can watch him for you when you’re working, like we used to. Help him properly.”

“Help him properly?” he asked, frowning. “What does that mean?”

“You have utter strangers watching him while you work,” Ramon said. “You bring… Her, back into his life.”

“I’m his mother,” Shannon said, standing.

“You gave up on your marriage, twice, and abandoned your son!” Helena snapped. “You don’t get to call yourself his mother.”

Buck glanced over, wide-eyed, at Maddie and Chimney. They were both edging away from the table, abandoning him as they attempted to subtly escape the blast radius.

“She didn’t abandon anybody,” Eddie grounded out, and Buck resisted the urge to say that, yeah, she kinda did. “She left to take care of her mother.”

“He has no stability here, Eddie,” Ramon told him. “He bounces between homes and strangers. We told you, before you left. We told you not to drag him down with-”

“That’s enough!” Buck shouted, catching the attention of the others around them. Using the table, he leveraged himself to his foot, leaning against it heavily. His leg was hurting, it was well past time for his next dose of pain meds, but it was secondary to the burning anger he was feeling at these people. How dare they stand there and talk to Eddie like that? How dare they? “Eddie is a wonderful father. And Shannon might have made mistakes, but she is making up for them. You two don’t get to come in here, make him feel shitty for his choices, and try to drag him and Christopher off where you can, I dunno. Control them.”

“We’re not trying to control anyone,” Helena said.

“And you don’t get a say in this,” Ramon told him.

“Neither do you!” Buck snapped. “Not after the, uh… The custody agreement!”

“Custody agreement?” Eddie asked, sounding confused.

“Yeah, the one the judge and everyone agreed to and signed off on,” Buck said, looking him in the eye and trying to get him to understand.

“He’s right, you can’t move to Texas with Christopher,” Shannon said, catching on faster than her ex-husband. “Not without my permission. And I’m not giving it.”

“Well, surely a judge would be willing to-”

“It doesn’t matter what a judge would be willing to do or not,” Eddie said, interrupting his mother. “Chris and I have a life here, with family. We’re staying. I’m not going to uproot him again.”

“Chris hasn’t been here long enough to put down roots,” Helena protested. “He spent the first six years of his life in El Paso, with us.”

“And now he’s here, with us,” Shannon said. 

Ramon opened his mouth to continue the argument, but Eddie cut him off.

“Dad, mom, enough,” he said, clearly trying to keep from biting their heads off. “Christopher and I are staying here, with Shannon and Buck, and with Abuela and Pepa. We’re not moving back to El Paso. That’s final.”

It was obvious that neither Helena nor Ramon felt it was final, but they understood they weren’t going to win the argument right then. They huffed and grumbled, but Buck watched with relief as they stomped off, to be met by a scolding Abuela. She had clearly heard some of what was said, and was not happy with them.

“Buck,” Shannon said, catching his attention.

“Yeah?”

“Marry me.”

“Our divorce is still not finalized,” Eddie said, not sounding nearly as amused as he had the first time he said it.

“Listen, one of us needs to marry the man now, and you’re taking too long,” Shannon told him, sending both him and Buck into sputters.

“What-”

“That isn’t-”

“I want more cake after that,” Shannon said, ignoring them. “Maddie?”

“Yeah, I could go with more cake,” his sister said, standing up and joining her, Chimney following her heels.

“Hey, get me more cake!” Buck called after her.

“No!”

“Get Eddie to do it,” Shannon said, and then she and Maddie both started giggling. That was shaping up to be a friendship he was not going to enjoy, Buck just knew it.

Buck had spent his time in the hospital, trying to figure out ways to prevent Bobby from interfering with his ability to work in the future. He already had plans to try and get his doctor to do a scan and find the blood clots before his embolism, but that was no guarantee. Especially when there was the chance Bobby would still use the blood thinners as an excuse to keep him away, whether he vomited up blood in front of him or not.

It was when he’d been laying there, wishing he could ask Dr. Copeland for advice, that he realized what he needed to do. A quick email exchange later and here he was, opening the door to his apartment and letting Chief Alonzo in.

“Sorry about any mess,” he told him, ducking his head. “It’s been kinda difficult getting around the place to clean.”

Carla had been letting herself in regularly, after Eddie had given her a copy of the key. Whether she had Chris or not, she would come in and help pick up, make sure he was taking his meds, and cook for him if need be. She even helped him shower, much to his embarrassment. He felt much better, this go around, than he had when he was stuck on the couch of his loft after Ali had left him.

“It’s quite alright, son,” Alonzo told him, patiently waiting for him to limp to the recliner, which had become his new favorite piece of furniture with his leg. The chief took the couch. “How is everything?”

“It’s okay, sir,” Buck told him. “They replaced the rod and did some bone grafts.”

“Well, hopefully you’ll be back out there soon,” he said. “But that wasn’t what you asked to meet with me about.”

“No, it was about… I had a therapist once, who said that trauma had a splash zone,” Buck told him, remembering what Copeland had said. “That it didn’t just happen to the victim, but also to everyone around them. I had my leg crushed by the truck, yeah, but everyone else had to watch.”

“And you’re worried about PTSD for them?”

“Yeah, kinda, or something like it,” he said. “Especially Bobby. The kid, Freddie? He asked for him specifically, right? I just… I’m worried he might be feeling guilty, that what happened to me was somehow his fault.”

“I think I understand,” Alonzo said, stroking his chin. “So what do you suggest?”

“Me? Uh… Well, I know the department is going to mandate therapy for me before coming back, so… That? For Bobby? For all of them?”

“It’s not a bad idea,” the chief said. “I’ll see about looking into it.”

He stood, and shook his head when Buck started struggling to grab his crutches.

“No, son, I’ll let myself out,” he said, shaking his head at him and walking for the door. “And Buckley?”

“Yes sir?”

“Keep me in the loop, about your leg,” he ordered. “I want to know how your recovery goes.”

“Uh, yeah. I mean, yes sir.”

As he stared at the door after Alonzo closed it behind him, Buck felt, for the first time since his leg was once again crushed, that things were starting to look up for him.

Thin Lines

Recovery this time was not any faster or slower than it was the first time around, although Buck still grumbled about it. His leg constantly ached, even through the haze of the painkillers, when he actually took them. He had never been fond of being on them before, and after his brief flirtation with alcoholism earlier in the year, he was even more hesitant of taking them. Especially when he realized how well they helped him fall into a dreamless sleep at night, how he would actually feel calm after taking them, and how much he had started looking forward to his next doses specifically for that reason.

It was a fine line, trying to get through it without falling into the same pit Bobby had. He constantly felt like he was walking a tightrope, and every pill he shook out of the bottle threatened to send him tumbling down with the greatest of ease. Carla was helping him with it, though. She and Eddie finally had enough with him purposefully dodging doses, and lying to them that he wasn’t, and confronted him about it one day while Chris was with Shannon.

It was a somewhat awkward conversation, having to admit out loud that there had even been a problem to begin with, but they helped. Of course they helped. Carla even went with him to his doctor, to discuss switching to a different medication. The one he was on now wasn’t as strong, but there was also less of a danger of addiction.

Once again, he couldn’t help but think that Abby and all the pain she caused him had been worth it, just so he had Carla in his life.

It helped that Buck very rarely went a day without seeing someone else. If it wasn’t Carla coming over, with or without Christopher, then it was Maddie or Eddie. Occasionally, even Abuela and Pepa would visit, carrying containers of homemade meals, or ingredients to cook them in his kitchen. Bobby, of course, would also come over to ensure he wasn’t wasting away. There was a tall stool now by his kitchen counter, where he would sit and either help or talk to whoever was cooking for him at the time.

Occasionally, while watching Bobby cook or impressing Abuela with his (atrociously accented) Spanish, he’d find himself comparing it to how things were Before, by that last Christmas. When he was ignoring the cracks in the foundation, refusing to admit that things were not okay. When his family had fractured and broken around him, and he clung tighter to Taylor, because she had come back and chosen him, where everyone else was leaving and choosing other people. When his loft had been cold and empty, even when she was there. Especially when she was there.

He regretted how he had panicked and ran, like a proper Buckley, but he didn’t regret having a chance to undo all the hurt.

A few weeks after Chief Alonzo’s visit to his apartment, Eddie stomped through his door and flopped onto the couch, face first, exactly like a teenager. Buck, sitting in the recliner with his leg propped up, muted the crappy daytime soap opera he’d been watching and stared at him.

“I’m guessing Chris is with Shannon, then?” he asked, and got a muffled grunt as an answer. “What, did they make Chimney acting captain again?”

“Dios, no,” Eddie said, sitting up. “They’re making us all go to therapy.”

“Finally,” Buck said, and the other man let out a wounded noise. “I talked to the chief weeks ago.”

“You talked to-? This is your fault!?”

“I mean, technically it’s that Freddie kid’s fault…”

“Buck,” Eddie whined, and he couldn’t help smiling at how similar he sounded to Chris at that moment. “I don’t want to go to therapy. I don’t need therapy.”

“If you don’t need it, then it shouldn’t be that difficult,” Buck said, shrugging. Truthfully, Eddie was the one he wanted to get into therapy the most, right after Bobby. He didn’t think he was likely to join a fight club this time around, not with Shannon alive and when Buck had no intentions of filing a lawsuit, but one could never be certain. “But c’mon man, they told you why, right?”

“Because of lingering mental trauma from witnessing the truck bombing,” Eddie recited.

“Hey, it traumatized me, and I barely remember any of it.”

“Yeah, but it happened to you.”

“It happened to you, too,” Buck said, shrugging. “And I’ve put together enough from what you and Shannon, and your family, have mentioned to know that, yeah, you probably do need therapy.”

“I don’t-”

“Eddie, you came home injured and didn’t have a chance to actually heal before you were having to juggle a failing marriage, learning how to be a father, and paying the bills. I don’t know how you earned that silver star,” he lied, “but I know you never earn them by experiencing something pleasant.”

Eddie glared at him, that familiar mulish set to his jaw, and Buck knew he wasn’t going to get anywhere by pushing.

“I should be getting my cast off soon,” he said, changing the topic. “And then it’s getting ready for recertification.”

“Gracias a Dios, because I miss having you watching my back,” Eddie said, sinking into the couch cushions. “I almost bit the floater’s head off the other day. He was just… Mouthy.”

“I’m mouthy.”

“Yeah, but I like you,” Eddie said, and Buck had to look away to hide the dopey grin on his face.  “Do you know what day they’re taking it off? I’ll see if I can’t drive you there and back.”

“Yeah,” Buck said, reaching for his phone. “I have it on here…”

The concept of Buck’s personal boundaries had always been more theoretical for his sister. It was a carryover, perhaps, from losing Daniel at such a young age and then being saddled with raising him while their parents mourned. It had been fine, when he was a kid, but as an adult after several years of radio silence from her, it was a bit aggravating. At the time he had been too overwhelmed with surprise and relief to really have a problem with it, but in hindsight, there were many red flags in how she reentered his life the first time around. How she got the landlord to let her into Abby’s apartment while he was out, and then immediately told him that Abby was probably cheating on him.

Was Buck allowed to still be annoyed by it, when it never happened this time?

The problem was always that she knew best, or at least believed she did, and didn’t put much effort into understanding why others disagreed with her. It translated at the moment into her trying her damndest to get him to slow down on his continued efforts to get back to his job, because no matter how glacial it felt to him, it was still too fast for her taste. She was worried, and he understood that, but he was a fully grown adult with the ability to comprehend what he was doing and make his own informed choices.

“I’m just saying, Evan, that you don’t have to rush into this.” Maddie had been waiting for him at his apartment when he got back. It had been a couple weeks since the cast had come off, and one week since he went back with complaints of “leg cramps” and they found the beginnings of blood clots. As he hadn’t even started training for recertification yet, there’d been no accusation of it somehow being his fault, and no reason for them to try sticking him on light duty while they figured out what caused them. They’d even caught them early enough that it wasn’t going to delay anything.

The blood thinners were going to be on a need-to-know basis. That meant only his doctor, the department brass, and Eddie and Carla knew at the moment.

“I’m not rushing, Mads,” Buck told her, already tired of this conversation.

“Yes you are, you just got the cast off, and you’re already wanting to get back to work.”

“I’m wanting to build back the strength in my leg,” he said. “So does my physical therapist. You know, the guy who has a degree in this.”

“Are you sure that he knows what he’s doing though? I mean, if they’re worried about blood clots…”

“If they’re- What?” His eyes wandered to his coffee table, where he’d left yesterday’s mail. Mail that included an invoice from his insurance for the ultrasound they did to find the clots. “Maddie, did you invade my privacy?”

“I didn’t invade your privacy, I’m your sister,” she said, rolling her eyes. 

“That… Is your being my sister evidence that you didn’t invade my privacy? Or are you saying that, because you’re my sister, it doesn’t count?” She didn’t answer, and he didn’t expect her to. “I have spent weeks doing nothing more than laying, sitting, and hobbling around. Actually exercising my leg isn’t going to put me at any more risk of a blood clot.”

“Well, do they know what’s causing them?”

“I never said I had any blood clots,” Buck pointed out. She had probably gone through his medicine cabinet, to be so certain of it. “Did you come over just to snoop and get into a fight with me? Or did you want to actually visit?”

“Visit,” she conceded, letting the topic go. It was a nice afternoon spent with his sister, after that. They had dinner and watched one of the many movies Chimney kept suggesting to them. He did like spending time with her, when she wasn’t trying to dictate his life.

The next day was an unpleasant reminder that people liked to gossip about him, his sister and her boyfriend included. But at least Eddie was there to tell him it was happening.

Chim just told everyone about your blood thinners.

How did he find out?

Mads snooped

saw insr n mail

wnt lkng n med cab

Was that even English?

Cap looks worried, he’ll probably call

Great. Just… Great.

Trust is a Key

“I am so sorry,” Chimney said the moment Buck answered the door to his frantic knocking. It was the first time he’d actually laid eyes on the man since Eddie’s shield ceremony. They spoke on the phone, and they texted, but neither he nor Hen had managed to find or make the time to stop by. It was much the same as the last time he’d been laid up recovering from the ladder truck, so he truly hadn’t been expecting much else.

It was the day after Chimney told everyone about his blood thinners, and two days after Maddie snooped through his apartment while waiting for him to get home. Contrary to Eddie’s belief, Bobby hadn’t called him yet. Whether it was because he’d been too busy or putting it off, Buck didn’t know. Perhaps the captain was stress-baking at home with plans to ambush him with baked goods while heaping disapproval and paternal concern down upon him.

(It was a shame Harry didn’t have his own phone yet, or else he’d ask him if he heard anything.)

“What exactly are you apologizing for?” Buck asked, reigning in the immediate reflex to forgive him.

“The blood thinners,” Chimney said. “I didn’t realize they were supposed to be a secret until Eddie said something, and I am so sorry.”

“It’s fine.” Hearing that had him settling somewhat. He hadn’t thought Chimney would purposefully go ratting these things out to everyone else, but then again, the man had happily gone around telling everyone about his “invisible girlfriend” Before. “I’m assuming Maddie came by or called the other day, ranting about me not being careful enough?”

“Pretty much, yeah.” Chimney sighed. “Your sister is just worried, man. She cares.”

“Too much, I think,” Buck said. 

“What does that mean?”

“You know that I didn’t tell her about the blood thinners, right?”

“Then how did she…? Is she psychic, too?”

“No, she isn’t- She has a key, and the urge to poke around when I’m not here.”

“Oh, wow, okay.” Chimney’s eyes were wide.

“Yeah, listen, she’s gonna be pissed at me soon, so just… Bear with it?”

“Why is she going to be pissed at you?” the paramedic asked. “What are you doing?”

“Changing the locks.”

Buck wasn’t certain if there had been a schedule worked out for who would take him to his rehab appointments, but it definitely seemed like there was one. He could easily imagine Eddie, Carla, and Bobby doing rock-paper-scissors for who would take him and on which days. His insecurities wanted to believe that it was the losers who were stuck ferrying him about, but the wiser, therapied part of him could easily imagine them trampling each other to volunteer for tribute. The worry that they were only doing it out of obligation or guilt was still there, but it was nowhere near as strong as it had once been.

On a day that it was Eddie’s turn to take him, he presented his friend with a new pair of house keys. Both were hot pink, one with tiger stripes and the other leopard print.

“Why?”

“I changed my locks,” Buck said, shrugging. “One’s for Carla, obviously.”

“Obviously,” Eddie agreed, rolling his eyes as he took them. “Because of Maddie?”

“Yeah, because of Maddie.” She had been… Not well pleased, when he told her what he was doing. But Copeland had always been insistent that he needed to be firm with his boundaries. While he was locking his door with his own - not pink - key, he asked, “how’s your therapy going?”

Eddie heaved a giant sigh as they made their way to the building’s elevator.

“Was that a good sigh? A bad sigh? C’mon man, give me more than that.”

“I’ve only had a couple sessions so far,” he answered. “And it’s mostly been to talk about how I felt during the truck bombing. Which is stupid, because I’m not the one who was trapped under the truck.”

“What, because seeing me in pain was nice for you?” Buck asked, shoulder checking him as they waited for the elevator. “Because I know how I’d feel if the situations were reversed.”

(Helpless. Horrified. Guilt ridden. Desperate to get to him, desperate to take the pain away, desperate to make sure he was okay.)

“The divorce is done,” Eddie said, switching topics as the doors opened and they stepped inside. “And we have an actual custody agreement now, instead of just lying about one to keep my parents off my back.”

“Yeah, Maddie told me she and her went out celebrating. You know, before she started yelling at me for changing my locks.”

“We should be worried about that, right?” Eddie asked, glancing at him. “That Maddie and Shannon are friends? Somehow?”

“I don’t know if we should be,” Buck answered. “But I definitely am.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?” Bobby asked, while driving him back to his apartment. It was weeks after Chimney had told everyone about them, so the captain had been sitting on it for a while. Probably talking about it to his priest and (hopefully) to the department therapist, getting advice before confronting him. “About the blood thinners.”

“Because it wasn’t your business,” Buck told him, too tired to really mind his tongue. Rehab that day had been harsh and painful, and Buck had maybe cried a bit in between snapping at everyone around him. Possibly. “Not yet anyway.”

“Not my-? Buck, what?”

“It wasn’t your business,” he repeated. “You didn’t need to know. Literally no one knew, except for people who needed to know.”

“And Eddie needed to know?” There was a tinge of hurt to his words, and Buck found himself feeling bad for putting it there.

“He’s the one who took me to the doctor’s appointment,” he told him. In lieu of saying he didn’t want him to know because he didn’t trust Bobby to not impede his return to work out of guilt and a twisted urge to protect him by hurting him, he went with an equally true statement. “I didn’t want you to worry, I’m getting enough of that from Maddie.”

“She’s your sister Buck, of course-”

“Yeah, yeah, everyone’s been telling me that. And I get it. But it gets to the point where it’s obvious she doesn’t trust me to make my own choices, and I didn’t want to hear it from you, too.” He rested his head against the car window. “I had every intention to tell you before I came back to work, I swear.”

“I do trust you, kid,” Bobby said, and Buck almost rolled his eyes at that.

“This isn’t going to be a problem with me coming back to work, right?”

“I mean, do they know what’s causing them? The clots?” the captain asked, and this time Buck did roll his eyes.

“And there we go,” he spat. “That’s why I didn’t tell you.”

“If it’s caused by something you’re doing to get back to work, then-”

“Something I’m doing?” he asked, voice shaking. “First you say you trust me, and now you think it’s something I’m doing that’s causing the clots. This is why I didn’t tell you.”

“Well, do they? I need to know.”

“Why? Why do you need to know? Why can’t you and Maddie at least trust my doctors, if not me? If they don’t think I’m putting myself at risk, why do you?”

“I don’t think that,” Bobby said, in a voice that was probably meant to be calming but only came across as patronizing. “I’m just worried. We’re all just worried.”

“Maybe you’re too worried about me.”

It was lucky that they were at a red light, because Bobby twisted his head to stare at him.

“What? What does that mean?”

“Maybe you’re too worried about me to be my captain,” Buck said, meeting his eyes. “Because I am going to be a firefighter again, and I would really, really like to be a firefighter again at the One-Eighteen. But if you’re too worried about me, about the blood thinners, then…”

And Buck mostly didn’t mean what he was implying. The 118 was his home, and had been ever since the actual first time he sat at the dining table in the station’s loft with them. But he was tired, and he was hurting, and he didn’t want to have this fight again. He would, if he had to. He would claw and bite and do anything it took to be back on the trucks with his family, even if that meant going through another lawsuit and making himself the bad guy again.

But he didn’t want to.

“Are you… Buck, are you giving me an ultimatum?”

“I am asking you to be objective, cap,” he told him. “I know you feel guilty, like what that kid did was your fault-”

“Of course I do, it would never have happened if he wasn’t angry with me.”

“But that’s why they have you going to therapy, isn’t it? So you aren’t taking it out on me?” He turned away, and gestured towards the road ahead. “The light’s green.”

They were both silent the rest of the drive to his apartment.

The Surprise Party That Wasn't

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Recovery this time around hadn’t been any faster, but it also hadn’t been any slower. Come the last week of September, Buck was once again breaking records recertifying. He was even a couple seconds faster this time, because he had done the course before. Bobby hadn’t made any noises about the blood thinners since their confrontation in the car, the implied ultimatum causing him to step back and rethink what he was doing.

Athena, when she called to check in, had mentioned that he had started going to more AA meetings. When Buck had voiced his sense of guilt over that, she had shot him down almost immediately.

“All you did was speak your truth, Buckaroo,” she had told him. “How he responded to that is not on you.”

As far as Buck was aware, Bobby and everyone else had finished the therapy they were mandated. Eddie had grumped and grumbled at him after almost every session, either over the phone or in person. Buck wasn’t sure if it had helped any, because Eddie’s first instinct with his emotions had always been to “suck it up and move on,” and that didn’t involve talking about them. It was a tendency that Buck was definitely going to need to break him of, and soon. Else there was every bit the chance of being blindsided by another Christmas announcement.

Buck could not help but contemplate how much of that had influenced Chris into bottling everything up until he exploded all over the holidays. Chris had told him, while they were stuck on a firetruck surrounded by water, that he had tried complaining once and it hadn’t worked. And he hadn’t even cried when Buck told him about his dad being shot, even being the one to offer comfort instead. How much of that was Chris being the strongest kid he knew, and how much of that was simply him sucking it up and moving on? How much of that was Chris, and how much of that was Chris acting like his father?

Chris, Before, had the tendency to seem perfectly fine until he suddenly wasn’t, and that worried Buck.

He’d had two years, or there about, to sit on that problem and think about it, but Buck still hadn’t figured out how to address it. He was even less of a parent to the kid now than he had been Before, with Shannon still alive and no Will giving him guardianship in the event of Eddie being unable to care for his son. And he knew, with how Eddie’s parents treated him, that the man would not react well to any perceived critiques of how he was raising his kid. Even if they were coming from Buck.

It was a problem that would have to remain on the backburner, until inspiration or something like it came to him.

The situation with Maddie was similarly stalled out. She was still hurt that he had changed the locks on her, hurt by the very concept that Buck needed boundaries against her. It had taken time to get back to civil conversations with her, time for her to finally realize that he wasn’t going to cave on this even in the face of her sisterly anger, and that to keep pushing the subject was to only hurt herself. It meant that they were always on the edge of heated feelings and pointed words whenever they spoke, cutting calls and visits short to prevent full-blown arguments from erupting. Buck wanted his sister in his life, but he didn’t want to keep defending his life from her.

He wondered if it was this that led to his sister not driving with him to the Grant-Nash house for his surprise party. He wondered if it was their mutual desire to avoid being stuck in a car together, unable to leave if words became loud and sharp again, or if it was simply a by-product of him living somewhere else this time around. Perhaps it was both. Perhaps the latter was an excuse to avoid the former.

Athena opened the door when he knocked, grinning brightly at him.

“Buck, I’m so happy you were able to make it.”

“Thanks for having me over, I appreciate it,” he told her, following her down the stairs. Having everyone suddenly shouting “surprise!” still had him jumping, even when he was expecting it. Standing at the bottom of the stairs, looking at his family gathered around to support him, he heart was fit to burst. It wasn’t quite his entire family yet. He could almost see the gaps where Ravi and Albert would be, where little Jee-Yun would be. But the family he had now, even with the stress he’d put on some of them, were there. For him.

Eddie was the first to pull him into a hug, followed by Bobby and Hen, and then Maddie. After that, the party went much the same as the first time around. Chris gave him the adorable card, which was going to be stuck on his fridge until the heat death of the universe. Then Hen and Karen showed him the baby photo of their intended sperm donor, and Buck was still trying to figure out how to subtly and gently crush their hopes about that when he suddenly had an armful of emotional Karen.

(Maybe he didn’t have to say anything? They got through the disappointment okay last time. Or maybe he could just casually leave foster parent pamphlets around the station.)

After a short check in with Maddie and Chimney, which he ended while the words were still friendly teasing and not cutting, he turned around and found Bobby right there, waiting to talk.

“They’re sending me the paperwork in the morning,” he said. “And then you will officially be back.”

“And you’re okay with that?” Buck asked, because he needed to know. “I mean, if you’re still too worried to be my captain, to let me back, then…”

“I don’t really have a choice, do I?” he asked. “Not when you made it clear that you’d go elsewhere.”

“I don’t want to go elsewhere,” Buck told him. “I hated not being with you guys.”

“We missed you too. It’ll be nice to have the whole team back together,” he said. “But Buck, with the blood thinners, you need to be careful.”

“Hey, I’m not going to spontaneously bleed to death, Cap. If it’s something surgical glue can’t handle, then you’d be sending me to the hospital anyways, right?” 

“That’s… Probably true.”

“Oh it’s definitely true. And uh, Cap? Thanks. Not just for all of this,” he waved his hand around at the entire yard, filled with balloons and people from the station. “For being there, for the surgeries and the rehab. I know I was not the easiest person to be around, sometimes.”

“You weren’t that bad.”

“Pretty sure Eddie would disagree with you,” Buck said. “Hey, do you know who came up with the cake? Because I have critiques.”

“Critiques?” Bobby’s eyebrows started rising.

“Yeah, like- Remember the cake we got for Chim?  After the rebar?” He waited for his captain to nod in recognition. “Why did he get a fun cake and I get a boring one?”

“A fun cake?”

“Yeah! With the liquorice rebar.”

“I hesitate to ask, but what would you have wanted instead?”

“I was thinking- hey! Don’t roll your eyes at that. I was thinking a cake in the shape of a firetruck on its side and under it-”

“Oh my Lord, Buck…”

“And under it, a firefighter action figure! And maybe with another one standing by it, with a little vest on?”

“You have put too much thought into this,” Bobby said, looking heavenward for strength.

“He’s put thought into something?” Eddie asked, joining them. Buck pouted at him for the implication.

“He wanted a cake recreation of the bombing.”

“Buck, what the fuck?”

“Hey, that rhymed!”

Buck managed to enjoy his party to its end, this time, with no coughing and no blood. Well, some coughing, when Chris managed to time a joke just as he was drinking. It had sent him into a minor panic, half-expecting to taste blood in his mouth again, but he thought he managed to hide it pretty well. At the very least, no one looked any more worried than they typically would be to see him choking on coke. And at the party’s end, because he was a weak man and a yawning Chris had asked, he followed them to theirs.

(He ignored the knowing looks he was sent as they left, because they didn’t really know anything.)

A couple days later, with the paperwork filed, he opened his email and found the confirmation of his return date.

It nearly stopped his heart, when he saw it.

September 28th, the day of the tsunami.

Chapter End Notes

I'm going to have to write something fluffy, to balance out the next chapter.

Edit: changed the date of the tsunami, because I realized it was a Monday and that Chris should have been in school.

The Water Will Take

Chapter Notes

*casually ups the Rating*
See end notes for (spoilery) content warnings

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The day had been hell, and the evening had somehow been worse. Bobby had tried to sideline Eddie early on, which had almost resulted in physical violence. If Buck hadn’t been there, it probably would have. The captain had eventually been convinced that it was better to have him there with them, rather than risking him diving into the disaster without any back-up beyond Buck.

(Because if he sent Eddie away, Buck would follow, and everyone knew it.)

Bobby finally left them at the VA hospital with Lena Bosko of the 136, arguing that everyone would be filtering through there. It was sound logic, Buck knew. Logic he had followed the last time, and logic that led him to the happy ending he was so desperate for now. Because there had to be a happy ending, there had to be, and he wasn’t sure what he would do if there wasn’t.

“Hey, excuse me,” he said, flagging down a volunteer. Eddie had stopped talking to anyone by this point, his face wet from sea water and tears both. Buck’s wasn’t any better. “We’re looking for a kid and his mom?”

“What do they look like?”

“The kid, Christopher Diaz, he- He’s nine, with brown hair, and he has CP,” Buck told her. “And his mom, Shannon, she’s shorter than me, also with brown hair.”

He held his breath as the volunteer quickly flipped through the papers on her clipboard. When she solemnly shook her head, he was brutally reminded of the last time he had lived through this.

“They’re not listed here,” she said, a tired apology to her tone. “You might want to check the black tent.”

Eddie sounded like the air had been punched out of him, leaving him gasping for breath. They both knew what she was implying.

“C’mon, you can just… Just sit over here, okay?” Buck said, trying to lead him to a nearby bench. “I- I’ll go look, you don’t need to-”

“No, I have to,” Eddie said, the first he spoke since the sun set. He tugged himself out of Buck’s gentle grip and made for the tent’s entrance. “I have to. I have to make sure.”

“Okay,” Buck said, walking in beside him. “Okay. I’m here with you.”

The black tent, the make-shift morgue that they had set up, was large. Inside were rows and rows of still, nameless bodies. Every once in a while, someone who was making the same desperate search as them would collapse with a cry. The two of them made their way together, down one line and up another. Hoping and praying that they wouldn’t find them here, that there was still a chance.

A quarter of the way through the fifth row, under a sheet much too large for what it was covering, that hope was crushed as ruthlessly as Buck’s leg had been.

Before

The days leading up to the last weekend of September were filled with an odd mix of dread and anticipation. Buck was torn on what to do. Well, not really, but he was feeling torn about it. He had spent that day helping who-knows how many people, before and after losing Chris. Part of him thought he needed to be there, to help those people again. A bigger, louder part of him, the traumatized and cowardly part of him, was relieved to have an excuse not to be.

At least he knew Chris wasn’t going to be there. Last time, the boy had only been in danger because Buck had put him in danger. This time, since Shannon was going to be watching him, Chris would be safely ensconced in his mother’s house for the day. In-land and miles away from the danger.

There was also the question of how much weight an anonymous warning would have, if he tried it. Would anyone listen? Would they close the pier for the day, or keep a better eye out, just in case? Or would they blow him off as a loony trying to cause a panic? There had to have been some prior warning, a seismic event of some sort that would have been cause for concern. Perhaps that, in addition to an anonymous phone call from a worried psychic?

No, they’d probably thank him for his concerns with condescension and then tell him that there was nothing to be worried about, that NOAA was keeping an eye on everything.

The morning of, Buck woke up early and went through his routine. He spent far too much time in front of his bathroom mirror, primping in an attempt to look good for his first day back and to distract himself from his nerves. He felt guilty, knowing about the tsunami and doing nothing. But there wasn’t anything he could do, really. He couldn’t control the ocean, and no one would listen to him if he said anything.

“You don’t worry about the things you can’t do anything about,” Bobby had once told them, a year ago now. Natural disasters unfortunately fell into that category. It didn’t help him feel any better as he walked into the station unaided for the first time since the bombing.

“Buckaroo!” Hen shouted, greeting him with a hug and smile, when he joined them in the loft after changing. “Look at you.”

“Lazy-bones is finally off his butt,” Chimney said.

“It’s good to have you back, kid,” Bobby said, setting a plate of breakfast in front of him as he sat at the table.

“Where’s Eddie?”

“Right here, I had to take Chris to Shannon’s,” the man announced, joining them. He and Buck grinned at each other as he sat down, and Buck felt the nerves finally settle.

The day, for all that it was destined to go differently, started off calm. A minor fender-bender, followed by a call to a hot dog vendor that had caught fire. He hadn’t kept track of the clock when he was having fun with Chris, so he wasn’t sure when the wave hit, but he knew it was getting close. He was twitchy with nerves, jittery and bouncing on his heels.

“What are you smiling at?” he heard Hen ask, and turned to see Eddie looking at his phone.

“A picture Shannon sent me of Chris.”

“It’s good you two are still friends.”

“Yeah, we’re trying,” Eddie told her. “For Chris.”

“What are they doing?” Buck asked as he ambled over. “Watching movies together?”

“Nah,” Eddie answered. “She surprised him with a trip to the pier, apparently.”

Buck nearly tripped over himself.

“W- What?”

“Hey, did someone leave a hydrant open?” Bobby asked, and Buck could see the dawning horror on Eddie’s face as the alert came in on his phone.

After

Eddie was utterly silent. He had collapsed at the sight of a pale, unbreathing Chris beneath the white sheet, a puppet with all his strings cut. They still hadn’t found Shannon, but the energy to continue the search had been leached away with their hope. She could have been in another row, beneath another sheet. Or she could have been out there still, waiting to be rescued or to be recovered.

Buck wasn’t certain how, precisely, they had managed to manhandle Eddie away from his  son. He had radioed Bobby to tell him they had found Chris, and the pain in his voice must have been enough for him to understand what wasn’t said. The captain had shown up alongside a blood-covered Athena - “It isn’t mine.” - and somehow through the combined efforts of all three of them, Eddie was lifted to his feet and steered out into a night that was suddenly so much colder.

It was Athena that took them both home, Buck refusing to leave Eddie’s side and no one even bothering to suggest it. Bobby had stayed behind, promising to oversee what needed to be overseen. Not that Eddie had acknowledged it, quietly allowing himself to be steered in and out of Athena’s cruiser and then through his front door.

“Will the two of you be okay?” Athena asked, lingering on Eddie’s doorstep.

“No,” Buck told her, and then shut the door before she could ask any more stupid questions. In the time that took, Eddie had wandered away. It didn’t take long to find him, the place being as small as it was. There was only one place he would be.

Stepping into Chris’ room, he found him exactly where he thought he’d be. The man was sitting on the bed, back bowed and silently shaking. He was gripping his St. Christopher medallion in his fist, so tightly that Buck worried it would start cutting into his palm. He didn’t say a word as Buck sat down next to him, nor did he resist any when he gently pulled him into his side.

“I’m here, Eds,” he said. “I’m here, just let it out.”

Buck could hear the echo of his heart shattering in Eddie’s wail.

It seemed like forever before Eddie eventually cried himself out, the exhaustion catching up to him. He fell asleep against Buck’s tear soaked shoulder, and he gently lowered him onto the too small bed. He’d have to be moved, Buck knew, but he didn’t have the heart to try it yet. Instead, he left him there, turning off the light as he silently padded to the kitchen.

On autopilot, he grabbed a glass from the cabinet and went to fill it at the sink and then, half-way to doing so, changed course. It cracked as he slammed it onto the counter, and then shattered when he did it again. With a wordless shout, he spun and threw the remnants into the wall before sliding to the floor. The sharp pain in his palm and fingers, and the blood dripping from his hand like water, told him how stupid that idea had been.

It didn’t matter.

Christopher was gone. His Superman was gone, and his best friend was as broken as the glass Buck had just thrown. Christopher was gone, and it was all his fault, he knew that it was. If he hadn’t been such a selfish coward, if he had gone to the pier instead of sticking his head in the sand, he could have done something. He could have been there, he should have been there, like he was Before.

But he hadn’t been, and now…

What Buck wouldn’t give to redo this day like he had so many others. What he wouldn’t give to rewind it and unfuck everything. The loop he’d been stuck in last May had been painful, but nowhere near as agonizing as this. He almost wished he was back there, constantly dying again and again until-

He froze, staring at his bleeding palm, which showed no sign of slowing thanks to the blood thinners.

Could he…? But what if it didn’t work? Eddie could wake up alone to an even emptier world.

But if it did work…

After using the counter to pull himself up, he blindly groped for the block of kitchen knives, never taking his eyes off his wounded hand. Once upon a time, he had taken a life to protect his sister and his friend. It had been easy, frighteningly so. This time it would be even easier, if not as clean.

Anything, anything, for his family.

Anything, anything, for the boy he thought of as his own.

(He’d always been the expendable one.)

“You are very lucky dead things aren’t entertaining,” Ichabod told him when he opened his eyes.

“Because we both know that’s what matters,” Buck said, slowly getting to his feet.

“My entertainment is the only thing that matters,” the entity said, smiling at him.

“Yeah, yeah, whatever.”

“You were livelier the other times you died.”

“Well, Ichabod,” Buck ground out. “I’m sorry if losing my s- My friend’s kid has put a damper on my mood.”

“Was it really much of a loss, though?” he asked, tilting his head. “He was a rather defective child.”

“CHRIS ISN’T DEFECTIVE!” Buck roared, getting into his face, but Ichabod didn’t even blink.

“You’re treading a thin line there, boy, to be yelling in my face when I can send you all the way back to the beginning again.”

“I don’t care, do it,” he said, squaring his shoulders. “Do it, if that’s what you want, if that’s what it takes. Chris is more important than anything else. I would live through the last two years over and over again if it would keep him safe. Hell, let the truck take my leg this time, I don’t care. Chris is more important.”

“The child isn’t even yours.”

“That doesn’t matter!” Buck shouted. “I’ll still do any-”

A long, cold finger to his mouth silenced him.

“Those are dangerous words to speak aloud in a place like this,” Ichabod said, voice low and serious. “You are very, very lucky you started saying them to me, instead of something far less kind.”

Buck stayed quiet, swallowing against the sudden fearful lump in his throat.

“This is the only time I’ll let you get away with this, by the way,” the entity told him, lowering his finger. “The next time you kill yourself for a do-over, I will send you to the beginning again. Or let you stay dead.”

“But dead things aren’t entertaining.” The words sounded trembling even to his own ears.

“No, but what gets left behind can be.”

When Buck once again opened his eyes, he was in bed with his alarm ringing to get him up for his first day back to work. He scrambled for his phone, groaning when he realized how little time Ichabod had given him to work with. When he called, Bobby answered almost immediately.

“Hey-”

“Bobby, I can’t come in today.”

“You can’t- Buck, I’m confused.” He could hear the frown. “You fought with everyone to come back as soon as you could, and now you’re not coming in?”

“It’s- Something’s come up, or- Or something will come up, I-” How could he explain this? Fuck, he didn’t have time to explain this. Shannon could already be at the pier with Christopher, or on her way, and he needed to get there so he could get them both away. “Bobby, I just need you to trust me, okay?”

“Of course I trust you, Buck, but I don’t understand.”

“And I’ll explain it to you, I promise,” he said. And he would, even if that meant explaining everything. “I just- You’ll understand, I swear. Just trust me.”

And then he hung up, because he just didn’t have the time.

Chapter End Notes

cw: (off screen) child death; implied suicide; minor ableism

We Sell Our Lives to the Sea

“Is something wrong, Cap?” Hen asked when she and Chimney climbed the steps to the loft.

“I don’t know,” Bobby said, staring into his coffee, which had cooled to room temperature long ago. The phone call with Buck had left him feeling unsettled, and cooking breakfast for the team had been forgotten. “Yes. Maybe?”

“Okay,” Chimney drew the word out as he sat down. “Do you want to give us some context here?”

“Buck called in.”

“What?!” the paramedics screeched.

“Did he tell you why?” Hen demanded, invading the captain’s space. “Is it his leg? Did something happen with the blood thinners?”

“He didn’t say,” Bobby answered, finally looking up. “He didn’t sound…”

“He didn’t sound, what?” Chimney urged.

“He didn’t sound like he was in trouble. But he was also in a hurry to get off the phone.”

“Well, what did he say?” Hen asked.

“That something had come up. No, no, he said something had or was going to come up.” It hadn’t made sense, and even with the promise of an eventual explanation, Bobby still wanted to call him back and demand to know what was going on. “Then he told me to trust him and hung up.”

“I don’t think I’ve known that boy to willingly miss a day of work,” Hen commented, frowning. “And he was determined to come back as soon as he could.”

“Maybe he was having a psychic moment,” Chimney offered, and the other two rolled their eyes.

“Buck isn’t psychic,” Hen told him.

“He said you wouldn’t believe me…”

“Believe what?” Eddie asked, climbing up the loft stairs. “Where’s Buck? Is he not in yet? I thought he’d get here early, or at least before me.”

“He called in,” Bobby said, lapsing back into quiet contemplation as the two paramedics filled the former army medic in on what the captain had told them. There was something going on, that much was obvious. Buck hadn’t sounded like he was in trouble, but he had sounded… Worried wasn’t the right word. Anxious, perhaps? He had sounded anxious over the phone.

“He isn’t answering.” Eddie’s frustrated words drew him out, and he looked up to find the man scowling at his phone. “It’s ringing, but it keeps going to voicemail. He always answers when I call.”

“Should we call Athena?” Hen asked. “Have her start looking for him?”

“She’s not at work,” Bobby told her. “She and May are having a spa day, I think.”

“Maybe-” Chimney started to say, but the station alarm interrupted him. None of them were happy about it, but they did have a job to do. Everything felt off, all of them left unsteady and questioning what was going on. The first call, a minor fender bender, was at least calm. The one that followed, a hot dog vendor that had caught fire, was somewhat more demanding of their attention even as it wasn’t labor intensive.

  Bobby caught the others checking their phones when they could, each hoping to get word of just what precisely was going on with their prodigal teammate. He couldn’t reprimand them for it, either, because he was doing the same. Each time, he was faced with an utter lack of notifications, and the queasy feeling in his stomach got worse.

“Anything?” he heard Hen ask Eddie, who had his phone out again. They’d put the fire out and shut off the hoses, or at least Bobby thought they had. There was standing water in the street, too much to not be coming from an unsecured hydrant somewhere.

“No, just a text and a picture from Shannon,” Eddie answered, tilting his screen so Hen could see. “Nothing from Buck.”

“Hey, did someone leave a hydrant open?” Bobby asked. An alert rang on Eddie’s phone, and he heard Hen heave a sharp gasp and cover her mouth.

“No, no, no. Dios, no. Por favor, Dios, no,” Eddie was saying, frantically calling someone and cursing as they didn’t answer.

“What is it?” Chimney asked, rushing over. “What’s going on?”

“A tsunami hit the Santa Monica Pier,” Hen said, meeting their horrified stares as Eddie tried calling whoever it was he was trying to reach again. “Shannon was there with Chris.”

Shannon didn’t truly know her ex-husband’s coworkers too well. Outside of Eddie’s shield ceremony, she hadn’t truthfully interacted with them much. She felt like she knew Buck, though. Eddie spoke of him often and fondly, as did Chris. It was a fact that caused more than a little bit of jealousy, like she had been replaced in both their hearts. But then, she didn’t really have anyone to blame but herself, did she? She was the one who had left in the darkest hours before dawn, after all, and then didn’t look back.

Meeting the man in person, seeing him interacting with her son and husband in person, had cemented that feeling. Her son still loved her, and she knew he always would. But there was now a third person who had hung the stars in his sky, and seeing the two of them together had hurt. Seeing the way Eddie had watched them together, eyes full of adoration, was simply a twist of the knife.

The realization that he had begun to move on from her, even if he hadn’t realized it yet, was one of the reasons she had decided for a divorce. She hadn’t told Eddie that, of course. She had given him different but equally true reasons at their soured dinner date. Their marriage hadn’t been working long before she left them, long before he left her, and perhaps never had been. It was just Christopher binding them together, and the sense of obligation and duty impressed upon them by Eddie’s parents.

Their marriage had been dead, perhaps, long before either of them left the state of Texas.

Shannon didn’t think Buck liked her much, or at least, she got that impression from him the handful of times they talked. But he had stood up to her former in-laws, defending Eddie and her both from them, and then handed them a way to forever ward off their attempts to take Chris. When Eddie had mentioned a month before that Buck had suggested a custody agreement, she had been ready to gouge the man’s eyes out. That it turned out to be a way to protect her parental rights, just as much as it was to protect Eddie’s, was sufficient to appease her. Even if that hadn’t been the man’s intentions.

And the man tended to pop up at the most random of times in the most random of places. First, the day after she asked for the divorce. She had been a bit snappish with him when he asked how her dinner with Eddie had gone, she could admit that. But who wouldn’t be, when faced with their future replacement?
