Luckily - and she felt bad for thinking it - the car crash had interrupted things before she could really embarrass herself.

(She hadn’t been wrong, though. Buck did love her ex-husband, and her ex-husband loved him in return, even if they were both too damn stupid to see or realize it.)

Now here the man was again, this time to interrupt her mother-son day at the pier.

“There you are,” he said, running up to them. Relief was evident in his voice, and Shannon got the impression from the way he was breathing that he’d been running the entire length of the pier.

“Buck!” Chris cheered, stumbling over to hug him at the waist.

“Buck, what are you doing here?” Shannon asked. “I thought you were working today.”

“I was supposed to, but-” Buck cut himself off, bending down to scoop up Chris. “We don’t have time, we need to go.”

“Go? Go where?” she asked.

“There’s no time,” he said, and he kept glancing at the ocean behind her. “We have to go. Now.”

He grabbed her by the wrist, grip tight enough that she knew it was going to leave bruises, and almost dragged her along behind him as he started to run. She tried to tug her wrist free, tried to ask him what was going on, but he wasn’t answering. It was frightening, and she was about to start screaming for help, when other people started screaming and running. The sight that greeted her when she craned her neck to look back would haunt her dreams for years to come. 

The entire ocean, rising up to crush them all.

They reached a firetruck, left there as its firefighters and paramedics attended to the mascot she and Chris had passed earlier, and she watched as Buck gently pushed her son through the open window. Then, with barely a care for her comfort, he grabbed her around the waist and shoved her in as well. She barely managed to contort and twist herself to avoid landing on Chris.

And then the wave hit.

Eddie had been looking forward to this day for what felt like ages. He was finally going to his best friend, his partner, at his side again. After months and months of working without him, things were finally going to be as they should have been. There wouldn’t be any more strangers trying to fill that gap at his side, their wrong presence rubbing at him like too-tight shoes.

He had been looking forward to this day.

And then Buck called in.

He didn’t call in sick, or injured, he just called in. With no reason beyond that something had come up. He hadn’t even mentioned anything to Eddie, leaving him to learn it second hand. Which stung far more than he wanted to admit. And then he wouldn’t answer his phone, when he always answered if Eddie called or texted, and so there had to be something wrong.

But sadly, whatever was going on with Buck wasn’t the most immediately pressing of concerns. Because a tsunami had hit the Santa Monica pier. And Eddie learned this while looking at a text from Shannon, saying she had taken Chris there for the day.

Eddie was trying to have hope, was trying to not fall into despair every time he tried his ex-wife’s phone and was immediately sent to voicemail. It would have been easier, if Buck had been there with him, and he tried not to be angry with him for his absence. It didn’t help that he still wasn’t answering, either.

Bobby had attempted to bench him, when he realized what was going on. Eddie had nearly punched him for it, and probably would have if Hen and Chimney hadn’t worked together to separate the two. It was Hen who convinced Bobby that keeping him away wouldn’t work, that he would just go running into the disaster zone anyways, and wouldn’t it be better to have him close by? After all, they would need the extra pair of hands in a situation like this.

Eddie was trying to have hope, but it was waning as the hours went by. They went into the wreckage, keeping an eye out for Shannon and Chris, only finding destruction and a fellow firefighter named Lena Bosko of the 136. As time passed with no sign of them, he retreated further into himself, grunting or nodding when Bosko asked him something or when Bobby gave him an order.

Eventually, Bobby used Bosko’s injured ribs as an excuse to leave them both at the VA hospital, where they’d set up an emergency triage center. Eddie hadn’t fought against it, had run out of the energy to fight against anything sometime after the sun had set. He followed Bosko into the make-shift field hospital, intending to force her into getting checked out before searching through the patients in the hope he’d find his ex-wife and son, when a voice called to him.

“Eds! Over here!”

He turned, and found Buck sitting in one of the cots, looking battered and bloodied and bruised, hooked up to an IV. Christopher was in his lap, head tucked under his chin as he slept, and Shannon was in a chair beside him. Physically, he had to have crossed the space between him and them, but he didn’t remember doing it. One moment he was beside Bosko, the next he was across the room, pulling Chris into his arms.

“Gracias a Dios,” he whispered. “Gracias a Dios.”

“Daddy?” Chris mumbled, reaching up to rub the sleep from his eye.

“I’m here, buddy,” Eddie said. “You’re okay?”

“Mostly,” Shannon told him, patting Buck on the leg. “This one got a bit beaten up, though.”

“I’m fine,” Buck protested.

“So fine, they’re doing a transfusion?” Eddie asked, checking the lines while he held Chris close to his chest.  “And giving you antibiotics.”

“It’s a precaution.”

“Buck, you took a piece of the pier to the back while on blood thinners,” Shannon said, rolling her eyes.

“It was just a scratch.”

“But besides that? You’re all okay?” Eddie asked, starting to check them over himself. It was difficult to do one-handed, but he wasn’t about to set Chris down yet.

“We’re all fine,’’ Shannon reassured him, and he felt the weight fall off his shoulders as that reality sunk in.

“Good, good, that’s- I need to tell everyone else,” he said, reaching for his radio. “Hey, Cap?”

“Eddie?”

“I found them. They’re at the field hospital. With Buck.”

“With Buck?” Bobby’s voice had an odd tone to it, though it was hard to figure out what the tone was over the radio. “I’m on my way.”

“Well, I’m not going anywhere,” Buck said, though he didn’t sound overly excited by the fact.

Bobby was worried about Buck, and so Athena was worried in turn. They hadn’t started off on the right foot, but he and his sister had both grown on her. According to her husband, he had called in on the morning of what was supposed to be his first day back to work, with no reason given beyond that something had come up and that he promised to explain later. And then, for some reason, he had wound up at ground zero of a natural disaster. Where he then, apparently, managed to save Christopher and Shannon and a dozen others.

The promised explanation had been delayed, because when she and Bobby arrived at the field hospital - her covered in Captain Cooper’s blood - it was to find him looking worryingly pale. Instead, they had allowed him to slip away to his apartment, where he could lick his wounds in peace. Wounds he received by somehow being at the right place at the right time to save people, when he was supposed to be miles away.

Bobby didn’t know what to do, and he told her as such.

“Well, we’re all off today,” Athena had said. “And he’s had time to sleep. Let’s go get that explanation he promised you.”

It turned out that visiting Buck that day hadn’t been an original idea.

“Eddie, you’re not with Chris?” Athena asked when they joined him in front of Buck’s door.

“Abuela’s mother-henning him,” he explained. “What are you two doing here?”

“To talk to Buck,” Bobby said. “And you?”

“To talk to Buck,” Eddie echoed. He flipped through his keys, pulling out a pink leopard-printed one that Athena raised her eyebrows at and unlocked the door.

“Hey, Eds,” Buck greeted from the kitchen area, looking only moderately less pale than he did the night before. He glanced up from the coffee he was pouring and sighed when he saw Eddie wasn’t alone. “So… Is this another intervention?”

“Buck,” Bobby said. “You’d said you would explain.”

“Now?”

“Now.”

Buck sighed again and limped for his recliner, sinking into it. The limp was worrying, but not surprising.

“Fine, but you’re not going to believe me,” he told them.

“Try us,” Athena said, sitting down on the couch. Bobby sat next to her, while Eddie remained standing.

“I want to start by saying that I’m not crazy…”

The Echo in My Words

“I want to start by saying that I’m not crazy,” Buck said. He wasn’t looking at them, keeping his eyes focused on the cup of coffee in his hands, twisting it about between his palms. He wanted to be up and pacing, but his leg was vehemently against the idea of that after the day it had. “I know you’re going to think that I am, I know that it’s going to sound like I am, and I have no idea how to convince you otherwise. But I am not crazy.”

“None of us are going to think you’re crazy,” Bobby said, and he just managed to resist snorting at that.

“Don’t make promises you can’t keep, Cap,” he said. “I don’t know where to start, so I guess I’ll just… Start. I’ve lived through the tsunami three times now. Not a tsunami, that tsunami. The first time, they didn’t catch the blood clots early enough and I had an embolism at the party. They kept me from coming back to work, and I wasn’t doing well with that, so I went to the pier with- I was at the pier, when the wave hit. And then there was yesterday, when I knew Shannon and Chris were at the pier, and I knew…”

“How did you know they were at the pier?” Eddie asked. “It was a surprise.”

“I just did,” Buck answered, resolutely not looking up at him.

“What about the third time?” Athena asked, catching on before the other two. “You said you lived through the tsunami three times, but you only mentioned two. What about the third?”

“Yesterday was the third.”

“Okay, then the second-”

“I’m not going to talk about the second,” Buck snapped. The sight of an unbreathing Christopher beneath a white sheet, the sound of Eddie’s pained wail, none of that was ever going to leave his memory. But he was not ever going to talk about it if he could avoid it. “You’re not here to talk about the tsunami, though. Not really. You want to know why I called in yesterday and why I was at the pier, and I’m telling you: it’s because I’ve lived through it before and knew it was coming and knew Chris and Shannon were in danger.”

“How, though?” Bobby asked. “You say you lived through it before, but how is that possible, Buck?”

“I was… I was really, really lost, one Christmas,” he said. “It felt like everyone was leaving, and I was terrified of ending up alone again, so I ran away. I got into my jeep and I drove and I drove until I didn’t know where I was anymore, until the jeep died in the middle of nowhere. There was a crossroads, and a stranger standing in the middle, and he- He asked me what I wanted.”

“And then?” Athena prompted.

“And then I woke up on the morning of my first day as a probie,” Buck said, shrugging.

“So you believe you’ve been living the last two or so years of your life over again?” Bobby asked.

“I believe-? No, Bobby, I-” He finally looked up from his coffee in time to see the captain and his wife exchange loaded glances. “You do think I’m crazy.”

“We didn’t say that,” the officer said. The tone of her voice said otherwise, like she was trying to keep some stray dog calm while she called animal control. “It’s just that we’re having trouble understanding parts of it.” 

“The truck bombing,” Bobby pointed at his leg. “Did that not happen the first time?”

“No, it, uh. It did.”

“So you let yourself be crushed by the truck?” the captain asked, incredulity lacing his words.

“No, I didn’t let- I mean, I did, but…” Buck chewed on his lip, knowing this wasn’t helping his case any. “It had to happen. It was better that it happened.”

“It had to happen.” Bobby’s eyebrow rose to join his hairline.

“Yeah, uh. My leg was going to get hurt anyways, and… And you weren’t going to get your job back, otherwise.” He watched as Bobby and Athena exchanged glances again, and his temper got the best of him. “If you think I’m crazy, just fucking saying it.”

“We don’t think you’re crazy,” Bobby said, clearly trying for reassuring but only coming across as patronizing. “But I am… Concerned.”

“Concerned,” Buck echoed.

Bobby sighed and stood, crossing the small space to place a hand on his shoulder.

“It has been a stressful summer,” he said. “I think, perhaps…”

“Perhaps what? Fucking say it, Bobby.”

“Buck, there’s no need for that,” Athena told him, crossing her arms and giving him a disapproving scowl.

“Perhaps it would be best for you to wait before coming back,” Bobby said, and Buck’s heart dropped. “Maybe go for a few more counseling sessions? The trauma you’ve gone through in just a few short months, anyone would have trouble with it. And you weren’t well, even before the bombing.”

“You want me to wait.”

“Just a bit longer, Buck.”

“Or what?”

“Or I go to the chief with my concerns,” he said.

“I don’t know which is worse,” Buck said, sneering up at his captain. “That you think I’m crazy but refuse to just say it, or that you’re trying to use it as an excuse to keep me from coming back after you couldn’t use the blood thinners.”

“No one is keeping you from coming back,” Athena said. “And you’re the only one using the word crazy.”

“Because you both keep pussyfooting around it!” he shouted at her.

“Buck-”

“I want you to get out, please,” he said. “Now. If you’re going to keep being patronizing, then go.”

“Okay, if that’s what you want,” Bobby said, stepping back. “But we’ll talk to you about the counseling later, when emotions aren’t running so high.”

“You mean when I’m not acting crazy,” he scoffed. “I’m not doing any more counseling, Cap. I’ve already been cleared to come back by a department therapist. They didn’t think I was too traumatized to work.”

“He’s right,” Eddie said, speaking up for the first time since he asked how Buck knew Chris and Shannon were at the pier. “He’s cleared to come back. Whatever he believes, it wasn’t enough for them to think he was too unstable to return.”

“I’ll see you bright and early, Wednesday morning,” Buck said, watching Bobby and Athena head for the exit. The captain looked like he wanted to say something, but he was evidently going with the better part of valor. He wasn’t certain if Bobby really would go to the chief, and he didn’t know what would happen if he did. It was a nuclear bomb, and he didn’t think the captain was willing to deal with the fallout that would ensue if he dropped it. He didn’t think, but there was that uncertainty that had always plagued him.

When Bobby and Athena were almost out the door, he blurted out,

“Michael’s going to be diagnosed with cancer just before Christmas. If you don’t believe me now, you will then.”

“We’ll keep that in mind,” Athena promised, and closed the door behind her.

“Do you think I’m crazy?” Buck asked Eddie in the silence that followed, leaning forward with his elbows on his knees.

“I think you sounded crazy,” he said, coming over to sit on the coffee table in front of  him. “But I also don’t care.”

“You don’t care?”

“Not one bit,” Eddie said, reaching to grab onto his shoulder. “Do you want to know why?”

“Always.”

“Because if you hadn’t been there, my son would be dead,” he said, looking him in the eye. “I know that beyond a shadow of a doubt. I knew he was dead the moment I got that alert on my phone, and in that moment I was dead. But Chris isn’t dead, and neither is Shannon, because you were there to save them. Whether you were there because you’re psychic, or because you lived through it before, or because the ghost of Elvis came down from Mars and told you to be there,” Buck let out a wet laugh. “It doesn’t matter. Because either way, my son is alive because of you.”

“Of course I was there, I couldn’t- I’d do anything for that kid, you know that.”

“I do,” Eddie confirmed, resting his forehead on Buck’s.

“And uh, thanks. For being here with me, for helping with Bobby.”

“I didn’t help much,” he said. “But of course. You have my back, I have yours-”

He cut off suddenly, jerking his head back to stare at him, eyes wide.

“What?” Buck asked, worried. “What is it?”

“Nothing,” Eddie said, shaking his head. “It’s nothing. Hurry up and get your shoes on.”

“Why?” He stood, gingerly putting weight on his very sore leg. Running up and down the pier looking for Chris and Shannon hadn’t been kind to it, nor was all the debris banging against it as he hung off the side of the firetruck, or the fact that instead of stretching it out and massaging it before bed, he had crashed into sleep almost as soon as he got to the apartment. It meant he had woken up with it stiff and aching.

“You’re coming home with me. Abuela is motherhenning Chris and Shannon, but she wants to motherhen you, too. You got hurt saving her favorite bisnieto, after all.”

“If it means I can get some of her cooking, then I’m game.”

As Eddie watched his Abuela harass his best friend over his pronunciation of Spanish words in between plates of her food that she kept forcing upon him, with Chris laughing gleefully and Shannon watching on in amusement, he couldn’t help but dwell on the realization he had made. Or, the realization he thought he’d made. He’d been unwilling to ask, unwilling to learn if it was the actual truth of things.

“You have my back, I have yours,” he had said, and as those words left his mouth, he remembered when Buck had said something so very similar in vastly different circumstances. Perhaps it was the discussion that had preceded it, his assertion that he had lived through these years before, that he had somehow traveled backwards in time.

“You have his back, he has yours,” Buck had told Lola, that day he was trying to talk her down from the overpass, before her husband arrived. The day he had told her about the man who had left him on Christmas, because his kid was scared. The day he had told her how he realized he was going to be alone again, just like before, just like always.

Buck had been talking about him, he knew that now. He’d been talking about him and Chris. But Eddie didn’t know what to do with that information. He didn’t even have all the information he needed, because for all that Buck had sounded and described being hurt in his monologue to Lola, it had been so very light on actual details.

Why had Eddie left?

Or, why was he going to leave?

Belief in Hindsight

Just like he promised Bobby, Buck walked into the station on Wednesday, bright and early. He had spent the night before with the Diazes, sleeping on the couch before being woken up with Eddie by Christopher screaming in his sleep. He hadn’t been there the first time, to help with the boy’s nightmares, something he regretted and now had the chance to make up for it. It meant that he and Eddie had carpooled to work, and so the man was right behind him as he climbed the loft stairs to the station’s kitchen, desperate for coffee.

Bobby was already there, standing at the stove as he made breakfast.

“Cap,” he greeted as he went to the cabinet to fetch mugs for himself and Eddie.

“Buck.” The captain lowered the heat on the burners and turned to face them. He looked conflicted, and Buck knew this was going to be an awkward morning, and probably an awkward shift. Eddie was at his back, though, and he was so very thankful for that.

“I didn’t get any notice from the brass telling me I was benched until further notice, so I’m assuming you didn’t go to the chief.” He handed the mugs to Eddie, letting him get the coffee while he talked.

“No. No, I didn’t.”

“Does that mean that you believe me?” he asked. “Or does that just mean that you didn’t want to admit that you think I’m crazy?”

“I don’t know what to believe,” Bobby admitted. “And I don’t think you’re crazy, Buck. I just… I don’t know what to believe.”

“Is this really where you want to be having this conversation?” Eddie asked, handing Buck his coffee. The man had a point, they were in the middle of the open, literally waiting for the others to join them for breakfast.

“You’re right,” Bobby said, turning back to the food. “This isn’t the place, or the time.”

“Buckaroo!” Hen cried when she crested the top of the stairs, Chimney right behind her. She hugged him tightly, and Buck felt himself relaxing into her hold. “You had us worried when you called in.”

“Sorry, I didn’t mean to,” he said.

“You’re looking rough, still,” she said, checking him over. “But at least you’re not so pale.”

“Why were you at the pier?” Chimney asked.

“Because the ghost of Elvis came down and told me to be,” Buck answered, smiling when he caught Eddie rolling his eyes.

“Wait, really?”

“No, Chim.”

“So then, what?” the paramedic asked. “Did you have a premonition or something? Like on that one show, with the witches.”

“You mean Charmed?” The others all stared at him in varying degrees of surprise and incredulity.  “What? I had a bum leg, a Netflix account, and time to kill.”

“Breakfast is ready,” Bobby said. “And I have an announcement to make.”

They all paused in getting food to stare at him in anticipation.

“Well, don’t keep us waiting,” Hen said.

“Station One-Thirty-six was in the middle of the impact zone, so their crew is being temporarily reassigned while it gets fixed up,” the captain said. “So we’re going to have one or two of them joining us within the next week.”

And Buck had to hold in the groan, because that meant Bosko. Bosko, whom he never actually met outside of a couple moments. Bosko, who had dragged Eddie into the fight club mess, which could have cost him his career and Christopher. Bosko, the woman Bobby had replaced him with, however much he tried to play it off as anything but.

(Buck had never asked who taped over his name on the locker for his turnout gear, nor had he asked how many of the others had seen it and thought it perfectly okay. Some questions were just too painful to ask.)

The shift bounced between busy and slow. They would have periods where they’d leave a call only to respond to another right away, and then they had periods where they spent a solid two hours vegetating in front of the television. It was an array of labor-intensive calls, like a car’s engine bursting into flames while merging into another lane, and stupidly simple calls, like the one with the child stuck in the tree, and the awkwardly hilarious calls, like the one with the couple whose attempt at spicing up their bedroom life led to them being freed with bolt cutters.

It was during one of the Q-word periods, after Buck had lost a round of Mario Kart to Hen, that Bobby called him into his office.

Bobby didn’t know what to believe. He had always been a religious man, his faith a life raft in the stormy seas that followed the apartment fire. But he had always tried to be rational about it. Things happened for a reason, but God didn’t reach down and physically move the pieces. The world ran on logic. The full moon didn’t influence behavior, ghosts didn’t call 9-1-1, people weren’t psychic, and time travel wasn’t possible.

(Jinxes were definitely real, however, and the Q-word was one.)

But…

But Evan Buckley had always been oddly prescient during certain calls. Chimney had been calling him psychic for years, and Buck himself had always shot him down, saying that it was just good instincts or good hearing. Buck himself had never, ever claimed to be psychic, at least to Bobby’s knowledge. Which made sense, if he believed himself to be a time-traveler instead. Believed himself to be, because surely he couldn’t truly be? But then…

But then.

There were facts, so small and so easily overlooked, that were glaring at him in the face as he looked back. How Buck knew his way around the station even on that first day, how he would know what tools a call required before even Bobby was certain. The way that Buck would, at the beginning, say or hear something and then look beside him, as if expecting someone to be there to share the joke. The way Buck would do that same thing now, except with Eddie standing there to laugh with him.

(And Buck had seemed so excited and happy in the days leading up to Eddie joining them, as if he really had been expecting him.)

There were other facts, too. Facts that would worry him, if what Buck said was true. Facts like the way he used to flinch away from Chimney, if the paramedic was suddenly in his space or seemed even a bit upset. Not Bobby, not any of the other men in the station, only Chimney. What did that mean? Did he even want to know?

Bobby didn’t know what to believe.

But did that matter?

“So we’re having the conversation now?” Buck asked, closing the office door behind him.

“I didn’t want to keep putting it off,” he said.

“I didn’t lie to you, Cap,” Buck said. “I told you I’d explain, and I did. I didn’t lie to you.”

“I’m not calling you a liar. I’m also not calling you crazy.”

“So you do believe me, then?”

“I don’t know what to believe,” he repeated. “I truly don’t. Because if I believe your story, then…”

“Yeah, I- I get that, I really do,”  Buck said, rubbing at his arm.

“I meant it, though, when I said I was concerned,” Bobby told him, raising his hand and rushing to talk when he saw the younger man scowl and open his mouth. “I’m serious, Buck. Even without that, you’ve been… You weren’t well after Christmas. And ever since the bombing you’ve been angry. I can’t force you into more counseling, but I know more than anyone that being cleared to return isn’t the same as being okay.”

“What do you expect me to do, Bobby? I can’t exactly go to a therapist about this and have them take me seriously.”

“You need to talk to someone, though,” he urged. “Eddie, or me. Someone. Some of the things you said the other day, if they’re true-”

“If?”

“They worry me. The way you said your leg was going to be hurt anyway, like you knew it for a fact. The way you insisted it was better that the truck bombing happened. The way you knew Chris and Shannon were at the pier, and how you said you lived through the tsunami three times but refused to talk about one of them.”

“I don’t- Cap, please. I don’t want to talk about it, I really don’t. Please.”

“Fine,” Bobby sighed. “Then-”

The office door opened, interrupting what he was about to say. Eddie edged his way in, glancing around before settling his gaze on Buck.

“Is everything okay in here?” he asked, not even bothering to pretend like he was including Bobby in that question.

“We’re good,” Buck answered, smiling brightly at him, and dear Lord, they were both ridiculous. “We were just talking.”

“Just talking?”

“Yes, Eddie,” Bobby said. “We were just-”

The alarm rang, and he sighed.

“I guess we’re done talking,” he said, following them as they rushed out.

That Bitter Taste

The fire drill, as mandated by the city every three years, was supposed to be a surprise. Supposed to be, but that didn’t take into account people having lived through the exact drill before. Of course, he couldn’t just tell Bobby what day and at what time the drill was going to be, because it would defeat the entire purpose of the exercise. He could, however, make sure they avoided the stalled bus on Grant by taking a different route.

(Buck’s memory was far from eidetic, but just about everything from the tsunami through the lawsuit had been seared into his brain as he spent night after night going over ways he could have done things differently.)

“My God,” Chimney said as they all hopped out of the trucks in front of the office building. “That’s the biggest damn fire I’ve never seen.”

“I hate fire drills,” Hen complained as she and Eddie got the hoses attached to the hydrant.

“City mandates we do ‘em every three years,” Eddie said. “Can’t fight city hall.”

“Fire alarm was triggered at Twelve-Twenty, call came in thirty second later,” Bobby announced, looking at his watch and then to his tablet. Buck peered at it over his shoulder. “Boots down, hoses out by Twelve-Thirty-three.”

“Six minutes under the allotted response time.” And ten minutes better than the last time around. “Go team.”

“Get to work,” the captain ordered, rolling his eyes at him.

“C’mon, Eds,” Buck said. “We need to make sure there’s not a logjam at the stairwells. You get points docked if, say, someone takes a tumble and sends a whole crowd of people falling down the stairs.”

“Really now?” Eddie asked, following along after him.

“Yeah, I know I did when I was stuck playing fire marshal the first time around.” He was a few steps ahead before he realized Eddie had stopped. He turned, finding the other man looking at him with an odd expression. “What?”

“Nothing, it’s just… That’s the first time you’ve casually referred to something related to the thing without couching it as being psychic,” he explained, catching up to him.

“The thing?”

“Shut up, what do you want me to call it?” he asked. “When we’re in public, surrounded by strangers?”

Buck rolled his eyes.

“C’mon, stairwell.”

With the two of them taking control of the flow of traffic, they were able to get people out of the stairs and to the exits far quicker than they had been. This meant that when one of the office workers had a seizure after losing his sunglasses, there wasn’t an awful domino effect all the way to the bottom. Buck even managed to catch him before he hit the person in front of him, lowering him to the floor while he shouted for Hen.

So busy with the seizing man was Buck, that he didn’t take note of who had been behind him. Buck didn’t notice Chase Mackey was even there until the lawyer was hurrying past him, chasing after the paramedics as they rolled the seizure patient out. And when he did, he wasn’t sure if he wanted to run in the other direction or vomit then and there.

“Buck? What’s wrong?” Eddie asked, grabbing his shoulder.

“Nothing, Eds,” he said, shaking his head and resolutely deciding to pretend the lawyer didn’t exist. “C’mon, we should make sure everyone’s cleared out upstairs.”

The first time around, Buck never actually spent a shift with Lena Bosko. With being relegated to what was in essence a desk job (which would have actually made the blood clots worse, if he stuck with it) and then suing the city, he didn’t get back to work until she was back at the 136. The most time he actually spent with her had been at the rage room, when Bobby told him he was being reinstated. So actually working alongside her was an adjustment.

It didn’t help that he was still bitter at her, both for being his replacement and for getting his best friend into an illegal fight club. He was trying not to be, or at least he was trying not to show it, because Bosko hadn’t meant to replace him, nor had this version of her even suggested fighting to Eddie. At least, no one else had called him out for it, so he figured he was doing a good job on concealing, even if he was still having trouble with not feeling.

It did not help that she called him Diaz, and he answered to it, when he specifically said he wouldn’t.

To add to that was Maddie. Chimney had told him and Eddie about her reaction to breaking a plate, and there hadn’t been any good advice that Buck could give him. Trauma was difficult and confusing and required more patience than action. Even if she hadn’t still been annoyed with him for enforcing his boundaries  - though they were slowly getting past that - he knew she wouldn’t appreciate him trying to help.

And then there were Chris’ nightmares again, though they were thankfully not as bad as they had been Before. At least, he wasn’t dreaming about his mother drowning. It was still harrowing to wake up on Eddie’s couch to the sound of Chris’ cries. And it was frustrating to have the boy tell them that he was fine, when he was so very clearly not fine.

(Yes, Buck was very well aware of the hypocrisy. No, he was not taking suggestions at this time.)

Actually going on calls with Bosko was an adjustment. She served much the same role as Buck did, and so sometimes he couldn’t help but feel superfluous whenever Bobby would send her in instead of him. And the captain did it just often enough that Buck couldn’t help but feel it was almost on purpose. He knew that it (probably) wasn’t, but still. Like the car on the side of the cliff, with the mother and her two kids. Buck could have just as easily rappelled down there with Chimney, but instead, he was stuck up top. 

He tried not to let it show how much it bothered him, whenever this happened. She wasn’t replacing him. She was temporary and she would be returning to her station by the end of the month, he knew that. But her very presence just kept reminding him of when she had replaced him. When Buck saw the tape across the top of her temporary turnout locker, he remembered seeing his name taped over with hers. When Buck saw her with Eddie in the gym, offering advice to him about Christopher’s nightmares, he remembered when his best friend had gone to her instead of him, even before the lawsuit.

None of that was her fault, though. She hadn’t done anything to deserve the bitterness he felt towards her. So he mostly tried to avoid her, and tried his best to be friendly when he couldn’t. The others gave him odd looks sometimes, so he knew he wasn’t always being as subtle about it as he was trying. But they didn’t say anything, so clearly it wasn’t obvious enough to cause concern.

It was Bosko herself who finally confronted him, a day after Eddie called him complaining about a guy in a knee brace giving him trouble for parking in a handicap spot while dropping off Chris. A guy that he didn’t get arrested for assaulting, so Buck was counting it as a win. But she ambushed him while he was going at the punching bag, not really paying attention enough to make an exit before she was there.

“You’re punching this thing like it insulted your mother,” she said, putting out her hand to catch it as it swung back towards him.

“Bosko,” he said, putting on his best smile. “I thought you were with the others.”

“You don’t like me,” she said. “What’s your problem?”

You’re my problem, is what he wanted to say, but the parallel felt a bit too on the nose.

“I don’t have a problem,” he said instead.

“Yeah, no, you clearly do,” she refuted, letting go of the bag. “You are like, almost constantly angry. I’m pretty sure the others have noticed it.”

“I’m not constantly angry,” he protested.

“Sure, yeah, you’re not angry whenever Diaz smiles at you,” she said, sending Buck sputtering. “But you seem angry almost every time I see you.”

“Maybe it’s you,” he offered, going back to punching the bag.

“I thought you said you didn’t have a problem?” Bosko countered.

“If I told you it was me, not you, would you go away?”

“Nope,” she said, stepping back to watch him punch. He tried to ignore her, but her presence bothered him, and the longer she was there, the more he was bothered. Eventually, he punched the bag hard enough to send it swinging wildly, and she whistled in appreciation.

“Why are you here?” he asked, trying not to sound too biting, catching the bag with a grunt before it could hit him in the face.

“You are literally a powder keg,” Bosko told him.

“No one else thinks so.”

“They do,” she said. “They just don’t want to risk being the reason you blow.”

“But you don’t care?”

“Oh no, I care. I just think you’re going to blow either way, and the last thing anyone needs is Cap’s wife arresting you for punching some guy.”

“So, what then?” he asked, starting back on the bag again. “Are you going to suggest anger management, Ms. Touchy-Feely?”

Bosko shook her head.

“I know a place. It could be a healthy outlet, help you work things out.” Was she seriously…? “Punch people who want to be punched, before you-”

“No!” he snapped, loud enough that she blinked and jerked back in surprise. The quiet conversation in the loft above cut off.

“Hey, okay, it was just a suggestion,” she said, holding up her hands.

“A stupid suggestion,” he spat. “I’m not going to join a fight club, or whatever the hell your idea is.”

He glanced up to where Eddie and the others were looking down at them, all of them frowning in concern. Shaking his head at them, he turned and headed for the showers. Did he really seem that angry that often, for her to come to him with the offer instead of Eddie? He knew he had been snappish with people, a bit shorter with his temper, but surely that was reasonable? He was, after all, pretty much railroaded into letting the truck crush his leg again, an event that ensured Bobby got his job back, but which was also the reason Bobby tried to keep him from coming back.

Everyone had been worried, Buck knew, Bobby had said as much. He just hadn’t thought the problem was so bad, and so obvious, that Bosko saw him as prime fight club material. It gave him the same stomach twisting feeling he got as he watched Eddie pour beer after beer into his sink, those many months prior.

Standing in front of the door after knocking, Buck shifted from foot to foot. He wasn’t entirely certain that this was the right course, but it wasn’t like he had many other options available to him.

“Buck?” Athena sounded surprised to see him, when she opened the door.

“Hey ‘Thena,” he said, awkwardly waving. “Is, uh, is Bobby busy?”

“He’s cooking dinner, but come on in.”

“Thanks.” He followed her down the stairs  and to the kitchen, where she waved him on through.

“I’ll let you two talk about whatever it is you need to,” she said. “Holler when the food’s done, Bobby.”

“Yes ma’am,” her husband said, saluting with a spatula.  To Buck, he said, “You’re here late.”

“Yeah, I-” He stopped to swallow around the lump in his throat. “You, uh, you said you were concerned. About me.”

“Because I am.”

“I thought that it was just you being you, and Eddie being Eddie, but… Is everyone else?” he asked. “As worried about me as you?’

“Does this have anything to do with whatever happened between you and Lena earlier today?”

“A bit,” he admitted. “She called me a powder keg. She said you were all worried I might blow.”

Bobby sighed.

“I told you, that you’ve seemed angry since the bombing,” he said. 

“Because I have been,” Buck admitted, almost at a whisper. “I have been so angry at, I don't know. Everything. Everyone. And I’ve been trying not to be, because it’s not even you guys I’m angry at, not really. But I’m still angry, and I couldn’t even tell anyone why I was angry, and… Is the offer still open, to talk? About the, uh. The thing?”

“Always,” Bobby promised. “But are you sure you want to talk to me about it? What about Eddie?”

“I- I can’t,” he said. “Not about- I can’t.”

How could he tell Eddie that he was only here because even the mere possibility of him leaving had frightened him so? How could he tell Eddie of all the times he utterly failed to have his back? How could he tell Eddie that one day, his son might be so frightened for him that he'll see no other alternative but to quit his job?

He couldn’t.

“Alright,” the captain said. ‘Then we’ll talk after dinner.”

“Uh, okay, then I’ll-”

“You’ll stay right here and help,” Bobby said, gently pulling him to stand beside him at the stove. “I need my sous chef.”

Little Talks

When most people think about depression, they imagine someone being sad. They imagine dark rooms, self-isolation, lethargy. Depression was, typically, associated with “negative” symptoms, things that are taken away from the one suffering. A lack or a loss of something. A lack of interest in what used to bring joy, a lack of motivation to carry out daily tasks, a lack of happiness. A loss of sleep, a loss of appetite, a loss of energy.

Depression, in actuality, could also be expressed in “positive” symptoms, symptoms that exist that wouldn’t typically be seen in normal conditions. Eating more, for instance, or sleeping more. An unhealthy fixation on sex. Increased anxiety and restlessness. An increase in reckless behavior, engaging in actions with little to no care about their own well-being. A dependency on drugs or alcohol.

Depression could express itself in irritability, in agitation. The person’s tolerance is lower, their temper is shorter. Everything and anything can get on their nerves.

Sometimes, depression was anger.

And a lot of times, the best way to deal with anger was to simply talk about it.

“I don’t actually know where to start,” Buck said. “And I don’t know how much I want to tell you, or how much I can tell you.”

After dinner, after he helped Athena wash the dishes, he and Bobby sat back down at the dining table while she busied herself elsewhere. As far as he knew, Athena still thought he was crazy, or was heavily leaning that way, so he wasn’t certain what it meant that she was excusing herself from this conversation. Maybe she was just giving them the privacy to talk, since he had mentioned Bobby specifically.

“You can start at the beginning,” Bobby offered.

“I’m living in a Moebius strip, cap,” he said. “Where the hell is the beginning?”

“Okay, then how about you tell me what your problem with Lena is?” the captain asked.

“That’s just it, I shouldn’t have a problem with her. Not this version of her, at least. And I know it isn’t logical, and that she doesn’t deserve me being angry with her, but it isn’t helping me not to be.”

“Tell me anyway.”

“You replaced me with her,” Buck said. “The, uh. The other you, I mean.”

“Why the hell would I do that?” Bobby asked, screwing his face up in confusion.

“I don’t know, you- He- You kept saying that it wasn’t the case, but I mean. I walked into the station one day with her using my turnout gear locker and my name taped over, so…” He shrugged. “She also dragged Eddie into a fight club, so that was a thing.”

“I’m sorry,” Bobby interrupted, leaning in. “She what?”

“Yeah, I don’t know how things went, exactly, but he was angry about a lot of things. Like, he got arrested for punching a guy and she bailed him out. I guess she thought it would be a healthier way for him to vent, because apparently she isn’t a fan of traditional therapy, but he got deep into it.”

“How deep?’

“He punched a guy’s nose hard enough they choked on part of it, and was earning enough money off fights to buy a new truck,” Buck said. “But I managed to fix things so that won’t happen.”

“You’re certain?” Bobby asked, concern bringing out the lines on his forehead.

“Well, I’m not suing you and the department this time around, so…” He trailed off when he saw the blank stare on his captain’s face. “That was a, uh. That was a thing. That I’m not proud of.”

“Why?”

“Because you - that you - were keeping me from coming back to work, and I’d had that ambulance chaser talking in my ear,” Buck explained. “I really should have gone to the union, instead. Or, I don’t know, sucked it up and moved on.”

“If things after that bank heist went the same for him as it did for me, then it’s probably a good thing for him that you didn’t,” Bobby said, leaning back into his seat. “The only reason I was reinstated was because - in Chimney’s words - I was a hero on the six o’clock news. If you went to the union with an accusation that I was unfairly blocking your return to work, and they found it credible, I would have been out.”

“Yeah I uh, I already figured out the truck bombing was what led to them reinstating you.”

“You did mention it was better that it happened,” Bobby said, referencing their talk at Buck’s apartment, after the tsunami. “You never explained how you knew that.”

“Because I- I found the bomb on the truck, the second time. And the third. And a lot of times after,” he said, chewing on his lip as he remembered. “And each time, I’d find out that they fired you instead of giving you your job back.”

“Okay, I’m confused. How many times have you relived the past couple of years?”

“Most of it, only twice. Some of it, more than.” Buck looked down at the table. “After I stopped the bombing, I kept- My leg kept getting hurt, and- Well, I kept getting a redo for parts of it, until I let the bombing happen and let my leg get crushed.”

He couldn’t bring himself to tell Bobby that he got the redos by dying. He wasn’t sure what the captain would do if he heard that, if it would tip things back into fearing for his mental health instead of being willing to listen.

“Well, that explains part of the anger, at least. Actually, knowing you were forced to relive the truck bombing, and that you were already expecting to have to fight me for your return, explains a lot of the anger,” Bobby noted. “What else is different between this time around and the- Your original time?”

“A lot, but also not?” Buck shrugged. “I didn’t inflict Buck One-point-Oh on all of you this time.”

“Buck One-point… What?”

“Buck One-point-Oh,” he repeated. “And then Buck Two-point-Oh, and Three-point-Oh. It was how I put things behind me, when I decided to change. Eddie called it a software update, once.”

“Okay, so what was so bad about the original release?”

“He stole the firetruck for a hook-up,” he answered, looking anywhere but his captain’s eyes.

“What!?” Bobby looked close to bursting out laughing.

“I grew up, okay? I only did it the once,” he said. “Buck One-point-oh also couldn’t cook, or tie a tie. You, uh. You were the one who taught me, actually.”

“To cook or to tie a tie?”

“Both,” Buck said. “You helped me get ready for my first actual date. I changed that, this time. We didn’t- We haven’t had that moment, and I don’t know how I feel about that.”

“Well, maybe I can help you get ready for your next one,” the other man offered. 

“Yeah, uh. I’d like that,” he said, the words sounding lame to his ears. There wasn’t going to be another date, not with the way his heart was set on someone he couldn’t have.

“Speaking of Eddie-”

“Wait, what?”

“You didn’t really give a clear answer on why you’re not telling him any of this,” Bobby said, ignoring his confused sputtering. “He seemed to believe you far more readily than I did. Why me, and not him?”

“Because, it’s- I dunno, more difficult with him? I promised to have his back, and I ended up failing him in so many ways, Cap.”

“I doubt that.”

“But I did,” Buck protested. “Not that it really matters, I guess. I just don’t see the point in telling him about things that will hurt if they’re not going to happen, y'know?”

“Because they still happened to you,” his captain countered. “Because they’re still hurting you. But you don’t have to tell him everything, just like I know you’re not going to tell me everything.”

“I’ll think about it, okay?” Buck promised.

“I guess that’s the best I can ask,” Bobby sighed. “For now, I want to hear more about this date I helped get you ready for.”

“Okay,” Buck chuckled. “Uh, remember Abby, my dispatcher friend? Well…”

Talking with Bobby didn’t magically take the anger away, but it did help. During downtimes at the station, the captain would find excuses to keep Buck busy so he didn’t have to interact with Bosko as much. Usually this translated into helping in the kitchen, though sometimes it also involved inventing a chore for him to do, usually inventory. This meant that this version of his family quickly learned to dread the sight of him with a clipboard in hand, much as the other version had. 

All of it helped, and he had never been more thankful for his captain, except for all the other times he had reason to be thankful for the man. None of that meant he was magically anger free, though. The anger was just no longer quite so constant, now that he finally had someone to confide in, even if he couldn't confide fully.

It had him actually considering his promise to Bobby.

He finally relented after their team outing to the rage room, this time joined by Eddie. There was just something cathartic about smashing things to bits with a sledgehammer, and for once he wasn’t on the verge of biting Bosko’s head off. They actually ended up laughing together at some stupid joke he said, much to the obvious relief of the others

Afterwards, he followed Eddie to the Diaz home, and was both disappointed and relieved when he remembered that Chris was with his mom for the weekend. He stood there, watching Eddie putter around picking up, before he blurted out the first thing he thought of.

“I hated you, the first time I met you.”

Eddie turned and scowled at him in confusion, one of Chris’ action figures held loosely in his hand.

“¿Qué?”

“The other you, I mean,” he continued, leaning against the back of the couch. “It took me months before I truly felt comfortable at the station, before the others even really liked me. Then you came in, with Cap already telling us how wonderful you were, and everyone wanted to be friends with you right away. I was such a brat, because I was certain that I was going to be pushed out and replaced with you. It’s why I was getting so angry around Bosko, actually. Because she did replace me, even if only for a little bit.”

“So, what changed?” Eddie asked, tossing the toy onto the coffee table.

“We got a live grenade out of a dude’s leg together,” Buck said. “And you, I don’t know. You saw me, I guess. No one had ever actually looked and seen me, before. Not even Maddie. We dug a live grenade out of that guy’s leg, and you’ve been my best friend ever since.”

“Hold on,” Eddie said, holding up a finger. “I just realized. You knew that grenade was live the entire time, even before you and Bobby took him out of that house.”

Buck’s shrug was sheepish.

“I wanted my best friend back,” he said. “I woke up on the morning of my first day as a probie, and I was certain it had all just been some crazy, realistic dream. And then I got to the station, and Bobby and Chimney and Hen were there, and I had to accept that it wasn’t. But I also had to accept that I was alone.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, my family was there, but they weren’t my family. They didn’t know me, and they weren’t the people I knew, not yet. And Maddie was still with Doug, and you and Chris were still in Texas. I ran away that Christmas because it felt like everyone was leaving and I was terrified that it meant I was going to end up alone, and because of that I did end up alone. And I hate myself for it.”

Eddie frowned at him and stepped forward to guide him around the couch, softly pushing him to sit, taking the spot next to him.

“You said that the stranger at the crossroads-”

“Ichabod,” Buck interrupted. “He said his name was Ichabod.”

“Okay, Ichabod then. You said Ichabod asked you what you wanted. What did you tell him?”

“That I wanted to fix whatever broke everyone,” he said. “Whatever it was that caused everyone to splinter apart.”

“Then it doesn’t sound like you really chose to end up back here.”

“I chose to run away, though,” he argued. “I panicked and I ran away, and that was my choice. I don’t know how this whole thing works, if that time even still exists, but I know that I left them. I abandoned them.”

“Buck, you first instinct upon meeting a demon-”

“He’s not a demon,” Buck corrected. “He’s really insistent on that.”

“Whatever the fuck he is, your first instinct was to ask for a way to help everyone else. And you have. I mean, Shannon’s still alive, isn’t she?”

Buck twisted his head around to stare wide-eyed at him.

“Don’t give me that look,” Eddie told him, shoving at his face. “I’m not an idiot, Buck. You just happen to be at the scene of a traffic accident with a car that drove through pedestrians, on your day off, at the same time as her? It might not have been obvious then, but it’s pretty damn glaring in hindsight.”

“You loved her, and Chris loved her,” Buck said, shrugging. “I couldn’t just not do anything, not if I could help. I still ran away, though.”

“Join the club, then,” Eddie said, jostling him with his shoulder. “You, me, and Shannon. We’ll hold elections for president later.”

“And Chris.”

“Chris has never run away, though,” he pointed out.

“Yet. He hasn’t run away, yet,” Buck countered. “On a related note, make sure he can’t use your phone to order an uber.”

“Ay Dios. Do I even want to know?”

“Probably not,” he answered, grinning at him. “But I’m going to tell you anyway, because I get to make fun of you.”

He watched Eddie roll his eyes, but he was smiling too. And Lena had been right, the other day, because the anger and frustration really did go away whenever Eddie smiled at him.

Proceed With Caw-tion

Bosko returned to the refurbished 136 just before Halloween, and Buck wasn’t exactly sad to see her go. Her mere presence wasn’t quite so intolerable as it had been, but she was still a reminder of one of his biggest regrets. He did manage to get along with her, on her last couple of shifts. They wouldn’t ever actually be friends though.

A couple days before Halloween, they were called out to a pumpkin farm. One of those that seemed to make most of their business in the fall, with the seasonal set-ups. They arrived to find a field trip worth of children holed up in their school bus, their teacher only willing to crack the doors open just enough to talk to them.

“Two of my students, they were attacked by crows,” she said. “They’re trapped in there.”

She pointed at a large red barn, surrounded by a murder of crows.

“I think I’ve seen this movie,” Chimney quipped.

Under Bobby’s orders, they got into their full turnout gear, the better to protect themselves from being murdered by the murder. They were edging towards the barn with a gurney when Chimney’s nametag fell to the ground.

“Damn clasp,” he cursed, bending down to pick it up.

“It’s fine Chim, forget the nametag,” Hen told him. “We all know who you are.”

“Yeah, Albert,” Buck quipped, biting his cheek to keep from smiling when the Chimney swung around and gave him a look.

“This is weird,” Eddie remarked. “You see crows all over the city. Never heard of them attacking anybody.”

“That’s because-” Buck and Hen started at the same time, stopping to stare at each other.

“After you,” Buck said, complete with a mock bow. She rolled her eyes at his antics.

“That’s because crows are very docile,” Hen continued. “They don’t attack unless provoked. No sudden movements, and we should be good. And why are you smiling at me like that?”

“Because now you can never make fun of me again for spouting off random facts,” Buck said. “Did you know crows hold funerals? They’re very social and family oriented-”

“Damn it.” He turned to see that Chimney had lost his nametag again. He started to bend down to pick it up again when a crow landing nearby caused him to freeze.

“Just leave it, Chim,” Bobby ordered.

“Copy that.”

“Everybody stay calm.”

“Eh, we’re fine,” Buck said, finding endless amusement at his family’s minor freakout over the birds. “We’re not the ones they’re pissed at.”

They got to the barn and carefully opened the doors. The two boys were sitting inside, one seemingly unharmed - though Eddie and Buck went over to make sure - and the other a bloody mess. As the paramedics took care of the worst of his cuts, they managed to get out of the kids that the injured one had thrown rocks at the birds.

“And now you’ve learned why that was a dumb thing to do,” Buck said, earning a warning scowl from Bobby.

“Cap,” Chimney called out from where he was peering out the window. “They know we’re in here.”

“They know they’re in here,” Hen corrected him. “Crows are smart and they hold grudges.”

“You think they’re waiting for these boys to come out,” Bobby concluded.

“They’ve been known to remember the faces of their tormentors years later and still attack.”

“And!” Buck interjected, unwilling to be out-done. “They’ve even been known to tell all their crow friends about them so that they attack, too.”

This fact clearly did nothing to settle the kids’ nerves.

“Oh, they’re bye-crows, great,” Chimney said, and Buck stared at him.

“The hell is a-?”

“How do we get these guys past them?” Eddie asked, interrupting him.

“They’re looking for two kids,” Hen said.

They eventually decided on wrapping the injured kid in enough gauze to make him almost unrecognizable, nearly mummifying him. The other kid was decked out in Bobby’s too-big turnout coat and helmet, which would have been the most adorable thing Buck had ever seen, if he was living a life deprived of Christopher and Jee-Yun.

“What happens if they fly over here?” Chimney asked as they slowly escorted the kids to the ambulance.

“Well, if you make eye contact with a crow, it could change its behavior,” Hen said.

“For better or worse?” Eddie asked.

“Unclear.”

“They won’t attack if you make eye contact,” Buck said, feeling stupidly smug. Eddie could clearly tell, because he rolled his eyes. “They’re not dumb, they know they’re more likely to get hurt if you see the attack coming.”

On cue, one of the birds landed in front of them, making eye contact with Chimney. They abandoned the nervous man to his staring contest with his new feathered friend, quickly taking the opportunity to get the kids into the safe metal box that was the ambulance. The paramedic rejoined them shortly after, and wouldn’t answer Buck when asked if he won or lost the contest.

On the day of Halloween, Buck brought in a few dozen cupcakes, to mark an occasion that was lost on everyone else. He hadn’t told Bobby or Eddie how the only ones to properly welcome him home had been Hen and Chimney, the former with a cake and the utter refusal to follow Bobby’s lead. Buck just didn’t see the point in telling either his captain or his best friend something he knew they’d feel needlessly guilty about. If it wasn’t fair to Bosko, blaming her for something the other version of her had done, then it wasn’t fair to them.

(He still wanted to celebrate the day that Eddie forgave him, even if no one else would know about it.)

“What’s the occasion?” Chimney asked when he grabbed one of the cupcakes.

“Is today not enough of one?” he asked.

“Okay, but why red velvet?” Eddie asked, reaching past him to grab one of his own.

“It bleeds when you cut it,” Buck answered, and something in his voice must have given the significance away, judging from the way Eddie looked at him. He ignored it. “I saved one at the apartment for Chris.”

“Great, more sugar,” he griped.

“Hey, at least it’ll be Shannon suffering for it tonight,” Buck said, grinning at him. “She’s gonna send you pictures of him in his outfit, right?”

“She’ll probably send them to you, too.”

“Good! He’s going to look adorable.”

A few hours later, it turned out that he didn’t need Shannon to send him any pictures. She showed up at the station as they were giving out candy, Christopher in tow. The little boy was dressed up as a pirate, complete with an eyepatch - which was pushed up - and a red bandana.

“Superman!” Buck cried, abandoning his station to grab him, swinging him up into his arms. “Have you found much treasure yet?”

“Yeah!” Chris answered, giggling.

“So much sugar,” Shannon said, ambling over. She was holding Chris’ candy bag, and it was bulging heavily.

“Aw, and you’ll have him all night,” Eddie said, joining them. “Darn.”

“Don’t worry, I’m sure he’ll still have plenty to eat tomorrow night,” she said, smiling cheerfully at him.

“Thanks,” Eddie drawled.

“Did you see any scary decorations?” Buck asked.

“There was a giant pumpkin,” Chris said.

“Was it a scary pumpkin?” he asked, and Chris giggled while shaking his head.

“There were a few decorations this year that were far too realistic,” Shannon told them. “I almost called you guys at one house, before I realized it was fake.”

“Yeah, some of them are ridiculous,” Eddie agreed, but Buck stopped paying attention. Because the lady with the dude in her windshield had completely slipped his mind, and now he needed to come up with a reason to go help, since Bobby wasn’t going to send him home early this time around.

Actually…

Athena pulled up to the gas station a few hours before midnight, meeting her husband there as requested. The fire captain was standing outside one of the 118’s ambulances, Buck and Eddie beside him. She stepped out of her cruiser, curiosity piqued.

“Alright, you said there was something I needed to see,” she said, walking up to them. “What is it?”

“Well, I know Cap says he believes me-”

“Because I do,” her husband interrupted to say.

“But I’m still pretty sure you think I’m crazy?” Buck continued, the statement turning into a question at the end. It had Eddie frowning at her, disapproval radiating from him.  “And I remembered there was something I needed to do tonight that would prove to you both that I’m telling the truth.”

“Alright,” Athena said, crossing her arms. “Show me.”

“I think she should be getting here- There!” He pointed at a golden sedan pulling into the pumps. There was a realistic looking body, arranged to look like they were sticking through the windshield. The officer scowled at it, because as much effort as the driver had clearly put into it, it would only serve as a distraction to everyone else on the road and almost inevitably cause an accident.

“I think that’s the car dispatch told us to be on the lookout for,” she said, following him as he started across the parking lot to it, her husband and Eddie following along. “But I don’t see how- Holy Mother of God!”

The foot of what was clearly an actual, live person jerked on the hood. Athena ran past Buck to intercept the driver as she headed in to pay.

“Ma’am!” she shouted, waving her down. “Stay where you are!”

“What?” the woman asked, stopping to look at her.

“She has a head injury,” Buck said, catching up to her. Bobby and Eddie were aiding the man trapped in the windshield. As Athena got closer to look at the driver, she could tell that he was right. There was a giant swollen knot, just above one of her eyes. “Uh, you should probably call for another RA unit.”

She stared dumbly at him as she did so, and then helped to get the driver over to the ambulance. The woman was obviously confused, not quite understanding why a cop was stopping her from getting gas for her car.

“What kind of cancer did you say Michael will have?” Athena asked. Buck smiled grimly at her.

“If I told you he gets a boyfriend out of it, would you worry about it less?”

“No.”

“I didn’t think so.”

Nothing is Ever That Easy

Sometimes, the worst part about knowing what was happening was being unable to prevent it from happening. Buck spent every moment of every day feeling like he was trying to stop a speeding train with nothing but his bare hands, unable to even slow it down as it barreled towards absolute disaster. For instance, there was nothing he could do in the face of the upcoming pandemic, except stock up on facemasks to hand out when the time came. Nor was there a damn thing he could have done to help Hen and Karen’s chances with the in vitro fertilization.

“I wish I could help her,” Chimney said, echoing his unspoken sentiments. They were at Buck’s apartment for dinner, him and Maddie both. Well, they’d had dinner, now they were helping to clean up. Buck and Maddie’s relationship had been steadily improving, but he had the peculiar feeling that tonight was going to see that progress getting tanked. “But she’s not talking to me about it. I’m not sure she’s talking to anybody.”

“There’s definitely something going on with her,” Buck commented. Chimney paused on his way to putting dishes in the sink to point and stare at him.

“You know what it is,” he accused.

“No I don’t,” he hurried to say. “Maybe it’s the Santa Anas. They, uh, they make people act weird. Right?”

“I don’t think it’s the wind,” Maddie said, laughing at him.

“And it totally wasn’t a ghost that called last year,” Buck retorted.

“Maybe it’s something personal she doesn’t feel like sharing,” his sister said, ignoring him. He had to bite his tongue, unwilling to disrupt the peace by pointing out the hypocrisy.

“Well, historically speaking,” Chimney said, glancing over her shoulder at Buck. “Hen and I tell each other everything.”

“Wait, everything?” Maddie asked, anxiety in her voice. Buck knew what she was afraid had been shared by her boyfriend. “Did you tell her about me?”

“No. I mean, I would have if I felt like she was listening,” Chimney said. “Maddie, you know she’s my best friend. I need to talk to someone.”

“I know, it’s just, you tell her, she tells Buck,” she said, and Buck must have been glaring at her back based on the way Chimney winced. “Maybe everything doesn’t need to be shared with the One-Eighteen.”

“But what else would we do on a twenty-four hour shift, if not gossip about each other?” Buck asked. 

“Okay,” she said, sighing as she turned to face him.

“Hey, you don’t have to-”

“It’s fine,” she said, cutting Chimney off. “I’m in therapy, mandated by my boss.”

“Why?” Buck asked, although he knew exactly what happened.

“A woman filed a complaint against me,” Maddie explained. “She said I was stalking her, but I think that’s an overstatement?”

“Is it?”

“A woman called nine-one-one, and Maddie thought she was in trouble,” Chimney said, doing his best to make it sound like anything but what it was. “So she just tried to help.”

“Yeah, but she didn’t want my help, because she thinks I’m a crazy person who invaded her privacy.” Maddie picked up her glass of wine and shrugged. “Maybe there’s a lesson in there for the two of you.”

“A lesson in there, for me?” Buck asked, placing his hands on the counter behind him and leaning back. “So, let me get this straight. Mere months after I changed the locks here because you invaded my privacy, you went and did it again? To a complete stranger?”

“That isn’t what happened,” she denied.

“Clearly Sue thinks it is, or she wouldn’t be reprimanding you,” he pointed out. “So what happened, huh? Did you enter their place while they weren’t home and go snooping through their mail? Their medicine cabinet?”

“She’s being abused, Evan!” Maddie snapped at him. “I was just trying to help her get out like I got out.”

“Guys…” Chimney tried to get between them, head swiveling between both siblings.

“You wanna know a lesson you taught me?’ Buck asked. It was rhetorical, because he was going to tell her anyway. “You can’t force your help on someone in that position. You can tell them how awful their partner is, how much of a dickbag they are. You can beg them to run away with you, because you know things aren’t as okay as they pretend it is. But unless they want to leave, there is nothing you can do except make sure they know they’ll always have a safe place with you.”

Maddie stared at him for a moment in stunned silence, and then looked around the apartment, as if taking it in for the very first time. Her eyes paused on the closed door of the second bedroom, before turning back to him.

“You knew…?”

“Unless this woman wants to leave, there is nothing you can do,” he told her, ignoring the half-whispered question. “But it doesn’t really sound like she wants to leave, or that she’s ready to leave. That’s her choice, just like it was your choice. And you can’t take that choice away from her. You can disagree with it, you can hate it, you can be pissed off at her for it. But until she chooses to leave, there’s not a damn thing you can do.”

“I just wanted to help,” Maddie said, almost pleading.

“But she didn’t ask for your help,” Buck said. “And thinking that she needs help doesn’t excuse invading her privacy, Mads. Being worried about someone doesn’t mean you can ignore their boundaries.”

He watched his sister rapidly blink, watched her lips start to wobble. She set the wine glass down with a harsh thud and turned on her heel, almost running out of the apartment. The door closed with a slam in her wake. Chimney chased after her, leaving Buck to finish cleaning up alone.

“I have no idea what to do,” Buck said, pacing in front of Bobby’s desk. He had dragged Eddie in there with them as soon as they got to the station together, having been carpooling in the jeep everyday ever since the A/C in Eddie’s truck gave up the ghost. Since he didn’t have the extra income from the fight club, he couldn’t just impulse buy a replacement vehicle, nor could he afford to get it fixed yet. “I have been racking my brain for a week now, and I’ve got nothing.”

“Okay, first, why don’t you sit down?” Bobby suggested, gesturing at the chair next to Eddie. Buck stopped pacing but didn’t take the seat. “And then explain to us both what’s going on.”

“We’ll get a call to an online shopping warehouse today, one of the workers pees on a robot and it takes offense.” Both he and Bobby turned their heads to stare at Eddie when the man let out an honest-to-God giggle over it.

“Sorry, sorry,” he said, trying to straighten his face. “Continue.”

“Anyway, while Hen and Chimney are taking him to the hospital-”

“Wait, does the robot try to kill him?” Eddie interrupted to ask, eyes going wide. “Hold on, no, don’t look at me like that, I need to know. Are there killer robots in the future?”

“I think that’s something we can worry about later,” Bobby said.

“I’m worrying about it now!”

“Your technophobia will have to wait,” Buck said. “As Hen is driving the ambulance, she T-bones another car at an intersection. Some girl, a couple years older than May, I think? She doesn’t make it.”

“Dios…”

“What happened?” Bobby asked, the captain mask out in force. “How did it happen?”

“Something to do with the traffic lights, I think?” he offered. “Hen said her light was green, and I think the vic’s light was green, too.”

“Was she- Will she be found at fault?”

“No, no. I don’t know the full explanation of what happened, it’s not like I was expecting to be able to undo any of it, but I know she was cleared in the investigation. Will be cleared.” He scrunched his nose up. “Trying to keep the tenses straight still gives me a headache.”

“Maybe we can have her avoid the intersection?” Eddie suggested. “Wait, do you remember what intersection it was?”

“West Olympic and Main,” he said. Every time he went through that intersection afterwards, he couldn’t help but remember what happened. He knew Hen had avoided driving that way again, if she could help it. “But what if avoiding this crash just causes another one sometime later?”

“What do you mean?” Bobby asked.

“I mean that something happened with the traffic lights. We could have Hen avoid it, only for an entirely different traffic accident to happen there.”

“Was the patient critical?” the captain asked. “Was it a minor injury, like a broken bone? Or was it a life-or-death matter?”

“There was arterial bleeding,” Buck said, chewing on his lip as he tried to remember. “He crashed at the scene, before they could get him loaded. But what does that matter?”

“If they needed to hurry, Hen would have used the traffic preempt switch-”

“Which causes the traffic lights in their way to change,” Buck said. “But if something is wrong with the circuitry at that intersection somewhere-”

“Then she and the other driver both get green lights,” Eddie finished.

“But what do I do?” Buck asked.

“You do nothing,” Bobby said. “I’ll make sure someone knows there’s been a report of an issue with the traffic lights in that intersection, and then tell everyone here at the station the same thing. Problem solved, crash prevented.”

“Just like that?”

“Just like that.”

Buck stood there, gaping at him, before falling into the empty chair with a thump.

“Huh.”

It was not that simple. The city maintenance workers sent to look over the traffic lights at Olympic and Main found nothing wrong with them. Instead, when Hen went down 11th to avoid the supposedly faulty traffic lights, the accident happened at the intersection of that street and Main.

Buck wanted to punch something.

No Glory

His name was Ichabod. 

It wasn’t his only name, nor was it his original name. He didn’t remember that one, truth be told. It had been lost to the fog of time, like so much else of what was his. For as long as he could remember, and he could remember a very long time, he had been stranded at the crossroads, unable to leave, only able to interact with those truly lost souls that stumbled across him. He didn’t remember why he was stuck there, didn’t remember how.

Had he chosen to be there?

Had he been chosen?

Was it, perhaps, a punishment? A reward? A mistake?

Ichabod did not remember.

He assumed he served a purpose, although he could not truly remember what that purpose would be. But all things served a purpose, and so that fact must be true for him as well. But what was his purpose? Was it merely to stand as witness to the stories of others? Was it to merely lend aid to those lost souls that found their way to him? 

Every person that found his crossroads was asked the same question. He didn’t know why he asked, it was almost a compulsion. He was compelled to ask the question, just as they were compelled to answer it true.

“What do you want?” he would ask, or some variation of it. The answers all varied. They were all, in some way or form, selfish at heart. Not that it was their fault, he thought. Life was selfish, and so it made sense that living creatures would be, too. He would give them what they said, even if usually it came in ways they did not expect or appreciate. His existence was dull, after all, and the only times he could interact with anything beyond his bubble of reality was when fulfilling those desires. As such, there was much incentive to fulfill them in ways that amused him. A husband’s love became a deadly obsession, and a man became rich overnight only to lose it all just as quickly.

What happened to the Blues singer was entirely his own doing, and Ichabod had nothing to do with it. The music itself had been all the entertainment he needed.

Only lost souls could find him, truly lost souls. Not just physically, but in everything. They had to be losing hope, they had to be aimless, they had to be on the verge of true desperation. These souls were rare, and so his visitors were few and far between.

And then, one day, the most lost soul of all found his way to him. And when Ichabod asked,

“What do you want, Buck?”

The answer he gave was the most golden of opportunities.

Buck had been missing for an entire week. 

Eddie had expected a reaction, when he gave them all the news of his decision. He had expected shouting, he had expected questions. He hadn’t expected Buck to just turn and walk away. He hadn’t expected his friend to just leave like he did. He had known Buck wouldn’t take it well, he had known that he would ask him to rethink it. It was why he hadn’t talked to him first, so Buck didn’t have the chance to make him second-guess anything. He had to do this, he had to leave. For his son.

Never, in all the ways he had imagined this moment, did he think Buck would ever just run away from it. He hadn’t even said goodbye, hadn’t even stopped to see Christopher before he left. He just got into his jeep and fled.

(“But you were running away, too,” Buck had said, that very first Christmas.

“Yeah, but I got to pretend like it was for a noble cause,” had been Eddie’s reply.)

They had all tried calling him, over and over again. He didn’t answer any of them, not even Taylor. Not even Eddie. Eventually, he either turned his phone off or it had died, because they all started being directed straight to voicemail. 

At the start, Eddie had been angry at Buck for running away. 

By the end of the day, that anger had turned to worry.

By the time they were counting down to midnight at the end of the year, that worry had long given way to fear.

What Ichabod could do was limited to what was asked of him. He could arrange for a man to run into a music teacher, he could twist a husband’s affections and reignite them, he could help another play the odds and receive a sudden windfall of funds. But once that was done, so was his ability to interact with anything beyond his small bubble of liminal space.

He had asked,

“What do you want, Buck?”

And Buck had answered,

“I want to fix whatever broke my family but I don’t even know what that was. I don’t even know when it was.”

And Ichabod could work with that. So specific, yet so broad. He picked Buck out of the river of time and set him down, mind and soul, in the place of his younger self. Almost immediately, another branch twisted out from that point, a branch that Ichabod could play with and keep playing with until Buck managed his task. There were limitations, of course, to what Ichabod could do. But as long as it could be considered helping Buck to achieve what he wanted, it was almost fair game.

The first time he truly had the opportunity to take an active role was after the truck bombing that wasn’t. He watched, peering up into the river of time, as Buck discovered that his precious captain would no longer be his captain. It was a fracture in the family that had not been there before, and Buck had asked to fix what broke his family.

It was easy to reach out and manipulate the odds.

A little stress there, some lose dirt there.

Buck was doomed to always injure his leg, it was a fact that not even Ichabod could alter. He could have easily stood by and allowed it to be injured in any number of nonfatal accidents, just like the truck bombing. But Nash’s actions during that night had been what saved his career, and while Buck could have limped his way back into firefighting, it would have been boring and left his desire unfulfilled.

So much more entertaining, then, to send a boulder tumbling down upon his pretty little head and send him back to try again.

And oh, did Buck try. Again and again, avoiding the truck bombing and letting the captain lose his job, giving Ichabod the excuse he needed to have a little fun. Once by drowning, once by burning. He even got a little creative with it, once setting off a domino effect with weights and wires.

Every time, after every death, Ichabod would unweave the branch to the morning of the truck bombing. There was no need to have a clutter of branches filled with dead and broken clients, after all.

(“I know it irritates you, but he wanted to fix whatever broke, and so I am giving him the opportunity.”

The blue butterfly resting on his hand was silent, but he understood all the same.

“Well, maybe if you visited more often, I would not need to find entertainment elsewhere.”)

Eventually however, coming up with ways to kill Buck while injuring his leg - and thus fulfilling the cosmic mandate - became boring. Besides, he was compelled to help him achieve what he wanted, after all. So he told him a secret of the universe, of things that could be changed and things that could not be changed.

Perhaps Ichabod took too much pleasure in rubbing salt into the wound, telling him how Nash had benefited from his trauma. But he had never claimed to be kind. So he gave him a choice that wasn’t a choice, and sent him on his way.

When Buck later used what he learned from the loop - that in dying, he could have a chance to try again - to save the defective child and his mother, Ichabod was both overjoyed and irritated.

(He allowed that branch to last a bit longer than he had the others, because while dead things were not entertaining, what got left behind very much was. It still got unraveled after a while.)

The morning after the tsunami, Eddie woke up in a bed far too small for him with his eyes puffy, his head aching, and his legs cramped. He was briefly confused, because why was he in Chris’ bed? Where was his son?

And then he remembered.

Somehow, that hurt more than when he first found his son. For the briefest of moments, he had forgotten how empty his world now was. For the briefest of moments, his son had still been alive.

He wasn’t certain how he got home, so lost was he in his grief, but he remembered that Buck had been with him the entire way. Where was Buck now?
