He pushed himself up in his son’s bed - his son was gone, gone, gone - and, for a moment, simply sat there. He didn’t know what to do, didn’t know how to exist after this. How had Bobby not simply ceased to be, after he lost his children?

“Buck?” he called out, his voice scratchy and his throat sore. He eased himself to his feet, his knees and back protesting his choice in sleeping arrangements. His home was quiet, far too quiet. Had his friend left? Was he still asleep?

He padded softly into the hallway, the air still.

“Buck?” he called again, to no reply. Which was concerning, because if the man was there, he would have answered by now. He checked the living room and saw the couch didn’t even have any sheets or pillows. He was about to leave, to see if Buck had taken his bed, when the smell reached his nose.

It was a coppery smell, so thick he could almost taste it.

Under the kitchen door, he could see something red pooling along the floor.

“Buck!?”

His name was Ichabod. 

It wasn’t his only name, nor was it his original name. He had been called so many things by so many people, and he had called himself just as many. This one was the one he was most fond of, however. He liked the form of it, the way it felt as it left his mouth, the way it sounded when it reached his ears.

Ick-a-bahd.

He liked the meaning of it, “no glory.” There was no glory to be had in his existence, nor any to be found in his small patch of time and space. There was only an eternity of solitude and boredom, interspersed with brief moments of distraction that never lasted. He was stuck, forever peering up into the reality beyond. Lost souls did not find glory when they stumbled upon him, merely a solution for their desperation.

Like the lost soul coming now, rumbling towards Ichabod in his truck.

Not Quite There

The time after Hen’s accident was difficult, to say the least. Buck felt awful for her, he truly did, but he was also angry and frustrated that it happened again at all. For the shortest of moments, he had let himself believe that everything was going to be as easy as Bobby claimed. But the universe seemed to enjoy reminding him of his impotence.

“I just don’t understand,” Bobby had said, a day or so after it happened. “You were right about literally everything else. And Hen wouldn’t have even been at that intersection if I hadn’t warned them about the other one.”

“I guess this thing was just carved into stone,” Buck had replied, recalling Ichabod’s words to him just before he allowed the truck bombing to happen. His captain had looked equal parts confused and concerned, but he shrugged it off and left to vent his frustrations out on the station’s gym equipment.

He was not the only one confronting their inability to help where it truly counted. One day, he was once again arriving at the hospital to support his sister, after she had saved the life of an abusive husband after his battered wife had shot him.

“Finger thoracostomy, kinda badass,” he remarked as he handed her a cup of the hospital's spectacularly bad coffee. “You saved his life, even if he didn’t deserve it.”

“No one deserves to die,” she replied.

There were still nights that he woke up thinking his hands were covered in blood that had never been there, but Buck could never regret choosing to take the weight of it upon his own shoulders. Not when it meant that Maddie didn’t have to bear the guilt of taking a life to save her own. Between her and the world, he had promised, and he would always keep that promise.

“Ms. Buckley, sorry to keep you here so long,” an officer Buck vaguely recognized - Williams, according to his name tag - said, coming over to where they were sitting. “You can head home now.”

“You don’t want to take my statement?” Maddie asked, getting to her feet.

“Detectives talked to Mr. d’Agostino before he went into surgery,” Williams said. “He said he shot himself by accident.”

“An accident?” Maddie scoffed.

“Yeah, that’s what I thought, too,” the officer sighed. “You folks have a good night.”

The two of them watched as he turned and left, Maddie in silent disbelief and Buck in resignation.

“I still don’t get it.” He hadn’t realized he voiced the thought out loud until he noticed his sister frowning at him. “I- I mean-”

“Maddie, I’m so glad you’re still here! I wanted to thank you,” a blond woman said, rushing over to hug her. There was a piece of gauze taped to her temple, one of her eyes was bruised, and her lip was busted. “Thank you so much.”

“Tara, what’s going on?” Maddie asked, gripping at her arms. “The officer just said-”

“He said he could forgive me if I would forgive him,” Tara explained. “If we could- If we could make things work.’

“What? No-”

“It can be different now,” Tara said, and she almost sounded like she believed it. “We can be different. He promised.”

She smiled at them both, something too small and fragile to truly be convincing, before rushing away from them and back to her husband’s bedside. Buck placed a comforting hand on his sister’s shoulder.

“C’mon, let’s get you home.”

“So she shoots him and then takes him back?” Eddie asked, carrying plates in from the living room to put in the kitchen sink. He and Chris had come over for a boys’ night, playing video games and eating pizza.

“Didn’t understand it the first time, don’t understand it the second time,” Buck told him, leaning against the counter. 

“My marriage problems were nothing compared to that,” Eddie said. “How’s your sister taking it?”

“Not well,” he answered. “She thought she could save Tara from Vincent, but she’s realizing that awful lesson: sometimes there’s nothing you can do.”

Eddie grimaced at his words.

“Still, uh. Still angry, then?”

“Nope,” Buck denied.

“You punched the firetruck.”

“I didn’t say I wasn’t angry then,” he said, opening the fridge to get something cold to drink. There wasn’t anything alcoholic, all of that had been unofficially banned from the apartment for months now, but there were glass bottles of sodas. He handed one to Eddie, before opening up his own. “I’m saying that I’m not angry now. Some things just can’t be changed, and I’m following Bobby’s advice about that: don’t worry about the things you can’t do anything about.”

That was a bald-faced lie, because he was worried. He was worrying a lot. But he smiled and said he was fine, and whether or not anyone believed it, he wasn’t going to change his tune.

“Well that’s good, I guess,” Eddie said, sounding unsure, as he twisted off his drink’s cap. “I was afraid we were going to have a repeat of before, with Lena.”

“What, were you afraid I’d actually join the fight club this time? Or just start taking swings at people?”

“Nah, that isn’t you.”

“You’re right, that’s more your thing,” Buck said, grinning at the eyeroll that got him.

“Ay Dios, let it go,” Eddie begged. “It wasn’t even me.”

“Y’know, there was one time I was certain that you- That he would take a swing at me,” he said. “It was during the lawsuit, we ran into each other at the grocery store one day. Well, I went there hoping to run into you- Him. It was before the fighting started, I think.”

“What happened?”

“There was a lot of yelling, some uh- Some words were said.” You’re exhausting. “Still kinda think you were punching the wrong people when who you were really wanting to punch was….” He gestured at himself.

“I refuse to believe that there is a version of me that could possibly consider punching you,” Eddie said, reaching between them to grip his bicep. “But I would never hit you. Especially when you’re on blood thinners.”

“You used that excuse last time,” he said, ducking his head and missing the way the other man frowned. “I’d still take you, though.”

“You think so?” Eddie asked. His voice was pitched lower, and when Buck looked up, he found the other man’s face had suddenly gotten a lot closer. “Because you’re welcome to try.”

He met his eyes, and could not look a way.

“I- I know-”

“Dad!” Chris called, and Eddie automatically stepped back, letting go of his arm to see what his son wanted. Buck sagged against the counter as he watched the other man cross the kitchen.

“Coming, buddy.”

What the hell was that? Was Eddie flirting with him? But that- That didn’t make sense. Eddie was straight. Eddie wasn’t interested in him like that, he’d never been interested in him like that. There were literal years of evidence to back that up, so what the hell was that?

He took a swig of his soda, and wished it was something hard.

(God, phrasing.)

Buck having plotted behind their backs to save Christmas solidified what Eddie had realized in the wake of the tsunami. There had been a token effort to deny it, but really, there was no use. The truth was the truth, no matter how one looked at it. But it didn’t mean he knew what to do with that realization, especially in the face of everything that he did know.

“I’m in love with Buck,” he blurted out the moment the door to the captain’s office closed behind him, a couple days before New Years.

Bobby raised his head up from the paperwork he’d been working on and looked at him, but he didn’t say anything.

“Cap?”

“Oh, sorry, was I supposed to say something?” he asked, leaning back in his chair.

“You aren’t surprised,” Eddie remarked, sitting down. “You knew?”

“I suspected,” the captain said. “When are you going to tell Buck?”

“I’m not.”

‘I’m sorry, what?”

“I’m not going to tell him.”

Bobby squinted at him, brows pinching together.

“You know he feels the same way towards you, right?” he asked, jabbing at the desk with his finger to emphasize his words. “He outright told Chimney about it a year ago.”

And Chimney had probably told Hen, who then told Athena, who then told the captain. But they were all wrong however, because,

“He doesn’t love me.”

For the briefest of moments, he was certain that Bobby Nash was going to do something violent, like slam one of their heads into the desk until a consensus was reached.

“He doesn’t- We are talking about Evan Buckley, right?”

“Do you know any other Bucks?”

“I don’t, but apparently you know one that doesn’t love you, and I haven’t met him yet.”

“Buck doesn’t love me,” he insisted, and he could literally watch as the captain swallowed back the initial words he wanted to say to that.

“I am almost certain,” he said, “that Buck has been in love with you since before you even stepped foot in this station.”

“That’s the problem, Bobby,” Eddie said, leaning forward on his elbows and dragging his hands down his face. “Buck doesn’t love me, he loves the other Eddie Diaz. The one that left him on Christmas.”

Bobby stared at him in utter silence for several moments, long enough that the former army medic was genuinely worried the man had suffered a stroke. Then, just as Eddie was about to ask if he was okay, he finally spoke.

“What the fuck are you talking about?”

Brothers

By March, Buck once again had the rod and screws taken out of his leg and was off the blood thinners. It had been a weird few months since Eddie maybe flirted with him in his kitchen. He hadn’t asked, afraid of getting his hopes up, and the other man had simply acted like it never happened. It was frustrating as hell, and apparently it was infectious, because he caught Bobby sending frustrated looks at Eddie almost once a shift. That had started shortly after the holidays.

Christmas had been fun. That Christmas was going to be the last “good” one for the next couple years, since the next one would be essentially canceled on account of plague, and the one after that, well… Buck had plenty of incentive to reinvent the wheel and plagiarize himself with the party at the station. He had a copy of the group photo they took hanging on his wall at the apartment, and every time he looked at it and saw Shannon standing on the other side of Chris, he was reminded that he could actually change things for the better.

Even if he couldn’t change everything.

With March came Chimney’s birthday, and with his birthday came cake and an expected unexpected guest.

“Hey, Chim, do you mind if I take home some of this cake for Harry and May?” Bobby asked, after they’d celebrated the paramedic’s birthday. They were hanging around the kitchen area, enjoying the downtime before the next call.

“How are they doing? Michael and everyone?” Buck knew they’d all be okay in the end, even after the things he planned on preventing, but he still worried about them in the moment.

“Upbeat and fighting,” Bobby answered him, and then to Eddie and Chimney, “Radiation was supposed to be his best shot. Now we’re going with his second best, surgery.”

“How are the kids handling it?” Eddie asked.

“Harry’s okay. I’m worried about May, though,” the captain said. “She’s got a better understanding of what’s going on.”

“That’s because older siblings don’t have the luxury of blissful ignorance,” Chimney chimed in, grousing. “They understand the truth even if they don’t want to.”

Bobby and Eddie glanced at each other, and then turned expectant looks on Buck.

“His younger brother Albert is in town,” he told them.

“You know-?” Chimney rolled his eyes. “Of course you know. And he’s my half-brother, from Korea. Showed up on my doorstep and crashed my dinner with Maddie, wasn’t quite the birthday surprise I was expecting.”

“That’s awesome, I didn’t even know you had a kid brother,” Eddie said, and then shot a reproachful glare at Buck. Had Buck not mentioned that? Surely he had. Though, he did tend to avoid talking about things that hadn’t happened yet, so he probably hadn’t.

“When do we get to meet him?” Bobby asked.

“That doesn’t really seem necessary,” Chimney said. “He’s going to be leaving soon anyways, my dad insisted on it.”

Buck tried to stealthily shake his head at the other two, but the paramedic caught the movement and turned to glare at him.

“What does that mean?” he demanded. “Was that a psychic moment? Wait, since when did they start believing you were psychic?”

“He’s not,” Eddie said, and then grinned at the scoff Chimney let out.

“Come on, you have a chance to get to know your brother, don’t waste it,” Buck said, thinking of Daniel. “Trust me.”

His tone must have given away some of his feelings towards the topic, because he caught the others frowning at him.

“I don’t know, it just feels weird to me,” Chimney argued. “Sure, we share some of the same DNA, but he’s practically a stranger to me.”

“I keep telling you, family comes to us in different ways, Chim,” Hen declared, walking over to join them, handing out papers to everyone. “And don’t think you’re gonna send him home without meeting all of us.”

“What is this?” Eddie asked, waving around his copy of the paper.

“Talking points regarding Henrietta and Karen,” Bobby read aloud, looking up to look questioningly at Hen. Buck stared down at his own copy, grinning at it.

Nia! Nia! Nia!

“Social services is vetting Karen and me to become foster parents,” Hen explained to them. “We listed each and every one of you as references so when they call, I need you all to sing our praises.”

“You mean these specific twenty-six praises?” Eddie asked, and Hen let out a small laugh.

“Karen made the list, she’s very thorough,” she said, and Buck could hear the adoration she felt for her wife.

“Hen, we know you,” Bobby assured her. “We don’t need some piece of paper to remind us of your many wonderful qualities.”

“I appreciate that, Cap, but I’d rather you didn’t improvise. The stakes are very high.”

“Hen, can I say something without you strangling me?” Buck asked.

“I make no promises,” she said, crossing her arms.

“I don’t think they’re going to care if you can play the bassoon.”

Hen frowned at that, double-checking one of the copies she still had in her folder.

“I didn’t- She just put down that I played a musical instrument, how did you…?”

Oh shit.

“Because he’s psychic!” Chimney crowed.

“Huh,” Hen said, blinking at him from behind her glasses. “Well, memorize the list anyway. All of you!”

She pointed at each of them in turn before walking off.

“Wait, no, hold on!” Chimney called after her, but she either didn’t hear him or ignored it. “Nearly three years I’ve been saying you were psychic, and it’s the bassoon that gets her to believe it?”

Buck shrugged.

Buck had missed Albert. Sure, he was a massively annoying roommate, but he was still his little brother in all but blood. Having him back in his life felt like another piece of the puzzle slotting into place. It was too bad that he had forgotten how much Chimney resented him at the start.

It first became (re)apparent when Albert dropped by the station unannounced, while Hen and Chimney were on their way back from taking the partially eviscerated guy to the ER. Chimney was silent as he sat through lunch with them, scowling as everyone chatted with the younger Han. It reminded Buck, on a visceral level, of how he was those first couple of shifts with Eddie.

(With hindsight, Buck could see just how similar he and Chimney really were. It wasn’t something he liked thinking about, especially considering the man was going to have a baby with his sister.)

The resentment was impossible to ignore during Chimney’s birthday party at the karaoke bar, when the man let it spill out everywhere.

“I get it, you know?” Buck said as they were playing pool. “Sometimes you have to take some time and distance between yourself and where you come from, to figure out who you are and what you want.”

“Hell, if I hadn’t enlisted, I’d still be working with my pops,” Eddie threw in.

“Eddie, don’t encourage him to go off to war,” Maddie scolded from where she sat beside Chimney.

“There is as much virtue to the noble warrior as there is to the most enlightened of scholars,” Albert said. This version of him was so young, so earnest. Too bad that wouldn’t last the year…

“That,” Eddie said, pointing at him and grinning adorably. “What he said.”

“Listen, everyone has their path,” Hen said, dispensing her wisdom. “Just do you, Albert.”

“I will. I will do me,” the younger man said, causing them all to laugh.

“Phrasing!” Buck called from the other end of the pool table.

“I just need a little bit of my brother’s courage,” Albert told them. “You know, he did not let father dictate his life. He took a stand, got out. Came to America to follow his dreams.”

He grinned broadly at them, aiming the pool cue to take his shot. Behind him, Chimney scowled darkly and set down his drink.

“There was no stand,” he said, drawing everyone’s attention. “I didn’t get out, I was left behind.”

“Chim…” Maddie tried, but he ignored her.

“See, most of my life, all I wanted was for him to see me, to be proud of me, be proud to call me his son. But no matter what I did, I was always invisible. Because you are the only son he cares about.”

From where he stood, Buck couldn’t see Albert’s face, but he could see the stiff way he stood and the way his shoulders curled just the slightest bit inward.

“You have all his attention, all his love, and you just walked away from it. Which I guess is easy for you, because you’ve never had to work for it,” Chimney continued, seemingly oblivious to the way everyone was glancing around, uncomfortable. Well, not everyone. Buck couldn’t take his eyes off the train wreck repeating itself in front of him “No, everybody loves Albert. This entire table is proof of that.”

“You do not know what my life was like at home,” Albert said.

“I know you’ve always had a family,” Chim steamrolled. “And I have always been trying to piece one together. Well, these people are all that I have. You don’t get to take them, too.”

“I do not wish to take anything from you, Howard,” Albert denied, earnest and pleading. “I’m your brother.”

“You are not my brother, I had a- Hey!”

Buck had had enough, grabbing Chimney by the arm and physically yanking him out of his seat, dragging him away from the others. He didn’t look at him, ignoring the way the older man tried tugging himself free, until they got out the doors and into the night air.

“What the hell?”

“You are not being replaced,” Buck said, letting him go and voicing the words he wished someone had told him, back when he was acting like a brat towards Eddie. “We can be friends with him and with you.”

“You dragged me out here just to say that?”

“No, I dragged you out here because you were being a dick to your brother.”

“He’s not my brother,” Chimney denied. “My brother was Kevin.”

“Maddie and I had a brother,” Buck told him, the words sending the other man into stunned silence. “He died when I was still in diapers. I’m not even supposed to know about him, but all my life, I’ve been living in his shadow. I spent years competing with a ghost for my parents’ love and affection and attention. So trust me, Howard, when I tell you that I understand. I probably understand how you’re feeling right now better than Maddie or the others ever will.

“But bad parents are bad parents. They don’t pick and choose which kid to be a bad parent to, they do it to all their kids equally. You look at him and think he grew up loved and cherished just because your father was present in his life, but you don’t go running from a good childhood. I certainly didn’t. Maddie didn’t.”

Chimney stared up at him, mouth agape. Buck sighed and rubbed at his face.

“Look, he came to you. That means something, Chimney. Don’t ruin it because of the insecurities your shitty father gave you. And uh, look. Maddie doesn’t know that I know about our brother, so uh. Try not to tell her that I told you?”

When the man nodded but still didn’t say anything, he sighed and walked back into the bar, leaving him out there to think. Maddie met him halfway, and he pointed her in the right direction before she had a chance to ask. The mood at the pool table was far more subdued than it was at the beginning, and Albert was looking like a kicked puppy where he sat.

“Your brother will get over it,” he told him, patting him on the shoulder. “I have a spare bedroom, you can stay at mine for the night.”

“Thank you,” Albert said, looking up at him, trying for a smile that came out as more of a grimace.

“Eh, you’re his brother,” Buck said. “Makes you family.”

Two days after the second attempt at celebrating Chimney’s birthday, hosted by Eddie, Maddie showed up at Buck’s apartment, pounding on his door. It was early, a couple hours before his shift, and he was still rubbing the sleep out of his eyes as he let her in. A single look at her face told him exactly why she was there.

“He told you.” He lasted longer than Buck had thought he would, but not as long as he hoped.

“He told me,” she said. “How? How do you know?”

Buck thought for several moments, and then went out on a limb.

“You told me.”

“What?”

He sighed.

“You told me, after I found a picture of him in your baby box,” he told her, and then headed for the kitchen. “Sit down, we need coffee for this and I need to text Bobby that I’ll be late.”

“I don’t understand,” Maddie said, sitting on the couch.

“Do you remember after the earthquake?” Buck asked, getting both of them cups. “When you asked how I knew to send you that text?”

“I know that Chimney thinks you’re psychic,” she said, rolling her eyes.

“I’m not,” he said, reentering the living room and handing her coffee to her. “I told you the truth that day. I am from the future.”

Maddie stared at him.

“Explain.”

Limitation, Accommodation

Buck didn’t tell his sister everything, of course he didn’t. Buck hadn’t even told Eddie everything. He gave her the same brief rundown he did Bobby and Athena, the day after the tsunami: one Christmas, he stumbled across a black-eyed stranger named Ichabod who sent him back in time to his first day on the job. It said a lot about how big of a secret Daniel's entire existence was, that simply knowing it was all it took for Maddie to believe his unbelievable story. There had still been questions, obviously. He answered most of them, some of them only vaguely, edging around the truth of it.

“What about Doug?” had been one of her first questions she asked, to which he replied with the honest, “He’s not around.”

“Okay, so how old are you now? I mean, technically,” Maddie asked, her coffee forgotten in her hands.

“Oh God, I don’t know,” he replied, scrunching up his face as he tried to think. “You know I’m awful at math. Uh, thirty-something? And a half? Maybe?”

“And a half, maybe,” she repeated, laughing at him.

“It was on Christmas, Mads, not my birthday. Or, actually, I think it was technically the day after Christmas by that point.”

“Excuses,” she teased. “Who all knows about… This?” She waved her hand around, as if she could encompass the entirety of his situation with it.

“Bobby and Athena,” he said. “And Eddie.”

“Of course Eddie knows.”

“What does that mean?”

“You know exactly what it means,” she told him. “And Chimney and Hen both think you're psychic.”

“You never know, perhaps I am psychic,” he told her, nudging at her leg with his foot. “Maybe I actually dreamed up the entire future and didn’t do any actual traveling.”

“That wouldn’t explain the demon guy, though,” she pointed out.

“Ichabod isn’t a demon,” he corrected her.

“Well, whatever he is-” She froze, a look of dawning realization creeping across her face. “Oh my God.”

“What?”

“Oh. My. God.”

“What!?”

Twisting around, she looked in turn at the quartz crystals in the corners of the room, at the dreamcatcher hanging from the ceiling, at the horseshoe nailed above his front door. She turned back to him, eyes wide and jaw hanging loose.

“Oh my God,” she repeated. “A ghost called nine-one-one.”

“I told you!” he crowed, jumping to his feet and pointing at her in victory, nearly spilling his coffee in his excitement. “I told you!”

“I don’t know what’s worse,” Maddie said, still wide-eyed as she looked up at him. “That ghosts might actually be real or that I know you’re never going to let me live this down.” A pause, during which she grimaced as he did a victory dance in front of her. “The latter. Definitely the latter. Are you sure you’re thirty-something?”

“And a half!”

“Maybe.”

Going to parent-teacher night with her ex-husband was a challenge, but for Christopher, Shannon was willing to put up with it. It helped that Carla was with them, a buffer between them and the faculty. Somehow, neither of them had managed to find the time to actually meet or interact with their son’s teachers before now. But the number of times they got called Mr. and Mrs. Diaz all in one breath, as if her identity was still tied solely to her failed marriage, was enough to have her contemplating murder. She really should have gone back to her maiden name, but the paperwork hadn’t been worth it. Now, though, she was definitely rethinking it.

And the teachers’ jokes weren’t even funny.

(Except maybe the chemistry one, that one got a sensible chuckle out of her.)

The worst of them, though, was Christopher’s English teacher, Ms. Flores. She didn’t come in with a corny joke or pun, but there was something about her that had Shannon having to resist sneering. Perhaps it was the way she pretty much ignored her, or the way she tried flirting with her ex-husband, just subtle enough to be missed. Shannon didn’t know what it was, but there was something that had her wanting to claw out her eyes and pour salt into the sockets.

It didn’t help that she was late to their conference.

“So sorry to keep you waiting,” Ms. Flores said, finally entering the room. “My last student’s father asked a surprising amount of questions.”

“I’m sure he did,” Carla said, smirking.

“Good to see you again, Mrs. Price,” she said, shaking the aide’s hand. “And you must be Mr. Diaz.”

“Please, call me Eddie, it’s short for-”

“Edmundo?” Ms. Flores cut in.

“Most people guess Eduardo.”

“Growing up, I had a grandfather named Edmundo,” the teacher said, attempting to smile coyly at him. “He was my favorite.”

“Hi! I’m Shannon,” she announced herself, loudly. It had not gone unnoticed by her that the teacher hadn’t even bothered looking her way the entire time, her attention entirely focused upon Eddie. “Chris’ mom.”

“Right! Let’s, uh, let’s talk about Christopher.” Ms. Flores said, smiling a bit too big to be real, looking through the notes on her desk. “He’s been doing really well in my class, his verbal skills have definitely improved. He’s still a little shy about reading out loud, but he definitely understands the material. I attribute that to him being read to from an early age, so bravo there.”

The way she was smiling at Eddie, and only Eddie, showed Shannon who she was congratulating. Eddie must have noticed the way his ex-wife’s hands twitched because he was quick to correct the teacher.

“No, that was all her,” he said, pointing at Shannon.

“Christopher told me you kept it up since she left, though,” Ms. Flores said, and Shannon just about lunged across the desk to wring her neck.

“All of us have been doing our best to keep up with the reading,” Shannon said, her smile more of a baring of teeth than an actual smile. “Carla and Eddie, and myself. And Buck of course.”

“Buck.” The way Ms. Flores said the name, it was obvious Chris had spoken about him in class before.

“He does the voices better than me,” Eddie said, smiling warmly. And a small part of Shannon almost felt sympathetic for the teacher, because her ex-husband was too far gone on one Evan Buckley to ever be truly receptive to the flirting. It was a small part of her, though. Itty-bitty, teeny-tiny. 

“Oh, I’m sure you’re no slouch,” Ms. Flores said, undeterred.

“Oh, no, he isn’t,” Carla chipped in.

“You know, speaking of Buck,” Shannon said, playfully slapping her ex-husband on the arm. Or, it was supposed to be playful. It might have been a bit too hard to count, from the way Eddie tried to subtly rub at the impact site. “We really should have brought him with us. His sister would have understood if their night got pushed back a day.”

“Who, uh, who is Buck, exactly?’ the teacher asked, her pretty little smile looking a bit strained.

“He’s my-” Eddie started, but Shannon interrupted.

“He’s Eddie’s partner,” she said, smiling brightly at the teacher. On the other side of Eddie, Carla tried to pretend like her burst of laughter was a coughing fit. Did it make her a bad person, that she took some enjoyment in the way she could see the small glimmer of hope die in Ms. Flores’ eyes? “Chris adores him.”

“Oh! Uh, okay.” The teacher cleared her throat and busied herself with pretending to shuffle through her notes again. “Well, Christopher is one of our most popular students. He loves making the other kids laugh.”

“Is that a problem?” Eddie asked, frowning, discussion of Buck forgotten.

“Not at all,” Ms. Flores assured them. “He’s a very sweet and kind boy. You’re doing a great job. Uh, the both of you, and Buck.”

“Thank you,” Shannon answered for them, and then practically herded Eddie out the door.

After the skateboard incident, and the way Chris reacted to the talk about limitations, Eddie practically ran to Buck’s apartment. Surely, surely, this had come up in the other timeline. How did the other Eddie get through this? How did the other Chris react to it?

“He called me a liar,” he said the moment he let himself through Buck’s door. The man himself was lounging on the couch, reading what looked like someone’s biography. “Chris, I mean.”

“Oh, it’s time for the Jim Abott talk,” Buck said, closing the book and setting it on the end table, moving his stupidly long legs to make room.

“Jim Abott?” Eddie asked, sitting down next to him, close enough their shoulders touched. “The baseball player?”

“Pitched a no-hitter in the Nineties, born with one hand, yadda yadda,” Buck explained. “Listen, Eds, I am too old to walk you through this again-”

“Too old?”

“Yes, too old. I’m like, thirty-something.”

“Hey!” Because Eddie was in his thirties, and he was not old!

“So I’m going to skip to the end. Just because Chris can’t do things the same way as the other kids, doesn’t mean he can’t do them at all,” he said. “The word of the day is accommodations, Eddie. Not limitations.”

“Okay, I’m liking the positivity,” Eddie said, watching as Buck reached for his phone. “But this helps me, how?”

“Accommodations,” Buck repeated, and then shoved the phone into his face. On the screen, once Eddie could focus on it, was a diagram for a contraption of some sort.

“What is this?”

“It’s what we did Before. It’ll help him stay on the skateboard,” he explained. “I already have the parts, I think. Somewhere. I’ll have to double check.”

Santo Dios, how was this man even real? Eddie refused to believe that the other version of him had ever been so stupid as to pass him up. Maybe that’s why he left? Maybe they had tried for something and it ruined everything? But that wouldn’t explain the comment about Chris being scared…

Actually, there was another thing bugging him.

“Hey, Chris’ teacher, is she-?”

“Yeah, she’s the one you were too busy chatting with to notice that your son snuck out of your house. On crutches.”

“Well, that’s a mistake that won’t be repeating itself,” Eddie said, mostly to himself.

“Which, uh, which part?” Buck asked..

“Hey, how did the talk with Maddie go?” he asked instead of answering. “You came in late that shift, and we haven’t really had the chance to talk about it.”

“It went fine. She, uh. She asked about Doug.”

“And what did you tell her?”

“Well definitely not the entire truth,” Buck said, rolling his eyes. “Just that he wasn’t around.”

“What happened to Doug?” Eddie asked, and then clarified, “That Doug, I mean.”

“He took Maddie,” he whispered, gaze locked on his lap. “He stabbed Chimney and left him for dead, dragged Maddie off to Big Bear. By the time I found her, she had- He was dead, and she wasn’t.”

When he looked up, Eddie could see tears gathering in Buck’s eyes.

“Am I a bad person?” he asked. “Because I don’t regret it. I don’t. What Doug did, what Maddie had to do, it- I would do what I did a thousand times over if it meant she didn’t have to go through that again.”

“Buck, you just gave me a way to help my kid skateboard,” Eddie said, gripping him by the shoulder. “I’m horribly biased, but I’m going with no. Now, do you want to hear some of the really bad jokes Chris’ teachers came up with at parent-teacher night?”

“Um, sure?” Buck sounded uncertain, blinking at the sudden change in topics.

“Okay, uh… What do you call a number that won’t sit still?”

“What?”

“A roamin’ numeral.”

They were really bad jokes, but at least they got Buck to laugh.

Chapter End Notes

Listen, I figure this is obvious between this fic and Take My Hand, but I Do Not like Ana Flores. The moment the words, "our limitations tell us when to stop" came out her mouth, that was all there was to it. There was a kid at my school, a couple grades above me, whose arms didn't develop properly. They were like t-rex arms. He did everything with his feet. He wrote with his feet, he used utensils with his feet, he played the drums with his feet, he drove with his feet. Once you've been in a car with a guy who's steering and shifting gears with his foot, the concept of "our limitations tell us when to stop" dies a cold death.

So the fact that Ana Flores looked at Chris and was like "welp I guess he'll never skateboard ever" just infuriates me.

The Oracle of Los Angeles

“But am I happy?” Chimney asked Hen and Eddie as the three of them got changed into their uniforms. It was the start of the shift, their first day with Reynolds subbing in for Bobby while the captain was on that camping trip with Michael and Harry, and the paramedic had just finished telling them about the conversation with Albert the night before. “Albert is annoying, but maybe he’s right. Things with me and Maddie are great, but we’re not exactly lighting the world on fire.”

“Does it matter what he thinks?” Eddie asked, fiddling with the collar on his button up. “Only you know how you feel about Maddie.”

“I really care about her-”

Hen’s almost disgusted scoff interrupted him.

“The dreaded C-word,” she said, and then gestured at her shoes. “I really care about good arch support. That’s not how you feel about your significant other.”

“Obviously,” Chimney said, rolling his eyes. “I care about her more than good footwear.”

“Okay, but how much more?”

“A lot,” he said, dropping down to sit on the bench.

“Do you love her?” Eddie asked, doing up his shirt buttons.

“Yeah.”

“Does she love you?”

“Unclear,” he answered morosely. The other two frowned at him. “I mean, I feel like she does, but neither of us have actually said those exact words out loud.”

“Maybe you should ask Buck,” Hen suggested.

“He isn’t a magic eight ball,” Eddie said, directing his frown at her. “But yeah, maybe you should. It is his sister we’re standing around gossiping about.”

“That’s why I’m not asking him about it. God knows I don’t want to risk bringing Angry Buck back,” Chimney said. “And with how her last relationship was, we just wanted to take it slow.”

“You’ve been together for, like, a year-”

“Ten months and three weeks,” Chimney corrected Hen.

“A year,” she repeated herself, rolling her eyes. “Glaciers move faster, Chim.”

“They’re also melting,” he countered. “So maybe fiery is overrated.”

“Hey, guys,” Buck interrupted, gripping the doorframe and leaning through the locker room entrance. He already sounded exhausted, and the day hadn’t even started yet. “Reynolds wants us to do a line up.”

“I can’t believe Cap left us with this guy,” Hen complained, stomping out of the locker room, Buck on her heels.

“I sure wasn’t gonna do it again,” Chimney told them. He and Eddie were almost out the door when the former medic stopped him.

“Hey, I get taking things slow,” Eddie told him. “But tomorrow isn’t promised to anyone. So if you love her, tell her.”

“That’s rich, coming from you,” Chimney said, crossing his arms and scowling.

“What does that mean?”

“I mean, you and Buck,” the paramedic said. “The way you two look at each other. If you’re going to give me advice like that, you need to follow it yourself.”

“You sound like Cap.”

“Wait, you’re not going to deny it?” Chimney asked, dropping his hands to hips and squinting up at the taller man. “I expected more of a fight.”

“It’s complicated, Chim,” Eddie said, shifting uncomfortably.

“No, it really isn’t,” he denied. “You love him, he loves you.”

“No he doesn’t,” Eddie said, smiling a little sadly.

“W-what?” Chimney stuttered out. Did his friend hit his head at some point? He didn’t think he had, but clearly the man was suffering from a concussion. He pulled his penlight out of his shirt pocket, shining it into Eddie’s eyes to check his pupillary response. “What year is it? Who’s the president?”

“Chimney-”

“Han! Diaz!” Reynolds called out, sounding impatient. Never before had Chimney seen someone look so relieved to be called for a line up, or in such a hurry to get to it.

“Note to self,” he muttered to himself as he followed at a more sedate pace. “Have Hen help me pin him down and check for a head injury…"

It wasn’t often that Buck went to the Grant-Nash residence while Bobby was away. He wasn’t certain why that was. It wasn’t that he and Athena had no relationship outside of his captain, because they did. She called often while his leg was healing, and she would still check on him independently from Bobby. It was just that, if he went over to visit, it was always to visit her and Bobby or just Bobby, never just her.

(In hindsight, he felt rather bad about that.)

So to have her invite him over while Bobby was off on the camping trip with Harry and Michael was unusual.

“Hey, Athena,” he greeted when she opened the door for him.

“Thank you for coming, Buck.” She was smiling warmly at him, which automatically eased his nerves.

“What’s the occasion?” he asked, handing her the bottle of wine he’d bought. He and Maddie had been raised by WASPs, after all.

“Well, now it’s to have a reason to drink this very nice wine,” Athena answered, reading the label as she led him down the stairs and to the patio out back, grabbing glasses from the kitchen as she went. She also snagged a thing of orange juice from the fridge, obviously with him in mind, which made him smile. “But I just wanted to chat. You know, touch base.”

“Right…” Buck wasn’t certain if he totally believed her reasons, but he wasn’t about to complain about an opportunity to spend time with someone he absolutely considered family. One of the people who, through everything, had never, ever let him down. “How’s, uh, how’s Harry enjoying the camping trip?”

“Oh, it sounds like he’s having fun,” she answered, pouring herself some wine and him the juice.

“Sounds like?”

Athena sighed.

“I’m worried about him, and I’m worried about May,” she said, swirling the wine in her glass. “And I’m worried about Michael.”

Buck got the suspicion that this wasn’t a social visit at all.

“That’s understandable,” he said, carefully. So very carefully. “But they’re all dealing with it okay, right? You’re all handling it okay?”

“Buck.”

“Athena.”

She set the glass on the patio table and set her gaze on him, and suddenly it wasn’t just Athena, his captain’s wife across from him. Instead, it was Sergeant Grant, and he had somehow stumbled into an interrogation.

“I have never asked much about the future, since Halloween.”

“And I’m thankful for that.”

“Buck, I need to know,” she said. “The other day, May just casually mentioned the possibility of Michael being gone in a year. I need to know, is he?”

“Do you?” Buck asked. “Need to know, I mean.”

“What does that mean?”

“‘Thena, I could give you a laundry list of all the things that are going to happen, but how will that help you? There are things that will happen regardless of how much we try to prevent them. How will knowing about them help you?” he asked. “If I told you Michael is dead next year, how will that help you now? How will that do anything but cause you pain now?”

“So it’s true?” Athena’s voice broke a bit. “Michael, he…?”

“No,” Buck sighed. “He’ll be fine. I told you, he gets a boyfriend out of it. Actually, they got engaged before…”

The officer sunk in her seat, covering her mouth as she let out a broken sob of relief.

“Thank God,” she said, the words trembling. “Thank God.”

“But Athena, I can’t- Bobby told you, right? How we tried to save Hen from accidentally killing that girl, but it happened anyway?” He waited for her to nod. “I cannot, I will not, put the weight of that on anyone else’s shoulders. Not unless I need to. Not when it might happen anyway, no matter how much we try.”

“So instead you’ll carry on alone, trying to do it all by yourself?” Athena asked, scoffing.

“Hey, if it ain’t broke,” Buck protested, shrugging. “It worked out before.”

Athena narrowed her eyes, clearly unconvinced as she picked up her wine glass again.

“Well, how about something small, then,” she said. “Does May go to USC?”

“Oh! Uh…” he busied himself with drinking the orange juice, shrinking under Athena’s gaze. “She, uh. She stays close to home.”

“So she does go to USC?”

“Uh, well…”

“Buck.”

“College isn’t for everyone, y’know?” Buck broke, trying to smile brightly at her. “I mean, uh. I dropped out during my first year. And- And Eddie didn’t go at all. And Maddie isn’t even using her degree!”

“Evan Buckley,” she growled, and Buck curled in on himself. “Are you telling me that my baby girl wrote that essay about how I’m the enemy, and got accepted into a university with it, and she doesn’t even go?”

“Well, uh, look at the bright side,” Buck tried, and then flinched back when she slammed her wine glass down.

“The bright side?”

“She won’t go into debt with loans?”

“I am going to kill her.”

“She hasn’t done anything yet,” he pointed out. “And doesn’t this prove my point? How knowing the future doesn’t actually help?”

“Buck.”

“Yes ma’am?”

“Shut up.”

“Yes ma’am.”

Chimney stood at the table, frowning down at his phone. Maddie wasn’t answering. She said that she loved him, the very first time she had ever said those words to him, when at their date she had said she had used those words as a shield against Doug and so thought she could never say those words to him. And now she wasn’t answering. Not his texts, not his calls. Nothing.

Worse still, when he tried to call 9-1-1 in a last ditch effort to reach her, he got a message about a high call volume.

Screw it, he thought, and pressed call for a different contact.

“Go for Buck,” the psychic answered.

“How come Nine-One-One doesn’t respond when I call?”

“I think I’ve heard this riddle before…”

“It’s not a riddle, okay?” Chimney said, rolling his eyes, even though he knew the other man couldn’t see him. “I just tried calling and got the high call volume message. Did I miss an earthquake or something?”

“No, pretty chill- Wait, why are you calling Nine-One-One?”

“Your sister said that she loved me-”

“Fuck!” Buck yelled, and Chimney yanked the phone away from his ear, wincing at the volume. “That’s today!?”

And then he hung up, leaving the paramedic to stare at his phone. Now he was very, very concerned.

Athena had just hung up with May and pulled into the intersection at 9th and Los Angeles, a car accident blocking the way, when her phone rang again.

“Buck, I’m busy right now-”

“A bunch of art thieves have taken the dispatch center hostage.”

She paused in the process of getting out of her cruiser, staring in horror at the phone on her dash.

“What?”

“A bunch of guys took over the dispatch center, they’re redirecting units so some others can steal a bunch of art from a museum. It’s near an intersection with a car accident, uh, Los Angeles and uh…”

“Los Angeles and Ninth,” she finished for him, staring out her windshield to the aforementioned accident. “I’m already there.”

“Okay, so they’ll probably-”

“Seven-Two-Seven-L-Thirty,” a male voice interrupted from her radio. “They’re requesting you at One-Nine-One-Two-Four Sunset. Assault and battery in progress.”

“Copy,” Athena said into the radio, trying to sound all business. “Dispatch, at Ninth and Los Angeles. Non-injury car accident.”

“Yes, units are already en route to that location,” the dispatcher lied. “Please proceed to assault and battery in progress.”

“Copy that,” Athena said into the radio and then, after taking a moment to make sure it was off and they could not hear her, said to Buck, “I’m going to hang up now and call Maynard.”

“Wait, wait, wait!”

“What?” she asked, getting impatient.

“You can’t just send in SWAT. They’re in the dispatch center, they’ll know you’re onto them.”

“I’ll take that under advisement. But Buck?”

“Yes ma’am?”

“If I see you anywhere near the dispatch center, I will have your hide for a new couch cover. Do I make myself clear?”

“As a whistle,” Buck’s strained voice answered.

Later, when Athena went to the dispatch center to see things for herself and found both Buck and Chimney waiting for her outside the building, the former smiling brightly at her as if it would spare him from her maternal wrath, to say that she was angry was a vast understatement.

The Well

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The first clue the others had that the day was going to be a shitty one was how silent Buck got the moment they pulled up to the farm house. They didn’t pay too much attention to it, considering the call was about a missing kid. Everyone knew how much Buck adored children, they had all seen him with Chris, and the ones who had been there remembered how he had been with the baby in the wall. So it wasn’t too out there to think that he might have just been taking the call extra seriously.

The second clue was how he didn’t even join them in the house for the rundown of what was going on. When Bobby and Athena sent the others out in all directions to find Hayden, Eddie found him on the other side of a small, fenced in garden. He was crouched down, gazing at the mouth of a narrow metal pipe, moving aside the last of what looked like wooden planks.

“Is that…?”

Buck just nodded.

“Hey guys, over here!” Eddie called out, the others running over.

“Cap, the human dowsing rod found him,” Chimney announced into his radio as Eddie called the kid’s name into the well.

It took the rest of the day and into the evening to get everything set up. They lowered a camera and got visuals on the kid, they contacted the city for maps of the pipes, they ordered a drill and got it set up to dig a parallel tunnel. Throughout it all, Buck said nothing, looking increasingly anxious as the sky grew cloudier. Eventually, it began to storm in the distance, and he couldn’t seem to keep his eyes off it.

“Buck? Are you okay?” Eddie asked as they worked together to set up the radio so they could talk to Hayden.

“Yeah, just… Just really hoping I didn’t step on a butterfly somewhere,” he answered, which didn’t really answer anything at all.

“What?”

“We’re ready to put the radio down!” Buck called over to Bobby at the screen set-up, where they could see the top of Hayden’s head, instead of solving Eddie’s confusion. “Gonna drop it to forty feet!”

Even across the several feet of distance between the mouth of the well where they were crouching and where they had the screens, Eddie could see the way the captain frowned at the erstwhile time traveler. Instead of voicing any of the concerns he had, however, he nodded for him to go ahead. With the radio in place, after a bit of trial and error, they managed to make contact with Hayden, with first his mother and then Eddie speaking to him.

Soon, much too quickly for anyone’s liking, the storm reached them. The downpour slowed the drill, and every time there was a crack of thunder, Buck seemed to leap out of his skin. Bobby shot down the city commissioner’s concerns about the drill rig acting as a lightning rod, before giving marching orders.

“Get the winch and the harnesses,” he said. “Once we hit depth-”

“I’ll go in,” Eddie said. Beside him, Buck let out what he could have sworn was a whine, although it was almost lost to the wind.

To say that Bobby was concerned as they lowered Eddie into the well was an understatement. He was concerned about the boy, Hayden. He was concerned about the storm. He was concerned about how Buck had gone almost entirely mute the moment Eddie had volunteered to go down.

He was also concerned about the way the radio was cutting in and out.

“Eddie, do you copy?” he tried. “Tell me what’s going on, Eddie.”

“Cap, I think he’s out of range,” Hen said.

Bobby watched as the minutes counted down on his timer, pacing around the well opening. Every once in a while he would glance back at Buck, who still hadn’t said anything. Surely if something was wrong, their youngest would say something. But he stayed silent, and Eddie hadn’t pulled on the rope.

And the minutes kept ticking down.

With less than three minutes to go, Chimney called him over to the video feed.

“I’ve lost the signal,” the paramedic complained, gesturing at the screens that said exactly that. “I think we need to run another line.”

“No time for that, Chim,” Bobby said, holding up his arm so the other man could see just  how little time they had.

After another minute had passed, after another garbled message on the radio and another failed attempt to get Eddie to answer, Bobby really had no choice.

“Prep the rig,” he ordered Buck. “We’re bringing him up.”

“No.”

Hen and Bobby both turned to look at him, shocked with the outright refusal.

“Excuse me?”

“He needs more time.”

“He doesn’t have it,” Bobby countered, pointing at the timer, its red digits almost mocking them. “We’re almost down to one minute.”

“Cap, please-”

“No, Buck,” the captain said, stepping up beside him. “I can’t risk it.”

As if on cue, the timer went off.

“Time’s up,” he said, taking over the winch from Buck. “We’re pulling him out. Now.”

It didn’t happen immediately. They got to thirty feet, then twenty-five. It was at twenty that things took a turn he really probably should have expected, because Buck and Eddie could be alike in all the worst ways.

“The weight’s gone!” he yelled out, continuing to run the winch..

“What does that mean?” Chimney asked.

“He cut the line.” Buck’s voice was monotone, almost emotionless.

“What?” Bobby asked.

“Oh my God!” Hen cried out from the mouth of the tunnel they’d dug, holding up the tattered end of the rope. “He cut the damn line.”

“Why?” Bobby asked, tearing his eyes away from the rope in Hen’s hand to Buck, who had slumped against the side of the fire truck that was parked behind him. “Why would he do that?”

“He needed more time.”

Chimney thought, stupidly, that things were going to be okay after he was lowered down and found both Hayden and Eddie, wet but alive. He made a quip to the firefighter about not cutting his next line and then brought the kid to the surface, greeted with applause and adoration. With mother and son reunited, Bobby started making plans to bring Eddie back up.

And then things went to shit.

Lightning struck the drill rig, and as he watched it collapse, Chimney had the time to think, “Oh, that explains why Buck didn’t like the thunder.” And then he realized that the way the rig fell had collapsed the tunnel they had dug. He watched, transfixed, as Buck leapt to his feet from where he had pulled Bobby to safety, only to run to the former dig site and literally started clawing at the dirt, screaming as he did so. The anguish in his voice as he cried his partner’s name put to bed any doubts that their feelings weren’t mutual.

God, Eddie was an idiot. Maybe he could get a recording of it from the news people and force him to watch it?

After Bobby had to bodily stop Buck from digging through the wet earth with nothing but his two hands, Chimney lost track of him. It wasn’t until they were regrouping on the porch of the farmhouse that he noticed he was missing entirely.

“Where’s Buck?” he asked.

“Hell if I know,” Hen said.

“Shouldn’t we, I don’t know, go find him? Ask him what to do?”

“Seriously, Chim?”

“Hey, he knew where Hayden was, and I’m pretty sure he knew Eddie was going to cut his line. The man’s psychic, I don’t know why I’m the only one willing to take advantage of that on calls.”

“Psychic?” the Search and Rescue commander asked, looking between them.

“I should have listened to him,” Bobby said, fingers pinching the bridge of his nose. “Buck told me he needed more time, I should have listened.”

“You couldn’t have known, Cap,” Hen tried reassuring him, but the captain only scoffed and shook his head.

“How long can my man last down there?” he asked the SAR commander.

“We’re talking thirty feet of wet earth coming right down on top of him,” was what the man gave as an answer. Chimney and Hen glanced at each other in concern, because what the hell were they going to do if they couldn’t get Eddie out? How they hell would they get Buck through that?

Twice, Buck had to watch as Eddie was lowered into the drilled out tunnel. Twice, Eddie cut his line when they tried to pull him up before he could get to Hayden. Twice, lightning struck the drilling rig, sending it falling to the ground and collapsing the tunnel. Twice, he found himself trying to claw his way through the dirt to get to Eddie beneath it.

And now he was here, sitting at the water’s edge, hoping he hadn’t stepped on a butterfly somewhere along the way and fucked everything up. The others were still gathered in front of the farm house, planning out recovery operations. Because they were all certain that Eddie was dead, with maybe Bobby as the exception. But Eddie couldn’t be dead, Buck refused to even accept that as a possibility. And if it was somehow the reality of things, then Buck would gladly risk Ichabod carrying through with his threat.

It would be as worth it now as it was after Chris and the tsunami.

Beneath the waters of the artificial lake, he could make out a faint green glow that got larger and larger, closer and closer. Buck held his breath, and kept holding it until Eddie’s head breached the surface. If he hadn’t already been sitting, he probably would have collapsed in relief.

“Eds!” he called out, getting to his feet. His voice was hoarse from the screaming he had done earlier. ”Eddie! Over here!”

Eddie paddled across the water to him, and he helped pull him onto the shore. He was muddy and soaked and trembling and beautiful, and Buck clung at him for several moments.

“Fuck you,” he said when he pulled away, though there was no heat to the shaking words. “Fuck you for putting me through that again.”

“Were you really,” Eddie panted, shivering. “Just waiting for me here?”

“The others are back up there planning to use thermal cams to find your heat signature.”

“Wouldn’t be easy, I’m-”

“Pretty cold, I know,” Buck said, letting out a relieved breath as he tugged one of his arms over his shoulders. “C’mon, let’s get you checked out so we can get you home. Chris will be disappointed if he can’t show you off on Friday.”

“Oh yeah,” Eddie sighed. “Big date. Can’t miss it.”

Chapter End Notes

This chapter was entirely brought to you by the image of Buck sitting patiently by the water for Eddie.

The Symbolism of Red

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Here’s the thing about Red Delacroix: Deep down inside, there was an inescapable part of Buck that hated the man. Not because he was a jerk or a bad guy or anything like that - because he was actually the exact opposite of those things - but because Red was his future. He had known it when he first met him, when everything still seemed hopeful and bright, and he knew it now, after Maddie and Chimney had left him, after Eddie had started for the door. He looked at Red, the retired hotheaded firefighter, all alone after everyone he cared about left him behind one way or another, and he could only see himself thirty, forty years into the future.

It would probably be better to say that Buck hated what the man represented.

The fact that the first time Buck met him, it was because everyone he cared about was too busy with their own families to have time for him, really helped to drive the comparison home.

Perhaps it was because he was actually a masochist, or perhaps it was his innate urge to try and fix things, or perhaps it was because he was still trying to prove to himself that he wouldn’t be alone in his final days by not letting Red be alone in his. Whatever the reason, Buck once again passed on the offer from Eddie to help wrangle a bunch of children during Chris’ first time hosting a sleepover - not that the offer had ever been serious, not the original time and definitely not this time - and slunk into the bar he knew Red was waiting at. It wasn’t even one he typically frequented, he couldn’t even remember what had brought him to it that first go around. He honestly wouldn’t doubt it if someone said it was the universe itself trying to make a point. But he found himself there again, this time with a goal in mind beyond drinking away his loneliness in public.

It was a testament to how lonely the old man was, that he didn’t even question Buck joining him with a coke.

“I’m telling you, we’re just bringing down the last of this litter, and that mother bobcat, she’s got a laser-beam focus on Mac and me,” Red was telling him, an hour and several beers later, the two of them having moved to one of the booths. He kept blinking as he spoke, he was so drunk. “And she’s saying, ‘Forget about the damn bushfire, you better not harm one hair on any of my babies.’”

They both laughed, and then the retired firefighter sighed, his mood dropping.

“Oh, Mac. He bought it in Two-Thousand Two,” he said. “Powerlines. Chatsworth.”

“I’m sorry,” Buck said, grimacing. “Do you still talk to any of your old crew?”

He knew he didn’t, but a part of him still hoped for a different answer. A stupid, naive part of him.

“At first, you know, there were barbecues and parties and swapping war stories.” Red laughed softly. “And then, there were Christmas cards and emails about the grandkids. Nowadays, the only thing that gets us all together in the same room is when another one of us is dead.”

The worst part was, Buck could see it. He could see the barbecues and the get-togethers that were held at the Grant-Nash residence, or occasionally at Hen’s or Eddie’s, and he could easily envision them just stopping one day as they all moved on. After Eddie leaves and he’s no longer part of the 118, too busy with whatever new and safer thing he moves onto to find time for Buck. After Bobby retires and he just wants to enjoy his golden years with Athena in peace, Buck’s presence exhausting and unwelcomed. After Hen becomes a doctor and becomes too busy saving lives in surgery to keep in contact with any of them, letting them go just as she and Chimney had let go of those that were there before Buck.

And Buck could easily, far too easily, imagine the station filling with new faces as the old familiar ones disappeared. Buck could easily imagine himself becoming a ghost at the station, just as he had been in Abby’s apartment, left behind and forgotten and refusing to accept that the people he loved and considered family had all moved on without him.

“We’re all gonna go eventually, kid,” Red continued. “You just don’t want to be the last one left.”

“It’s an awful feeling, isn’t it? Realizing you’re being left behind.”

Red barked a laugh.

“You’re far too young to be sounding that old.”

“I’m an old soul,” Buck joked.

Eventually, Red reached the point of being almost too drunk, and the much more sober Buck escorted him home. The older man complained about it, of course, in the same way that Buck complained about it whenever someone heaped concern upon him. He said the lines, the whole time hoping someone would read between them for the pleading that was truly there.

“Enough good deeds, you can get home,” Red told him, turning on a floor lamp in his living room and stripping off his coat. “I’m all right.”

“Oh, hey.” Buck ignored the words and focused on the pleading between the lines. He pointed at a black and white group photo on the wall. “This is your house, right?”

“Yeah, that’s my family. Fightin’ One-Thirty-Four,” Red said, coming up beside him, fondness lining his tone. He pointed at each face in turn as he listed their names. “That’s our cap, Al Prescott. And then Phillie, I told you about him.  And then there’s Arno, Mac, and that’s me. We were about your age around then.”

“John Delacroix,” Buck said, reading it off the Certificate of Commendation hanging in a frame by the photos. He had forgotten that Red wasn’t actually his name, spending so long calling him that in his head. To be fair, he also sometimes forgot that Chimney’s name was actually Howard.

“The guys used to call me Code Red because I was a bit of a hothead when I was young,” he said, playfully punching at him and causing them both to laugh. “You know about that, don’t you, Buck? The hotheads?”

“And uh, who’s this?” Buck asked, holding up the photo of a young Red and a blond woman. He remembered she was his could-have-been, and that she had dementia now, but he could not for the life of him remember her name.

“Cindy, the one that got away,” Red told him. “We were gonna be married.”

“What happened? Was it the job or…?”

“The job,” he sighed. “Keeps us pretty busy. It’s hard for someone not to feel like they’re always coming a distant second. She got us tickets for the World Series in Eighty-Eight, home game for the Dodgers playing Oakland.”

“But the job got in the way.”

“The job got in the way.” Red nodded. “I had already scheduled a shift, and I figured, nobody was gonna beat the A’s anyway. So I told her I’d make it up to her later.”

“But there was never a later.”

“She was gone by the fifth game,” the old man said. “You got anybody kid?”

The question actually made him laugh, which surprised the older man.

“Not really, but there was someone…” Buck sighed. “We worked together, and then he, uh. Got hurt on the job, and his kid was scared, so he decided to leave.”

It was only after he said it that he remembered Red was not of his generation, nor even Bobby’s, and he swirled around to face him in a panic. But Red was merely smiling sadly at him, with a hint of disappointment.

“And you didn’t follow him?”

“This job is my life,” he said, and the words sounded pathetic even to his own ears.

“No it isn’t.” Red was shaking his head at him. “It can’t be. You can be the hero, save lives, but you can’t neglect having one of your own. The last thing you want is to be at the end, holding nothing but regrets.”

He gripped Buck’s arm lightly.

“Trust me, kid. I know.”

“Red is a forty-year veteran of the department. Two citations of bravery,” Buck was telling them. He had been off the entire shift, quiet and subdued even on scenes, and it had taken all day for Eddie to get him to crack. And when he did, sitting off to the side as everyone else took turns at shooting pool while they took advantage of the break between calls, he told them about the retired firefighter he’d met at a bar, which raised multiple levels of concern for Eddie. Starting with: did he need to go through his apartment before things became a problem again? And including: why the hell did he pass up helping Eddie with Chris’ sleepover to chat up an old drunk? “Now he’s alone in an apartment he pays for with his pension.”

“From the way you described him,” Eddie said, lining up a shot. “It sounds like he’s okay with that.”

“No he isn’t.” Buck said it with such a conviction that Eddie jerked his head up to look at him. “And I’m not okay with it.”

“So it’s all about you,” Chimney said, only to shrivel under the strength of Eddie’s glare.

“That’s not what I’m-” Buck cut himself off with a sigh. “Whatever.”

“It does seem like his situation is bothering you more than it bothers him,” Bobby chimed in, trying to be diplomatic.And failing at it, in Eddie’s opinion.

“Of course it bothers me,” Buck said, settling his chin on top of his arms, which were crossed over the back of the chair he was sitting in. “He has no friends and no family, the guys from the One-Thirty-Four don’t talk anymore. They all just… Left him.”

Eddie met their captain’s eyes over the pool table and saw the same concern he was feeling. He heard the words and couldn’t help but remember the crazy woman on the overpass and everything Buck had said to her.

(“And he tells you that he’s leaving, just like everyone else leaves, and you realize that you’re going to end up all alone. Again. Just like before, just like always.”)

“I’m sure they didn’t mean to, Buck. Life gets busy,” Hen said, lining up her pool cue and taking a shot. “Especially when you don’t work in the same firehouse anymore.”

“And that’s supposed to make it better, how?” he asked.

“I…” she trailed off, uncertain, and looked at Bobby for help.

“That won’t be the case with us, Buck,” the captain said, Chimney nodding in agreement. “We’re family.”

“Yeah, it’s never gonna change,” Eddie said, and turned to look at Buck just in time to see his face somehow fall even further. He frantically gestured at Hen and Chimney. “You two! You still keep in touch with the guys that used to be here, right?”

Please say yes, please say yes, please say-

“Um,” Hen started, and that one syllable was a knife to Eddie’s hopes. The paramedics shared loaded looks. “I don’t know if we’d call some of them friends.”

“I spoke with Tommy last year,” Chimney offered, and the fact that Eddie didn’t even know who that was did not bode well. “I was calling to ask for a favor, but…”

“Anyways!” Eddie turned back around to meet Buck’s eyes. He wanted to grab him and shake him and promise him that he wasn’t going to be like the other Eddie, that he wasn’t going to leave him. But he didn’t know the words he needed to say to make him believe. “That won’t happen to us.”

Buck didn’t say anything. He just got up and headed for the loft stairs, not looking back at any of them as he climbed down them to the bay.

“Should we be concerned about that?” Chimney asked after he was gone.

“Yes!” Eddie hissed.

“You two couldn’t have just lied to him?” Bobby had his arms crossed across his chest and the disappointment coming off him in waves was almost palpable.

“That was an option?” Hen glanced at Chimney.

“Lying is always an option!” Eddie snapped. “You’re a parent, you know that!”

“I think the real question, Hen,” Chimney said, rolling his pool cue between his hands. “Is which one of us is going to end up leaving?”

When Maddie came over - full of sisterly concern because no doubt Chimney had run off to gossip with her as soon as the shift was over, if not before - he distracted her with the tales of how badly he had screwed up the first go around, with Cindy and Red. He had given the old man the option of meeting her, this time able to warn him ahead of time about the dementia, but he had declined. He wanted to keep the memories of her as she was then, he told him, and not ruin them with the ghost of how she was now.

“I was such an idiot, trying to help him,” he told her. “She didn’t even know who he was. She was afraid of him. You don’t get over that so easily, I know Abby didn’t, when her mom had moments like that.” He had told Maddie a bit about Abby, both how she’d been his friend in this timeline, and how she’d been more in the other. “And I know how much it hurts to have someone you love look at you but not actually see you, y’know?”

“You mean, when you first…?”

“Yeah. I walked into the station that second first day, absolutely certain I’d just had a screwed up dream.” Buck laughed a little. “And then there they were, sitting at the table, eating. They didn’t even recognize me, which, duh. I was just some new probie, replacing someone that was actually their friend. Or, not friend, I guess. Hen and Chimney don’t even talk to him anymore.”

“So, I’m just going to go out on a limb here,” Maddie said, moving from his recliner to sit closer to him on the couch. “And say that I think everything with and about Red is hitting a little close to home. I mean, a lonely hero firefighter, pining for his lost love?”

“I’m not always lonely,” he told her, not meeting her eyes.

“When you’re with Eddie and Chris, you mean?” she asked, sighing when he blushed but didn’t say anything. “Listen, I don’t know what happened in the other time, but this Eddie? He loves you. The only one blind to it is you.”

“Maddie, he’s straight.”

“Is he, though?”

“I have an entire timeline that says he is.”

“Do you, though?” she asked. “Did that Eddie even know you weren’t straight?”

“I… Huh.” He blinked. “But, there was a girlfriend. And Shannon. He never mentioned anyone else, guy or girl…”

“Did you?” Maddie asked.

“Well-” he started, and then stopped, because no, he hadn’t. By the time Eddie showed up in his life he wasn’t talking much - if at all - about his romantic and sexual misadventures before Abby, utterly embarrassed by the way he used to be. So the Eddie of Before would only have the partners of Bucks 2.0 and 3.0 as evidence for his sexuality, and they had all just happened to be women. “Huh.”

“Listen, like I said. I don’t know what happened in the other time,” Maddie said. “But maybe Eddie has always known he was attracted to guys and just didn’t say for whatever reason. Or maybe you were his closet key. Or maybe sexuality is a confusing mess and we’re both thinking too hard about it. What’s the worst that could happen? If you go up to him today and confess your feelings to him. What’s the worst that could happen?”

“He could leave.”

Chapter End Notes

3.16 and everything to do with Red was always going to be a good source for dramatic irony in this story. I've been wanting to get to this chapter, and the next one, for ages.

The Ghost of You(rself)

Chapter Notes

I am posting this, and then I am going to go into hiding. Enjoy! :')

He had been expecting the call about Red being in the hospital since, pretty much, the moment he gave the man his number. That didn’t mean Buck was ready to walk into the room to find him in a hospital bed, hooked up to oxygen and an IV. That didn’t mean seeing how close to the end they truly were wasn’t a punch to the gut.

“Hey,” he said as he entered the room. “I came as soon as I could. What, uh. What happened?”

“I’m sorry,” Red groaned. “I didn’t know who else to call.”

“Hey, it’s fine,” Buck told him, pulling up one of the uncomfortable chairs so he could sit at his bedside. “That's why I gave you my number, so you could call it.”

“I’ve been arguing with these doctors for the last hour,” the old man complained. "They won’t release me, so I think you wasted a trip down here.”

“I’m visiting a friend. I don’t think that’s a waste.”

“Oh, you stupid kid,”  Red scolded, shaking his head. “You’ve picked a bad time for that. I’m on the express out of here. Mesothelioma, got diagnosed last year. I actually lasted longer than they thought I would, but you know me.”

“Stubborn.”

“Stubborn,” the old man agreed, nodding. “Don’t ever want to quit. Until now.”

“Hey, bad time or not, I’m not going to just leave you,” Buck told him. “No one deserves to be alone, especially when…”

Red barked out a laugh.

“What do you know? Maybe it wasn't a screwed up dream after all.”

“What wasn’t?” Buck asked, blinking at him in confusion.

“It was uh, after Mac passed. In Two-Thousand Two, remember? I was maybe a bit too drunk to be behind the wheel, y’know? But I was also too drunk to know that I was too drunk, so.” He shrugged his paper gown-covered shoulders and laughed at himself. “Anyways, there I was, drunk as a skunk and utterly lost, when suddenly I’m- I dunno, I was on a road I had never seen before. And there in the middle of the intersection was this creepy guy, dressed all in black, with this hat on.”

Buck stared at him, unable to form any appropriate response to the story yet, because holy shit.

“My car dies, I get out, and the guy comes up to me. He’s all, ‘howdy stranger’ and then we talk for a bit, because I was too drunk and stupid to recognize a bad idea when I saw one. But he was easy to talk to.” The old man sighed. “He said his name was, uh. Ick-something. Icki- Icko-”

“Ichabod.’

“That’s it!” Red snapped his fingers and grinned at him. “You met him too?”

“Once or twice, maybe,” he said dully, still trying to formulate a proper response to everything.

“Huh, small world,” Red chuckled. “Well, we talk for a bit, and then he asks, ‘what do you want, Red?’ And I tell him, ‘I don’t want to be alone at the end.’ And then I woke up in my car, parked in front of my place. Didn’t even remember the drive home. I probably should have been more specific about what I wanted, I guess.”

“What do you mean?”

“Kid, I’ve been alone up ‘til now, haven’t I? But now it’s the end, and…” He flicked his hand limply in Buck’s direction. “What was it you said? He asked you, didn’t he?”

“I wanted to fix something,” Buck told him, feeling solemn.

“Well, you’re forty years too late to fix me,” Red said, laughing to himself. 

“Okay, so what can I do?”

“Sit with me for a while,” the older man said. “I never told you about how Arno broke his nose, did I? He was always pretty clumsy…”

“He passed away at Five Twenty-Three this morning,” Buck told Maddie as they both sat at his dining table, mugs of tea forgotten. “The department’s going to pay for the funeral.”

Maddie had invited herself over, concerned for her brother and how he was handling everything with Red. It turned out to be justified, as she had found the door unlocked and him sitting alone in the dark. She was so proud of him, for going out of his way to make sure an old man didn’t spend his last moments alone and forgotten. She was even prouder still, that he had probably known exactly who Red was and what was going to happen, and yet still opted to open himself up to that pain.

“At least he wasn’t alone in the end,” she offered him. “You were a good friend.”

“I still don’t know if I didn’t just do that thing that I always do,” he said. “Make it all about me, try to fix things to make myself feel better. Eddie once said I was the guy who liked to fix things.”

“There’s nothing wrong with that,” Maddie told him. “It’s one of the reasons we all love you.”

“I was literally born to fix something,” Buck grumbled. “Even if I failed then, too.”

“You didn’t fail at anything there,” she told him, reaching forward to grab his hand. “I don’t know the way I ended up telling you, but obviously I dropped the ball somewhere if you think that you failed. Because what happened with Daniel was not your fault. His life and his death were not your responsibility to bear, and to hell with whoever let you think that it was. And if it was me, well then. Fuck me.”

“Maddie!” Buck gasped. It was so stupid, but her brother was smiling, so it was a win in her book.

“And with Red, you were there when no one else was, both times,” she continued on, squeezing his hand. 

“The job was all he wanted to talk about,” Buck told her, his smile slipping. “It was all he had to talk about.”

“Evan, you’re not him. His life isn’t your future.”

Maddie didn’t know what she expected in response to her statement, but it definitely wasn’t the dark, bitter laugh that erupted from her brother.

“You don’t know that,” he told her, shaking his head. He drew his hand out of her loose grip, wrapping his arms around himself. “You really, really don’t know that."

“Yes I do,” she told him. “Because he didn’t have a sister. He didn’t have me.”

The way his eyes flicked over her, unconvinced and disbelieving, had something twisting in her stomach. She wasn’t certain what it was about that look, but it unsettled her. Then he looked away, the ambient lighting in the room not enough for her to make out his face and really figure out what that expression was.

“I know that I left you twice, once with mom and dad, and then again when things got rough with Doug, but I came back,” she said, trying to reach for him again. “Because you’re my brother and I love you.”

“I love you, too,” he told her, voice barely more than a whisper.

“You’re never going to be left behind, okay? No matter what.” She held up her hand, pinky out. “I promise.”

Buck turned his head to look at her, and then down to her hand. He reached out and then gently, oh so gently, pushed her pinky down to join her other fingers in her palm.

“Evan…?” she asked, his name shaking as it left her lips, because no. No, no, surely not. No.

“Don’t make promises you can’t keep, Mads,” he told her in a broken voice, and she could swear that she felt it as the world crumbled beneath her.

“Is everything okay, honey?” Athena asked. There had been anger surging through her, along with disgust and a distinct feeling of powerlessness that she hated. She had just gotten done at the scene, having watched through some of the videos they had found at the Not-Just-a-Peeping-Tom’s house, and really all she wanted was to decompress with some wine. But as she entered her kitchen to do exactly that, she found her husband stress baking.

Bobby looked up, opening his mouth to answer, only to frown at whatever he saw on her face.

“I could ask you the same,” he said. “What’s wrong?”

“You go first,” she told him, grabbing down a glass and fetching the half-full bottle that Buck brought the other week, when she invited him over to ask about Michael. “Mine is a bit… Case sensitive.”

“I’m worried.”

“I gathered that from how you’re making bread at- What time is it?” She checked the clock on the wall. “Nearly midnight. What are you worried about?”

“Buck,” Bobby told her, going back to directing his anxieties into the dough he was kneading. “The future. Buck and the future.”
