“This is about that retired firefighter,” Athena guessed, and he nodded. “I think it’s sweet, what he did for him. He’s such a kind boy.”

“He was desperate that Red not be alone,” he told her.

“Because Buck’s heart has always been too big for his own good.”

“No, Athena, I mean-” He let out an aggravated sigh. “I think…”

“You think…?”

“He’s never told us how far back he traveled. He’s never told us much about what happens,” he told her. “We all told him that what happened to Red was never going to happen to us, but he looked at us like… Like we were telling him the sun was always going to stay in the sky after he’d personally seen it set. And there’s what Eddie’s mentioned to me, and what Chimney just told me Maddie said…”

“What do you mean?” Athena asked, perching on the nearby stool, cup of wine forgotten.

“You remember that woman on the overpass, right? Wanted to be seen by her husband, pulled a gun?” Ahena nodded, gesturing for him to get on with it. “From what I understand, when Buck was talking to her, he took the opportunity to vent about the future. And Eddie was able to hear some of it.”

“Okay, so what did our boy say?”

“According to Eddie, he… He told her about someone he was close to leaving him on Christmas. About how they told him he was leaving because their kid was scared of losing their father.”

Athena drew in a sharp gasp.

“You think he was talking about Eddie?”

“Eddie thinks he was talking about Eddie,” Bobby told her, and she watched as he just about throttled the dough. “You weren’t there at the station, when Buck told us about Red. You didn’t see the way he just walked away when Eddie tried to promise that what happened with Red wouldn’t happen to them. To us.

“And he told us, Athena. The day after the tsunami. He told us how he felt like everyone was leaving him. We just missed it because we were too busy worrying he’d had a psychotic break to listen.”

“You haven’t told me about what Chimney said. What happened with Maddie?”

“I didn’t understand most of it, and I don’t think he did either,” Bobby said. “But apparently she tried to promise that he wouldn’t be left behind, and he just… Shut her down. Told her not to make promises she couldn’t keep.”

She took a long drink of her - really very good, props to Buck - wine.

“And you’re worried that you just got a glimpse into why he was frightened enough to run straight into the arms of… Whatever it was that sent him here.”

“I’m worried that I’ll end up failing my kid again,” he told her. He let out a sigh and let go of the dough, turning to face his wife. “What was it that made you upset?”

“That man I arrested the other day at your scene? With the drone?” Athena waited for him to nod before continuing. “I thought he was just using his drone to be a voyeur.”

“But…?

“But he’s not just anything,” she said, the darkness of her tone getting across what she couldn’t outright tell him. “And we let him go. Because the Feds didn’t want to drive all the way across the city just for a run of the mill Peeping Tom.”

“Oh God.”

“Honestly, on my way home, I was debating the pros and cons of asking Buck for help,” she confessed. “But there’s the risk that we never caught him again, or that he doesn’t remember the details. And I don’t want to treat our boy like he’s just a source of information.”

“Ask him anyway,” Bobby told her, shrugging when she raised an eyebrow in question. “Maybe he can help. Maybe it’ll help take his mind off Red. If nothing else, it’ll give you an excuse to check in with him.”

“Please,” she scoffed, rolling her eyes. “I’ve never needed an excuse.”

Buck couldn’t say what was fueling his decision to do this. Maybe it was reliving everything with Red, and therefore being reminded of him and Cindy. Maybe it was the discussion he’d had with Maddie, and the realization that he’d been working on faulty assumptions for years. Maybe he was panicking about what he’d unintentionally revealed to Maddie and was just running away from it and to this as a distraction.

No matter the reason, he was finally doing it.

The apartment was mopped and swept and vacuumed and dusted. There was no trash to take out, there were no dishes to be washed. It was as pristine as the day he moved in. Buck had even cooked them dinner, making something simple that he knew Eddie would love. He had almost dressed up for the occasion and gotten flowers, but he hadn’t wanted for everything to be overwhelming, he hadn’t wanted to be too much.

God, he was so nervous, but if it all went the way everyone seemed so sure it would…

The door opened and Buck froze mid-pace, spinning around to grin brightly at Eddie.

“Eds! You came!”

“Yeah. You asked me to,” he said, sniffing the air as he walked in. “What is that? It smells delicious.”

“It’s just, uh, something Bobby taught me how to make,” Buck said, wringing his hands.

“Are you okay?” Eddie asked, eyeing him up as he slipped off his shoes and set them by the door. “You seem… Nervous.”

“Well, I am.” He shrugged at his friend’s questioning eyebrow. “It’s not because of anything bad, I promise. It’s, uh. It’s actually a good thing? I hope?”

“You hope?” Eddie chuckled. “Whatever it is, I’m glad you’re not taking everything about Red as hard as you were.”

“I’ve been through it before,” he told him. “Speaking of! Apparently Red ran into Ichabod.”

“What?” Eddie stared at him, wide eyed, as he took a seat at the dining table.

“Yup. Apparently he ran into him after a funeral for someone from his station,” Buck explained, setting out the food. “Ichabod asked what he wanted, Red said he didn’t want to be alone at the end, and…” He waved at himself with his free hand. “What he wanted most in the world was to just… Not be alone.”

“I meant what I said that day at the station, Buck,” Eddie said, fixing him with brown eyes gone impossibly soft. “That won’t happen to us.”

Buck smiled at him and he wanted to believe, because he knew, logically, that leaving the station didn’t mean leaving him. Except logic rarely got along with fear, and there was too much evidence stacked up against him to believe that someone would actually stick around once they started edging for the exit. But it was Eddie, whom he loved so very much, and he wanted to believe him. He was desperate to believe him.

He took a breath and took the dive.

“I love you,” he blurted out, and Eddie froze. This wasn’t some mumbled answer to Taylor’s half-assed comment. This was the truth, his entire truth. So he said it again. “I love you. I don’t know when it happened, because I didn’t fall in love. It was too gradual to be a fall. You know how they say that if you stick a frog in a pot of water and slowly bring it to a boil, that it will stay in there until it boils alive? It’s not true, it’ll hop out as soon as it gets too hot. But it was like that.

“I think it started after the grenade, after you told me I could have your back and I told you that you could have mine. Or, or, maybe it was that day at the station with Chris. Or maybe it was every day in between and every day since, but I love you. It happened so gently and so gradually that I didn’t even realize how much I loved you until you were gone and I was alone. I didn’t realize until you weren’t there how lonely my world was without you in it.

“I love you, Eddie.”

Eddie’s face was a mask of… Something. Something far too close to heartbreak, although that couldn’t be it. Maddie, Shannon, they seemed convinced that Eddie felt something for him. And there was that night in the kitchen, when he was certain that Eddie had been flirting with him. Why would he look like hearing Buck say those words physically hurt him?

And he wasn’t saying anything back.

“Eddie?” he tried. “Eddie, please, say-”

“No, you don’t.” He shook his head, words filled with anguish.

“W-what?”

“You don’t love me.”

“What? Yes I do! I just told you that I-”

“You love the other Eddie,” he said, and that answer was so unexpected that Buck was shocked into silence. “The Eddie you were a brat with at the beginning, but who forgave you. The Eddie whose wife died, the Eddie who joined a fight club and screamed at you in a grocery store. The Eddie whose kid managed to sneak out for an uber while he was too busy chatting with his teacher girlfriend. You’re in love with the Eddie who left you and who you ran away from.”

Buck stood there and didn’t know what to say, didn’t know how to begin to even comprehend what he was hearing. That wasn’t- None of that was true. It wasn’t true. It couldn’t be true. He was in love with Eddie. Just Eddie. The only Eddie Diaz that there was.

“You’re not in love with me,” the other man said, either ignorant or heedless of the pain his soft and gentle words were causing him. He was smiling at Buck, a small and sad thing with tears. “You’re in love with a ghost.”

And Buck had been wrong, so very wrong, in what he told Maddie before.

This was the worst that could happen.

Aftermath

Chapter Notes

Posting this a bit early, because I have a migraine and I didn't want to leave you all hanging.

Ever since he had told them about Red, Hen had been concerned for their youngest member. Sure, okay, she didn’t understand why Buck would be so torn up over a lonely man that, to her, didn’t sound torn up about it himself. But Buck had seemed so uncharacteristically subdued ever since that day, worryingly similar to how he’d been with the boy in the well. Chimney seemed to think it meant that one of them was going to end up leaving, sometime in the future.

Perhaps Buck had seen her own departure, as she chased after her new found dream of being a doctor. Not that she had mentioned it to her wife or her best friend yet.

Hen didn’t know the relationship Red had with the people of his firehouse, so she couldn’t truly compare it to her own experiences. Was the 134 of Red’s day like it had been at the 118, before Bobby and Buck? Or was it like how the 118 was now? Although they couldn’t have been, not if the old man was truly as alone as Buck said he was. Chimney, Bobby, Buck, Eddie: they were her family, just as much as Karen and Denny, and now Nia. Short of something catastrophic, like what happened to that station in Texas, she couldn’t imagine them not being there years and years into the future. Even if she did manage to become a doctor and didn’t work with them every day.

Then again, maybe she couldn’t understand Buck’s fears and worries because she, unlike him, had someone to come home to. She had Karen, and she had Denny, and so she knew she would not be alone in her twilight days.

Who did Buck have?

Eddie, was the immediate answer. 

But who did he have outside of the station? Who did he have that wasn’t so intertwined with his job? There was Maddie, but considering she had gone no-contact before, after being minimal contact for years before that, Hen could see why Buck couldn’t trust her to continue being a permanent presence into the future. Plus, Hen didn’t trust Buck not to assume that Maddie would start putting boyfriend over brother.

Everyone’s happiness before his own.

So Buck’s behavior after meeting Red was concerning, even more so as he seemed to sink deeper and deeper into - as Chimney called it, when it was just the two of them - Sad Buck. Considering he hadn’t even known Red for a full week, he took the old man’s death rather hard. Then there was whatever had happened between him and his sister, which Hen still wasn’t sure about the details. Chimney had gone on about a pinky promise, but he’d been too busy panicking over an upset Maddie for her to get anything useful out of it.

And then, their last shift a couple days ago. Buck had come in with… Not quite his old bounce, but a new resolve. As if he had decided to do something and having decided, was able to look at the future with more hope than fear. 

Now, at the start of their next shift, she was hopeful that he would continue with that upward momentum. Except, that didn’t seem to be in the cards, because,

“Buck called in,” Bobby told her and Chimney as they joined him in the loft. When the shorter paramedic immediately opened his mouth, looking startlingly worried, the captain hurried to add, “He said that he wasn’t feeling well.”

“Buck called in sick?” Hen glanced at Chimney and saw the same disbelief in his eyes. “Should we take the ambulance over, make sure he isn’t actually dying as we speak?”

“Okay, but did he actually sound like he wasn’t feeling well?” Chimney pressed, “Or did he sound like there was, say, another tsunami and he needed to be heroic again?”

“I asked Athena to go check on him,” Bobby said.

“Check on who?” Eddie asked, cresting the top of the stairs. “Is, uh. Is Buck not in yet?”

“He called in,” Hen said, and watched as what looked uncomfortably like guilt flickered across his face.

“Oh,” the man said. Just,

“Oh?” Chimney repeated. “Buck willingly called in, when the last time he did that he ended up saving your kid and his mother from a natural disaster, and all you have to say is, oh?”

“Did he seem okay when you saw him?” Bobby asked.

“When I saw him?” Eddie asked, looking momentarily panicked.

“C’mon, Eddie, we all know you practically live out of each other’s pockets,” Chimney said, rolling his eyes. “You’d have a better idea of if he was sick than Maddie would.”

“He, uh. He didn’t seem sick when I saw him,” the former army medic answered, not looking at any of them. “But I haven’t talked to him in a couple days, so…”

He trailed off to pull out his phone, his face a mixture of expressions that Hen couldn’t really place. Fear and hope, followed by disappointment and guilt. At the same time, Bobby’s own phone chimed and he let out a small curse when he checked it.

“Athena says he wasn’t home,” he told them, sounding worried.

“He’s with Shannon and Christopher,” Eddie said, frowning at his screen. He showed them the picture his ex-wife sent him of his son and Buck on a playground somewhere.

“Well, if something was going to happen that we needed to be worried about, I’m sure he would have said. So there’s nothing to be worried about,” the captain said, sounding even more worried than he did before. “Eddie, maybe you could stop by after shift?”

“I, uh. I don’t think that’s a good idea, Cap.” He sounded guilty, and wouldn’t look away from the picture on his phone to meet their eyes.

“Why?” Hen demanded. “What, did you two have a fight?”

“Something like that.”

“Someone’s calling you,” Shannon said, eyeing Buck's phone where he had it laying on the picnic table. It was on silent, vibrating against the wood. Buck didn’t even glance at it, opting to instead grin and wave at Chris when the boy called his name. After spending two days wallowing in his bed, he had called Shannon and asked to crash her mother-son time.

“It’s probably just people wondering why I’m not at work.”

“Yeah, why aren’t you?” she asked, setting her elbows on the table and leaning on them. “You have the same schedule as Eddie, unless he’s taking overtime. I get the weekends he has a twenty-four hour, which is this weekend. So…”

“I just wasn’t feeling well,” he said, giving her the same excuse he gave Bobby.

“But you’re feeling well enough to run after Chris.”

“That’s easy, he’s not very fast,” Buck quipped, trying to smile. He wasn’t sure how convincing of a smile it was, though. It had been easier around Chris, because his Superman could make him smile on even the darkest of days, but now it was just him and Shannon. Actually, it might have been the first time it was just him and Shannon in… Ever.

“That sounds like something Eddie would say.” Though he tried to hide the wince at his name, she must have seen it anyway. “Okay, what did my ex-husband do?”

“W-what?”

“What did my ex-husband do?” she repeated.

“He didn’t do anything,” he denied.

“Right, and that’s why you looked like I stabbed you when I said his name.”

“We, uh. We had a disagreement.’

“What sort of-” Shannon cut herself  off to glance at his phone again. “Okay, who’s Police Mom and why does she keep calling you?”

Buck almost killed himself diving for his phone to answer it.

“‘Thena!” he greeted her, fixing his biggest grin on his face, even though the police sergeant couldn’t see it. “How are you on this fi-?”

“Boy, do you know how many times I’ve called you?” she growled, and he swallowed at the tone. “I stopped by your place to check on you and you weren’t there.”

“Y-yeah, sorry, I’m at-”

“The park with Shannon and Chris,” she said, cutting him off. “Bobby told me.”

“How did Bobby know?”

“I sent Eddie a picture,” Shannon answered, which made sense, he guessed. 

“Oh, uh. Okay. Was there something you needed or…?”

“I need you to answer your phone when I call,” Athena said, and he started nodding frantically.

“Yes, ma’am,” he said, when he realized she still couldn’t see him. 

“But Bobby was worried about you.”

“I told him that I just wasn’t feeling well,” Buck said, the excuse sounding lame even now. It was true, though. It just so happened that “not feeling well” in this instance translated to heartbroken.

“You’ll have to forgive him the concern, Buckaroo,” Athena said. “Considering the last time you willingly missed work, you showed up in the aftermath of a natural disaster.”

“No disasters this time.” Except his life. “I promise.”

“Good,” she said, and the sigh of relief she let out made the line crackle. “Then I’ll let you go and tell Bobby everything’s fine. I need to get back to this case.”

“Case?” Buck asked, sitting up.

“Don’t you worry about it, Buckaroo,” she scolded him. “Just enjoy your day at the park. But then we will be talking about whatever is troubling you.”

“Yes, ma’am,” he agreed. When she hung up and he set his phone back down, he looked across the table to Shannon, whose eyebrows were raised in judgment. “What?”

“You sounded exactly like I used to when my mother got upset with me.”

“Well, she cares more than my actual mom.”

It felt like Bobby was constantly worried whenever it came to Buck, especially since the truck bombing and then the tsunami. For those brief months after Christmas, things had started looking up and he felt like he could breathe easily. And then Buck came into the station that day and told them about Red, and from there he showed a small yet terrifying glimpse into what the future might hold.

He wasn’t sure which worried him more now, however: the young man calling into work, or him showing up on Bobby’s doorstep in the middle of the night.

“Hey, Bobby.” Buck smiled, or tried to smile. It looked more like a grimace. “Am I, uh. Am I interrupting anything?”

“Nope, it’s just me tonight,” the captain assured him, letting him through the door and leading him to the living room. “Athena’s still at work.”

“Oh, that case, right?” Buck’s voice had an odd tone to it.

“Yes,” he said, drawing the word out as he took in the sight of the young man before him. Buck looked tired, and perhaps a bit stressed, shifting his weight between his feet and rubbing at his arms. “Is that what you’re here to talk about?”

“No.” The answer came with a ducking of his head. “I actually- I probably should have done this at the station, but I didn’t want to risk…”

“Risk what?” Bobby asked, concern skyrocketing.

“I can’t be on A-shift,” Buck said, still refusing to meet his eyes. The statement took the captain’s breath away. “I am here to request a shift change, at least for a little while.”

“May I ask why?”

“If I told you it was personal, would-?”

“Buck.”

Bobby watched his Adam’s apple bob at his throat. The young man took a long, deep breath, and then let it out.

“I can’t work with Eddie.” He sounded pained as he said it. “I can’t even- I just can’t.”

“Buck, what happened?”

“I told him I loved him.”

And Bobby could guess exactly how that went. The talk with Eddie just before New Years had been one of the most frustrating conversations that he could remember having. And the worst part was, the captain couldn’t even say he had been entirely wrong in what he said then. Buck had trouble at times differentiating between the people of this timeline and the people he knew in the other, he had even admitted to such when opening up about why he was so hostile towards Lena Bosko. Bobby had experienced his own frustration with that, when Buck had described the actions of his counterpart as if the Bobby he was talking to had been the one to do it.

But did that make Eddie right to think that Buck didn’t truly love him at all?

(Personally, Bobby thought the man was being an idiot.)

“I could move him, instead.”

“That would just be punishing him,” Buck said, sounding as tired as he looked. “And that wouldn’t- He doesn’t deserve to be punished for how he feels.”

“The option is still there, though.”

“I know,” and he finally gave a real smile, small though it was. “Thanks, though.”

“Do you want to talk about what happened?”

“No,” Buck said. “Can I just… Do you have any ice cream?”

“I think Athena and May will understand if we break into their stash.”

Stupid Choices

Eddie Diaz hated himself. He hated that he couldn’t just accept Buck’s feelings, and he hated that he broke the man’s heart, and he hated that he ran away from the destruction he wrought. He hated the Eddie Diaz that left on Christmas, and he hated the one who had to stand there and listen to Buck’s confession, both on the overpass and in his apartment. The worst part was that, when Buck first started speaking at their failed date - and it was a date, Eddie should have realized what was going on when he opened the door - Eddie had been so… Excited. Overjoyed.

And then…

“... I didn’t even realize how much I loved you until you were gone and I was alone.”

Any possibility of deluding himself into believing that Buck had been speaking about him died with those words. Because when had Eddie ever just left him before that night? When, in all the days and weeks and months and years up to that point, had he allowed Buck to ever be alone? It just made it all so very obvious: the man he loved didn’t love him, not truly. He loved the ghost of a man that existed only in his memories.

Eddie didn’t have those memories, he didn’t live those experiences. When Buck told stories of the other him - always with such painful fondness - he had trouble recognizing himself in the words. He could not see himself ever just raging at Buck in the middle of the store, could not see himself becoming so distracted by a pretty face that he lost track of his own son. He could not see himself acting in such a way that it convinced Buck that he would ever want to purposefully hurt him.

Had Shannon’s death affected him that much? Because that was not him, could not be him.

Eddie Diaz hated himself.

He had not been looking forward to their first shift together after Buck’s love confession. There was no way either of them were going to be capable of working together, much less existing in the same building, without something snapping and exploding. But it turned out that he needn’t have worried, because Buck had apparently wanted to put himself through it even less than he did.

Hearing that he called in filled him with guilt and relief, and then even more guilt because of the relief.

The others went along with Buck’s excuse that he was simply sick, although Eddie wasn’t certain if they actually believed it. They definitely knew something had happened between the two of them, because Bobby had asked him to drop by after shift and Eddie had to explain that it wasn’t perhaps the best of ideas at that moment. The assumption that they’d fought wasn’t too off-base, except for how it was entirely off-base. But Eddie wasn’t about to explain to Bobby and the others that Buck had confessed his love, only for him to shoot it down because Buck was actually confessing his love for a ghost. Not there at the station, and hopefully not ever.

(Buck wasn’t the only one perfectly willing to run away from things.)

Just before the end of their twenty-four hour shift, they were called to help reign in a runaway hot air balloon, and to rescue the little girl trapped in its basket. It made Buck’s absence, already impossible to overlook, an almost aching wound for Eddie. He knew the man would have had a trivia fact or ten at the ready, just waiting for the opportunity to be blurted out if he had been there. But Buck wasn’t there with them that day, because Eddie had taken a hammer to his heart and cried while he did it.

Afterwards, when the shift was over, Eddie almost decided to stop by Buck’s and… He didn’t know. Talk? Apologize? Ask to start over? It didn’t matter, because he took the path of least resistance and just went home, figuring he’d push off the awkwardness until their next shift.

Except Buck wasn’t there for that shift, either.

“Buck has asked to be switched over to B-shift,” Bobby told them as they gathered around in the loft. “Only temporarily. “

“What? Did he say why?” Chimney demanded.

“Personal reasons,” the captain said, and from the way his eyes flickered over to him, Eddie knew that Buck had told at least some of the details.

“Well, what kind of personal reasons?”

“The kind that are personal.”

“What sort of fight did you two have?” Hen asked, and Eddie turned to find her staring at him intently, eyes narrowed behind her glasses in a way that reminded him far too much of his neighbor's cat growing up, the one that used to leave dead birds on the porch.

“Uh- I-”

“Diaz! My office,” Bobby interrupted, and Eddie wasn’t sure if he was being saved or just switching torments. He caught Chimney mouth ‘Diaz?’ to himself as he passed the paramedic on his way to the captain’s office, feeling very much like he did whenever he got called into the principal’s office at school.

“Okay, I can explain-” he started as soon as the office door closed behind him.

“No.” The captain’s tone had his mouth clicking shut. “I’m talking right now, you’re listening. Clear?”

Eddie nodded.

“Good. Buck’s shift change is only for a couple weeks, maybe a month,” he continued. “Now, I don’t know precisely what went on the other night, but I know enough to understand exactly why the two of you may not be able to work together for the moment. As your captain, I am telling you this: the two of you will talk about this, and you will do it soon, and we’ll decide whether or not the two of you are able to continue working together in the future.

“Now, not as your captain: you are an idiot.”

“Bobby-”

“You’re still not talking,” Bobby snapped. “I understand why you feel the way that you do, and that is the only reason I am merely annoyed, instead of raging. My wife - you know, the police sergeant with a gun? She will not be so understanding. You are extremely lucky that she’s been too busy with work of her own to hear about any of this. And you best pray that your luck continues to hold out, because I will not be getting in her way.”

Eddie had never actually been in this position before, facing the anger of a significant other’s parents. The fact that Buck wasn’t his significant other, and that Bobby was not actually Buck’s father, did little to disabuse him of the comparison. It was a position he desperately did not want to be in again, and this was only Bobby.

The idea of facing down Athena in all her wrathful glory terrified him.

“So, what will you be doing? As soon as possible?” Bobby asked, and it took Eddie a moment to realize he was expected to respond this time.

“Talking to Buck.”

“Good. You’re dismissed.”

Eddie had never scurried out of a room faster.

Buck wasn’t certain if this was the best of ideas. Actually, that was a lie. Buck was entirely certain that this was a very bad idea. But at this point, what the hell did he have to lose?

(Literally everything, but that was logic speaking, and there was no place for that at this moment.)

In his memories, Studio Self Storage was… Dark. Imposing. Ominous. In the full light of day, with working power, it wasn’t any of those things. It was just an ugly cement building. The young man working the front didn’t even look up as he entered, airpods securely in place. Luckily, he wasn’t needed.

The entrance to the stairwell was already propped open.

Buck wasn’t sure what his game plan was here. He just had the vague notion of hovering nearby, maybe waiting at the coffee shop across the way, so he could ensure that Athena wasn’t alone and vulnerable. But at some point between opening the jeep door and stepping out, ‘being nearby’ became ‘being there,’ became ‘have a look around himself.’

Even with the fluorescent lights working, the inside made him feel claustrophobic. He remembered vividly that night, following after Bobby to where Athena was laying, bloodied and beaten. His feet took him in that direction now as he crept up the stairwell and onto the floor the sergeant had been - would be - on, wincing as the door closed with a metal clang behind him. Around a corner, and he was in the right hall.

There, a few units down, he could see one open. There wasn’t anyone nearby, and there wasn’t anyone in the unit itself, which contained a bed and a bunch of random junk, including a bike and paper towels. It looked more like a makeshift home than a storage unit.

He pulled out his phone, prepared himself for the anger he was invoking, and hit the call button.

“What is it, Buck?”

“Okay, now don’t be mad.” The silence that followed that request was telling and full of judgment. “‘Thena?”

“I make no promises.”

“I’m at this place, Studio Self-”

“Damn it, Buck!” He winced at the venom in Athena’s voice.

“So you, uh. You made the connection already?”

“Yes,” she snapped. “I’m on my way. Stay there and wait for me.”

“Yes ma-” The lights went out above him, plunging the halls into darkness lit only by the red glow of the emergency exit signs and the light of the setting sun through the window at the far end. “Oh damn it, the tree lady.”

“Tree lady?” The confusion of the topic change seemed to have distracted her from how angry she was with him, so that was a plus. “What tree lady, and what does she have to do with any of this?”

“She was uh, upset with some tee trimmers, I think?” He remembered her mostly for how amusing the lady had looked, with her hair all puffed up like an angry cat. “I don’t know, but she stole their truck and took out a power line.”

“Okay, well, this is going to be a mess and a half to drive through,” she said. “I’ll be there as soon as I can. In the meantime, don’t do anything. Don’t touch anything, don’t go inside-”

“Uh, well…”

“Damn it, Buck.”

“I’m not like, in his storage unit proper, right? I’m just in the hall…”

“Get out of the building and wait for me.”

“But you said not to do any-”

“Buck.”

“Heading outside now, yes ma’am.”

He hung up with her and tucked his phone in his pants. Taking a deep breath to fortify himself for her anger when she arrived, he turned for the stairwell-

Only for something heavy and metallic to slam into the side of his head. It sent him stumbling to his knees, clutching his head. Another strike sent him to the floor entirely.

“You’re not my usual type, I prefer them softer,” Jeffrey Hudson said, tossing aside the pipe he’d used to hit him. It clattered loudly against the cement of the floor, and for the pain that flared in his head at the noise, Buck felt like he’d been struck again. Hudson knelt down by his head. “You are pretty, though.”

The sun had set entirely by the time Athena pulled into the spot next to Buck’s jeep. The jeep’s owner wasn’t anywhere to be seen, and she began to seethe with anger. She had told the boy - the stupid, stupid boy - to be out here waiting for her. But where was he? Not where she could see him. Probably still inside, poking around. God help him if she found him in the storage unit itself.

Looking around the entrance, and finding it abandoned, she spotted a propped open door. Her flashlight illuminated the stairs on the other side.

“Dispatch,” she spoke into her radio. “Seven-Two-Seven-L-Thirty at Studio Self Storage doing a business check.”

“Copy, Seven-Two-Seven-L-Thirty,” Maddie Buckley’s voice responded.

The sergeant pulled out her sidearm and used her foot to kick the door open wider, slowly making her way into the cavernous stairwell. There was still no sign of Buck, no sign of another person at all, and worry started to push its way past the anger. Stepping onto the floor with the units, she shone her light into every shadowy corner, hoping to find her boy.

“Buck?” she called out. “Buck, where are-?”

A pained moan answered her, and she hurried around the corner, her light bouncing as she ran. There, in front of an opened storage unit, she found him. He was curled up in the fetal position, his hair matted with blood and the side of his face a mess of darkening colors.

“‘Thena?” he groaned, squinting up at her against the light.

“Oh God,” Athena gasped. She reached for her radio. “Dispatch, Seven-Two-Seven-L-Thirty, I need an RA unit at Studio Self Storage, along with backup and detectives. I have a possible-”

Someone slammed her into the wall with a cry, and then did it again, pressing her against it. She let go of the radio, stabbing her elbow into whoever was on her. They grunted in pain and slammed her into the wall again, before she managed to turn enough to push them away. The man - it was clearly a man, even in the darkness - punched her across the face, sending her stumbling back, before he grabbed her by the arm and threw her into the opposite side of the hall.

She barely caught herself before he was on her again, grabbing her by the hair to smack her head into the wall, making her see stars. Her gun fell from her fingers.

Athena kicked and punched and clawed and bit and elbowed. She tasted blood and was not sure whose it was. She lost track of what was happening beyond her bubble of survival, lost track of anything in the darkness except for this man and the need to survive.

And then he was gone, a dark shape tackling him to the ground. They landed in the pool of light made by her dropped flashlight, Buck on top of her assailant. She scrambled for her gun, just as she saw the man pull something out of his pants that glittered in the light.

“Buck!” she shouted, just as the man stabbed the knife into his side. 

Buck gasped and went limp, the man taking the chance to push him off, rolling him to the side. The man started to rise to his feet, only to freeze at the sight of her gun pointed at him.

“Do not move,” she snarled. Sirens were audible in the distance, quickly coming closer. Hudson - she could see it was him now, could recognize the face of the bastard she let slip through her fingers, even under the blood that covered it - eyed her, getting tenser and tenser as they could hear cars pulling up. “Don’t…”

Athena could see in his eyes the moment he decided, was ready as he lunged. Her finger squeezed the trigger before he even took a step, the knife slipping from his fingers as he fell, clutching at the bullet wound in his chest. Holstering her weapon, she ignored his unmoving form as she rushed to Buck’s side, falling to her knees.

“Buck?” Her hands pressed down on the bleeding wound in his side and he groaned in pain. “Buck, I need you to stay awake.”

“‘Thena?”

“Yeah, it’s me, honey,” she said, pressing down harder and ignoring the guilt that tugged at her when it made him whimper. “Help is on the way, I promise.”

“I- I tried…” he slurred. “My head hurts.”

“I know, it’ll be okay, I-” She was interrupted by him turning his head and retching onto the floor, and she automatically took a hand off the stab wound to keep his face out of the puddle of puke. She could hear booted feet running up the stairs to them. “It’ll be okay. It’ll be okay…”

In All the Ways That Count

Chapter Notes

Sorry this is late, my body decided to force a mini-vacation.

Note: The only medical knowledge I have comes from wee-woo shows. Do not @ me about any medical inaccuracies herein.

“Howdy, stranger.”

“And I’m back here again. Are you going to have me redo the day or send me back to the beginning, like you threatened last time?”

“Oh, no, you didn’t die.”

“Then- No offense, but what am I doing here, then?”

“Visiting.”

“Visiting… Alright, I’ll roll with it. Hey, uh, I don’t actually remember much of what happened…”

“That would be the head injury.”

“Right, but uh… Did he, uh… Did he…?”

“No. Apparently, you weren’t his type.”

“Not his type!? I’m everybody’s type!”

Maddie rushed into the hospital, almost barreling over the people in her way. She didn’t even stop to apologize, deeming them unimportant. It had been bad enough, having to listen to Athena get attacked and be unable to even offer reassurances that help was on the way. But then the sergeant had shouted her brother’s name, pain and terror clear as day in her voice. Maddie hadn’t even known her brother was there, hadn’t even known he was in danger. She had thought he was safe at work, with Howie and the others. Josh had immediately told her to go, the moment they got word of which hospital he was headed for.

When she came rushing into the waiting room, she found the whole team already there. So was Athena, still in uniform with her face bruised, hunched over a bit in her seat with an arm wrapped around her middle. Howie spotted Maddie first, and he rushed to wrap his arms around her.

“Any news?” she asked over his shoulder. Bobby paused in his pacing to shake his head.

“Not yet,” Howie said, stepping back to look at her but not letting go. “He’s still in surgery.”

“How bad is it?” she asked, and when silence greeted her, asked again. “How bad?”

“Based on the placement and the bleeding, we think the knife might have nicked his spleen,” Hen said, infuriatingly gentle. “He also showed signs of a severe concussion before he lost consciousness.”

“There was a metal pipe on the ground, near where I found him,” Athena said, looking up at her. “We think Hudson must have ambushed him with it, before I got there.”

“Who’s Hudson?” Maddie asked, and then immediately shook her head. “Never mind, I don’t care.”

She took the empty seat on the other side of Athena, right next to a deathly silent Eddie. He hadn’t said a word since she joined them, his eyes focused on some point between himself and the wall on the other side of the room. His fingers, she could see, were clutching tightly at the arms of the uncomfortable chair he was perched in.

“Eddie?” she tried, and got a grunt in response. “Where- Who has Christopher?”

“Carla,” he answered, tonelessly.

“Does he know? About what happened?”

“Not yet,” he said, and then, “I’m not leaving.”

“No one’s suggesting that,” she said, glancing over at the others. “I’m just… Who’s going to tell Christopher?”

“I’ll tell Carla, when we know more,” he answered. “And then she can tell him, or bring him here so I can. But I’m not leaving.”

Maddie sighed, accepting that she wouldn’t be getting anything else out of the man for the moment. She looked down at his hand, whiteknuckling the plastic armrest, and reached down to gently pry his fingers loose. Her own fingers wrapped around them, and she held down the wince when he squeezed them so tightly it hurt.

And Buck had tried to tell her once that the feelings weren’t mutual. God, her brother could be such an idiot.

“I’m guessing I didn’t keep her from being attacked, then. Was it one of those-?”

“No.”

“No?”

“I am not letting you blame the consequences of your bad choices on the unfathomable forces that dictate the movements of the universe.”

“What? But-”

“If you had stayed outside the building and waited for her, like a good puppy, it wouldn’t have happened. Probably. Instead you were an idiot and went poking around.”

“Wow, tell me how you really- What was that?”

“Hmmm?”

“It sounded like… Christopher?”

“Before we go inside, mijo, I need to tell you that it might look a little scary,” Eddie said, kneeling down in front of his son, just outside of Buck’s room. It was the morning after now, and Christopher had thrown a full scale tantrum at the idea of going to school instead of seeing his Buck. Carla hadn’t the heart to force him, opting instead to bring him to the hospital, to meet with his father and go from there. The others, with the exception of Maddie, had all gone home to rest. Well, Athena had gone directly to the station, to give her statement on what had happened.

(The sergeant had gotten out of it with bruises and a fractured rib, and none of them wanted to contemplate what could have happened if Buck’s concussed self hadn’t intervened when he did.)

“He’s not hooked up to any machines,” Eddie continued. “But his face is… He’s really hurt.”

“Okay, can I see him now?” Chris asked, swaying impatiently.

“Yeah, c’mon.” He stood up and held open the door for his son. Buck didn’t look any better than he had when Eddie had stepped out to see Chris and Carla. He was even paler than he normally was, which made the bruises beneath his eyes and that covered the side of his face even more stark in contrast. There was a bandage wrapped around his head, his disheveled curls poking out from beneath it..

Eddie had to stay in the doorway and spend a few moments breathing, lest he give in to the urge to throw something out a window. The correct target would have been Hudson, but nobody could ever accuse Athena Grant of being a lousy shot.

“Hey, Chris,” Maddie said, smiling wanly at him as he made his way to Buck’s bedside. She hadn’t moved from the chair she had claimed when she was allowed to see her brother, and the exhaustion was drawing lines on her face. But no one had tried to convince her to go home and sleep, not after the way she had nearly snapped Chimney’s head off when he attempted it.

“Hi, Maddie,” the boy said. “Someone hurt Buck?”

“They did,” she nodded.

“Can I sit with him?” he asked, looking back at his father. Maddie glanced at him, too, and he nodded with a sigh. Together, the two adults managed to get Chris in the bed next to Buck, situated so he wasn’t in any danger of yanking on the man’s IV.

“Has he woken up at all?” Eddie asked when they were done, taking Maddie aside and keeping his voice low. The doctor the night before, when they finally got news, had informed them that there hadn’t been any immediate signs of damage beyond the skull fracture. But they also said they wouldn’t really know until Buck woke up. The ‘if’ had been unspoken, but each of them had heard it all the same.

“Not in the twenty minutes it took you to go down, get Chris, and come back,” Maddie said, shaking her head.  She sounded grim, and he understood why. Both of them knew the dangers of head injuries, and what it could mean if Buck didn’t wake up soon.

“Dad?”

“Yeah, mijo?”

“Can Buck hear me?”

“Uh…” He looked at Maddie for help.

“Of course he can,” she said, shrugging at Eddie when Chris wasn’t looking. As they watched, he bent his head down and started talking about what he did at school the day before. It would have been a sweet scene, in literally any other context.

“And then Jimmy brought the worm in, but Ms. Flores screamed and made him throw it out…”

“Can I ask you a question?”

“You just did.”

“Oh, you are just hilarious. But seriously, I want to ask you something about Eddie.”

“And you are asking me, why?”

“Well, because you are literally the only other… Person? I’m gonna go with person. You are literally the only other person here. And unlike Bobby or Athena or Maddie, I know for a fact that you don’t care about my feelings enough to lie.”

“Hmmmm. Your relationship drama is entertaining enough, I guess. Carry on.”

“Right, I forget. I exist solely for your entertainment… When I told Eddie I loved him, he said I didn’t. He said… He said I was in love with a ghost.”

“Because you are.”

“But what does that mean!?”

“Would you say that the person you are now is the same as the man-child that first entered the fire station?”

“Well, no, I- I’ve changed. Or, I like to believe I have.”

“So if I took away all your memories since then and set you back to that point, you agree that you would not be you, yes? And if you went through wildly different experiences from that point on, that you would not be the same that is standing here, yes?”

“I- I guess, but… I wouldn’t be that different, right?”

“The core of you, perhaps. The broken child your parents made would still be there.”

“Hey! Getting a bit personal there.”

“You went back in time to fix things, expecting everything to somehow still be the same. But some things become defined by the cracks in their being. Your captain would be a vastly different person if you somehow managed to prevent the fire that took his family or prevented the injury that led to his addiction. Same for your sister, if you had managed to stop her from marrying her late husband.”

“What are you saying, exactly?”

“You cannot undo a crack so large and expect them to be the same. It defined everything the original Eddie Diaz did afterwards, and it is that Eddie Diaz you were in love with when you met this one.”

“But I- I-... I love them both.”

“Then convince him of that.”

The first thing Buck noticed was a weight pressed against his side, followed by a cottony feeling in his head and a dull ache. Blinking his eyes open, he almost immediately squeezed them shut when it felt like someone was trying to jab them out with flaming pins. He must have made some sort of noise, because he heard a rush of movement and then felt someone grabbing his hand.

“Buck?” he heard Maddie say. “Evan? You can open your eyes.”

He did, slowly, hesitantly. It was darker now than when he first tried it, the lights dimmed. Someone had placed Chris in the bed beside him, and the boy was dozing against his shoulder. The sight of it had him smiling.

“How are you feeling?” his sister asked.

“Like… Like I am on very good pain meds, and my head still feels like it’s trying to kill me.”

“That would be the skull fracture,” she said. Now that he could focus on her, he could see just how tired she looked, even with the smile she was shining on him.

“How long…?”

“A day,” she said, typing at her phone as she spoke. “We weren’t sure when… What do you remember?”

“I was at… I was going to…” He frowned, trying to figure it out. “Uh, I was on my way to a storage place…”

“Studio Self Storage,” Maddie supplied. “That’s where Athena found you.”

“Athena!” The outburst felt like it split his head open, but that wasn’t important. “Is she-?”

“She’s fine, you got the worst of it, whatever happened,” she told him. “A fractured rib and some bruises.”

“And me?”

“You had a nicked spleen, but they managed to fix that,” she said. “They were mostly worried about your head. He hit you with a pipe.”

He didn’t really remember being hit with a pipe, but that was concussions for you. Buck could, vaguely, remember the lights going out wherever he was.  He could remember with a dreamy haziness a shape in the darkness rushing into Athena. But everything was jumbled, and there were more blank spots than blurry images. And trying to remember just made his head hurt worse.

“Who brought him here?” Buck asked, nodding his chin at the still napping Chris.

“Carla dropped him off,” Maddie said. “Eddie went to find a vending machine. I texted him-”

The sound of running feet interrupted her, and they both looked up to see the man in question come to a sliding stop at the door. He clutched at the doorway, nearly falling on his face. Eddie didn’t look as if he had slept any more than Maddie had, his hair sticking up in all directions as he stared wide-eyed at Buck.

“Hey, Eds,” Buck said.

“Hey,” Eddie said, breathless.

Maddie glanced between them before getting to her feet, letting go of her brother’s hand and patting his leg.

“I’m going to go find a nurse and tell them you’re awake,” she told him. “And then let the others know.”

Buck nodded at her absently as she squeezed past Eddie and into the hall. The two men were silent for several long moments, before,

“I’m sorry,” they both said.

“Wait, what are you sorry for?” Eddie asked, creeping up to the bed, like he was afraid Buck would jump up and bite him or something.

“For hurting you,” he said. “For hurting you and not even knowing it.”

“Buck…”

“No, let me…” He sat up as much as he could without waking up Chris. “I’m not in love with the Eddie whose wife died. I’m in love with the Eddie who dropped everything to rush to his Abuela’s side when she was hurt, the Eddie whose aunt called him a saint for everything he did for his son. I’m in love with the Eddie who filled his son’s room with life and love, even while his own is still so bare. I’m in love with the Eddie who saw me for me, in a way no one else had ever done before.

“The two of you are the same in so many ways, in all the ways that made me love you. Him and you. But you’re…” Buck stopped to swallow against a suddenly dry throat. “You’re right, the two of you are different people, too. I was so busy trying to keep bad things from happening that I didn’t realize how much that would change the people they happened to.”

“It felt like you weren’t seeing me,” Eddie confessed, and he sounded so hurt that Buck wanted to cry. 

“I think… I think I was so focused on what was the same, and you were so focused on what was different,” he said. “That we weren’t seeing each other. Because in all the ways that count, in all the ways that I love, you two are the same. I don’t love you because you look like him, or because you remind me of him, or because I can’t have him. I love you because you’re you.”

“You keep saying him,” Eddie noted, reaching out to take his hand. “Before now, it’s always been, ‘you did this’ or ‘you did that,’ as if you were telling stories I should have remembered doing.”

“I’m sorry,” Buck said again. “I wish you had said how much it was hurting you. Then maybe I would have gotten here without needing to actually get some sense beaten into me.”

“I think it’s too soon for the jokes,” Eddie said, smiling down at him. “But for the record? I love you, too.”

“Mr. Buckley!” The doctor loudly greeted as he entered the room, his volume causing Buck to wince and Chris to stir. Eddie twisted his head around to glare at him. “How are we feeling?”

“Like someone took a metal pipe to my head,” was Buck’s cheerful answer, and he smiled up at Eddie when the man directed the glare his way.

A Long Time Coming

“I think I’m just going to chain you to one of us from now on.” The sound of Bobby’s voice had Buck opening his eyes. The captain and the sergeant were both at the doorway, apparently waiting for permission to come in. Like they needed his permission. Bobby looked tired but happy to see, while Athena…

“God, ‘Thena, your face,” he said, and when she narrowed her eyes, hastened to add, “Looks just as beautiful as ever, the captain is a very lucky man.”

“Uh-huh.” She walked stiffly when she came in, and Bobby hurried to help her into one of the chairs. The glare that got him was softened by fondness. “Where’s your sister? And your shadow?”

“Probably wrestling over who gets to stay nights,” Buck answered. “The argument got pretty heated earlier, I think the nurses were about to throw them out before Chris told them off for being too loud.”

It was adorable. Chris had raised his head and scowled at them and said, “Your voices are too loud, you’re hurting Buck.” It had shut them both up immediately, both of them falling over themselves to apologize in whispered voices. Eddie had left shortly after, to get Christopher home and get himself a change of clothes, while Maddie had gone to talk with Josh and Sue.

“So, how long did they say you were staying?” Bobby asked, settling a hand on his wife’s shoulder.

“A few nights, at least,” Buck told him. “Skull fracture and all. And I haven’t even asked about work yet.”

“Oh that will be at least a couple months,” the captain said, smiling at the groan of dismay that Buck let out. “But I am really, truly debating the pros and cons of just keeping you at the station regardless. What were you even doing there to begin with? I know I switched your shifts like you asked-”

“Wait, why did he switch shifts?” Athena asked, tilting her head back to narrow her eyes up at her husband.

“Oh, uh.” The sight of Bobby sweating bullets was as amusing as it was unusual. “There was- Uh, he and Eddie-”

“There was a thing with me and Eddie,” Buck cut in, bestowing mercy upon the man. “We’re better now.”

“Better?” Bobby asked. Athena raised her eyebrow as she turned her head between them.

“Better,” Buck nodded. “We talked.”

“A good talk…?” Athena asked.

“A good talk,” Buck confirmed, averting his eyes as he tried to fight off the blush he could feel blooming on his face. “So there’s probably, like, paperwork? To fill out?”

“It’s already filled,” Bobby said, waving it away. “The two of you just need to blow off the dust and sign it.”

“Blow off the-? How long have you had it ready?”

“Your first shift back after the tsunami,” Bobby answered, not even pausing to think about it. To his wife, he said, “It has been a very frustrating year.”

“Oh, poor you,” Buck drawled.

“You still haven’t explained why you were there.”

“Oh, uh, that was where Hudson was hiding out,” he said, scratching sheepishly at his neck. A thought struck him and he started giggling. “Oh man, he literally stored himself there. He stored himself at Studio Self Storage.”

“Hiding out?” Bobby’s brow furrowed in confusion. He looked down at his wife. “He went there looking for the Realtor Rapist?”

“Apparently, I should have taken you up on your idea of asking Buck for help on that case,” Athena said, crossing her arms and glaring at the bedridden young man. “Maybe that would have kept this idiot child from getting hurt.”

“Going in there by myself to look around wasn’t one of my smartest moments,” he admitted. “What happened to him, anyway?”

“Nothing you need to worry about,” she assured him, reaching an arm out and patting his leg.

“So have you and Maddie worked out the custody agreement yet?” Buck asked, watching as Eddie set down his old army duffle beside the rollout bed the nurses had brought in. “Or should I expect her to come rushing in here with a folding chair?”

“I think I could take her if she did that.”

“I bet you, you couldn’t.” Buck watched as Eddie unzipped the bag and pulled out a bottle of mouthwash, which he then handed to him. “What is this for…?”

“It’s Abuela’s secret remedy for male-pattern baldness,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes. “It’s mouthwash, idiota. What do you think it’s for?”

“You are a very rude boyfriend,” Buck said, and then dutifully took a mouthful of the off-brand Listerine as said boyfriend stared him into compliance. He swished it around, cheek to cheek like an overgrown chipmunk, until the other man held up the nearby waste bin for him to spit into. “Okay, so why did I-?”

Eddie interrupted him the best way possible: with his mouth on his. Kissing Eddie was the best thing ever, Buck was quickly deciding. If he could do nothing else, from now until the heat death of the universe, except kiss Eddie, Buck would be okay with that. He clung to the man and did his best to pull him into the bed, ignoring the way it pulled at the stitches in his side..

Except Eddie was (usually) the more sensible of the two, and he pulled away before they took it too far, chuckling at how Buck pouted and whined at him for it.

“To answer your question, it was because I didn’t want our first kiss ruined by halitosis.”

“You call that a kiss?” Buck asked, breathless. “That- That wasn’t a kiss. Get back here and try again.”

“Right.” He rolled his eyes. “You definitely sound, and look,” his eyes darted down the bed, which made Buck preen even as he adjusted his sheets and hospital gown, “Like you didn’t enjoy it.”

“It was awful. Zero stars out of ten.”

Eddie opened his mouth for another witty retort, but Buck’s phone broke the banter. Someone - Eddie or Maddie - had placed it on the table beside the bed and plugged it in to charge. That would have been thoughtful, except Buck’s concussion meant he couldn’t look at screens, so it was just tortuous temptation instead.

“Just ignore it. Unless it’s Athena, then answer it right the fuck now.”

“It’s Chimney,” Eddie said, swiping his finger across the screen and hitting the speaker button.

“What the hell do you want?” Buck groaned in aggravation.

“Hen! She’s cheating on Karen, isn’t she?” Chimney slurred through the phone. 

“Are you drunk?” Buck asked. Eddie’s look of bafflement mirrored his own.

“No!” Karen shouted down the line. “Maybe! Yes.”

“Didn’t Hen say she was sick?” Eddie asked him, to which Buck could do nothing but shrug.

“Oh shit, Eddie’s there too?” Chimney asked.

“Yeah, who did you think-? Never mind. What’s going on?” Buck asked.

“My wife is a cheating cheater!” Karen answered, sounding like she had her face right by the phone. “Who cheats!”

“Okay, let’s use our indoor voices,” he said, rubbing his head, which did absolutely nothing for the pain their shouting was causing him. Eddie, in a move that made Buck love him even more, thumbed the volume down on the phone. “And then explain - softly - why you called me about this.”

“Because, Mr. Psychic!” Chimney whisper-shouted down the line. “We need you to tell us if Hen really is cheating-”

“She is!” Karen interrupted.

“And who this Imil- Imels-”

“Imelda!”

“Right! That person! Who that is!”

“You interrupted my time with my boyfriend, to ask me if Hen is cheating on Karen?” Buck asked, laying back against his pillows.

“Again!” Karen threw in.

“Your boyfriend?” Chimney sounded shocked and dismayed. “Does Eddie know? Are you cheating on Eddie?”

“I am the boyfriend, you idiot,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes at Buck.

“Oh! Congrats man! When did-? Ow! Right, right, sorry. Hen! Cheating! Yes? No?”

“Why in the world do you think she’s cheating on Karen?”

“Again!”

“We have dates!” Chimney said. “And a hotel! And she went to a restaurant and said it was for my birthday, but I didn’t go with her! It was a teppanyaki restaurant, Buck! I love teppanyaki!”

“I- I’m still not understanding why-?”

“Because you’re the psychic!”

“Hen isn’t cheating on Karen,” Buck said.

“Liar!” Karen shouted at him through the phone.

“If you weren’t going to believe me, why did you even ask?”

“Because Chimney said you would know!”

“And I do! She isn't cheating on you!” In the background, he could hear the sound of Chimney’s apartment door open and closing.

“Hey Howie, I- What the hell is going on here?” Maddie did not sound very pleased about whatever she was seeing.

“Hen is cheating on me!” Karen’s voice was muffled now, so Buck figured she was facing away from the phone.

“And I called Buck to ask if she was, and he said she wasn’t, but-”

“They’re both drunk,” Eddie said, grinning at the phone. “They’re your problem now.”

“Good luck, Mads!” Buck threw in.

“What? No-” Whatever protests Maddie had were cut off as Eddie’s thumb slid across the screen to end the call.

“So, that was dramatic,” Eddie said, placing the phone back on the bedside table. “It was like one of Abuela’s telenovela’s.”

“You mean the ones you watch with Chris and claim it’s to practice his Spanish?” Buck asked, grinning at him as he sputtered out denials. “Face it, snookums. I know your guilty pleasures.”

“Snookums?” Eddie asked, sounding amused.

“What, you don’t like that one? What about…” Buck hummed in thought. “Sweetcheeks? Honeybun? Sugarplum? Hotpants?”

“Ay Dios.” He rolled his eyes, but he was smiling too widely for the irritation to be anything but a front. “Is Hen really cheating on Karen?”

“No,” Buck said. “I mean, I can understand why Karen would jump to that conclusion.  She’s done it before, with Denny’s bio-mom. That was a train wreck. But no, this is…”

“This is…?”

“I think this is when she starts thinking about med school,” he said. “Hey uh, semi-serious question. When Chris was here, before I woke up, did he say anything about a worm?”

Chimney had moved from the couch to his dining table, clutching the glass of water that Maddie had forced into his hands. Hen had come and gone, dropping the bombshell announcement that she was seriously considering becoming a doctor. Karen had been overjoyed, both with her wife’s decision and with the fact that her relationship wasn’t in any real danger.

But he couldn’t find the joy.

“You’re not happy for her?” Maddie asked, reaching over to stroke a hand through his hair.

“I just can’t get past the fact that she’s leaving me,” he confessed. “I mean, it’s been me and her at the station for years now. I can’t even begin to imagine what it’s going to be like without her there.”

“Hey, there’s years to go before then,” Maddie said, trying her best to smile at him. She still looked so tired, he thought. He felt selfish for putting this on her, after everything with Buck. “It’s not like she’s going to earn her medical degree overnight.”

“I guess you’re right,” he sighed. “Sometimes I really hate that he’s psychic.”

“Who?”

“Your brother,” he said. “It’s handy a lot of times, like with the chocolate that one time. Or that Jason guy he warned me about, right before our first Christmas together. But with the whole thing about that old guy. Red? I knew that Buck had seen that someone was leaving. I just didn’t think it would be Hen.”

He looked up to find Maddie frowning at him, and he wanted to reach up and rub away the crease it made in her forehead.

“Howie, what Jason guy?”

It's a Train Wreck

“Explain to me again why I’m here and not at Eddie’s? Or at least the loft?” Buck asked with a groan. And then, when he realized what he said, “My apartment. I meant, at my apartment.”

“We all took a vote,” Athena said, shaking out a blanket and handing it to him where he sprawled across her couch. Harry and May were in their rooms, the former playing video games and the latter probably obsessing over the merits of still having her graduation party with her mother injured, minor though it was this time around. “And it was a unanimous decision that we will not be taking our eyes off you until you’re cleared to return to work. And since I’m still on paid leave until the investigation is over-”

“Wait!” Buck interjected. “You didn’t do anything wrong, though. I mean the guy had literally just stabbed me.”

Or at least that was the order of events he had put together from what he had heard and been told.

“Protocols, Buckaroo,” she said. “I shot and killed a man in the line of duty, there has to be an investigation. And besides, my rib would be keeping me on desk duty, anyway.”

“How is your rib doing?”

“It’s sore, but healing. Better than your head.”

Everything was better than his head. There was still a persistent ache, impossible to ignore even while it was muffled by the heavy duty pain meds he’d been prescribed. Those had been immediately handed off to Eddie, who had then passed them onto Athena for the evening. Buck still didn’t trust himself with the bottled temptation in any form.

He had needed his department issued sunglasses to get out of the hospital when he was discharged, the sun almost making the idea of clawing out his own eyes worth it. Bright lights and loud noises were not his friends at the moment, and that was probably the only reason he was at the Grant-Nash residence instead of the station. The mere idea of the station alarm ringing while he was there was enough to set off phantom pains throughout his entire being.

And none of that was taking into account the stab wound in his side which, considering it could have easily taken out his spleen, was honestly the least of his worries.

When he had been discharged from the hospital, after four days under observation, Eddie had taken him directly to his place. The man hadn’t even given him the chance to argue, and already had a change of clothes for him at casa de Diaz. Someone had taken advantage of his key privileges, but Eddie had always been the only one who could do that and get away with it. Spending a night in bed with his boyfriend was wonderful in theory, except in practice it was a massive tease. The man absolutely refused to do anything beyond kissing, what with the head trauma and the stab wound and all.

And it had taken a lot of pouting and some minor manipulation to keep Eddie from just taking the couch.

(“But if you’re all the way in the other room, how would you really know if something was wrong…?”)

The sound of Athena snorting to herself in amusement drew Buck out from his thoughts.

“What is it?” he asked, twisting his head so he could see her better. She had her phone out, smirking fondly at something she was reading.

“Your boo-”

“Oh, that’s a good one. I’ll have to use that one next time I see him.”

Athena rolled her eyes.

“Eddie brought in pamphlets for a summer camp and now Bobby is regaling me with fond memories of Camp…” She squinted at the screen, clearly trying to figure out if she was looking at an actual word or an impressive typo. “Weegeewagen?”

“Ugh, the summer camp,” Buck groaned. The day before he was discharged from the hospital, Chris had trundled in, full of excitement at the prospect of going with all his friends. Buck could not share his joy. Nevermind the horrifying prospect of the boy being so far away for two whole weeks, there were also the dangers that people were only just now taking notice of.

“You don’t approve?” Athena’s lips quirked in open amusement. 

“It’s not that- Actually, no, I don’t approve!” he said, sitting up. “That farm to fork thing is actual child labor. But no, it’s not… It’s not the camp itself.” Buck let out a sigh. “It’s going to get canceled before the first week is through and Chris is going to be heartbroken.”

“Canceled?” Athena echoed. “I’m afraid to ask, but is this related to the recent news? And your stockpile of face masks that Eddie said he found?”

“If I told you that there was absolutely nothing to be worried about, would that help at all?”

“No.”

“Figures. I’m not that good of a liar.”

“Nine-One-One, what’s your emergency?”

“There’s been a train derailment. Pacific West One-One-Three-Five. We were heading from Phoenix into Union Station. We’ve crashed somewhere close to the LA County line.”

“Okay, so how many-?”

“There are multiple injuries. This is a mass casualty situation…”

The 118 hadn’t even been on site for that long and Eddie was already exhausted. It was just… Well, it was a train wreck. There was a reason people called awful, messy things train wrecks. Bobby had split the team up when they arrived, hesitating a moment when he sent Eddie to see if one of the cars could be safely secured. Eddie could see when he had to stop himself from telling an absent Buck to go with him.

And honestly, Eddie would have felt a lot more comfortable if Buck had been there.

There was a woman, a few years older than him with strawberry blond hair and large glasses, arguing with a couple of men from the 153.

“Please, if you can just let me up into the car,” she was begging. “Please! I’ve gotta get up there.”

“Guys, guys, I’ve got it,” Eddie said, waving them on to deal with more important things, taking on the duty of talking the woman down himself. Up close, he could see she had a cut near her temple. “Ma’am, I’m sorry. We can’t let you inside. It’s too dangerous.”

“I know it’s dangerous!” she snapped. “I need to get up in that car.”

“I hear you, I’m sorry.”

“Wait.” She peered up at the station number on his helmet. “Are you from the One-Eighteen?”

“Yeah.” Eddie had no idea what his station had to do with this, but-

“Where’s Buck?” she demanded. “He’ll help me, I know he will!”

“He’s not- How do you know Buck?”

“We’re- We were friends. I worked at the dispatch center.”

“Oh!” It was extremely worrisome that the moment she said they’d been friends, it automatically narrowed down who she could be, even before she mentioned her previous career. Buck really didn’t have many people outside of their little group, did he? “You’re Abby, the-” The ex in a different timeline. “-person who introduced him to Carla. Listen, Buck isn’t here. He got hurt.”

“Again!?” Which. Yeah.

“You were on the train, right?” Eddie asked, eyes flicking over to the blood on her forehead. He reached forward to steer her by the shoulder. “We need to take you over there and get you checked out.”

“No! I’m fine!” She snapped, stepping out of his reach. Gesturing wildly at the train, she said, “I need to get up there.”

“Ma’am, no, it’s far too dangerous-”

“I’m trying to find somebody!” she snapped. “Buck would understand.”

“I’m not Buck,” Eddie told her, trying to keep his frustrations at bay. “Just tell me who it is you’re looking for, and I’ll have everyone keep an eye out.”

“It’s my fiancé,” Abby said, frantic energy turning into burgeoning tears. “He fell asleep and I went to the bar.”

“Can you give me a description? So I can pass it on?”

“That’s him,” she said, pulling out her phone and showing him a photo of the two of them together. “We were in that top car right there, all the way in the back.” 

He followed the line of her finger and silently cursed. It was the car he’d been sent to find a way to secure, the car that was standing at an almost 90 degree angle on its end, and in danger of toppling down to the ground at any moment.

“We’ll find him,” he said, that being the most he was willing to promise. “What’s his name?”

“Sam,” she said. “Sam Egan.”

“Okay. Stay down here, and go get yourself checked out,” Eddie ordered, turning his back on her and heading to do his job. He reached for his radio. “Cap, I’m on my way to the car now. I have been asked to be on the look out for a possible survivor named Sam Egan, white male…”

“You know, I just realized,” Buck said, staring at the column fireplace in the middle of the Grant-Nash den. Athena was watching the tv, its volume muted. “I managed to save your fireplace.”

“Save my fireplace?” the sergeant asked, turning to look at him.

“Yeah, uh. The first time around, with Hudson, I wasn’t… There.” It was still one of the worst nights he had ever lived, having to listen to Athena being attacked and watch as Bobby slowly crumbled in despair before his very eyes. “And Bobby and Michael took their frustrations out on the fireplace. With hammers.”

“You weren’t there? Wait, is that why you were there this time?” she asked, and then didn’t even give him the chance to answer. “You sweet, stupid boy.

“Hey, your radio was on the entire time it was happening,” Buck said. “It was traumatizing and I’m blaming that for my actions.”

“That, or your pigheadedness,” Athena said, frowning down at him. She was definitely still angry about him going into the building on his own, instead of waiting for her to get there. “Well, thank God some good came out of the mess. I quite like my fireplace as it is, thank you very much.”

She turned back to the television and clucked her tongue.

“Speaking of messes…”

“Why? What’s going on?” he asked.

“There’s a literal train wreck at the county line. Looks like the One-Eighteen is there, along with a couple other stations.”

Train wreck? Train wreck…  Train wreck!

“Well, at least I won’t be there to piss both Eddie and Bobby off this time,” Buck told her.

“As opposed to how you managed to piss me off just the other day?” Athena asked, crossing her arms and imposing judgment through the judicial use of a single eyebrow.

“If I said I didn’t actually remember making the decision to go in, thanks to my very, very severe head trauma, would that make you less angry with me?”

“No.”

“Worth a shot,” he sighed. “But Abby was- Is there, right now.” He gestured at the television without actually looking at it. “My dispatcher friend, remember? You helped look for her mom. She and her fiancé were both on the train, and I might have promised to bring him back to her?”

“Of course you did,” Athena said, and Buck couldn’t see her face but the eyeroll was implied by her tone.

“Not my best moment, definitely not my worst,” he admitted with a shrug. “Bobby was not too pleased with me when Eddie ratted me out. See, Sam - her fiancé - he was pinned by a beam, but it was also pinning another survivor, so we couldn’t just lift it off one without crushing the other. I wanted to cut through the side of the car to get one of them out that way, but Bobby-”

He froze mid sentence, horror thrumming through his very core as the realization struck him.

“Oh God,” he whispered, covering his mouth and fighting back the urge to puke.

“Buck?” Athena sounded worried, dropping to her knees beside the couch and resting a hand on his shoulder. “Buck, what’s wrong?”

“They’re going to let him die,” he said. Oh God, oh God, oh God. “‘Thena, they’re going to let him die.”

Finding Sam alive had Eddie feeling a modicum of relief. He hadn’t exactly wanted to have to tell the poor woman that her fiancé was dead, even if he was currently pinned by a beam. It should have been simple, routine. Use the jaws or the ram to move the beam and then get the guy out.

Except, it’s never that simple.

There was a young woman, a girl really, pinned by the other end of that very same beam. Move it one way, it crushed her. Move it the other, it crushed him. And there was no third way that he or Bobby could see, not one that was safe enough to risk.

“Okay, I’m calling it,” Bobby told him and the guy from the 153 that had come up with Eddie. Davis, his coat said. “We start with the girl, we get her out.”

“Copy that.” He felt grim at the decision.

“Sir,” Davis said. “You know that if we do this…”

“He’ll probably die, I know,” the captain sighed. “But we need to save whomever has the better chance, and Eddie’s saying that’s the girl.”

“Her vitals are stronger,” Eddie added, and Davis nodded in acceptance.

Sometimes, this job just sucked.

Maddie paced her apartment, staring at the phone in her hand. She had nothing to do but wait while the pregnancy test did its thing, and Howie was still helping with the triage and clean-up at the train wreck site. Having time to waste was never actually a good thing, in her experience. It left too much of an opportunity for her brain to turn on itself. She would have gone to see Buck, bothered him while seeing for herself how well he was doing, but…

But.

There was something about Howie’s drunken story about Jason that bothered her. The timing of it, the way Evan had warned him away from the obsequious man. There were things her mind wanted to add together, like how he had started a downward spiral around the same time Howie had told her that the mysterious Jason finally got the hint and stopped bothering him. Things like the way Doug had been missing for months before she tried serving him divorce papers. Things like the way Buck had known the entire time how bad her marriage had truly been.

And how Doug once mentioned that his mother had almost named him Jason.

Taking a deep breath to fortify herself for the unpleasant, and hopefully entirely unnecessary, conversation to come, she dialed a number she could never truly forget. It rang for several moments, which made sense because it was terribly late over there. Looking at the time had her wincing, because it was not going to help make the conversation any more enjoyable.

“Hello?”

“Hi, mom,” Maddie said. “It’s me…”

“Maddie? Do you know how late it is?”

“Yeah, sorry mom, I just-”

“Couldn’t this have waited until the morning?” her mother rolled right over her. “Well, I guess I should just be happy that you’re calling at all without one of you being hurt. Or has Evan gone and done something for attention again?”

“He- He goes by Buck now, mom,” Maddie sighed. It hadn’t even dawned on her that she was yet to inform her parents about Buck’s most recent hospitalization. “I’ve told you this.”

“He’s still letting people call him that?” She could hear the borderline disgust in her mother’s tone, subtle enough to be missed by anyone who hadn’t grown up hearing it.

“I wasn’t calling about Evan,” she said, conceding the fight. “I was just… Do you still have any photos of my wedding?”

“Why? I thought when you finally had the sense to divorce him that you wouldn’t care about those things anymore,” her mother sniffed. She was still riding that high horse, apparently, and had been ever since Maddie had reluctantly informed her of the decision. “You know, I told you that he was no good. I kept saying you should have left him, but did you listen? No. Neither of you ever listened.”

“Yes, yes, you were right,” Maddie said, and the gall of saying it almost made her vomit then and there. “I just- I need a copy of one of the photos we took, of me and Doug. If you have one, could you email it to me? Please?”

All of her pictures of Doug had been left behind in Pennsylvania when she fled. There had been no need to bring any with her, no desire whatsoever. Except she needed one now, just so she could ask Howie and get an answer to that niggling question in her head.

“Fine, fine,” her mother said, waspish tone stinging at her ears. “I’ll have a look.”

“Thank you…”

Things Best Left Unsaid

It had taken the rest of the night for Athena to calm Buck down, following his realization of what consequences he had unknowingly wrought. And then he had sworn her to secrecy, because it would do neither Bobby or Eddie any good to know that they very well could have saved both Abby’s fiancé and the girl trapped with him. It wasn’t their fault, that they had gone the safer route. It wasn’t their fault that if they had even thought of the solution they’d gone with in the other timeline, they wouldn’t have even seriously considered it in his absence. 

Eddie and Bobby, they both had limits to how far they were willing to push the risks versus the rewards, the captain more so than the veteran. It was Buck, always Buck, who regularly campaigned for the options that were riskier, but that would have the most gains. It was Buck with the unstoppable compulsion to save everyone he could, no matter the danger to himself. In a very twisted way, his parents giving him such a poor sense of self-worth had been a benefit as a first responder. Not that he would ever, ever voice that thought aloud.

None of this changed the fact, however, that Sam Egan was dead because he had gone and gotten himself too injured to work. None of this changed the fact that, while Buck was burdened with the knowledge that Sam could have been saved, it was Eddie who had to be there for the results. The man had been somber when he picked Buck up and drove him back to the Diaz residence, the morning after, and didn’t say much about what had happened. Which was a flashing neon sign that it hadn’t been pleasant, because Eddie always talked to him about any calls he missed.

“How’s Abby holding up?” Buck asked Carla sometime later, when she came back to Eddie’s from dropping Chris off for one his last days of school. It was her turn to babysit him, apparently. He would probably have been at the Grant-Nash residence again, but Athena wasn’t home, busy at the station talking to people about Hudson.

“Not very well,” Carla said, sitting beside him at Eddie’s second-hand dining table with a sigh. “She’s handling it better than his girls are, apparently.”

And that’s right, Sam had daughters. He had honestly forgotten. His poor choices took their father away.

“I tried reaching out to her,” he said. “But I didn’t get any reply back. Not that I know what I would say if she did. Sorry I wasn’t there when you needed me?”

“Now don’t go blaming yourself,” the aide scolded. “And don’t try denying it, I know you are. There was nothing you could have done differently if you were there. And it’s not your fault that you weren’t.”

And that statement was just so absurdly untrue it would be hilarious, if he was in the mood to laugh.
