“She’s blaming me enough for the both of us, I’m sure.” The words made Carla scowl, which she immediately tried to cover up, so he knew he was right in the assumption. “If I hadn’t been such an idiot and gone rushing into the storage place, if I hadn’t let myself get my head beaten in, I would have been there. I would have been able to help.”

“You didn’t know what was going to happen.”

“Haven’t you heard?” he scoffed. “I’m psychic.”

“And I’m the Queen of England,” she said. Then Carla’s frown slowly morphed into a smirk. “So, I couldn’t help but notice that you spent the night here, but the couch doesn’t look like it’s been slept on.”

“Oh, uh…” Buck could feel his face heating up. “That’s because I slept in Eddie’s bed. With Eddie. Just slept!”

“About damn time,” she laughed. “Remember that parent-teacher conference a few months back? The one Shannon and Eddie both went to? She called you his partner, and he never denied it.”

“We had some issues to iron out first.” That was a damn understatement. “We’re still ironing them out, honestly.”

Buck was under no delusion that everything became unproblematic just because he and Eddie now spent a regular portion of their free time making out. He was seriously considering going to Dr. Copland again, but he had no clue how to even begin framing his problems in such a way that she wouldn’t deem him a potential danger to himself and/or others. And he was also making a greater effort in differentiating between the Eddies, to the point of referring to the other Eddie as ‘Edmundo’ whenever he came up in conversation.

(“Ana always called him that, and it annoyed me so damn much, Eds.”

“It annoys me, what the hell?”)

“Hey uh, since you’re here…” He wrung his hands in front of him, feeling somewhat embarrassed about the request he was about to make. Not as embarrassed as he would have been before his leg, when he had needed help getting in and out of the bath, but still. “Is there any way you can help me wash my hair? It’s getting kinda bad, and I can’t see what I’m doing well enough to avoid the tender spots.”

The words had Carla laughing good naturedly.

“Of course, boo. Get yourself to the bathroom and we’ll see what we can do.”

By the time of May’s graduation party, the symptoms of Buck’s concussion had lessened considerably. The headache and the sensitivity to noise and light were still plaguing him, but nowhere near as bad as it had been. Which was good, because he wasn’t going to miss out on one of the last large gatherings they’d get to have for a year or more. The graduation party, much like the Christmas party, had always been one of his more fond memories. He would have been there regardless, even if he had to borderline overdose on the pain meds.

(Not that anyone would have allowed that to happen.)

“Okay lovebirds, stop canoodling,” Chimney told them, walking up to where Eddie and Buck were lounging in the corner of the Grant-Nash’s living room, watching Chris and Denny make funny faces for the photobooth. Across the room, May was chasing after Harry, cake smeared across her face.

“We are not canoodling,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes

“We can start canoodling, if you’d like,” Buck offered. “That way you can actually complain about us doing it.”

“What does canoodling even mean?”

“I’m not sure, cupcake. I think it’s a sex thing.”

“Cupcake?” Eddie asked, eyes scrunched in amusement. “Better than snookums, I guess.”

“This might be the worst thing to have ever happened to me,” Chimney said, watching them with a face full of despair. “I take back all my encouragement to get your shit together, this is… This is unacceptable. This is worse than the pining. This is more painful than the rebar.”

“Look at it as karmic repayment for all of Interim Captain Han’s sins,” Buck offered.

“You still haven’t let that go? It has been a year, Buck!”

“You tried to make me wash your car!”

“Was there a reason you came over here?” Eddie broke in. “Or was this just a social visit?”

“Oh, uh, right.” The paramedic suddenly looked nervous, glancing over his shoulder at the room of people behind him. Actually, he was looking at where Buck’s sister was now chatting with May about something, the latter wiping her face clean with a paper towel. “Have you noticed Maddie acting a little… Odd?”

“Odd?” Buck echoed, scrunching his nose up. “Not… Really?”

Except, that wasn’t true, was it? There had been something in the way she talked to him recently, like there was something she was hiding. Like she had made a realization and didn’t want to say anything yet. Like she knew something and-

Buck’s face broke into a wide grin.

“What?” Chimney demanded. “What is it? What’s that smile for?”

“It’s a secret,” he said immediately, making the man huff in annoyance. “She’ll tell you soon. I’m not even supposed to know about it, yet.”

“And you still try to say he isn’t psychic.” The paramedic jabbed a finger at Eddie’s chest.

“He isn’t,” Eddie said, grinning as the shorter man rolled his eyes and stomped off to rejoin the crowd of revelers. “So, do I get to know what this secret is?”

Buck hummed in thought.

“Maybe, what do I get out of it?”

“My love and affection.”

“That’s cheap, I get that already,” he said. Eddie just shrugged and nodded, conceding the point. Buck smirked at his boyfriend. “I’m going to be an uncle.”

“You mean…?” Eddie trailed off, grinning at him.

“Yup. In, uh… Eight and…” He frowned and started counting on his fingers, whispering the names of the months to himself as he did so, before giving up. “Screw it, February. In February.”

“Oh man, you are as bad at math as me. Gracias a Dios, Chris has his mother’s skills…”

“I’ve heard that you have a new beau,” Athena said, sidling up to her ex-husband, a wicked grin on her face.

“What?” Michael squawked. “New-? Who told you that?”

“A little bird did.”

The man narrowed his eyes and swirled around, craning his neck to find the oversized golden retriever amongst the small crowd. 

“That’s cheating,” he grumbled, glaring at the psychic as he laughed with his own boyfriend. Hen’s foster-daughter was in his arms, slapping at his shoulder. “If he’s going to be using his powers to spread gossip, the least he could do is tell me my lucky lottery numbers.”

“Michael, you’re a successful architect in Los Angeles,” Athena said. “I don’t think you need to play the lottery.”

“It’s the principle of it, ’Thena!”

“Anyway!” The sergeant rolled her eyes. “Tell me about him. What’s his name and date of birth? Address?”

“David’s a neurosurgeon, not a criminal,” Michael huffed. “You don’t need to do a background check.”

“A neurosurgeon?” Athena’s eyebrows rose in approval. “Definitely a step up from the last one. Still,” she sniffed. “Not as good of a catch as me, I’m sure.”

Maddie sat on her bed, going through the postcards that Buck had sent her those years he was traveling the hemisphere. They were bundled together, tied with a string and tucked away for safekeeping. They were, perhaps, her most precious of possessions. Near the bottom of the stack was the one sent to her on his first Christmas as a firefighter. The Christmas she finally decided to leave. He was smiling at the camera, a Santa hat pulled low over his head, the ladder truck that would eventually crush his leg displayed behind him.

There was a thumbprint on the back, a smear of red that she tried to rub away, for all the good it did. 

Merry Christmas, Mads, her brother had written, in his sloppy handwriting. I’m still looking for an apartment of my own. I want to make sure there’s plenty of room for you. If you decide to visit. You would love it here.

He had known the entire time. Every postcard he sent since joining the 118, since being sent back in time, had been filled with pointed promises that she had a safe space to run to, if only she took him up on it. He had gone out of his way, with every written word, to make sure she knew she had the option, while knowing that it had to be her choice.

Exactly like it had to be Tara’s choice.

The night after May’s graduation party, she checked her email and found that her mother had indeed found and sent her one of the photos from her wedding. It had been painful to look at, the sight of her and him together. Seeing herself in that wedding dress - which had been torn and tossed away in one of Doug’s rages - filled her with a deep well of disgust and pity and hatred, all of it directed at the version of her who had walked down the aisle with that man, willfully ignoring every warning from her parents and her brother.

She had cropped herself out of the photo, the action filling her with an odd sense of catharsis, and then asked Howie to look at it.

“Oh! That’s the Jason guy!” he had said. “The one I told you about. Did you know him?”

“Yeah,” she said, her ears ringing. “Uh, I have something to tell you, though…”

The news of her pregnancy had been more than sufficient to distract him. Honestly, Howie had seemed to forget about Jason (Doug, her mind reminded her. It was Doug.) entirely in favor of the overwhelming joy and terror of impending fatherhood. But Maddie couldn’t forget about him, her stomach churning with more than just the beginnings of pregnancy-induced nausea.

Doug had been in Los Angeles, and her brother had known about it.

Doug had been missing for months before she filed for the divorce.

She flipped through the postcards, landing on a couple from a couple years before he became a firefighter. The one where he wrote to say he was joining the  seals - hooyah! - and then the one after, where he admitted to dropping out. Because he hadn’t wanted to be a ‘robot with red eyes,’ in his words. Because he hadn’t wanted to be an emotionless machine.

Not because it was too violent, not because of what active combat with a gun against other people with guns actually entailed. But because he hadn’t wanted to shut off his emotions. Maddie knew, far too intimately, that the most violent of acts were driven by emotions. She just could not, would not, imagine Buck doing them.

Yet, all signs pointed…

Some questions were perhaps better left unanswered, but she wasn’t sure if this was one of them.

Three Things Don’t Long Stay Hidden

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Chris’ sleep away camp was, just as Buck remembered it being, canceled only a week into it. The pandemic, and the news of it, was really picking up speed now, and life was coming to a screeching halt. Buck grimly divided up his stockpile of facemasks, sending them to the station and everyone’s homes. It wasn’t nearly enough, he knew, but it would hopefully keep them all covered until the gears got moving.

Once again, fear and paranoia settled over the station, but this time Buck wasn’t there to see it first hand. The earliest date for his return was in August, giving the fracture in his skull plenty of time to heal. It meant he didn’t start every shift getting his temperature taken or going through a checklist of symptoms, and it meant he wasn’t there as every cough or sneeze turned one into a pariah. He was honestly a little relieved, to be missing the worst of it.

(The worst of it. As if everything was peachy-keen by next year.)

The others were all terrified of getting their families sick and were starting to circle the wagons. Harry and May moved in with Michael, while Hen in turn moved into the guest room at the Grant-Nash house. And then there was Eddie and Chimney.

“Shannon and I talked about it,” Eddie said one evening, when he stopped by the apartment after shift, his hands still red from how thoroughly he had scrubbed them. “Since she’s going to be working from home for a while, and since I’m… It’s just safer to have Chris stay at hers.”

“That makes sense,” Buck said, running his fingers through Eddie’s hair. They were curled up on the couch together, the older man leaning into him. “How did Chris take it?”

“We haven’t told him, yet,” the man answered with a sigh. “In the other timeline, what did you and-” He scrunched up his nose. “Edmundo do?”

“Have I told you about the loft? The place I lived at, Before?” Buck asked, and Eddie shook his head. “I liked it, but it had its share of problems. Everything was open, the kitchen and living room was pretty much one long room. The bedroom was upstairs, in- Well, in the loft area. I had just moved in when my leg happened the first time.”

“Well that was poor timing.”

“No shit,” he snorted. “Not wanting a repeat of that was why I didn’t pick there this time around. But I had you and Chimney both staying over, at one point. With one bed, and an open floor plan.”

“Madre de Dios, where did everyone sleep?” Eddie asked, sounding equal parts appalled and intrigued.

“Well I slept in my bed,” Buck declared primly. “Chimney was stuck on the couch.”

“And Edmundo?” It was adorable, really, how his nose scrunched up whenever he said his own name like that. He really, truly did not like his full name.

“In the bed with me,” he admitted with a shrug. “Just two bros, y’know.”

“Just two bros,” Eddie muttered, and Buck narrowed his eyes at him.

“Are you…?”

“Am I what?” He wasn’t meeting Buck’s eyes, looking away while he worked his jaw.

“I woke up to him spooning me once,” Buck said, just to see, and broke into a grin when he saw the scowl bloom across Eddie’s face. “Oh my God, you are! You’re jealous!”

“No I’m not!”

“You are!” This was the funniest thing he’d heard in days. “You’re jealous of him! You do remember that you two were the same person once, right? You’re jealous of another version of yourself.”

“I’m- That’s not-” Eddie tried stammering out, face turning crimson. “Shut up!”

“Oh, no, I am never shutting up about this,” Buck promised, and then his grin turned salacious. “Not unless you make-”

Someone started banging at his door, and Buck threw his head back with a groan.

“Oh look, a distraction,” Eddie declared, getting to his feet and hurrying to open the door. Chimney barreled past him, bags in his hands, a wild look in his eyes. He was wearing two of the facemasks Buck had given everyone, one on top of the other, though he tore them off and threw them onto the table after he set down his things.

“Please let me stay here.”

“What’s wrong with your place?” Eddie asked, closing the door with a frown.

“My pregnant sister is there,” Buck answered for him, and his boyfriend nodded in understanding. Like Before, Chimney had no doubt been voicing his concerns at the station about getting Maddie sick. And besides, they had literally just been talking about this, before getting sidetracked by Eddie being jealous of himself.

“Exactly,” Chimney said. “So please? Can I stay in your spare room, until this all blows over?”

“Of course you can,” Buck said with a sigh. It was literally one of the reasons he chose a two-bedroom apartment, after all. This and Maddie. Though it meant he needed to get the man a copy of the key. “Quick question: leopard print or tiger stripes?”

There was something going on with Maddie. He hadn’t paid much mind to it, when Chimney had first brought it up at May’s graduation party, assuming it had just been about the pregnancy news she had yet to share. But there was still something clearly bothering her, whenever she and Buck talked. Like she was constantly on the precipice of asking him something, but chickened out every time.

He was about ready to demand she just spit it out, whatever it was. Except that there was almost always someone else with them, either Albert on her end or Chimney on his, and he knew for a fact that she would shut down any attempts in front of them.

Living with Chimney when the man had his own room to stay in was much better than the first go around, Buck was quickly deciding. They weren’t constantly on each other’s toes, and both could go to the respective hidey holes when the togetherness got too much. It helped, too, that Eddie was still staying at his own place, since Chris was living with Shannon, if only for the short term. Buck ended up spending a lot of nights over there, whenever the man didn’t have a shift.

Being separated from his child was not something Edmundo had dealt well with, Before, and it was not something that Eddie was dealing well with now. Luckily, Buck knew of a wide variety of ways to keep his boyfriend distracted from his empty nest. Even better, the stab wound to his side was healing nicely, and his concussion was barely more than an achy afterthought, and so Eddie didn’t need to be so concerned about hurting him if things got too rambunctious. 

And often, his distractions could get very rambunctious.

They fell into a routine during the summer. He would chat with Maddie and Chris over Facetime, and hang out with Chimney and Eddie at either the apartment or the Diaz home, whenever the two men weren’t on shift. If they were on shift, he often carpooled with one of them to the station, spending most of the day there so everyone could be assured that he wasn’t getting into any trouble. It meant he could make sure that the station alarm definitely wasn’t going to cause any problems with his post-fracture head, and that he wouldn’t be spending an entire day or more alone.

Buck desperately did not want to spend an entire day or more alone, not after getting so used to constant company once again.

At the station, he spent most of his time helping Hen study for her MCATs or in the kitchen with Bobby, whenever he wasn’t getting in trouble for distracting people, usually Eddie. The captain had pulled out the paperwork that both of them needed to sign and date, and it was indeed covered in a light layer of dust. Apparently, they really had been pre-filled and then thrown into the back of one of his cabinet drawers for safekeeping.

“Okay, so what about that day made you so sure?” Buck asked Bobby, idly spinning the pen between his fingers. He remembered that the captain had specified it was his first shift back after the tsunami that he got the paperwork ready. “What about that day had you going, ‘oh yeah this is definitely going to happen?’”

“When Eddie burst into my office during our talk to ask if everything was okay, and didn’t even look at me,” Bobby said. “And then the eyes you made at each other.”

“We don’t make eyes,” Eddie tried to deny, from where he was sitting close enough to Buck that they were practically in the same seat.

“Yes you do!” Chimney shouted from the couch, and Hen cackled beside him.

That was the routine, through the month of July and into the early days of August. And then, a few days before he was due to return to work, it suddenly changed. It was a day that Chimney was working a shift to cover another paramedic, and so Buck was spending it at the Diaz home, when someone came knocking on Eddie’s door. He paused on the way to answering it to put on a mask.

“Hel- Maddie?”

“Can I come in?” she asked, voice muffled by her own mask, and he quickly stepped aside so she could, following her into the living room. “Where’s Eddie?”

“Getting groceries for Shannon.” It had been part of what they’d come up with at the start of the mess, that Eddie dropped off whatever she and their kid needed. They were going to have to figure something else out soon, he knew, because Shannon was going to be headed back into work in a couple of weeks, and Chris was throwing tantrums to come back home.

“Good, that’s good.” With her face half-covered, Buck couldn’t really get a good read on her. There were new stress lines around her eyes, he saw, but she was standing as if a weight had been lifted from her shoulders. Her baby bump was already starting to show, and the sight of it filled him with happiness and concern, both.

(He really needed to figure out what to do for her PPD, when the time came.)

“What’s going on, Mads?”

“They found Doug,” she said, and the words nearly took him out at the knees, making him grab blindly for the couch. “Athena came and told me herself.”

“W- What?” he asked. “Where?”

“Wherever you left him, I would assume,” she said, looking him straight in the eyes.

And no, that wasn’t- She couldn’t- No.

“I have no idea what you’re-” he tried, but she shook her head.

“Doug told me once that his mother nearly named him Jason,” Maddie said, and Buck felt his stomach drop to his feet. “That was all I could think of, when Howie told me about the man you warned him away from. And then he recognized him in a photo I had mom send me.”

“Mom has pictures?” Buck asked. Stupid, so fucking stupid. He hadn’t even thought to ask his parents for help, had barely even thought about them at all since Ichabod. Stupid, stupid, stupid.

His sister nodded.

“I don’t know what happened,” she said, taking hesitant steps towards him. “I don’t want to know what happened.”

“Mads-”

“Thank you.”

“What?” That was not the response he had been expecting. He had expected disgust and fear and rage, not…Not gratitude.

“Thank you,” she repeated, reaching up to place gentle hands on his cloth covered cheeks. “You promised me, time and time and time again, that I would be safe here. That you would keep me safe. And you did.”

“He- I couldn’t-” He couldn’t get the words out, didn’t want to sully his sister with his actions in this timeline, or that man’s actions in the other. 

“And I am sorry, so very sorry, you had to go through that,” she kept saying. “But I need you to know that I am so very thankful.”

“I just- I had to keep you safe,” he sobbed out.

“And you did,” she told him, tugging his head down so it rested on her shoulder, her fingers going through his hair like when he was a kid. “I’m safe.”

Buck’s first day back at the station as an actual employee, rather than just a nuisance, was uneventful and boring. There were the regular mixed bag of calls, but people were still hesitant to go out and do stupid things, so the few calls they’d had were mostly medical emergencies. He didn’t really remember this day from the other timeline, days on the job tending to blur together over time unless it was something that stood out, but it seemed about right so far.

He was sprawled out on the couch, his feet hanging over one end and his head pillowed in Eddie’s lap. Chimney had made mocking sounds of disgust when he joined them in the den area, but they ignored him until he grew bored with it and turned on the news. At the sound of Taylor Kelly’s voice, Buck let out a sound of disgust and tuned out whatever she was saying.

“Have you and Shannon figured out what’s going on with Chris, now?” he asked, ignoring his alternate-timeline-girlfriend on the television.

“He’s moving back home with me,” Eddie told him. “It’s been a trial for the both of them. She was definitely not ready to be a full time mother again.”

“So what are you going to do dur-?” His question was cut off by Chimney’s shout.

“Oh! Buck, that’s that Jason guy!”

The words had him sitting up, his heart nearly stuttering to a stop. On the screen was a picture of Doug, not one of the wedding photos, so he had no clue where they got it from. For the first time, he started paying attention to what was being said.

“-the body found in Palos Verdes has been confirmed by an anonymous source to be Doug Kendell, of Hershey, Pennsylvania,” Taylor was saying, and out of the corner of his eyes, Buck saw Chimney turned his head to look at him.

“Doug? Maddie’s ex?” he tried asking, but Buck ignored him, busy trying to get a breath. This wasn’t- Why-

“Another source has confirmed that his last known sighting was in Twenty-Eighteen, when he had a violent encounter with his then-wife’s employer. It is not known at this time when or how he arrived in Los Angeles, and an official cause of death has not been given, but-”

“Buck?” Eddie’s voice was distant, as if the man was an ocean away instead of right next to him. He reached for him, but Buck batted the hand away as he stumbled to his feet. He couldn’t be here. He couldn’t be here, with Chimney staring at him in confusion and Eddie in concern. He couldn’t-

He couldn’t-

He was going to puke.

Buck ignored them yelling his name as he ran stumbling down the stairs to the bathroom, falling to his knees in front of the toilet bowl with barely enough time to spare. He continued kneeling there when he was done, shaking and gasping for breath.

Fuck, what was he going to do?

Chapter End Notes

I made a meme for you all.

The Reporter

2018, October

Taylor Kelly did not want to be stuck doing traffic reports on the radio for the rest of her life. Not only was that entirely dead-end, but she did not put so much effort into her hair for no one to see it. But it was what she had to work with, and she had learned from a very early age to make do with what she had. The opportunity for change came in the form of mechanical trouble, which sent the chopper she was reporting from cash landing into the bleachers for a sports field, and the handsome bunch of firefighters that came to their rescue.

It didn’t take much to convince her bosses to let her do a report on the station, because feel good stories about everyday heroes were catnip for viewers. They, in turn, helped convince the department brass. She didn’t actually care about the firefighters, or their stories. They were just a means to an end, an opportunity to prove that she deserved more than what the station had given her.

That wasn’t to say that the people there were boring, quite the opposite. There was Henrietta “Hen” Wilson, one of the only women on shift when she first showed up with her camera man in tow, and who had quickly caught onto Taylor’s angle in regards to everything. There was Howard “Chimney” Han, whose name most definitely had an interesting story behind it, and who was almost as desperate for his five-minutes of fame as she was. There was Edmundo “Eddie” Diaz, the - quite frankly, very attractive - army veteran, who very much did not like her.

The two that caught her interests the most, however, were the two that were the most desperate to avoid her. And in her experience, people so desperate to avoid sharing their stories had the most interesting stories to share.

There was Captain Robert “Bobby” Nash, who did not want her there, whatsoever. He would have certainly thrown her out of the station that first day if the chief hadn’t called when he did. There was definitely something he was hiding

And then there was Evan “Buck” Buckley, the cute puppy dog of a man with the interesting birthmark above his eye. He spent the entire time she was there avoiding her with more skill than anyone else. Actually, looking back, he had been avoiding her since the crash site, before she even had the idea of a story. No one that worked with him had anything negative to say about him, except for his recklessness at times. He was friendly, he was caring, he was loving. He was the station dalmatian she’d been looking for at the start.

He was also… Something.

“Don’t eat that!” Buck snapped at Chimney, when the blond had entered the loft to find them all eating brownies. Well, not all of them: Chimney had only just managed to get the last one and was about to eat it when Buck had smacked it out of his hands, and Taylor worked too hard for her figure to ruin it with fudge.

“What did the innocent brownie do to you?” the paramedic asked, sounding absolutely mournful over it. “It was fudge. With nuts. I love fudge with nuts. Why Buck, why?”

“Just - They were bad,” Buck stammered out, clearly trying to come up with an excuse for his outburst. “It was a bad batch. Like that cartoon.”

“A bad batch? How would you even know? Are you having a psychic moment?”

Taylor looked closer at the paramedic when he said that. He was honestly asking, as if his coworker being psychic was an actual possibility.

“Or just a loco moment,” Eddie added.

“Psychic?” Taylor wasn’t sure which angle was better, a firefighter who was legitimately psychic, or an unstable one who merely thought he was. Either way, this was something she could work with. “What does he mean by-?”

The station alarm interrupted her, and she had never seen a man seem so relieved to be headed for an emergency. Oh well, at least the captain was staying at the station for this call. She had the chance to crack him open while everyone was gone.

And then the brownies that Buck had been so concerned about turned out to be dosed with LSD, and oh! It was a damn goldmine of material, right in front of her camera. It was too bad the department lawyers were scarier than the news station’s. But still, that Buck had known…

2018, November

The next time Taylor Kelly had a chance to pin Buck down for her to ask about his ‘psychic moment’, it was almost an entire month later. She was at the karaoke bar nearest her news station, the one frequented by first responders of all stripes. Buck was across the room, sitting alone, staring morosely at the stage where Chimney was singing with a woman she didn’t recognize. It was a love song, so she assumed it was a new lady friend.

When Buck got up to order a drink, she told the bartender to give him a bourbon, in an effort to win him over. Except he had looked at the drink, and then over at her, and started to leave, without even taking the drink. Which just didn’t happen. She didn’t buy a guy a drink for them to just leave.

Especially not someone she could get a story out of.

“So, Buck,” she said, managing to intercept him before he got to the bar’s exit. “I see Chimney’s got a girlfriend.”

“What do you want, Taylor Kelly?” he asked. “What are you doing here?”

“Stalking you,” she tried to joke, but it obviously fell flat. “I’m kidding, the station is right around the corner, and I like to keep my ear to the ground.’

“Well, that’s nice, but I’m leaving now.”

“Buck, c’mon.” Taylor batted her eyes at him. “I just want to talk.”

“But I don’t want to talk to you.” And that was getting aggravatingly obvious. “Especially when I know you’re just fishing for a story. I haven’t forgotten what you tried to do to Bobby.”

“Okay, fine, you got me.” Maybe a little bit of honesty was the better approach. “It’s about what Chimney said, when everyone else was eating the special brownies. He asked if you were having one of your psychic moments?”

“You want to do a story on me?” Buck’s tone was an odd mixture of disbelief, amusement, and bitterness. “On that?”

“I’m just curious. A psychic firefighter? There’s a goldmine, right there.”

Something in Buck’s face changed, then, twisting it as he looked at her.

“Fine, y’know what? I’ll do a free reading, just for you,” he spat at her. “Your mother died and your father went to jail for it-” What the fuck? How did he know that? “-and he’s been denying his guilt ever since. You say that’s why you’re so obsessed with telling everyone else’s truth. You use your childhood to justify trying to ruin a good man’s life. But it’s all just an excuse, because you’re really just a loathsome bitch trying to make herself feel better by capitalizing on everyone else’s worst day.”

He sneered down at her, and she was too stunned to say anything back.

“You’re not pretty enough to hide that much ugly for long,” he said, and then turned his back on her.

Taylor didn’t chase after him, was too afraid to chase after him. How did he know that about her parents? How? She spent her entire adult life running from it, hiding from it. She didn’t even go by her last name anymore. No one in this city was supposed to know.

So how the hell did he?

2019, May

In the months following her brutal confrontation with Evan Buckley, she had done her best to avoid him. Luckily for her, he didn’t spend much if any time at the karaoke bar, not unless he was out with someone from the station, and that was only on rare occasions. That meant she could keep doing what she did best: listen to the conversations happening around her for interesting tidbits that she could make a story out of.

Honestly, it was a bit concerning how often the 118 came up in conversations. Those tidbits she tried to avoid like the damn plague. Anything to keep from running into Buck again and his far too personal knowledge of her. But still, they were interesting, like how they’d been framed for a diamond heist. Maybe, if one of the stories was worth it, she’d risk it.

“Did you hear about Nash?” a man near her said, talking to his drinking companion, and she paused to listen.

“What did that jackhole do now?” He was from the 122, Taylor thought. She’d seen him before, on a scene she had covered.

“He’s been sus- Holy shit!”

The loud outcry was joined by others, as everyone turned to look at one of the televisions hanging above the bar  It was showing a breaking news report, about a ladder truck being bombed, the injured firefighters being held hostage by some kid in a suicide vest. Taylor stared up at it, transfixed, and watched the drama unfold along with everyone else.

(In a different timeline, one where the bombing never happened, the firefighter would not have been interrupted. He would have finished his sentence, and Taylor would have moved to sit next to them, and listened eagerly as he told her all about Captain Bobby Nash and his suspension. And the story she made out of it would have been partially because of how sensational it was, and partially because she knew how much it would hurt one Evan Buckley.

But that wasn’t this timeline.)

2020, August

Dean Jacobs was a young officer on the force, and those were always the best to make friends with, in Taylor’s opinion. They were always so eager to brag, and always eager to make a pretty face smile. They had first met at the karaoke bar, before COVID restrictions had closed the venue down. One drink led to a quickie in the bathroom stall, and it turned out that officer Jacobs was very open with the pillow talk.

She was meeting with him at one of the city’s many parks, because he had texted her saying he had something she’d be interested in. Taylor sincerely hoped it was something she could use for a story, he wasn’t that good of a lay to be missing out on work for.

“So, what do you have for me?” she asked, sitting next to him on the bench and taking off her mask.

“You know those remains that were found in Palos Verdes last week? At the bottom of Vista Point?” Jacobs asked.

“It was the second body found there in the last couple of years, right?” she asked, clarifying. There had been another found, a hiker who’d been missing for years before that point. First responders had only found his remains because they were searching for an entirely different hiker.

“Yes, ma’am,” he said, smiling at her. Internally, she shuddered at the honorific. “But they got the dental records back.”

“And?”

“Doug Kendall,” he said, as if that name meant anything to her. “He’s been missing for a couple years now, apparently. He was last seen all the way in Hershey, Pennsylvania.”

“Okay, and?”

“Do you want to know who his brother-in-law was?”

Taylor resisted the urge to roll her eyes.

“You know I do.”

“Evan Buckley,” he said, and she felt her heart skip a beat. “That guy who was crushed by a firetruck last year, remember that?”

Slowly, Taylor felt the smile bloom across her face as she leaned into the young officer, placing a hand on his chest.

“Tell me more,” she purred.

The Story

“One week ago, a gruesome discovery was made at the bottom of Vista Point, in Palos Verdes. A pair of teenagers had run their boat ashore, and were trying to push it back to sea when one of them stumbled upon human remains. While the remains were in no state for an immediate identification, I can tell you now that the body found in Palos Verdes has been confirmed by an anonymous source to be Doug Kendell, of Hershey, Pennsylvania.

“Another source has confirmed that his last known sighting was in Twenty-Eighteen, when he had a violent encounter with his then-wife’s employer. It is not known at this time when or how he arrived in Los Angeles, and an official cause of death has not been given, but the investigation is ongoing.

“This is not the first time human remains have been found at the bottom of Vista Point. Also back in Twenty-Eighteen, first responders from the Los Angeles Fire Department responded to a call from an injured hiker and found the skeletal remains of another, who had been missing for five years by that point.”

The rest of the day following Buck’s panic attack did not go well. He spent much of his time between calls doing his best to avoid Chimney’s increasingly insistent questions, and everyone else’s concerned and confused gazes. Before, when Maddie came to him to say that he had been found, he hadn’t really understood what that meant. He had been too overwhelmed with the fact that his sister had at least an idea of what he had done, and was not condemning him for it, to really comprehend what could follow.

He did now.

Buck kept expecting for Athena to appear in the station bay, accompanied by Ransone or Romero. Or would they send someone else? Would they keep Athena distracted and busy, out of fear that she would try and warn him? He honestly wasn’t sure which would be worse, her being willing to put her career on the line for him, or that she would treat him like any other murderer she helped arrest.

Random trivia was once again his source of comfort, and he kept repeating the statistics in his head. Nearly a third of all reported homicides in the United States since 1965 had gone unsolved. In California, that number increased, to nearly two-fifths. In the county of Los Angeles, only a little more than half of reported homicides in that same period had been solved.

He had read once that the average person could walk past 36 murderers in their lifetime.

Every person in the station walked past one every day.

Unfortunately, he couldn’t avoid Chimney forever, because he had driven the man to work that day. Well, he could, but he wasn’t sure how it would look if he left Chimney stranded at the station. Buck regretted not doing so anyways about five minutes into the drive home.

“So Jason was Doug?” Chimney asked and kept asking. “That was Maddie’s ex-husband? Did you know? The entire time you were warning me, did you know?”

Buck bit his tongue and kept his eyes on the road, because there was no good answer to any of those questions. He could lie, but then he would have to keep lying, and eventually he’d trip up. Besides, his poker face was awful. Silence was the better option. Silence was always the better option.

“How did he even know Maddie was here?” The paramedic kept talking. “Oh man, she’s going to be so freaked. No, wait, she already knows. Doesn’t she? She asked me to look at a picture once, after I let slip about your warning.”

“Athena told her they found him the other day,” Buck said, because he couldn’t help but calm the man’s worries about his sister. “She didn’t tell me where.”

“Hey, wasn’t Vista Point the place with the hiker? The call you kept saying a ghost called Nine-One-One?”

“Oh look, we’re here,” he said, finally pulling into his spot at the apartment building. He waited for Chimney to grab his bag and hop out of the jeep, before saying, “I’m heading to Eddie’s.”

And then he didn’t even wait to make sure the paramedic made it inside before doing exactly that. Eddie was pacing the living room when he entered the residence, almost looking as stressed as he himself felt. The man barely waited for Buck to close the door behind him before grabbing and pulling him into a hug.

“You spent that Christmas here, with me,” he said, and Buck tried to pull back to look at him. “That’s when it happened, right? You were here, with me.”

“Eds, no.”

“Buck, yes,” Eddie said, finally letting go enough for him to step back a bit. “If anyone asks, you were here with me.”

“You’re seriously offering to lie to the police for me?” Not that Buck hoped it got that far.

“We promised to have each other's backs,” his boyfriend said, as if this situation was an obvious extension of that.

“Eddie, I wasn’t expecting you to help me cover up a m- murder when we said that.”

“What’s that quote? Good friends help you move, but best friends help you move a body?”

Buck didn’t get a chance to say anything to that before his phone started ringing in his pocket, causing them both to jump. He took it out and held it up as if it were a venomous snake, and let out a relieved breath when he saw it was his sister calling.

“Hi, Mads-”

“You were with me and Howie that Christmas,” she interrupted. He couldn’t help the small smile that formed at the words.

“I think I’ll let you two work this out,” he told Eddie, handing him the phone, and left to start on dinner while the two of them hammered out his alibi.

“A source close to the investigation has confirmed that the breaks found in Kendall’s remains are consistent with a fall occurring after death. This would mean, of course, that his body was dumped, likely from the top of the cliffs overlooking the shoreline. While the coroner has not been able to confirm the cause of death, the circumstances do point to homicide, although the police investigating the matter have not yet officially declared it as such.

“Doug Kendall was married to one Maddie Buckley, who divorced him in absentia in early Twenty-Nineteen. She moved to the city of Los Angeles without him in the latter half of Twenty-Eighteen. Her brother, Evan Buckley, also lives here, and works for the Los Angeles Fire Department. He was one of the victims of the firetruck bombing, back in May of last year.

“Ms. Buckley hasn’t answered our requests for interviews, and so we don’t know why exactly she moved to get away from her then-husband. But people at the hospital she worked at in Pennsylvania have described her coming to work with injuries on multiple occasions…”

“That loathsome fucking bitch!” Buck shouted at the television, and then quickly turned to Chris, “Do not ever use those words.”

Christopher had officially moved back in with his father, both of them having finally reached their limit in regards to their distance. Shannon had looked relieved when she brought him over, and Buck tried very hard not to judge her for it. He knew that it was vastly different caring for a four year old versus a ten year old, and there was a world of difference between being a part-time parent and a full-time one.

At least she was acknowledging her faults and was trying to make up for them.

“I think that’s a few dollars in the swear jar,” Eddie told a giggling Chris. “Why don’t you finish unpacking your clothes, okay kiddo?”

“Okay, dad,” the boy said, getting off the couch and heading to his room.

“Gracias a Dios, I am so glad to have him back home,” Eddie said, watching him go. “Even if it means figuring out childcare without Carla is going to be a pain.”

Carla had started cutting off clients in an effort to protect both herself and them. If they weren’t in desperate need of her services, then it was just not worth the risk of exposure. Unfortunately, it once again meant the Diazes were without her.

“Edmundo ended up leaving him at Hen’s while he worked,” Buck said, and it still felt odd referring to the other Eddie like that, even after months of doing so.

“That makes sense, Karen’s working from home, anyway,” he said, nodding. Then he pointed at the tv. “So, what did the loathsome bitch do now?”

“I’m pretty sure she just aired my sister’s abuse on live television,” Buck said, turning back to glare at the reporter on the screen. “She didn’t come out and say it, but it was definitely and heavily implied.”

“What a bitch.”

“I can’t believe I slept with her, much less dated her,” he grumbled, cursing his younger self. 

“You dated Taylor Kelly?” Disgust and judgment coated every syllable that fell out of Eddie’s mouth.

“Oh, you dated Ana Flores,” Buck countered. “Don’t get on your high horse.”

“Edmundo dated Ana Flores, I’m innocent of his sins,” Eddie argued back. “You, on the  other hand…”

“Look, I’m pretty certain it’s been made clear that rational thought in moments of panic is not my forte,” he said, crossing his arms. “And it was a stressful time, and she kissed me and then ran away and then came back, and that fact mattered.”

“That she kissed you and ran away?”

“That she came back,” he said with a shrug. He turned away from the television again in time to see sympathy filling his boyfriend’s eyes. Yeah, after Shannon, Eddie would understand why that mattered. “And I kept telling myself that she had changed from who she was when we first met her. But I don’t know if she actually did, or if I had just managed to delude myself the entire time.”

“Just to be clear, I am definitely still judging you,” Eddie told him.

“I’ve been judging myself for that choice since the second go-around with the brownies,” Buck said. He chewed on his lip. “Do you think they’ll let Athena be the one to arrest me?”

“No one’s being arrested for anything yet,” Eddie said, wrapping an arm around him.

“Yet.”

“Another confirmed sighting of Doug Kendall has been added to the timeline of events we’ve been putting together. It can be assumed that he took a plane to Los Angeles from Pennsylvania. He then rented a car from a small business near Burbank Airport. We know it was him, because one of the employees that worked there recognized him when they saw the photo in our report.

“The car he rented was initially reported stolen after he failed to return it when the rental contract expired, although it was eventually located at Burbank Airport. The GPS device attached to the car said it had been there since the late hours of Christmas, Twenty-Eighteen. Unfortunately, the owners of the business didn’t keep the full records, and so we don’t know where it was before that point.”

It was perhaps one of the more tense dinners Hen had ever sat through at the Grant-Nash house. She had moved back with Karen and Denny and Nia a couple weeks ago, but had dropped back in to see her friend. Things at the station had been weird since Taylor Kelly’s report on Doug Kendell’s death. Chimney had spent the entire day trying to get it out of Buck if he had known that “that Jason guy” was him when he warned the paramedic away, while Buck seemed to constantly be on the verge of a panic attack.

There were facts she had known before, and there were facts that the reporter was helpfully spreading out for all to see, and she was not liking the picture they made in her mind.

Neither were Bobby or Athena, it seemed.

“Athena?”

“Yes, Hen?” the sergeant asked, placing a too-wide smile on her face, the kind she wore right at the start of her and Michael’s break-up. She was clutching her glass of wine to her chest. Beside her, Bobby was dutifully cutting through his steak, mouth set in a grim line.

“I really don’t want to ask-”

“Then don’t,” the sergeant said, falsely sweet.

“But do you think-?”

“I said don’t!”

“Athena, come on!” Hen threw up her hand. “Things are looking pretty damn suspect. We all know something happened on Christmas that year, and now we know that Buck warned Chimney about a guy who turned out to be his now dead brother-in-law. Before Christmas!”

“I know nothing of the sort, Henrietta!” Athena shouted at her. She slammed her glass down hard enough that the wine sloshed out, and stood up so violently that her chair nearly toppled over. The kids were thankfully still with Michael. “And you will stop talking about it in my house!”

“Bobby,” Hen tried, looking to the captain for support.

“You heard my wife,” he said, not looking up from his food, which he had barely touched. 

The paramedic sighed and let it go. It was pretty clear now that they were both thinking it, too.

They just didn’t want to be thinking it.

She really, really did not want to be thinking it.

“Doug Kendall’s former brother-in-law, Evan Buckley works for the Los Angeles Fire Department, station One-Eighteen. It was the One-Eighteen who discovered the missing hiker at Vista Point before Kendall was declared missing. I did a series of interviews with most of the station One-Eighteen members back in October of that year, but Evan Buckley repeatedly refused to sit down for one.

“As if he had something to hide.

“One of Ms. Buckley’s former coworkers, when reached for comment, spoke of how Evan Buckley once tried for the Navy SEALs, but ended up dropping out…”

“Is this really necessary, Lou?” Athena asked, hands on her hips as she stood in the darkened observation room. 

“It is very necessary,” Lou Ransone said. “Even without Ms. Kelly’s own amateur investigation, things surrounding Kendall’s death already look sketchy. He and his sister would have been questioned anyway.”

“Look at that boy,” she said, gesturing through the one-way mirror. “There is no way you seriously-”

“Athena.” He was one of the few people who could interrupt her like that and get away with it. “You’re here as a courtesy.”

She swallowed down everything she wanted to say, because she knew she was already getting away with more than she should have been. If Lou hadn’t been her friend, she wouldn’t have even been allowed to bear witness to the questioning. The detective took her silence as the concession it was and left the room.

On the other side of the glass, Buck was sitting at the table, facing the glass. He looked so incredibly small for someone so tall. Beside him was a bronze-skin woman who had walked in with him when he arrived as requested to answer questions. She prayed that the fact he brought a lawyer with him was because he was being cautious, and not because he legitimately needed one.

“Mr. Buckley, Ms. Rose,” Lou greeted them when he opened the door to the interrogation room, moving to take the seat across from them. “Thank you for coming in today. We just had a few questions to ask…”

Questions of Innocence

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

It had been Athena who called and said they wanted him to come to the station for questioning. Buck wasn’t sure if she had been asked to do it or if she had volunteered, but either way, hearing it coming from her did very little to settle his nerves. But at least it was finally here, so he didn’t have to spend any more days-hours-minutes waiting for it.

Life had become very stressful ever since Taylor Kelly had started her systematic public flogging of his reputation. She didn’t come out and say he killed Doug, but she implied it hard enough. There was the allusion to Maddie’s abuse as a motive; there was the story of their call to Vista Point and the reiteration that they had been the one to find the five-years missing hiker; there was his background of SEALs training, however brief. If it was anyone but himself falling victim to it, he’d almost be impressed by her ability to tie it all together into a noose to hang him with.

The worst part was that she wasn’t wrong. Oh, the SEALs training hadn’t come into play at all, but everything else? Knowing that the hiker went unfound for years had been why he chose to dump Doug off the cliffs there, after all. And what Doug did to Maddie had been the motive, even if it was technically mostly what he was going to do.

Buck had called Attica Rose the moment he got off the phone with Athena, eternally grateful that he had kept her card from the bank heist fiasco the year before. She hadn’t sounded surprised to hear from him, apparently having followed Taylor Kelly’s reports as well. The public defender met him at the station, and with someone by his side, it wasn’t so scary to walk into his own interrogation again.

“Mr. Buckley, Ms. Rose,” Lou Ransone greeted them when he finally entered the interrogation room. Buck didn’t know him all that well, the most he had to do with the man was when Sue had been attacked in the other timeline, and he and Taylor had played amateur detectives. Fittingly, Taylor was helping to bring them together once again. “Thank you for coming in today. We just had a few questions to ask, regarding the events surrounding Doug Kendall’s death.”

“Is my client here because there is actual concern he was involved, or because of Ms. Kelly’s slanderous reporting?” Attica immediately asked, crossing her arms.

“Mr. Buckley-”

“Buck,” he interrupted, and immediately flushed when they both looked at him. “I- I go by Buck.”

“Buck,” Ransone amended with a slight nod. “Buck is here because we were simply wishing to clarify some things.”

“That were brought up because of that reporter, I’m sure,” Attica said. Ransone hesitated to answer, before sighing.

“Yes, her reporting did bring up some interesting questions,” he admitted. For some reason, that answer had the lawyer smiling slightly. “And some of those questions are what we were wanting answers to today.”

“Very well, let’s get this over with,” Attica said, settling into her seat. “So my client and I can both leave. He’s currently missing work, after all.”

“Mr. Buc- Buck, Doug Kendall was your brother-in-law, correct?”

“Yes.” He didn’t give any more details than that. He wasn’t asked for them, and he had learned from his brief foray into the true crime genre that details were where people tripped up.

“Were you aware of the abusive nature of your sister’s marriage?”

“I… I had reasons to suspect.”

“Was that why your sister moved to the city? To get away from an abusive husband?”

“Yes.”

Ransone looked at him for several moments, clearly mulling over his thoughts.

“This is what we’ve managed to put together so far,” he said, clasping his hands together in front of him and leaning forward. “Doug Kendall was an abusive husband, and when your sister finally had enough, she came to you. Mr. Kendall eventually tracks her down to Los Angeles and comes after her, renting a car from the place near the Burbank Airport. That was in November. The rental car is then reported stolen when he fails to return it at the end of the rental agreement, but it is eventually found at the airport.”

“That sounds an awful lot like what Taylor Kelly has been reporting,” Attica pointed out.

“Well, a lot of what she’s been reporting has come from our investigation.” He looked very perturbed when he said it. “As I was saying, the owners of the rental business said that the car’s GPS recorded it as being left there in the late hours of Christmas. That, combined with the autopsy report, tells us that Mr. Kendall probably ended up at the bottom of those cliffs around the same time.”

“Is there a question in all of this?”

“Where did you spend Christmas that year?” he asked, looking at Buck.

“Originally, I was invited to spend it with my captain and his wife,” he said, taking a deep breath. “I ended up spending the day with my sister, and then my boyfriend- He wasn’t my boyfriend then, but Eddie Diaz invited me over for the evening.”

“And if asked, they’d corroborate?”

“Yes.”

“It was the One-Eighteen that discovered the remains of the hiker that October, wasn’t it?”

“And we’re done here,” Attica Rose declared, getting up. “Because, considering that Mr. Kendall’s death hasn’t even been ruled as a homicide yet, you are certainly treating my client as a suspect for it. He’s answered your reasonable questions, anything else and you’ll need to actually give us proof that there was even a crime committed.”

“Fine,” Ransone said, looking as if he hadn’t been expecting anything different. “But if anything else comes up, we’ll be in touch.”

Buck and his public defender headed for the door, though he paused before stepping out. He glanced back at the detective.

“Hey, uh, no hard feelings?”

Ransone snorted in amusement.

“No hard feelings.”

Buck followed Attica through the station hallways, eager to get away. Once out the door, she paused and started digging through her purse for pen and paper, writing out a name and number.

“You’ll need this,” she said, handing it to him.

“What is it?” he asked, taking the slip of paper.

“A lawyer I know that handles civil suits. We’re not friends, but he gets results,” she answered, and the idea of another lawsuit almost had him balling it up and tossing it on instinct. “Taylor Kelly’s reporting on you in relation to Mr. Kendall’s death was the entire reason you were dragged in today, regardless of what they might claim. The detective even admitted to it. It’s defamation. Specifically, it’s slander per se.”

“So you’re suggesting I sue her?”

“You were nearly charged with a crime entirely based on her words,” she said. “Suing her is the least she deserves. What does she have against you, anyway?”

“I called her a loathsome bitch to her face, once,” Buck admitted, and the bronze-skinned woman burst out laughing.

“She is certainly earning that moniker,” Attica Rose said. “Keep my card, if you need me again, don’t hesitate to call. I enjoy keeping their jobs from being too easy.”

“No offense, but I really hope I don’t have to talk to you again,” he told her, making her laugh again as she headed for her own car. 

“None taken, Buck.”

Maddie Buckley was pregnant and tired and stressed when she arrived at the dispatch center for her shift. Her doctor had started limiting her caffeine intake, and she had nearly murdered Albert for his coffee that morning. She would blame these circumstances, along with a brief bout of clinical insanity, for her actions.

“Ms. Buckley!” Taylor Kelly shouted from where she was laying in wait. She wasn’t quite on the property, having already been warned away once. But still, Maddie had to walk past her from where she parked. “Do you have any comments on your brother being brought in for questioning in relation to your husband’s death?”

Nope, nope, nope. Ignore her, Maddie. She isn’t worth it.

“No comment at all? You haven’t spoken publicly about the abuse, do you think that’s-? Ah!” Taylor stumbled back, clutching the cheek where Maddie had slapped her. She hadn’t even realized she was doing it until her palm was cracking against the reporter’s face. And it made a very lovely sound.

“What I went through in my marriage is not fodder for your attempts at fame,” Maddie snarled at her, her mask doing little to muffle the absolute anger in her voice. “And what you’re doing to me and my brother is well-past reasonable reporting. Get out of here before I report you for harassment.”

She turned on her heel and marched for the doors, shaking out her stinging hand. Her phone started ringing and she pulled it out to answer.

“So I’m not being charged with anything,” Buck told her.

“That’s good,” Maddie said. “I just slapped Taylor Kelly in front of her camera.”

Her brother whistled in appreciation.

“I wish I could have seen that,” he said. “Hey, the public defender that helped me out gave me the name of another lawyer. A, uh. A lawyer that specializes in civil suits. Like defamation.”

“And are you going to take her up on that suggestion?”

“Mads, it… Does this even count as…?"

“That’s beyond the point,” she told him, pausing just outside of the elevator. “But I can see why you’d be hesitant. But you can’t tell me it isn’t making things difficult at work for you.”

“It’s really not, though?” he said. “Like yeah, I constantly feel like everyone’s tiptoeing around me in conversations, and I know I’ve walked in on people talking about me. I mean, outside of work my life has been stressful as hell, but at work? It’s…”

She could just about hear the shrug he ended that sentence with.

“Speaking of work, I need to get going,” Maddie said, glancing at the time on her phone. “But hey, send me the info for that lawyer. If you don’t do it, I will. She has no business dragging the details of my marriage out like she has been.”

“Yeah, I- I’m so sorry, Mads.”

“No one’s fault but hers.”

“Do you think he did it?” Hen asked Chimney while they were restocking the ambulance, Buck upstairs with Eddie and Bobby. The man in question had come in late for his shift, due to him being questioned for a possible murder he might have committted. The very idea of it, of their golden retriever of a coworker killing a person, absolutely blew her mind. Then again, she couldn’t really imagine Eddie killing someone, and that he served in Afghanistan was a commonly known fact.

“I…” He glanced around, nervous. “I don’t know. I mean, he spent like, entire months angry beyond belief. And before that, we all saw that downward spiral he took.”

“And he definitely knew Doug was in town before he went missing. You said so yourself.”

“But that doesn’t mean that he…” Chimney trailed off. None of them had ever even voiced the exact words yet, seemingly all under the belief that not saying it kept it from being true.

“I don’t think I would blame him if he did,” Hen admitted, and her partner sputtered in shock. “I nearly let Eva die, when I found her overdosing.”

“What the hell?”

“She was trying to take my kid away,” she said. It wasn’t the same, not nearly so. But she understood the need to protect one’s family, no matter what. Taylor Kelly’s own reporting had heavily alluded to what Maddie had suffered at Doug’s hands, and Hen could never hope to understand how Buck had felt, being unable to protect his sister from that. “So I don’t think I would blame him, if he did.” She set her jaw and nodded to herself, reaching a decision. “But he didn’t.”

Chimney stared at her, before nodding as well.

“But he didn’t.”

“According to Athena, they’re going to mark down Doug’s cause of death as undetermined and just let it go,” Buck told Eddie that evening. The sergeant had called him herself, to let him know. “Outside of Taylor’s claims, there’s not any actual evidence of what I did, so…” He trailed off with a shrug and rolled his head over to look at Eddie, sitting on the other end of the couch. Chris was asleep between them, having passed out in the middle of a Disney movie that had just come out, but which Buck had already seen a few dozen times before.

“So you are literally getting away with murder.”

“Can we not joke about this?” he begged.

“Sorry, corazon,” Eddie said, smiling apologetically at him. “So, I got to see your sister slapping Taylor Kelly on live television today.”

“Oh man, it was live?” Buck asked, sitting up. “I knew it was in front of a camera, but I didn’t know it was live.”

“Pretty sure Chimney swooned and started composing a sonnet for her right that moment.”

“I don’t think I want to ever hear Chimney’s attempts at poetry.”

Eddie hummed in agreement, settling further into the couch as he looked down at Chris, the boy somehow managing to sprawl across the both of them.

“What are the chances that she’ll stop with the story now?” he asked Buck. “I mean, with the police themselves saying there’s nothing worth investigating.”

“From my experience? She’s a dog with a bone.” He sighed, thinking back to what she had told him once, years ago and a year from now. “She once told me that unsolved mysteries never sat right with her, that the truth was worth everything. I don’t know how much of that was her actual feelings, and how much of it was justification, but…”

“So we should expect her to keep hounding you.”

Buck chewed on his lip, thinking.

“Attica- The uh, the public defender that helped me when we were questioned during the bank heist? I called her for help with the questioning today, and she gave me the number to another lawyer. She thinks there's grounds for a civil suit. A defamation case.”

“There probably is,” Eddie pointed out.

“Is it defamation if literally nothing she said was actually a lie?” Buck asked, struggling with the question himself. “I mean, I-” He glanced down, making sure Chris was still asleep. “I did kill Doug. I did dump his body at Vista Point because I knew it would take years for him to be found, because of that hiker call.”

“The police said there was nothing worth investigating further,” Eddie pointed out. “And you just told me she isn’t going to stop on her own.”

“You think I should go with the lawyer.”

“At the very least, she deserves to be raked over the coals for what she’s doing to Maddie. Your sister didn’t deserve to have her trauma exposed like that.”

“You’re right. You’re absolutely right.” Buck had killed a man to protect his sister, the action which started this whole mess to begin with. He could put aside his own doubts and file a lawsuit to protect her now. The paper Attica Rose gave him was still in his pocket, where he’d stuffed it without actually looking at it. When he dug it out and read the name she had given him, he couldn’t believe his luck was actually so awful.

Back at the crossroads, he was certain that Ichabod was laughing his ass off.

“What’s that face for?” Eddie asked. “What’s wrong?”

“I know this lawyer,” Buck said, unsure of if he wanted to laugh, or cry, or laugh and cry. “And he’s… He’s not a bad lawyer, he’s just a bad person.”

“Okay? Who is it?”

“Chase Mackey,” Buck said, handing him the paper to read for himself. “The guy I hired to sue Bobby and the department.”

Chapter End Notes

Now I feel I must make a note of my thoughts regarding Chase Mackey: He's an utter shithead, but he's obviously good at what he does, because he got the department to offer Buck a seven digit settlement. As their starting position. Like, say what you will about his ethics and him as a person, but...

Suits

Deciding to go with the suit, and with Chase Mackey in particular, was not a particularly easy or pleasant choice for Buck. He felt unclean for going through with it, and talking to the man brought up too many memories of when he was fighting against Bobby for his right to work. But he knew that Taylor wasn’t going to stop until either she got a suitable conclusion to the story, or she was forced to stop. And since the suitable conclusion ended with him in jail for premeditated murder, well…

The bright side was that he didn’t really have to interact with Mackey all that much, to be honest. On a day between shifts, he went to the building where they did the fire drill back in October, and was welcomed with open arms and a smile with too many teeth. He honestly shouldn’t have been too surprised, the man had probably caught the scent of blood when it became increasingly obvious that Taylor was trying to convict him in the court of public opinion.

“Honestly, I don’t care about my character,” Buck told him. “I’m mostly doing this because she’s dragging my sister’s trauma into it.”

“But she has basically accused you of murder,” Mackey pointed out. He was still smiling, it was starting to get creepy. “Didn’t she say you were questioned by the police?”

“Yeah. The detective said it was partly because of her.” He remembered the way Attica had smiled when Ransone admitted to that, and only now was he realizing why.

“At the questioning?” Mackey asked, and wrote something down when Buck nodded. “Well, I’ll be honest, I think this is going to be a walk in the park.”

“So long as she can’t use my sister for it anymore, I don’t care,” Buck told him, and watched as Mackey’s smile somehow got even wider.

“Don’t worry. By the time we’re done, she won’t be.”

“God, I just feel so… Ugh.” Buck gave a full body shudder. He was Facetiming his sister from Eddie’s kitchen, the only place he really felt comfortable talking about everything going on with Taylor. There had seemed to be a unanimous and unspoken agreement to just not talk about it at work, to the point where the television was never left on the channel for Taylor’s news station anymore. Doug had become a new version of the Q-word, unique to the 118, and absolutely no one seemed willing to bring him up in conversation, at least not where Buck could hear.

It was as if the entire station had all just woken up one day and collectively decided that if they didn’t talk about it, or acknowledge it, then it never happened.

“Is he really that bad?” Maddie asked him, and he could tell she was trying not to laugh at him.

“I would call him a shark, but I would be doing a disservice to those beautiful and misunderstood creatures,” Buck told her. “He just… He oozes slime, Mads. I feel dirty just being in the same room as him.”

“Then why did you go with him? Why not find another lawyer?”

“Because he’s actually very good at what he does,” he said, sighing and resting his head on his arms. “And I mean, he and Taylor seem to have the same ethics, so it’s just… Fight fire with fire, y’know?”

“I’m not sure that’s why we’re called firefighters, querido,” Eddie said, joining him in the kitchen.  “Is he going on about Mackey again, Maddie?”

“Yup.”

“He came in after talking with him the other day and spent about an hour scalding himself in the shower.”

“I felt dirty, okay!?” Buck whined. “And it wasn’t an hour. Your water heater isn’t good enough for an hour of scalding.”

“Just how often are you at Eddie’s now?” Maddie asked, propping her chin in her palm and smiling at him through the screen.

“About as much as before the kissing started,” he admitted. He let his eyes fall close when he felt Eddie start running fingers through his hair, and heard Maddie let out a quiet coo. “Well, okay, maybe a bit more now. Chimney spent a few days stressing the fuck out when I was at the apartment with him, trying not to ask anything after that first day. It just seemed… Mean, when I had somewhere else to go and he didn’t.”

“There is absolutely nothing stopping that man from coming home except himself,” Maddie huffed. “But besides making you feel dirty, how is everything actually going on with the suit?”

“Oh, fantastic,” Buck said, opening his eyes and lifting his head up. “The news station has already dropped the story entirely. They haven’t made any retraction or apologies or whatever, but they’re not talking about it anymore.”

“How’s life with Albert going?” Eddie asked, changing the topic. Buck could see the young man had appeared in the background, toweling at his hair. He perked up like a meerkat at the mention of his name.

“Remarkably similar to life with Buck, age nine,” Maddie commented drily. “Just with fewer injuries.”

“Hey!” Albert paused in drying his hair to scowl at her back.

“I swear to God, if you left another wet towel on the floor, I will strangle you with it,” Maddie tossed over her shoulder, not looking at him. Eddie and Buck sniggered to themselves as they watched the young man sheepishly step back into the bathroom and come back out a moment later with another towel.

“Don’t worry, Mads, you’ll get the other Han back soon,” Buck promised his sister. “I can’t really say it’ll be an improvement, but…”

“Was that a psychic moment?” Albert asked, moseying over to stand beside her. “Howie told me you had psychic moments.”

“He’s not psychic,” Maddie and Eddie said together. Albert blinked and shrugged.

“Okay.”

On the screen, Buck saw his sister scrunch her nose up and start sniffing the air around herself and Albert.

“Is that… Did you use my shampoo?”

“I ran out of mine yesterday.”

“So you used mine?”

“...Do you want coffee?”

“Yes, please.”

“Y’know,” Buck drawled as Albert scurried off screen to do his sister’s bidding. “Chimney won’t be happy with your drinking habits.”

“If Howie has a problem with me drinking coffee, he can come over here and pry it out of my cold, dead hands,” Maddie declared.

“Yeah, I can’t possibly understand why Chimney would be reluctant to return home to that,” Eddie said, draping himself against Buck’s back, resting his chin against his shoulder. 

“Are you saying my sister is not a delight to be around?” Buck asked, turning his head enough to grin at him.

“I’m saying there was a reason I fled to an active war zone when Shannon was pregnant, and she wasn’t suffering from caffeine withdrawal on top of everything else.”

“I thought that reason was finances and parental expectation,” Buck said, and Eddie shoved at his face.

“Let me have this.”

“No.”

“You two are adorable,” Maddie said, drawing their attention back to the screen. At some point, Albert had given her her coffee before scampering off. It was in the obnoxiously large mug that Buck had given her for her birthday that year.

“That is a cup of coffee,” Eddie commented.

“The doctor said one cup a day, she didn’t say anything about the size of the cup,” Maddie said primly.

“Did they just stick a handle onto a bowl?”

“I don’t know, ask your boyfriend. He’s the one who got it for me,” she said with a shrug, and then broke into a grin when she realized that it wasn’t a coincidence. “Oh my God, Buck, you really are the best brother.”

“So he is psychic?” Albert asked from off screen.

“No,” the three of them answered together.

Taylor Kelly was not having the time of her life. She had been flying high off the minor renown she made from the story of Doug Kendall and how Evan Buckley had obviously killed him, even if she never said that outright. She had been certain she was bound for a cushy anchor job or bigger stories that were actually worth her skill and time, something beyond the small pieces of gristle she had been reporting on ever since she managed to escape the traffic report. And then that man had waltzed into the station, walking with more self-assuredness than she could ever hope to actually feel, and demanded to see both her and her producers.

Ever since he served them with papers, she hadn’t been allowed anywhere near a microphone or a camera. Taylor had become persona non grata overnight, everyone whispering behind her back whenever she slunk into the building. It wasn’t fair, she just wanted the world to know the truth. And if it benefitted her, then all the better.

It had been an entire week and a half since Chase Mackey darkened the station halls, and now she was being called into a meeting with her bosses. She prettied herself up and put on her most winningest smile, but it melted off her face when she walked into the meeting to find that one of the station lawyers was waiting for her, as well.

“Thank you for joining us, Ms. Kelly,” her boss said, a stuffy man old enough to be her father. It didn’t escape her notice that the only seat left was on the far end from where everyone else was sitting.

“Is this about the suit?” she asked, trying to keep her voice from shaking as she sat.

“Yes, it is,” he said. “The suit is over.”

“That’s good! Then I can go back out there and-”

“No.” The single word echoed through the boardroom like the toll of a church bell.

“No? W- What do you mean?”

“I mean that you will not be going back out there, not as one of our reporters,” he said, glowering at her. “We decided to settle. Do you know how many thousands of dollars you have cost us, Ms. Kelly?”

“Thousands? B- But Buckley, he-”

“Enough!” he snapped, slamming his fist on the table. “To answer my own question: too many. You have cost us too many thousands of dollars. We should have pulled the plug the moment that it was obvious you were trying to convict an innocent man, but viewership was up. Except that all the profits we made from that are gone now, and then some.”

“That isn’t my fault.”

“Oh, but it is,” the man said. “And this isn’t even the first time your reporting has brought us legal trouble, except our lawyers-” He gestured at the man beside him. “-managed to step in before things got messy that time. And funnily enough, it involved the same group of firefighters then, too. I don’t know what your obsession with them is, and I don’t care. Because you are no longer our problem.”

“What do you mean?” Taylor asked, though she was afraid that she knew exactly what he meant.

“You are fired,” he said. “Effective immediately.”

“You can’t!” she tried to protest, looking desperately at the lawyer.

“Oh, but I can,” her boss said. “And I am. Because you violated the most important of our station’s ethics.”

He stood and leaned over the table, resting his hands on its surface, before telling her,

“You cost us money.”

“We would like to issue a public retraction of all of our former reporter’s accusations and allusions regarding the death of Doug Kendall, which has not been ruled a homicide and was never investigated as such,” the anchor on the screen said, eyes fixed beyond the camera to where a teleprompter was no doubt listing off the words she needed to say. Buck stood in front of the television at the station, feeling somewhat awed by it all. “We would also like to apologize to Mr. Buckley and his sister for the emotional toll our former reporter’s actions have caused.”

“So the lawsuit went well?” Bobby asked, coming up to stand beside him.

“Very well,” he said, tearing his eyes from the screen to look at him. Mackey had called him into his office a day ago to tell him that the station had offered to settle, practically dancing behind his desk as he showed him the amount being offered. It wasn’t anywhere close to what the city had offered Before, merely five digits instead of seven, but it was still a hefty amount.

“Our former reporter,” Eddie echoed from where he was standing next to them. “Does that mean…?”

“I felt a bit petty,” Buck said, shrugging. Mackey had said that he could easily get him a higher offer, but the money had never and would never be the point. The point was to keep Taylor from hounding him or anyone else close to him, and the station had jumped at the alternative to losing even more money. “She shouldn’t have brought up Maddie’s trauma like that.”

“How much did they give you?” Chimney asked, he and Hen coming over to join them.

“Enough,” Buck said. He hadn’t looked at the exact amount, and he knew a chunk of it would be going to Mackey. “I’m taking it and squirreling it away for a rainy day.”

He was already thinking of how he could trick Eddie into accepting some of it for a new truck, already structuring the argument in his head with just the right amount of Christopher-related manipulation. Maybe he could just do it like he did the coffee maker and frame it as a prank.

Actually, Eddie’s face if he walked out of his house to find it gift-wrapped in his driveway would be hilarious.

Of Things That Shake You

“The doctor said one cup a day,” Maddie said, and Buck could easily envision the face she was making, even without seeing the screen.

“Yeah, well, she’s the doctor,” Chimney said. “Not the parent.”

Buck couldn’t help but roll his eyes at the way the man was trying to helicopter parent an unborn child through Facetime.

“You know who gets the final say in what Maddie drinks?” he asked the paramedic, passing by him to get his own coffee. “Maddie. Maddie gets the final say.”

“Hey, go stick your face in your own Facetime.”

“Oh, go bicker with my sister in person. Hen and Eddie have both been back with their kids for months now. Hell, I saw Chris yesterday. You’re the only one still bunkering down like it’s World War Z.”

“I’m being cautious,” the paramedic retorted. “And we’re not bickering, we’re bantering. Playfully. Speaking of: shouldn’t you be in your room bantering with Eddie?”

“Did… Did you mean to make that sound dirty?” Buck asked, making a face at Chimney. He looked at his sister on the screen. “It’s not just me, right? That sounded dirty?”

“It sounded dirty,” Maddie agreed, Albert nodding along behind her.

“You are all disgusting,” Chimney groused.

“You’re the one making innuendos about my brother and his boyfriend,” she pointed out, causing Chimney to sputter out denials.

“I’m going to go take a shower,” Buck told them, before slapping the other man on the shoulder. “Shift starts in an hour. If you’re not ready in thirty, I will leave you behind.”

“That threat would be so much worse if I didn’t end up driving myself to work most mornings, anyway.”

 “Yeah, yeah,” Buck said, waving him off as he headed for the bathroom. “Just try not to, uh, banter with my sister for too long.”

“Disgusting!” Chimney shouted after him.

The weeks after Taylor Kelly was banished from their television screens had seemed to fly by, and before Buck knew it, it was the middle of September and microquakes were plaguing the city.
