That, more than anything, had helped him remember what day they were coming up on. After he and Chimney got to the station and changed for work, he hunted down his wayward boyfriend. The argument for getting Eddie a new truck with the lawsuit money had not been going well for Buck. The man just refused to accept charity for himself, no matter the source.

It was looking like he really would have to prank him with a brand new truck and ask forgiveness when the shouting was done.

“How was the drive this morning?” Buck asked when he found Eddie in the kitchen area, spilling himself into the seat next to him.

“It was fine,” Eddie said, eyeing Buck up like a threat.

“You know what would make it a better drive?”

“Buck…”

“I’m just saying. I have money I’m not going to spend, you have a truck that needs replacing.”

“My truck is working just fine.”

“For now. But you were just complaining the other day that the radio was acting up.”

“I can live without a working radio in my truck.”

“Can you?” Buck asked. “Can you really?”

“Buck,” Eddie said again, the warning tone a bit sharper this time, and he raised his hands with a sigh.

“Fine, fine, I’ll let it go for now,” he said, and then let himself fall against his shoulder. “It’s going to be a mess soon.”

“How so?”

“Uh, Caltech’s been tracking microquakes-”

“So you’ve mentioned.”

“Well, there’ll be a not-so-micro one at some point, which’ll cause a dam to break and part of Mt. Lee to come down.”

“That does sound like a mess,” Eddie agreed, and Buck could feel him nodding.

“There’ll be a bus in the side of a building,” he told him. “I still don’t know how that happened.”

“So we should definitely make sure the trucks are stocked,” the other man suggested, and Buck lifted his head to grin at him. “Why are you-? Oh no.”

“Oh yes,” Buck said, and then ran off in search of a clipboard.

An hour later, the earthquake hit, and things did indeed get messy.

“At least it’s not a tsunami,” Eddie said as the elevator doors closed, blocking their view of the bus, and Buck turned his head to glare at him.

“You know, for how much you insist that the two of you are different people,” he said. “Your awful humor is exactly the same as Edmundo’s.”

“You love it.”

“I mean, yeah. But still.”

The bus sticking out of the building went about the same as it did Before. Buck and Eddie went to the roof so Buck could rappel down and anchor everything while Bobby and the others got everyone off. And then they had to turn the whole thing into a teeter-totter to get some poor bastard out from under it. Honestly, Buck had forgotten about him entirely. Oops.

And then Bobby once again gave him a minor heart attack with the natural gas explosion.

Of course, the dam and the bus were never going to be the biggest problems of the day. No, no, that would be the landslide at Hollywood Hills that hit just as they were packing up to go back to the station, rerouting them to the impact site.

“Should we be worried about more of that hill coming down?” Eddie asked, joining Bobby and Hen where they were meeting with the incident commander, Buck and Chimney following behind.

“Yeah, we work quick, we work safe, we hope for the best,” Bobby told them, before turning back to the battalion chief overseeing everything. “Where do you want us?”

“The Hollywood sign,” she said, nodding up the hill.

“Which part?” Buck asked, because just as he remembered, a couple of the letters had moved, and one was missing entirely.

“The H,” she said. “It landed just west of here.  There were some hikers in the area.”

“Guess they should have bought a vowel,” Chim joked, and looked far too pleased with himself for it.

“Okay, Hen, Eddie, you’re with me at the sign,” Bobby said, giving out their marching orders. “Chimney, Buck, you stay here and help search for survivors.”

Buck nodded and headed to grab the gear he needed, but a hand at his shoulder stopped him.

“Athena was supposed to be here, helping evacuate residents,” Bobby said, keeping his voice low. “Is she…?”

“If there was reason to be worried for her, I’d tell you,” Buck said.

“No, you wouldn’t.”

“Okay, fair. But Bobby, if she wasn’t okay, do you really think I’d be wasting time here?”

It took a moment, but the captain eventually nodded and let him go with a pat on the shoulder.

Searching through the impact zone with Chimney was not any better the second go around. Actually, it was somehow worse, because he knew exactly how few people they were going to find alive. The hope that he had carried when he first lived through it had sputtered out, and now it was a matter of going through the motions. He tried not to let it show too much, though. Not when he knew how prone Chimney was to checking his reactions like a forecaster checking the clouds.

Hearing the baby’s cry was still like being struck by lightning and stepping into a sunbeam, all at the same time.

“It’s a baby monitor,” Chimney said, picking it up after digging it out from the debris. He turned in circles for a bit, before settling an expectant stare on Buck. “So where’s the baby?”

“Why are you looking at me like that?”

“You know exactly why,” the paramedic said, crossing his arms, the monitor clutched in his hand. “Where to, o’ human dowsing rod?”

Buck rolled his eyes and tried racking his brain for where they needed to go. He felt really, really awful for letting what they were about to find happen again, but it had been literal years from his point of view. It had honestly slipped from his mind between Eddie, his skull fracture, and everything surrounding Taylor Kelly.

Though, would he have even known which house to send the cops to, if it wasn’t covered by half a mountain?

He remembered there was a chimney. The pun stuck with him.

“I only heard a baby, not an adult,” Chimney commented as the two of them worked their way farther along the buried neighborhood. “When we heard the crying.”

“I’m sure their parents are there,” Buck said, remembering the house full of trapped pregnant women. 

“Or maybe they’re dead,” the paramedic countered. “Poor kid might be an orphan.”

“You never stop going with the worst-case scenario, do you?”

“I’m not psychic, but I think I’m sensing some judgment.”

“Yeah, because you’re having a kid with my sister, but you’re living in my guest room.”

Chimney gave an almost condescending sigh.

“To protect her,” he said. “And your niece or nephew. Maybe you’ve missed it, but the world’s taken an unexpected turn to crazy town. I’m just trying to keep them safe, until…”

“Until what? The world goes back to normal?” Buck asked, coming to a stop and slamming the pick he’d been using as a hiking stick into the mud. “Sorry to be the bearer of bad news, but it won’t. Not to how things were.”

“Then I’ll be a crappy dad over videoconferencing,” Chimney said, coming to a stop as well. “That’s actually something I got experience with.”

“You’re so afraid of what might happen that you’re running away. Trust me, Chim, that doesn’t solve anything. It just… It just makes what you’re afraid of come true.” He shook his head, and then pointed at the roof they’d stopped by. “We’re here, by the way.”

The other man leaped at the change of topics, turning to follow the direction of Buck’s finger.

“So how do we get inside?”

“Chimney.”

“What?”

“The chimney,” Buck said, rolling his eyes.

“You have kids, right? Family?” Sylvia asked. Athena had been trying to coax the agoraphobic woman out of her house when the landslide struck, bringing the building they were in down the mountainside. Now, the woman was trapped under a slab of debris, and the sergeant was trying to leverage it up enough to free her. Things seemed dire, not helped by Sylvia’s insistence she leave her behind and save herself, nor by May’s support for the idea over the radio.

But if things were truly so dire as they seemed, Athena had no doubt in her mind that Buck would have been there. She knew that the young man would have thrown himself into danger to help her, if things were truly as bad off as everyone else thought. That he hadn’t been waiting for her at the house when she arrived, a sheepish excuse at the ready, told her that if nothing else, she got through this in one piece.

“I have nobody,” Sylvia continued. “No one’s gonna miss me if I go down with this thing. You have people to go home to. Go. I deserve this.”

“You think you deserve to die alone in the dark, just because you lived your life alone?” Athena had heard a lot of stupid things in her life - a concerning amount of which came out of Buck’s mouth - but this just about took the cake.

“I deserve it ‘cause I never should’ve survived in the first place,” she said. “It was a car accident. I was driving, my sister was in the passenger seat. Another car came out of nowhere, and… I survived, and my sister didn’t.”

“I’m sorry,” Athena whispered, knowing full well how useless those words truly were.

“Afterwards, everyone told me I should get back out there and move on with my life, but without my sister in the world, I just… I just wanted to be in it less.” She was crying, and Athena paused in her efforts, sitting beside her and placing a comforting hand on her shoulder. “Eventually, I just stopped going out at all.”

“You gave up on yourself,” Athena concluded. “On life.”

“Wouldn’t you?” Sylvia asked, and then, “Of course you wouldn’t. You’re not a weak person.”

“I was attacked a few months ago,” the sergeant told her. “I was alone in the dark, and I never saw him coming. I have never felt more weak, or more powerless in my life.”

“Your trouble wasn’t your fault.”

“No, it wasn’t,” she agreed. “And someone helped me then, just like I’m helping you now. Because we’re never truly as alone in the dark as we think we are. I blame myself for walking into that building alone, and he blames himself for not being able to help me sooner.” Just like there was no doubt in her mind that Buck would have been there to help her again if she needed it, she knew he felt guilty for not doing more on that awful day. “Just like you blame yourself for driving and surviving. But that guilt is only going to isolate you.”

“I couldn’t save my sister,” Sylvia sobbed.

“But you can still save yourself,” Athena urged, getting back to her feet and grabbing her makeshift pry bar. “There’s no shame in fear, Sylvia. But you have to push through it. Through the fear and the pain, and out the other side.”

And Sylvia didn’t look quite convinced, not yet. But she set her jaw and nodded anyway, and they both went to work.

Two weeks after the landslide, Eddie found himself drawn outside far too early by the sounds of a tow truck. At first, he’d been terrified that his truck was being towed, though he couldn’t figure out a reason why it would have been. Instead, he found them doing a drop off.

It was a large black truck, four doors. A Ford, going by the logo. Eddie had seen it before, actually. Or at least a picture of it. On his boyfriend’s phone, before he mysteriously dropped the argument to let him spend money on Eddie. Except, it apparently wasn’t so mysterious now.

Ay Dios, there was even a giant red bow on the hood.

He yanked out his phone and hit call, not even giving the other man time to speak before loudly saying,

“What the fuck, Buck!?”

“Merry Christmas!”

“Halloween is still three weeks away!”

“Time is an illusion.”

“Buck!”

“Love you, see you at work, bye!”

Eddie glared at his phone as it switched back to his list of contacts. Oh, he was going to murder the man. He glanced back at the unwanted gift and scowled harder, because it was a very nice truck.

"Que cabrón.” What an asshole.

The Fear of Tomorrow, and the Days That Follow

Time after the landslide - and after Chimney moved back in with Maddie, switching living situations with Albert - was weird, moving so much quicker than the rest of the year had. It felt like Buck blinked and suddenly it was January, Halloween and Thanksgiving and Christmas having all flown by him. Eddie had taken weeks to forgive him for the gift he had given him in the early days of October, and even longer to actually admit he liked the new truck better than his old one.

With January came the reintroduction of a trait that both Eddie and Edmundo shared: technophobia. Because no matter what he said, the two of them were very much the same person where it counted. Seeing Eddie freak out over the HILDY Smart Home again was, perhaps, about as amusing as the man being jealous of himself and trying to deny it. More so, actually.

“Who would want to live like this?” Eddie demanded to know as they guided the gurney into the house. “Cameras and microphones everywhere, not knowing who’s watching or listening. And you have that smile again.”

“Just, fond memories,” Buck told him, and his voice absolutely gave away the adoration he was feeling for the ridiculous man.

“This is an Edmundo thing, isn’t it?”

“He was freaked out, too,” he said. And then, because he probably took far too much joy in seeing his boyfriend freak out, “Y’know, Eddie, if you have a computer or a smartphone, or really a smart anything, then anyone can spy on you.”

“Now I’m thinking I shouldn’t buy that fancy smart coffee maker I keep seeing commercials for.”

He wouldn’t have to, because Buck already had it queued up to order, just waiting for brilliant little Christopher to come up with the prank. Wait, how many expensive gifts did it take before he was considered a sugar daddy?

“Hello Eddie,” HILDY chimed in at just the right moment, making the man jump. On its screen on the wall, it flashed a picture of Eddie taken by the camera at the entrance, followed by a selection of coffee makers. “Here are some popular coffee makers. Would you like to hear the reviews?”

“You never did tell me if there were killer robots in the future,” Eddie said, wide eyed and apprehensive. “Is the future as terrifying as it seems? Because it seems pretty damn terrifying.”

“Eh, it was okay,” Buck said with a shrug. “You know, after the war was over and everyone submitted themselves to their robot overlords. I totally rocked the barcode tattoo.”

“That’s not a funny joke,” his boyfriend said. Buck just grinned and continued guiding the gurney to where it needed to go. “That was a joke, right? Right? Buck, c’mon! There’s not- They won’t seriously give us all barcode tattoos, right?”

“Here are some popular barcode tattoo ideas.”

“Buck!”

“This thing looks like a death trap,” Chimney declared, giving the baby crib he was assembling a shake and apparently finding it wanting. He glanced at the instruction booklet that came with it. “Oh, I think we mixed up the spacers with the supports.”

“Yeah, but they look the same.” So close to her due date now, Maddie looked very pregnant.

“Buck, did you steal the screwdriver again?” Chimney asked, kneeling down to fix where he messed up.

“Yeah, it’s all yours,” he said, tossing the tool across the room to him. “I am finally finished baby proofing everything. Still think we should put alarm sensors on these windows.”

“We live on the second floor,” Chimney pointed out.

“What’s your point?’

“I said you could baby proof the apartment,” Maddie reminded him, obviously not impressed with her brother’s paranoia. “Not turn it into an inescapable fortress.”

“I just don’t see a reason to underestimate my niece’s curiosity or drive to explore.”

“Niece?” His sister and Chimney shared a look before turning back to him.

“Oh, uh… Or nephew,” Buck said, doing his best to backpedal. “Nibling. My nibling.”

“What the hell’s a nibling?” Chimney asked.

“It's like sibling, but for your niece or nephew,” Buck explained.

“Is that a real word?” Maddie asked him, heading for the fridge in the kitchen area.

“Never mind if it’s a real word,” the paramedic said, setting down the screwdriver. “Maddie said the baby was in the wrong position to tell in the last ultrasound. It’s a girl?”

“I- I didn’t say-”

“Maddie, we’re going to have a girl!”

“Well, at least we can start narrowing down names, then,” Maddie said, reaching up to open a cabinet. Or she tried to, anyway. “Seriously, Buck? It’s an upper cabinet, how’s the baby gonna reach that?”

“Hey, she-  Or he! They! They could be walking in just… In just over a year.” Buck felt the smile on his face slip away with the reminder of how little time he had left. Would Jee-Yun even be in this apartment a year from now? He still had no clue how he was going to help Maddie with her PPD, not when he knew she was going to self-isolate. How could he help someone, when they didn’t want his help? How could he help someone when they weren’t going to even admit that they needed help until it was too late?

And the Jee-Yun of the other time, he would never get to see her walk. Hell, he didn’t even get to see her crawl. The last Buck had seen of her, she was screaming for her father as he obsessed over the video Maddie left him. And then Chimney had taken her with him on his cross-country journey to find a woman who didn’t want to be found, and his family had fractured and torn even further.

Now he didn’t even know if that time existed at all, still. He honestly didn’t know which option would be worse.

“Buck?” His sister’s voice drew him out of his spiral, and he looked up to find her frowning at him from across the room. “Are you okay?”

“I’m wonderful!” Buck answered, plastering on his best smile. He didn’t want to be here in this apartment anymore, not when it felt like he was talking to a pair of ghosts. But there was also a very real countdown of how many more days he could have with Maddie and Chimney, and he wasn’t going to squander them. “Anyway, uh… What were we talking about?”

The other two shared another look, and he could see the concern they were communicating to each other.

“Your paranoia regarding my unborn daughter’s ability to climb things,” Chimney said, picking up the screwdriver again.

“Hey, she- They! They’ll have Buckley genes, and God knows we manage to get into trouble.”

“Oh God, he’s right.” Maddie sounded absolutely mournful over it. She looked down at her belly. “Listen to me, Mango. Be less like your Uncle Buck and more like your dad. Or even your Uncle Albert.”

“Hey!”

“I remember quite well how often you got yourself hurt, you don’t get to be insulted by this!”

Chimney rolled over in bed and immediately woke up when he realized Maddie wasn’t there with him. He groggily pulled himself out from the blankets and padded into the living room, where he found her sitting on the couch, staring at nothing.

“Hey, you okay? Baby keeping you up?” he asked her, thinking it was just pregnancy related insomnia. At least, until he rounded the couch to find her teary-eyed. “Oh, hey, what’s wrong?”

“I think I’m scared,” she told him.

“About the baby?”

“Right now, everything’s great. The baby is safe and sound in here,” Maddie said, patting her stomach. “Probably safer than she ever will be. And then they’re born, and everything changes.”

“In a good way,” Chimney reassured her. “We finally get to meet our kid, our little girl. Hear their voice, get to know this person that we made.’

“But we’re not done making her yet,” she said, sniffling. “They go out into the world and that's when everything gets harder. Every decision, every choice, everything we do, it impacts who they become.”

“We’re going to make good choices.”

“Will we?” she asked. “What if… What if we’re not even here to make them?”

“Is this about Buck?” Chimney asked, taking one of her hands in his.

“He looks at me sometimes like he’s surprised I’m still here,” she said, and then shook her head. “No, no, that’s not right. He looks at me like he’s expecting me to be gone the next time he looks. It’s only whenever he thinks no one’s looking at him, but I keep catching him doing it more and more the further along we get.”

“Hey, hey, whatever it is you’re thinking, I’m sure it’s not that.”

“I just keep thinking back to the whole thing with Red,” she said, ignoring him. “How I tried to promise I wouldn’t leave him behind again, and he… How he told me not to make promises I couldn’t keep. I feel like- I don’t know, like he has a clock ticking in his head and it’s counting down to me leaving him again.”

“There’s a very simple solution to that,” Chimney told her, squeezing her hand. “Don’t.”

“But what if I don’t have a choice?”

“Then we try our best. That’s all we can ever do.”

“So what is going on with my ex-husband now?” Shannon asked.

“Oh, you know, the regular,” Buck said, pinning his phone between his head and shoulder as he put away the dishes he and Eddie had just finished washing. “Running into fires, helping the helpless, confronting his deepest and darkest fears.”

“He ranted to me last night for half an hour about the evils of technology that can watch and listen to you.”

“Only half an hour?”

“It might have been longer, I hung up on him part way through. I’m not even sure he noticed.”

“We’re currently kicking it old school,” Buck said, closing the cabinet door. “Honestly, I’m surprised he’s even still allowing our phones in the house. He’s unplugged just about every electronic that’s more high tech than a lightbulb, and even those are suspect in his eyes. I had to go out and buy a bunch of board games for Christopher.”

“That would explain why he was asking to come over in the middle of the week.”

“Yeah, he asked to go over to the apartment and play video games there. Eddie gave me that stare, you know the one.” From the other room, he heard someone knock on the front door and grinned to himself. “Hey Shan, I’m gonna have to hang up. I’m about to be yelled at.”

“What did you do?” she asked, already sounding amused.

“Oh, I’m sure Chris’ll tell you all about it,” he said, before disconnecting the call and stepping into the living room, just in time for Eddie to carry in a large box and start cutting it open. Buck winked at Christopher, busy doing his homework, and the boy smothered a giggle with his hand. It was with much anticipation that he watched as Eddie peeled open the cardboard flaps. Buck saw the moment the man’s eyes landed on the HILDY logo, and had to bite his lip when Eddie frantically tore off the bubble wrap and had a silent freak-out when he found the coffee maker.

Chris’ laughter gave the game away, and Eddie looked over to glare at the two of them.

“We got him,” the boy said.

“That we did,” Buck said, running a hand through Chris' hair.

“You- You-” Eddie was clearly struggling to find a child-friendly way to express his feelings at the moment, and having the other two giggling at his reaction was clearly not helping. “Thanks, Buck. Real funny.”

“You are welcome,” Buck said, very pleased with himself. He didn’t actually get to witness the reaction to it last time, and seeing it in person was worth every penny.

“I cannot believe you brought this… This…”

“Coffee maker?”

“Thing! This thing into our home!” Eddie huffed. Interesting word choice, but Buck decided to ignore it for now.

“Hey, technically? You brought it in yourself.” He walked over to pick up the box, kissing his boyfriend on the cheek in an ultimately futile attempt to cool his annoyance. “Let’s go set this up so it’s ready in the morning.”

“Oh, what? You expect me to actually allow this evil, soulless, treacherous thing to stay here? No, no lo estoy teniendo.”

Buck paused on his way to the kitchen, and then turned to grin at him, leaning in to whisper in his ear. A terrible, awful idea had come to him.

“Y’know, Edmundo threw his out without ever using it.”

Eddie stood there, glaring at him with his arms crossed and working his jaw. And then he huffed and grabbed the box from Buck’s hands, carrying it the rest of the way himself. Perhaps he should have gone for that tactic months ago. It sure would have made the truck argument easier.

Texas

Buck fell asleep to regular, dry air and woke up to what felt like being slapped in the face with a wet towel. He wiped his drool off the window and stumbled out, blinking at the smoke that was already starting to irritate his eyes. The base camp was a mass of motion around him, firefighters both local and out of state running around the place.

“I forgot how the air felt here.”

“You’ve been here before?” Hen asked, climbing out behind him.

“Once,” he said, glancing at his boyfriend when the man rounded the truck, bag in his hand.

“Welcome to Texas,” Eddie drawled.

“Y’know, sometimes I regret not checking out any of the rainforests in Peru,” Buck said, rubbing the sleep away from his eyes. “But this? This reminds me why I was wise to stick to the coast.”

“When the hell were you in Peru?” Eddie demanded, turning to stare at him.

“Between my time on the ranch and moving to LA.”

“Ranch?” And wow, Buck really did need to do a better job of bragging about his globetrotting days. Eddie had just accepted his Spanish skills at face-value and never questioned why a white boy from Pennsylvania could carry on a conversation in it, horribly accented or not.

“I was a real cowboy for a while there,” he said, and then waggled his eyebrows. “So, y’know, save a horse-”

“Nope,” Hen interrupted. “I had to deal with your snoring, I am not dealing with the flirting. We have places to be, people.”

Buck blew a raspberry, making Eddie laugh, and followed her to where they needed to go. The Deputy Chief’s briefing went much the same as it did the first time around, although this time Buck didn’t spend most of it staring at Firefox, trying to figure out where he recognized her from. That wasn’t to say there wasn’t any staring, however. Because…

“They’re staring at me,” he said, trying to keep his voice down. God, no wonder they both fussed at him for doing it last time. This was creepy.

“No, they’re not,” Hen denied, not even looking over at them.

“Actually, they kinda are,” Eddie said, glancing their way.

“Normally I’d be flattered that Firefox-”

“Firefox?” There was that tone to Eddie’s voice, the one that usually indicated that his boyfriend was feeling jealous and was trying to hide it.

“That’s what she goes by online, total badass,” he said, nudging him with his elbow. “She’s uploaded videos of a bunch of her rescues, gone viral a bunch of times.”

“And you think she’s-” Hen cut herself off when she, too, glanced over at the Austin firefighters. “Huh. They are staring. Maybe not at you, but they are staring.”

“Oh, this trip is already shaping up to be awkward as hell,” Buck groused.

“It’s not going to be that bad,” Eddie tried to assure him as everyone dispersed around them. “Maybe they just haven’t seen people as pretty as us before.”

“But, Firefox is right there.” The scowl his boyfriend gave him for that was very adorable, and thus worth it.

“Seriously, Buck?”

“Obviously she’s not as pretty as you, sugarplum.”

“Thank you.”

“Yeah, I’ve had enough of this,” Hen said, shaking her head and wandering off.

“I’m gonna get something to drink, meet you back at the truck?” Eddie asked, and he nodded and watched him head for the water station.

This trip was not going to be a particularly enjoyable trip, he knew. The other two were about to go off in their separate directions, leaving him alone with a bunch of strangers to dig a very long hole. And even worse than last time, there were people staring at him and he didn’t know why.

(He had a theory. He was ignoring that theory.)

Exactly like last time, the abandoners abandoned him. Hen went off to the medical tent - which made sense, he got the impression there was a concerning dearth of paramedics on site - and Eddie went off with Firefox to rescue a bunch of at-risk kids. And Buck was just realizing he couldn’t remember her actual name, that could get awkward eventually. A problem for later, maybe.

The fireline went pretty much the same as before. They dug, they raked, they bantered about their biggest or weirdest calls. Honestly, that tilted hotel during the earthquake trumped everything in his opinion.

And then a dog tried to run them over with a burning car.

“Maybe we should go out and help them search,” Marjan - Firefox - said, pacing the ground.

“Judd told us to stay here,” Eddie told her. Judd and Paul - two of the other 126 firefighters that came with - had taken off on one of the ATVs to search for the last missing boy, while everyone else escorted the other kids and their counselor to base camp. “That’s what we’ll do.”

“How can you be so calm under literal fire?” she demanded to know.

“Army medic,” he reminded her, grabbing his phone and pulling up one of his seldom-used apps. A moment later, Marjan’s phone chimed and she tugged it out to look.

“Seriously?” she asked, staring at him. “You want to follow me on Insta?”

“I’ve been told you put a lot of work into it.” There was no way she could be as impressive as Buck indicated she was. “Firefox.”

“I’ll show you mine if you show me yours,” she said, sauntering up to the picnic table he was sitting at.

“I haven’t been on social media in a while,” Eddie warned her. “The last post is from nine months ago, super boring.”

“I’ll be the judge of that,” she declared, accepting his follow request and sending her own. Eddie just shrugged and looked through what she had posted. And, shit. Maybe Buck hadn’t been wrong in his opinion of her, or at least what she posted.

“Is that a Prius in the air?”

“Tornado dropped it between two buildings,” she said, sounding smug about it. She held up her phone so he could see the screen. “Is this your kid?”

“Christopher, my world,” Eddie said, smiling at the picture of his son. “He’s with my ex-wife right now, his mother.”

“You did not build him a skateboard.” She had gone back to flipping through his scant photos.

“It was Buck’s idea.”

“Buck.” Marjan narrowed her eyes at her screen, and then looked back up at him. “Evan Buckley, right?”

“Right.” He drew out the word, immediately concerned with the way she knew his boyfriend’s full name. She glanced about, as if worried that someone might pop out of the bushes nearby, and leaned closer.

“So, do you think he did it?”

“Did what?”

“C’mon, you work with him-”

“I’m dating him.”

That statement made her blink and sit back, mouth opening and closing aimlessly.

“This is awkward,” she finally said. “Never mind, uh. Forget I asked.”

“I’m still not sure what you were asking,” he said, though that was possibly a lie. He thought he knew exactly what she was asking about, he just didn’t want to think that Taylor Kelly’s reporting had made it all the way to his home state. That could make reintroducing Buck to his parents even more awkward.

Relief shone on her face when dispatch interrupted to ask for the search team’s location, informing them that they were sending air support. He and Marjan stood by and listened as the 126’s captain, Owen Strand, helped Judd and Paul find the last boy, and then as Hen talked the pair of them through stabilizing him. And then the pilot sent out a mayday, the helicopter letting out plumes of smoke before crashing a distance away from them.

But Hen being in imminent danger was not his only pressing concern.

“I need to get back to base camp,” Eddie told Marjan, grabbing his medical bag off the picnic table and slinging it over his shoulder. “Now.”

“Why?”

“Because I think Buck is about to do something very stupid, and Athena will kill me if he breaks his skull open again.”

By the time Judd and Paul picked them up and they finally made it back to base camp, the sun had already set. The firefighters assigned to the line were making their way back for the night, and Eddie headed right for them, searching everywhere for his boyfriend before he could run off to do whatever he was no-doubt planning. The fact that he couldn’t find the long-legged man anywhere was not a good sign, in his opinion.

“Mateo!” Judd called, waving down their probie when he saw him. “Where’s TK?”

“And Buck?” Eddie demanded.

“Diaz, right?” Mateo asked. “Buck left with TK. He said to tell you that he was, uh. Doing the thing?”

“¡Me cago en la leche!” he swore, violently enough that even the ones who didn’t understand flinched back. Scratching at his head, he did his best to figure out what ‘doing the thing’ meant at that moment.

“Doing the thing?” Marjan repeated, looking at him for answers.

“Something that’s no doubt incredibly stupid and reckless and-” Eddie paused mid-sentence as he realized what the thing probably was. “He’s going to steal a truck.”

“And do what?” Judd demanded to know. “Drive up there on their own?”

“Probably,” Eddie said, already hurrying for where the trucks were parked, the others right behind him. His boyfriend wasn’t at the 118’s truck - Buck clearly had enough sense to not tempt Bobby’s wrath like that - but he heard voices coming from farther down the row.

“What are we waiting for?” Someone, Eddie assumed it was TK, was asking.

“We’re waiting for-”

“Hey, dumbass! Dumbasser!” Judd snapped, rounding the next truck and shining his light on them.

“That,” Buck said, pointing at them, squinting against the light. “We were waiting for that.”

“Have you considered the consequences of what you’re about to do at all?” the large Texan asked.

“The scary part is that Buck probably did,” Eddie told the group, and then corrected himself. “No, he definitely knows the consequences.”

“You two didn’t seriously think that you could sneak off and drive into wildfires, did you?” Marjan demanded to know.

“Yes?” TK offered weakly.

“I mean, we were waiting for you to get here,” Buck said, not sounding the least bit guilty. “You were a bit late, though.”

“Okay, what is your deal?” Paul asked, pointing at him.

“We don’t have time for this!” TK suddenly snapped. “My dad is out there!”

“He’s right, c’mon,” Judd said, holding out his hand expectantly. “Where’s the keys?”

“Nah, I’m driving,” Buck said, twirling them on his finger.

“What? No! It’s our truck!”

“Just… It’s easier if we just let him,” Eddie explained, the whole conversation exhausting him more than the fires had.

“Wow, Hollywood, you are whipped,” Judd said, and the words had his boyfriend waggling his eyebrows with a grin. Eddie rolled his eyes and climbed in, Buck going around to get into the driver seat. In the side view mirror, he saw Marjan stop TK, and he strained his ears to listen.

“Were you really going to go out there alone with him? You remember that news story!” he heard her say in hushed tones. Yeah, Taylor Kelly was still causing issues, even months later.

“Innocent until proven guilty,” he heard TK hiss.

“Hurry up, you two,” Eddie said, sticking his head out the truck window. “Or get left behind.”

They didn’t waste any more time after that.

“Y’know, we’re going to end up having spent more time on the road this trip than we did fighting wildfires,” Buck pointed out to Eddie. They had rescued Hen and Captain Strand, and were packing up to go home, after the commander had dismissed the out-of-state crews following the fires’ containment. Not that he was in much of a hurry to get home, knowing what, or rather who, would be waiting for him there. “Maybe we could spend another night or five here. Make the driving worth it.”

“I would very much like to sleep in my own bed, thanks.”

“I, too, would like to sleep in your bed. But it was a twenty hour drive down and it’s another twenty hour drive back up, and we’ve barely spent more than twenty-four hours here.”

“It’s probably for the best,” Eddie said, reaching out to play with a strand of Buck’s hair. “I think I know why they were all staring at you.”

“Mateo made it pretty obvious yesterday,” he sighed. “Poor kid stuck his foot in his mouth and TK stumbled over his own to cover for him. I just acted like I had no clue what he was talking about.”

“Well, it couldn’t have been any worse than what we have to look forward to,” his boyfriend said. “Remember, I did promise that we’d stop by my parents’.”

“Oh, God,” Buck groaned. “So, how are we going to play this? Are we going to pretend we’re still just friends or…?”

“What? No,” Eddie scoffed. “I’m going to tell them you’re my boyfriend and when they start something, we’ll leave.”

Buck’s only response to that was to kiss him silly, and when Hen finally joined them at the truck, she threatened to spray them with a hose until they separated.

(Eddie’s parents did start something, and the firefighters did leave early, but it wasn’t because of Buck. It was, of course, over Christopher.)

Parental Disappointment

“You’re here to tell me in person that mom and dad are coming,” Buck said when he opened his apartment door for his sister. They had gotten back from Texas just the other day, and he had been waiting for the announcement that their parents were on the way to see their favorite living child.

“How did you-? Right.” Maddie sighed as she took off her mask, walking in as he stepped aside and closed the door behind her. “Yeah, they’re almost here, but you know that.”

“I know it’s going to be a dumpster fire of a visit and I want no part of it,” he told her.

“Buck, c’mon, you don’t know that.”

“I’ve lived through this visit once already, Mads,” Buck pointed out to her. “Dumpster. Fire.”

“When was the last time you even spoke to mom and dad?” she asked, setting her purse down on his coffee table and taking a seat on his couch.

“From whose perspective?” He took a seat on the other end, leaning back against the arm. “If we’re not counting the time travel… I don’t know, definitely before I started at the One-Eighteen.”

“Oh my God, Buck. They’re our parents.”

“Who single handedly contributed to half the reasons I started therapy.”

“You’re in therapy?”

“Well, not now,” he told her. “Then. Before. I’ve thought about starting it again, but… If I told the truth about my issues, I’d probably get locked up as a danger to myself or others. If I lied, then it wouldn’t actually be very helpful.”

“They wouldn’t lock you up, Buck,” Maddie said, frowning at him.

“Uh-huh. Hello Dr. Copeland, today I want to talk about the guilt I feel for the very bad thing I did to prevent someone else from doing another very bad thing. How do I know he was going to? Because I’m from the future and wait, why are you coming at me with a straitjacket?”

Maddie gave him a very unimpressed stare.

“Maybe you don’t phrase it quite like that,” she suggested, rolling her eyes. “Why Dr. Copeland?”

“She was my therapist. She gave me a lot of de-escalation techniques for dinner with mom and dad, except they didn’t work, and the visit was a dumpster. Fire.”

“You don’t know that it’s going to be that bad this time,” Maddie said, almost pleading. “I mean, you… You know about it, now. Right? You can avoid whatever happened to make it so awful.”

“I am,” Buck said, nodding. “Mom and dad.”

“Buck, please,” she begged. “I just want my little girl to have a normal family.”

“Well, that’s too bad,” he said. “Because one of her uncles came from the future, and two of her grandparents are hiding the fact that they had a third kid.”

“Oh no,” she gasped. “They don’t know that you know.”

“Nope,” he said, popping the word. “And apparently Chimney doesn’t know that I know the full story, even though I’m the one who told him about Daniel.”

“Oh, I might have put too much emphasis on how mom and dad didn’t want you to know.”

“Well, at least he’s loyal to you,” Buck said, trying not to sound bitter about it. “I’ll put him out of his misery at work tomorrow. Or maybe I’ll watch him slowly break down trying to keep the secret. Depends on my mood.”

“Buck.” Maddie managed to sound both amused and disapproving.

“Maddie.”

His sister rolled her eyes and sighed.

“Whatever, have your fun,” she said. “But please, will you be there? Chimney will be there, and Albert. Maybe you can bring Eddie?”

“Oh fuck no.”

“I’m going to invite Eddie,” Maddie said, nodding to herself, pulling out her phone to tap away at the screen.

“Mads, c’mon. I love him too much to inflict our parents on him.”

“Too late,” she said, looking up from her phone and smiling at him brightly. “He already said he’ll be there. Which means you have to be there.”

Buck let out a groan and let his head fall back.

“So how bad is this visit actually going to be?” Eddie asked him the next day at the station.

“Dumpster fire,” Buck answered, voice muffled by the pillow he’d been trying to smother himself with. He was stretched out on the couch, so miserable that he was unable to find amusement in poor Chimney’s continued endeavor to not implode under the weight of a secret he didn’t have to keep. The timer on the oven dinged and he knew he needed to go help set the table, but couldn’t find it in him.

“Is he still moping about this visit?” he heard Bobby ask Eddie.

“I’m not moping!” he said, though the effect was ruined by the pillow he hadn’t moved off his face.

“Yes,” he heard Eddie say, and huffed in annoyance.

“What are they like?” Hen asked, and it sounded like she was walking across the room. “Your parents, I mean. Like, no offense Buck, but I look at Maddie, and then at you, and I think, ‘there’s a story there.’”

“You have no idea,” he heard Chimney say, and he finally moved the pillow to watch as the man realized his misstep and tried to backtrack. “None of us has any idea.”

“The story is that I was born for spare parts and it didn’t work,” Buck said, using the back of the couch to pull himself up. The others turned to stare at him as Chimney sputtered in shock.

“You know!?”

“Chim, I told you about Daniel,” Buck said, rolling his eyes. “Of course I know.”

“Spare parts?” Eddie had his arms crossed over his chest, glowering.

“Maddie and I had a brother, Daniel. Well, Maddie did, I never knew him. But he was sick, and he needed a bone marrow transplant, and they weren’t a match. So, they had me.” He waved at himself. “Made me, really. Except I was defective and it didn’t work, and they never quite forgave me for it. And they have spent the past nearly thirty years doing their best to pretend that he never existed.”

The others all stared at him in stunned silence, before Hen broke it.

“Good luck,” she said, patting both Eddie and Chimney on the shoulder.

“Dumpster fire,” Buck repeated.

Just hearing the way Buck referred to himself as defective, the self-deprecation that laced his words, immediately impacted Eddie’s opinions of the Buckley parents. The way his boyfriend was looking forward to the visit with utter dread had him ignoring all of Buck’s attempts to convince him not to be there, because there was no way in hell he was going to let his boyfriend suffer through this alone. Not when he knew Chimney - and Buck - would be focused on making things comfortable for Maddie.

Seeing how Buck’s eyes dimmed when his sister opened her door to their parents simply confirmed for Eddie that he made the right choice.

The first night was awkward, to say the least. Margaret Buckley managed to smile and sneer at the same time, acting as if her son’s mere presence was an inconvenience to her. Every time he tried to insert himself into the conversation, she hummed in disinterest and quickly moved on, doing her best to ignore him. The worst part was that Buck didn’t even seem surprised, and mostly stayed silent. Phillip Buckley at least didn’t give the impression that he resented his son’s presence, but he also didn’t do much to counter his wife’s behavior, seeming content to just follow her lead.

That was the first night, where their special brand of passive-aggressiveness had Eddie thinking of his own parents fondly. By the time he and Buck left, he was seriously regretting not taking Chimney up on his offer of tequila disguised as water, but he had wanted to be sober in solidarity with his boyfriend. At least the Buckleys weren’t homophobic, though that would require that they actually cared about their son in any way.

The second night, though. The second night was when limits were reached.

“Well, I’m just glad everybody’s okay,” Margaret said after Chimney was done retelling the story of Mad Stan the bomber. Albert had managed to wiggle out of being present this time, which Eddie was almost jealous of. But Buck was there, and so Eddie was, too.

“You all seem to have very dangerous jobs,” Phillip noted.

“Not really,” Maddie said, rubbing at her belly. “I mean, most of the time, it’s pretty run of the mill.”

“Yeah, and Stan wasn’t a bad guy. He just needed someone to see him,” Chimney said, and Buck raised his head from where he’d been silently picking at his food to share a loaded look with Eddie. They both knew how much it hurt to not be seen. “To understand how much pain he was in. He probably wasn’t going to actually blow up the place.”

“Still, it seems very risky,” Phillip said, shaking his head. “I mean, from what I hear, Evan has spent quite a lot of time in hospitals.”

Buck glanced at his father, but seemed to just let that statement go. Eddie wasn’t having it, though.

“What you hear?” he asked, his temper boiling over. “Your son has been in the hospital twice in the past two years with serious injuries and this is the first I’ve even laid eyes on you. But clearly you were able to drag yourselves here in an RV to see your daughter.”

“I’ve told Evan-” Margaret started.

“Buck!” Eddie snapped, loudly enough that the others all jumped. “His name is Buck.”

“I’m not good with seeing my children in hospitals,” she finished, voice trembling as she glared at him. “You don’t know!”

“No one is good with seeing their children in hospitals,” Eddie seethed. “But good parents still show up.”

Maddie and Chimney sucked in a breath, but it was Buck’s reaction that struck him the most. His boyfriend was looking at him in awe and surprise, as if he honestly hadn’t expected someone to stick up for him here. It struck him then that Buck had almost definitely sat through this exact dinner with these awful people before, and for the briefest of moments, Eddie hated Maddie for putting him through it again.

“I think we’re ready for dessert!” Chimney said, clapping his hands together.

“Oh, Howard, where’d you put that box we brought?” Phillip asked, jumping on the chance to change topics.

“More gifts?” Maddie asked.

“Not exactly.”

“It’s over by the couch,” Chimney said, getting up. “Let me grab it.”

“I like him, Maddie,” Margaret said, smiling down the table at her daughter. “You picked a good one this time.”

There was something in her tone, a mixture of judgment and reproach and condescension, that had Eddie’s hackles rising. But from everything he’d heard about Doug, he couldn’t say she was wrong. Chimney came back with a large wooden box and sat it down in front of Maddie, and Buck’s face seemed to drop at the sight of it before it went eerily blank.

“Your baby box,” Margaret explained when Maddie looked at her questioningly. “I thought you might want to pass on some of these things to your little girl someday.”

Eddie wanted to ask where Buck’s was, but he had the awful impression that the answer to that question would result in him flipping the table over.

“I can’t believe you kept all this,” Maddie said, looking through the contents of the box.

“You thought we’d throw it away?” Phillip asked, laughing as if that was a ridiculous notion.

“You mean like you threw away all of mine?” Buck’s quiet words drew everyone’s attention, though his eyes were fixed on his plate of almost untouched food. And yeah, Eddie was afraid that was the case. “You mean like you threw away everything of Daniel’s?”

In the silence that followed, someone could hear a pin drop in the next county over. Margaret and Phillip both looked shocked, while Maddie was closing her eyes against the inevitable, and Chimney looked torn between running away and staying to watch the fallout.

“Who- How-” There were tears gathering in Margaret’s eyes. “Maddie, how could you?”

“Oh, because I didn’t have a right to know?” Buck asked, finally looking up to glare at his parents. “I didn’t have a right to know why my mother couldn’t stand to look at me my entire life?”

“You’re not a parent!” Margaret cried. “You don’t-”

“Yes he is.” Eddie stated it like the simple, inarguable fact that it was. “And he’s a damn good parent, definitely better than you.”

“Don’t talk to my wife like that,” Phillip snapped, glaring at him.

“Then she shouldn’t talk to my boyfriend like she has been,” he said, not bothering to look at the man.

“I spent years wondering what it was about me that kept my parents from loving me,” Buck said, his words so very quiet. “But it was never about me. It was because you are both too selfish to look past yourselves and your own pain. Does Daniel even have a grave? Or did you just throw him away with everything else?”

“You don’t understand!”  Margaret tried again, and Buck scoffed.

“That you’re an awful mother who gave up on her kids when they were children?” he asked. Chimney was staring wide-eyed at them, Eddie could see, while Maddie simply looked heartbroken. “I understand.”

“Speaking of kids,” Eddie said, getting to his feet and urging Buck to stand as well. “It’s almost Chris’ bedtime and I promised him we’d call to wish him goodnight.” He paused to glare at Margaret and Phillip. “Because that’s the kind of thing good parents do. But you’re awful people, so there’s no way you’d understand that.”

There was silence in their wake when they left.

“So tonight was…” Eddie trailed off, clearly trying to find the right way to describe it. They’d gotten back to the Diaz residence and called Shannon, so they could talk to Chris before he went to bed. Hearing the kid’s voice was absolutely the best thing to help soothe his heart after dealing with his parents.

“A dumpster fire?” Buck suggested.

“That sounds about right.”

“The scary part is that I think it actually went better this time around.”

“Madre de Dios,” Eddie whispered, flopping onto the couch next to him. “I don’t know how the hell you two are as functional as you are, with parents like that.”

“There was one time, Maddie found an old bike in the garage,” Buck said, thinking back. “I fell off of it and got hurt. Dad acted all concerned at first, but then mom came out and got angry about the bike, and he immediately took her side.”

“What was it about the bike that had her upset?”

“It was Daniel’s, I think,” he said. “But they got really angry, there was a lot of yelling. And I remember Maddie telling me… People do that when they care. They overreact and then feel bad about it later.”

He heard Eddie suck in a breath, and he nodded.

“Yeah,” Buck said. He bit his lip, and then asked, “What did you mean earlier? When you said I was a parent?”

“C’mon, you know exactly what I meant,” Eddie said, looking at him with impossible fondness.

“But Chris-”

“Is lucky enough to have three parents who love him,” he said. “You’ve been helping to raise him since long before we figured our shit out. Hell, if something happens to both me and Shannon, you get full custody.”

“What.” He couldn’t possibly be talking about that, could he? Buck had just assumed that since Shannon was still alive, there wouldn’t have been a need for-

“I talked to her about it, after the well,” Eddie said, and yeah, that was exactly what he was talking about. “Or, I told her what I was wanting to do, and then she informed me that I was months behind her on it, because apparently she did it after the tsunami.”

“I love you,” Buck said, as if those three little words could possibly convey everything he was feeling in that moment.

“I love you, too, corazon.”

The Q-Word

“Trauma bag?” Buck asked, reading off the list on his clipboard, pen in hand. The Buckley parents had fled back to Pennsylvania, after making a minor attempt at reparations following the warehouse fire. This time, he hadn’t given it to them. He almost felt bad for it, but he just didn’t have it in him to try again. His parents were awful, selfish people, and he didn’t have to forgive them for it. They just were not worth the effort.

His feelings were valid, and losing a child didn’t excuse them for how they had treated him his entire life up until this point.

(“The other firefighters were very kind. We got to hear-”

“I don’t care. I want you to leave.”

“Evan-”

“No. I don’t want you here. I never wanted you here. Now go.”)

He did feel kind of bad for Maddie, who had been the one stuck dealing with them ever since that disastrous dinner. Then again, it was her fault that they were even in town to begin with, and her fault he had to go through all of that again, so…

“Yup,” Eddie said, grabbing the trauma bag to put into its proper compartment on the truck.

“Excuse me?” Buck put a finger to his ear. “What was that?”

“Check,” the other man said, rolling his eyes and smiling.

“AED?”

“Check,” Eddie said, the smile not leaving his face.

“Oh no, who gave you a clipboard?” Hen asked, her and Chimney coming up to bother the pair. “Quick, Chim, go call a hostage negotiator.”

“You’re hilarious,” Buck said, pointing at her with his pen. “Isn’t she hilarious?”

“Yes, dear,” his boyfriend dutifully answered.

“Thank you, pumpkin,” he said, glancing back down at the list. “C-spine bag?”

“Check,” Eddie said, carrying it over. “Hey, Chim, how’s Maddie doing after everything?”

“Better now that Margaret and Phillip are gone,” Chimney said, glancing at Buck. “It didn’t help that you left her to deal with them alone.”

“We didn’t leave her alone,” Buck corrected him, fixing him with a glare. “We left her with you. You need to start getting used to helping her deal with them. You’re family.”

“Well, technically-”

“Oh, no. Nope,” he said, cutting the shorter man off. “That’s your baby in her belly, you don’t get to ‘technically’ your way out of anything.”

“Hopefully, you won’t have to deal with them much,” Eddie said, leaning on the open compartment door of the fire engine. “Because there’s no way Maddie will invite them back down. Right?”

They all looked at Buck, who shrugged. He only knew they didn’t make another visit before Christmas.

“All I know is that I spent literal years without contact with them before now, and I will gladly go many more before I have to talk to them again.”

“Did it go that bad?” Hen asked, glancing between the three.

“Well, maybe if someone didn’t drop a major bomb about a secret he wasn’t supposed to know,” Chimney said, glaring at Buck. “It would have gone better.”

“No it wouldn’t,” Eddie immediately refuted. “If Maddie wanted it to go better, she shouldn’t have forced Buck to be there, because I was five seconds away from ripping Margaret’s head off for how she was talking to him.”

“That might have been the sweetest thing you’ve ever said,” Buck told him, leaning over to kiss his cheek, to the disgust of the paramedics. He turned to say something witty to them, but was distracted by who he saw behind Chimney. He grinned, bounced on his heels, and shouted, “Probie!”

Ravi, of course, was startled into dropping all the books he was carrying.

“I got it, don’t worry,” the probie said, waving him away when he moved to help.

“Sorry,” Buck said, feeling bad for scaring the kid. Again. “I didn’t mean to uh....”

“It’s fine,” Ravi said, standing back up.

“The new B-shift probie, right?” Eddie asked, coming up to stand next to the others. He shot Buck a look, probably because he’d been perhaps a bit too excited to see the guy again.

“Yeah- I mean, yes, sir,” the probie nodded, smiling widely. Ah, so young, so green, so innocent. Maybe Bobby could be convinced to steal him for A-shift earlier this time? “Just finished my first shift.”

“How was it?” Buck asked, the question tumbling out of his mouth before he thought better of it. He was just realizing his mistake, when-

“Pretty quiet.”

Fuck.

“Whoa!” Hen cried, holding up a hand as if warding off the word. “Did he just say…?”

“No!” Chimney whisper-shouted.

“Sorry,” the confused probie said. Ravi really did get the worst first impression of them. “I just said it was-”

“Don’t say it again!”

“Hold on, maybe if he says it a second time, it undoes the curse?” Hen suggested, sounding almost hopeful.

“And if he says it a third time, maybe the Candyman will kill us all,” Chimney scoffed. “Let’s not test that theory.”

“Well, today is gonna suck,” Buck said, making a head start for his turnout gear.

“I don’t get it, what did I do?” Ravi asked.

“You used the Q-word,” Chimney told him. “We don’t use the Q-word.”

“Who used the Q-word?” Bobby demanded, popping up to look down at them from the loft.

“What am I missing here?” Eddie asked, following his boyfriend. Buck, in lieu of answering, merely pointed up at the alarm just as it started ringing.

Eddie wasn’t entirely certain if he believed in the jinx, but he couldn’t deny it outright when he easily accepted time travel and black-eyed not-demons. Well, he could, and he did, because playing up the skepticism got Buck to make cute faces. Mostly he was just having difficulty with the idea that a single word could cause a bunch of people who hadn’t heard it to suddenly all end up in need of their assistance. Like the guy who duct taped himself to the billboard. It had to have taken time to do all that, right? Surely they would have been called out even if the probie - who Buck was obviously excited to see, so that was interesting - had kept his mouth shut and hadn’t uttered a word.

The day that followed was… Busy, that was undeniable. They spent more time in the truck than at the station, to the point where sometimes they got redirected to a scene on their way back from another. The progress was marked by the gradual crispiness of the captain’s casserole, until he eventually pulled it out of the oven with a plume of smoke to show it was basically charcoal. And, okay, the calls got weird. Especially the one with the octopus that attached itself to a lady’s face while she was on the toilet.

(“They’re scary smart, and can get out of just about anything,” his boyfriend informed them as they worked to coax it off. “There was one in New Zealand that managed to escape from an aquarium and back to the ocean, never to be seen again.”)

But just because it was becoming increasingly obvious that the jinx was possibly real, didn’t mean that Eddie was going to admit it. Because at this point, it was too much fun to keep poking.

“Man, that was a boring call,” he said as they all made their way back to the truck. “Two people stuck in an elevator. They didn’t even need medical attention or anything.”

“Don’t say it, Edmundo,” Hen said.

“Eddie,” Buck corrected, seemingly on instinct if the sheepish expression on his face was anything to go by.

“How can I not?” Eddie asked as he stowed away the gear they’d pulled out. “Y’all acting like a bunch of viejas. There is no curse.”

“Oh, he’s so definitive now,” Chimney said, climbing into the truck. Buck was staring at him though, wearing the same constipated expression he wore when he was struggling through Chris’ math homework.

“Nobody is saying you have to believe in curses,” Bobby told him as he got into the captain’s seat. “Just maybe don’t tempt fate?”

“How is that not the same thing?” Eddie asked, clambering into the truck behind the others and slamming the door shut. “It was a normal call. Went like clockwork. Wham, bam, thank you, ma’am.”

“You notice how you never hear anyone say, ‘wham, bam, thank you, sir?’” Hen asked, scowling at him.

“Buck says it all the time.”

“Could we keep it professional, please?” Bobby asked, paternal exasperation in his voice.

“Professionalism went out the window when everyone started blaming calls on jinxes,” Eddie said. “I just think that this proves the whole thing is a little silly and we should all be done with it.”

Suddenly, the truck rocked as something fell on top of it with a bang, a cloud of sparks curtaining the windows.

“Hey, Cap.” Chimney was staring holes into the side of Eddie’s face. “Did a live power pole just fall on the engine?”

“I believe it did,” Bobby said.

What followed was a chance to relax for longer than a breath, and he got to watch Chimney fall all over himself trying to find ways to break the curse. Apparently he was Googling it, because that’s what one does in the 21st century. He was even texting Josh - a coworker of Maddie’s - for help. He’d tried asking Buck, but the man had stayed silent and at some point started smiling at Eddie like he was in on a joke.

“Aha!” Chimney cried, holding out his phone in victory. “It’s a real thing. Okay, we have to move our hands in this kind of motion-” He demonstrated by waving his arms in front of him. “And ring the bells… Nine times.”

“That’s a way to break curses, but is this actually a curse?” Hen asked. “We’ve been calling it a curse, but I think it’s technically a jinx.”

“What’s the difference?”

“I feel like a curse implies that someone put a hex on you,” she explained. “And a jinx is more like a general angering of the gods.”

“Wait, so is a hex and a curse the same thing?”

“By that, you mean both are totally made up and not real?” Eddie asked. “Yes.”

“What more proof do you need?” Chimney demanded. “We are trapped in a death box with enough electricity coursing through every nook and cranny to fry us.”

“How about we don’t touch anything and nobody gets fried,” Bobby suggested. “With or without a curse, or jinx, or whatever.”

“There is no curse,” Eddie said. “Or jinx. Our crappy day didn’t happened because someone said the word qu-”

“Hey!” the captain interrupted. “Do not.”

“C’mon, Cap, you can’t really believe in all this.”

“Why can’t you?” Chimney asked, sounding frustrated. “Your boyfriend is psychic!”

“No he isn’t,” Bobby and Eddie chorused, and Buck snorted in amusement. Chimney looked about ready to resort to physical harm.

“You’ve had your fun, dumplin',” Buck said, reaching out with his foot to nudge Eddie’s. Ah, so that’s what the smile was for, he’d figured it out. “I think you should stop before Chimney sacrifices you in an attempt to placate whichever god Probie provoked.”

“The probie didn’t provoke anything just by saying the Q-word,” he said, Chimney let out a strangled cry beside him.

“I hate you so damn much, Diaz!” the paramedic shouted at him. “This whole time? This whole damn time?”

“It was funny,” Eddie said, shrugging.

“You kept saying it wasn’t real and provoking the universe,” Hen said, in the same tone she used for her most annoying patients. “Even though you actually do believe in it-”

“I wouldn’t go that far.”

“Just because you thought it was funny to watch us suffer?”

“No, I thought it was funny to watch you all get riled up over it,” he said, smiling widely at her. “I needed some way to entertain myself, it’s been a really slow- Ow!”

He reached down to rub his shin, where Buck had kicked him.

“I am in charge of a bunch of children,” Bobby said. “Buck, when do I retire?”

“Uh,” Buck blinked, seemingly startled by the question. “N- Never?”

“Damn.”

In a brief window of downtime at the station following the house fire that turned into a fireworks display, everyone had dispersed to their separate corners. Hen was studying and Chimney was napping, and Buck was searching for Eddie. He found him hunched over a laptop with Bobby in the loft.

“Yeah, well, that’s Aaron Harmon right there,” the captain said, pointing at something on the screen.

“Definitely not the guy,” Eddie said, sounding frustrated. “He said his name was Brian. You think he was a fake?”

“Who are we talking about?” Buck asked when he joined them.

“There was a guy at the fire earlier who helped out, said he was from the One Forty-Seven,” his boyfriend explained, and something about that sounded familiar. “I think it was the same guy who put ice on Ms. Flores’ burn.”

“I forgot you ran into her again today,” he grumbled.

“She called me Edmundo,” Eddie said, wrinkling his nose. “I’m even more annoyed by him now.”

“Who, Brian?” Bobby asked.

“No, Edmundo,” Buck told him. “It’s a whole thing- Oh! Brian! The fake firefighter?”

“Yeah,” Eddie nodded. “You remember him?”

“Well, it’s hard to forget someone who stole the engine.”

“I’m sorry,” Bobby reached over to shut the laptop, his full attention focused on the time traveler. “He does what?”

It turns out that one was easily solved: when they got to the call of the supposed gas leak, Buck made sure to grab the keys out of the ignition. Poor Brian hopped into the driver’s seat expecting to be able to drive away, only to be dragged out by an annoyed Athena Grant. All of the poor man’s hopes and dreams of helping people were extinguished then and there, rather than at the site of the five-alarm fire after a long and destructive car chase. 

Impersonating a firefighter was only a misdemeanor though, so he’d be fine.

“Shut up!” The kid on the roof - Buck thought he heard the negotiator call him Corey - shouted down. “I need to think!”

“Should have tried thinking before he ended up on a roof,” Eddie said, leaning against the fire engine as they all watched the tableau occurring. They’d been here for two hours so far, and Buck knew they’d be here for many more hours still. “I mean, he cornered himself.”

“That there is a whole series of bad life choices culminating in this one unfortunate moment,” Hen declared to them from where she was perched. “It’d be tragic if it wasn’t so moronic.

“And annoying,” Buck chimed in.

“Why don’t they just storm the roof?” Chimney asked. “It’s not that high. We can give ‘em a ladder.”

“It’s a tactic they use to drag out the process in order to wear them down,” Bobby explained. “Eventually, they hit a breaking point.”

“Or we do.”

“Ten bucks says he falls right off that roof,” Hen offered, and Buck saw a golden opportunity. Making sure none of the others were paying attention, he leaned over and whispered into his boyfriend’s ear.

“Twenty says someone climbs up there and pushes him off,” Eddie said, pulling out the money and offering it to Hen. The disapproving look from Bobby prompted him to explain, “Hey, someone’s bound to hit their breaking point.”

After Hen took Chimney’s money as well, Buck and Eddie snuck in a fist bump while the others weren’t looking.

Over the next several hours, they gradually got more and more bored with the tableau in front of them. Eventually, Hen and Chimney went to play cards in the back of the ambulance, while Bobby went to bother his wife.

“Y’know, it was this call that reintroduced me to Taylor,” Buck told Eddie, at the four hour mark. “I still keep expecting her to pop up here somewhere.”

“Is she even still in LA?”

“I'm pretty sure I saw her on Fox News when I was flipping through channels the other day, but I didn’t exactly linger to make sure.”

Eddie made a noncommittal hum, before asking,

“How much longer is this going to last?”

“I don’t even remember,” Buck groaned, letting his head fall onto his boyfriend’s shoulder. “Too damn long. I spent most of it complaining to everyone about my relationship woes, and I think you were bothering people for advice on how to tell Chris you were dating again.”

“Your relationship woes?”

“Oh, you’ll love this, it has enough drama to be in one of your telenovelas,” he said, lifting his head up.

“My abuela’s-”

“No, nope. I’ve walked in on you watching them too many times, by yourself, to believe that.” He laughed at how Eddie huffed in annoyance. “Okay, so after you- Sorry, after Edmundo started dating Ana Flores, I decided to try dating again and oh my God, how didn’t I pick up on that sooner?”

“Because you’re very smart but you can also be very dumb,” his boyfriend answered, smiling prettily at him.

“That’s rude. You’re very rude,” Buck pouted. “Did you want to hear me tell you an embarrassing story about myself, or not?”

“Yes, please,” Eddie said, and if they were back at the apartment or the Diaz residence, he’d probably have a bowl of popcorn at the ready.

“Okay, so. I matched with this woman named Veronica, and our dinner date did not go well. Like, literally everything I said, she found a way to make it negative. I told her to drive safe afterwards and she asked if I was saying that because I didn’t think a woman could drive.”

“Oof.”

“But it gets worse! Because she had just moved into the city, and I just got a new neighbor that I’d never met before.”

“Oh, no.” Eddie’s smile had grown, because he was a sucker for drama, even if it was derived from Buck’s past suffering.

“Yup, I get home from the second worst date of my life-”

“Wait, what’s the first?”

“My first date with Abby, when I nearly choked to death on bread and she had to do an emergency tracheotomy on the restaurant floor with a steak knife,” Buck explained, before waving it away. “Anyway. I go to take the trash out, and who’s also taking their trash out?”

“Veronica?”

“Veronica!”

“And I’m sure that was awkward.”

“Oh, very awkward,” he agreed. “And my brilliant self decided to have Albert play interference, distract her, y’know? Except he took to that task a little too well.”

“Wait, did Albert break the bro code?”

“Thank you!” Buck exclaimed, throwing up his hands. “Everyone else I brought it up with acted as if I was overreacting. But yeah, I go to her apartment to apologize for things being awkward, and the little shit walks out of her shower. And then, later, I come back from babysitting Chris while Ana Flores taught Edmundo math-”

“Wait, is that a euphemism?”

“No, he apparently took Chris’ math homework over there and that’s what they spent their date night doing.”

“That is…” Eddie was frowning heavily, obviously trying to find the right words for it. He eventually gave up, declaring instead, “I am very disappointed in Edmundo.”

“Eddie, we’ve spent entire nights trying to do Chris’ math homework.”

“We also did that before we got together, so I don’t think it counts,” he retorted. “Now, continue with the story, por favor.”

“Right, right. So I come back from babysitting to find them Netflix and chilling on my couch-”

“On your couch!?  He broke the bro code on your own couch!?”

“Yes! On my couch!”

“Okay, okay,” Eddie said, leaning in. “And then what happened?” 

“Albert invited me to dinner at Veronica’s, because apparently she wanted to patch things up,” Buck said, eyeing his boyfriend. He was getting far too invested into this drama. “And I, not wanting to be a third wheel, invited a plus one.”

“Please tell me it was Edmundo.”

“I wish I went with Edmundo, but I wasn’t going to invite my straight best friend- Yes, shut up. But I was certain he was straight, just like I’m pretty sure he thought I was straight. I wasn’t going to invite him on a double date with my failed date, especially when he had his own date. So I, uh…” He mumbled the rest of that sentence, scratching at his neck awkwardly.

“I didn’t catch that, dear.”

“I said I invited Taylor Kelly. And I might have failed to properly express what was going on, precisely.”

If someone didn’t have a calendar and only had the expression on Eddie’s face to go by, they could easily get the mistaken impression that it was Christmas. The man’s smile had grown impossibly large, and he sat up with his hands clasping his knees, looking very much like Chris hanging onto every word of their (heavily edited) work stories.

“Go on.”

“You know, you insulted me earlier. I think I should just leave you hanging.”

“No, Buck, c’mon,” Eddie whined. Again, very much like his son.

“Ugh, fine, put that pout away,” Buck demanded, caving as he poked at Eddie’s bottom lip. “So, that first night with my parents, you’d say that was incredibly awkward, right?”

“Right.”

“Well, the double date was… Kinda like that? Taylor did not like that she was blindsided by a double date.”

“Understandably,” Eddie said, and then he scowled. “Dios, I just sympathized with Taylor Kelly.”

“Some sharp words were said. Mostly from her. And I knew half of it was bullshit the moment she said it, cause like. Taylor said I was intimidated by strong women?”

That statement had Eddie blinking and rubbing at his ears.

“I’m sorry, there’s no way I heard that right. Intimidated by strong women?”

“Well, she wasn’t entirely wrong, because Athena intimidates the hell out of me.”

“Yeah, but that’s… It’s Athena,” Eddie said, as if that was all the explanation needed. And it really was. “And you just told me Abby did an emergency tracheotomy on you, with a steak knife. So I don’t see how anyone would honestly believe you were intimidated by strong women. But whatever, what happened then?”

“And then Taylor decided she didn’t want to stroke my ego-” His boyfriend snickered at that, because sometimes he wasn’t any more emotionally mature than Buck was. “That was her exact wording! She made some excuse about needing to prep for a story.” 

“And then what?”

“And then she called me needy on her way out.”

The other man stared at him in silence, his lips pressed into a flat line. He grabbed both of Buck’s shoulders in a tight grip, and asked,

“Why did you date her!?”

Eddie won the bet, of course. The homeowner finally had enough around hour eight and used his own ladder to climb onto the roof, where he then shoved poor, stupid Corey off the edge and onto someone’s SUV below. The man then told all the first responders and news reporters gathered to, in essence, fuck off.

They used their earnings to get McDonald’s on the way home.

(Judging from the look of mixed disapproval and amusement he gave them both, Bobby clearly knew what Buck had done.)

“Who are you texting?” Eddie asked, coming up to look over Buck’s shoulder.

“Albert,” he answered, leaning over the kitchen island in the station’s loft, frantically tapping away at his phone screen.

DO NOT GO ON THE 710

DO NOT

wow full words

and all caps

al i stg

DO NOT

“I don’t think he’s taking it as seriously as I would like.”

It was finally the day of Jee-Yun’s birth, not that she was named that yet. Chimney and Maddie were still struggling to find a name that they liked, much to both of their frustrations. The fact that the little princess was late to arrive - despite technically being right on time, from certain perspectives - was also causing stress. The expectant father had started cornering Buck to ask him when the baby was actually going to make an appearance, and the time traveler had begun to fall back on the cryptic, “Soon.”

Sadly, that answer seemed to only make Chimney more frustrated.

“What happens on the Seven-Ten?” Eddie asked, peering at Buck’s screen.

“Drunk driver,” he answered. “It’s times like this that I wish I thought to, I dunno. Get every detail and commit it to memory. I don’t know her name, I don’t know where she lives, I definitely don’t know her license plate. I’m just once again stuck waiting for something awful to happen that I should be able to stop.”

“It’s not like you expected to be back here to live through it again.”

“Her son’s in the backseat, Eds,” Buck said, shooting Albert another text reiterating the importance of what he was saying.

al r u lstng

DO NOT gt on 710

DO NOT

“He’s the one that calls Nine-One-One, and Maddie has to listen when…”

“Hey.” Eddie reached over to cup his chin, gently forcing him to meet his eyes. “Whatever happens isn’t on you. You know that right?”

“Isn’t it? I mean, I know what’s going to happen. I’m basically letting it happen again, just because I didn’t bother to pay attention to the details the first time.”

“You paid attention to the details of Hen’s accident, remember?” his boyfriend pointed out. “And we tried to stop it, and it happened anyway, remember?”

“Right. You’re right,” Buck sighed. “You don’t worry about the things you can’t do anything about.”

“Exactly.” He glanced around for a moment. “So I can’t help but notice that you’ve managed to avoid Chimney the entire day so far, at least when we’re not on a call.”

“Because he’s going to ask me again when Jee will be born.”

“Jee, huh?” Eddie was smirking at him for the slip. “And you can’t just tell him it’ll be soon, like every other time he’s asked?”

“It’s very soon,” Buck said, smiling at him. “Mads is in labor as we speak.”

“What!?” His boyfriend looked around again, checking that his outburst didn’t attract anyone’s attention. “But- But- She’s at work?”

“She also still thinks they’re Braxton Hicks, I’m pretty sure,” he said.

Eddie stared at him for a moment, frowning. He moved his hand from Buck’s chin to his cheek, his thumb stroking at a spot under his eye.

“What? What is it?”

“You don’t sound as excited about this as I thought you would be,” his boyfriend said. 

“What? Of course I’m excited.”

“Not as excited as I thought you would be,” he reiterated. “You were literally bouncing when you saw the probie-”

“Ravi.”

“When you saw Ravi. And I thought, if you’re about to meet your niece again, you’d be off the walls.”

“It’s complicated, Eds.”

“Complicated? What, does- Nothing happens during the birth, does it?”

“No, that-” Buck sighed again and reached up to hold Eddie’s hand, tilting his head to press a kiss to the palm. “That goes fine, it’s… What happens after.”

“Amor? What is it?”

“Something I don’t think I can do anything about, but I’m worrying about anyway.”

“I just want to hold her,” Buck said, gazing adoringly at the screen of his laptop. Eddie was thankful he wasn’t, because he didn’t think he’d survive the sight of his boyfriend holding a baby. He was barely able to keep from combusting whenever the man did something with Chris.

It was a couple days after the pile-up, where he got to watch the other man pace up and down the road repeatedly calling Albert on his phone, and then got to listen to the man yell at him for not picking up sooner. He wasn’t certain what, precisely, that was about. He just knew that Buck had seemed so very relieved when the younger Han answered.

“Soon,” Maddie said, and Eddie snickered at how similar that answer sounded to what Buck had been telling Chimney. “Dr. Heller just wants us to wait a few more weeks. And then you get to meet your Uncle Buck.”

He couldn’t see the screen from where he was sitting, but he was pretty sure that the last bit was directed at the baby.

“I can’t believe Chimney just missed the first ‘Uncle Buck’,” she continued.

“There’ll be others,” Buck said, waving it off. And though it was subtle, Eddie was certain he saw his boyfriend’s smile slip a bit.

“Okay, I am clean and ready to hold my girl,” Chimney said, finally joining Maddie and baby Jee at the laptop. “Uncle Buck! Was I the first one? I was the first, right?”

“Yeah, totally,” Buck said, nodding.

“Yes you were,” Eddie agreed.

“And Uncle Eddie!” Chimney said. “Who is not on the screen.”

“He’s camera shy,” Buck joked. “But I will leave you three to it, okay? Buck loves you, Jee. Buck loves- Oh shit you hadn’t told him, yet, uh… Okay bye!”

Eddie waited until he was certain Maddie and Chimney had hung up, before reaching over and wiping off a tear that had started gathering on his boyfriend’s eyelash.

“Are you okay?”

“Yeah, just. I missed her so much, you know?” he said, reaching up to close the laptop. “And now she’s here and I still can’t hold her.”

That wasn’t the only thing bothering him, Eddie could tell. But Buck still had the awful habit of not talking about things that happened in the other time until they were either about to happen again, or things had changed so much that they would never happen. So instead of trying to pull it out of him like teeth, Eddie opted to instead wrap an arm around him and pull him close.

Because what else could he do before Buck finally told him what was wrong?
