Which is to say, not well, because he was a self-sufficient manly man who didn’t like being a charity case. But that was okay, because the house was a thought for later. For After.

The After was also the reason he was here now.

“Hi, I uh, have an appointment?” he said, standing awkwardly in front of the receptionist. “Evan Buckley? I was needing to have my will witnessed and notarized.”

“Of course,” the receptionist said, and her voice gave the impression of a customer service smile, even if her mask hid it. “They’ll be with you in a moment.”

“Thanks.”

There was no shame in fear, Athena had told him, and he was very afraid of what might happen. But he knew what he needed to do, and part of that was making sure everything was properly tidied up, in case the worst happened. In case Ichabod decided that giving him another chance was less entertaining than the things that would be left behind.

There were some things he thought he managed to prevent, only for much worse versions to occur. “To her brother. I got a Dear John letter in video form.”

“But you… You found her,” Eddie said.

“I did, right where Buck said she was,” Chimney said, nodding. “God, I never changed my voicemail recording. I was so cruel to him. He was just trying to keep his word to her and keep me from spiraling, and I went out of my way to hurt him for it.”

“Fuck you for that, by the way,” Eddie said, tipping his bottle at him. “Maddie put him in an impossible spot and he didn’t deserve any of it.”

“No, he didn’t,” he said. “But it was easier to be angry with him than to accept that it was partially my fault for not doing a better job as Maddie’s partner. If I could go back and change one single thing, I’d make sure she wasn’t alone. Have the Lees take her and Jee in, or Karen.”

“There’s a lot of things I’d change, if I could,” Eddie said, taking a sip from his beer. “But right now? If I could, I’d go back to Christmas and take the battery out of his jeep. I’d like to watch him try to run away then.”

Chimney was surprised into laughter, almost choking on the gulp of beer he had just swallowed. He set the bottle down again, coughing and pounding at his chest.

“Man, I can just- That head tilt he does when he’s confused, you know? I can just imagine him trying to start his jeep in a huff and just doing that tilt when it doesn’t work. Like a confused puppy.” He let out a sigh. “How has Chris been handling it?”

“Not well.” That was an understatement. There had been more blow ups and tantrums and breakdowns in the past weeks than in the whole year before. His son was not handling Buck’s sudden and total absence any better than he was. “The exact opposite of well.”

“He’ll show up,” Chimney said, and the positivity was sounding painfully forced. “And if not, then... Maybe you can take your kid to go hunt your Buckley down, like I did mine.”

“My kid has school,” Eddie pointed out. “And I wouldn’t know where to even begin to look for him.”

“Maybe he’s in Boston, and we just missed each other.”

“Maybe.” He tried clinging to that hope, but calls to Buck were still going straight to voicemail, and that could only really mean a couple of things. “I just don’t feel…” Safe. “Comfortable leaving Chris behind to go on what could be a wild goose chase.”

“The option’s still there. And if he’s not in Boston, maybe he ran to somewhere he’s been before, like Maddie did,” Chimney suggested. “Probably not Hershey, though.”

“Definitely not Hershey.”

“But Maddie said he used to send her postcards, when he was traveling. Maybe we could make a list of places where he could be from them.”

And that’s how, instead of cleaning, Eddie and Chimney instead dug through Buck’s things until they found said postcards, and spent the rest of the night making a map of sorts of the man’s journey before Los Angeles.

In the end, it was Chris that drove him to it.

“What if he’s out there alone somewhere?” he asked, after waking up from yet another nightmare. “You need to find him, Dad. You need to find him.”

And what could Eddie do in the face of his crying son, but promise that he would?

In the middle of the thirtieth day since Buck had disappeared, Eddie packed a bag and dropped Chris off at Pepa’s, before setting off in the direction of the closest place on the list he and Chimney had made that night in the loft. The plan was to hit the ranch in Montana and then head for Boston, and from there down the Atlantic seaboard. The hope was that, by some miracle, he’d find Buck at one of those places.

He wasn’t sure he believed in miracles anymore.

He wasn’t sure he was actually brave enough to make this trip.

But Buck was out there, somewhere. Anything could have happened to him, could be happening to him. So Eddie could fake being brave for just a bit longer, he could fake being strong for just a bit longer. Because Buck needed him.

The trip started off fine, sorta. Getting out of the city was always a pain, and the sun was setting by the time he was putting the skyline behind him. Once he got too far out, the roads grew less and less familiar, and so eventually he had to put his faith in technology. Buck had gotten him a GPS for the truck one year; Eddie put his destination into it and hoped for the best.

It was a mistake.

“In five-hundred feet, turn right.”

“Turn right where-? Fuck!”

“Recalculating route…”

“Pedazo de mierda sin valor, I should just toss you out the window.”

“Recalculating…”

“Yeah, I know!” What Eddie didn’t know was where the hell he’d ended up. He wasn’t entirely certain how he’d screwed it up, but he must have put the destination in wrong or something. The stupid thing kept giving him the most unhelpful of directions, and they got worse every time he missed a turn or took a wrong one.

The sun had set, and the sky was filled with more stars than he was used to seeing anymore. He took the next right, and prayed it got him back on track. There was a four way up ahead, he could see. Maybe if he took a right there, it would take him back to the road he was supposed to turn right on originally, and then he could just turn left there…?

“Recalc-” The GPS died mid-word, and so did his truck, rolling to a stop just as it hit the crossroads.

“Que? Oh you have got to be…” Eddie huffed and reached down to pop the hood before hopping out, moving around to the front to see what, exactly, had gone wrong now.

“Howdy, stranger.”

The sudden voice had him leaping out of his skin, and he just about tripped over himself spinning to face the other person. Tall and looming, with a long coat and wide-brimmed hat. They were standing in the middle of the road, and he knew no one had been there when he got out. He edged towards his still open door, and to the bat he had stashed behind his seat.

“Hi,” he said, trying to sound casual.

“What’s got you out here so late at night?” the stranger asked, walking towards him. The motion had Eddie dropping the subtlety and rushing for the bat, pulling it out and gripping it tightly in his hand.

“My truck just died,” he explained, the weapon held to his side. “Stupid GPS got me lost and now I can’t get unlost.”

“That’s what happened,” the stranger said, and he was close enough now that Eddie could make out his features under the moonlight. A thin face, jutting cheekbones, deep-set eyes. More skull-like than some actual skulls he had seen. “But why are you here?”

“I’m looking for my friend,” he said. “Buck. He… He’s missing. He’s been missing.”

“Buck?” The name seemed to amuse the man. “Just how long has he been missing, now?”

“Thirty days,” he blurted out. “Thirty fucking days since he turned around and ran away, and I haven’t heard a damn thing from him since.”

“You sound angry.”

“You’re damn right I’m angry,” Eddie said. “He was supposed to be my friend, my best friend. He- I… He was supposed to have my back, and he just left.” He shook his head, unsure why he was telling this stranger everything. “That doesn’t matter. I need to… I’m going to grab my phone and call someone to come get me. It’s been nice talking to you, uh…”

“Ichabod,” the man said. “My name is Ichabod.”

“Ichabod. It’s been nice talking to you, Ichabod.” He turned to get into the safety of his truck. “Now, if you’ll-”

“What do you want, Eddie?”

He froze mid-motion, heart leaping in his chest.

“H- How did you…?”

“I know many, many things,” Ichabod said, and maybe it was just the way the shadows were falling beneath the brim of his hat, but his eyes seemed unnaturally dark. “But what I don’t know is: what do you want?”

“I- I-” He felt the words clawing their way up his throat, no matter how much he tried to force them down. This wasn’t natural, this wasn’t right, this wasn’t- “Buck. I want to find Buck. I want to know where he is, if he’s safe.”

Ichabod smiled, and even though it looked friendly on the surface, it did nothing at all to soothe his growing terror.

And his eyes were so very black.

A Burning Question

“It’s so much better this way,” Buck told him, and then he shoved Eddie backwards with enough force to send him stumbling. He had barely gotten his feet steady beneath him again when he heard that awful, familiar sound and then-

There was blood, spraying across the air and splattering across his face.

There was Buck, that smile slipping away with shock as he collapsed to the ground.

“Get down!” Captain Mehta shouted, tackling him into the side of the 133’s engine. A moment later, he saw the sparks as another bullet struck pavement, right behind where he’d just been standing. Chaos erupted around them, civilians and first responders alike all running for cover.

This didn’t make sense. This was Los Angeles, not Afghanistan. They shouldn’t be getting ambushed by sniper fire while doing their damn jobs. Buck shouldn’t be bleeding out on the pavement as bullets sparked off the vehicles around them and dug into the blacktop.

“Shots fired!” Mehta was screaming into his radio, using his free hand to push Eddie’s head down. “A firefighter is down. I repeat, firefighter down!”

Buck was laying right there, just out of reach. Buck needed help, and all Mehta was doing was shouting into the radio like back up would magically drop from the sky. But that was never going to happen, and by the time someone did arrive…

Gritting his teeth, Eddie shoved Mehta off of him and rolled under the truck. He army crawled until he could just about stretch an arm out and snag Buck’s wrist, dragging him to safety. There was a smear of blood trailing in their wake by the time he was back on the other side of the truck with Mehta.

“Get him into the cabin!” the 133’s captain ordered, and Eddie was already picking his boyfriend up and manhandling him into it before the captain was even done speaking. At some point, the battalion truck he and Buck had commandeered had - somehow - caught fire, but much like the bullets that were only just barely missing everyone, he paid it no mind.

This wasn’t the first time he had been forced to treat gunshot wounds while under enemy fire. Keeping his head down, he focused on ripping open Buck’s uniform shirt. There was so much blood already, and more pumping out as he watched. Even as he tore open a pack of gauze and pressed it to the wound, his mind was cataloging the placement and the possible internal damage. There were arteries, there were tendons and muscles, there was his lung.

“It’s gonna be… Okay…” Buck breathed out, weakly trying to reach up for him. Eddie grabbed his hand with his own, squeezing it tightly.

“Yeah, yeah it is,” he said, nodding, pushing the fear down. “Just hang on. You just need to stay with me and hang on, okay?”

Buck just smiled up at him as one of the others placed an oxygen mask over his face, his eyes never once leaving Eddie’s.

Time was an illusion in that truck. It felt like it took an eternity to get to the hospital, a lifetime stuffed into a handful of minutes spent trying to keep the love of his life from bleeding out beneath him. There was a trauma team rushing out with a gurney as the truck pulled to a stop in front of the ER entrance, and Eddie hopped up to help get Buck transferred over.

“Through-and-through, upper torso,” he told them, listing it off automatically. “Large caliber.”

“We’ve got a transfusion ready,” one of the nurses said. “Did you say large caliber?”

“It was a sniper,” Mehta answered.

“Pulse is weak,” someone said, and suddenly Eddie’s knees were, too.

“Trauma bay two,” the nurse directed as they rolled his boyfriend away. “Let’s set up for a thoracotomy.”

Eddie could only watch as Buck was taken farther and farther away from him. There was nothing he could do now. Everything was out of his hands, and he was stuck just waiting and hoping and praying.

How was it better this way?

“Any news?” Shannon asked, the moment Eddie walked through the door. He had called her and told her what happened, and she had immediately volunteered to help tell Christopher. He was thankful for that, so very thankful, because he wasn’t certain he was strong enough to do it by himself.

“No, nothing yet,” he said. “He’s still in surgery. Bobby or Maddie will probably tell everyone when he’s out.”

“Okay,” she sighed, nodding. She pointed at the envelopes in his hand. “What’s that?”

“A letter for Christopher,” he told her. “And one for me. Chimney found them at the station, along with one for Maddie. They’re from Buck.”

“A letter from…?” She shook her head. “So it’s like the tsunami, then. He knew it was coming.”

“Yeah, I think he did,” he said. “I haven’t looked at either of them yet. I wasn’t ready to read mine, and reading Chris’ felt… Wrong.”

The mere thought of reading Buck’s words to their son felt like a violation of the highest order. But he knew that he didn’t have to worry that whatever it said was appropriate or harmful, because they were Buck’s words, and he would never say a harmful thing to Chris. Especially if he had thought that the words would be…

“He’s in his room,” Shannon said, taking a breath and smoothing down her blouse. “I haven’t mentioned anything to him yet. Are you ready?”

“No,” he said.

“Neither am I,” she said, offering her hand. He took it willingly, thankful for the support. Bobby had said that having a kid was like having your heart outside your chest, and he had been so very right. And now Eddie was about to break his.

Christopher was sitting on his bed, playing on his Switch, when they stepped into his room. He looked up immediately, smiling widely at them.

“Hi, dad.”

“Hey, buddy,” Eddie said, sharing a look with Shannon before letting go of her hand and moving to sit beside their son. She sat down on the other side. “We wanted to talk to you about something.”

“Okay. Where’s Buck?”

“That’s what we wanted to talk to you about, honey,” Shannon said, reaching up to run her fingers through Chris’ hair.

“He got hurt at work today,” Eddie said.

“What happened? Was it in a fire?”

“No, not…Someone hurt him, Chris,” he said. “You remember how I got hurt? When I was gone? Before I came home?”

“Yeah…”

“It was like that,” Shannon said. 

“Is he gonna be okay?”

“I don’t know, buddy,” Eddie said, because he had promised not to lie to his son when it counted. “He has a whole team of doctors working to make him okay, though. And you know our Buck, he will do everything in his power to come back to us.”

Chris blinked up at him from behind his glasses, frowning at him. He reached a small hand up, patting his cheek.

“It’s gonna be okay, dad,” he said, and Eddie took that hand in his, much as he had Buck’s earlier in the day.

“Yeah. Yeah, it is,” Shannon said, sharing a look with her ex-husband across Chris’ head. Eddie wasn’t so certain of that, though. He wasn’t really certain if anything could ever be okay after this.

“Buck wrote you something,” he said, opening up the envelope and handing the letter to his son. “Before he got hurt.”

“What does it say?” Chris asked.

“I don’t know, I didn’t read it. It’s yours.”

He and Shannon sat and watched, bracketing their son as he read through the words on the page. The effect they had on Chris were immediate. His frown grew deeper with the very first sentence, and half-way through, his bottom lip began to wobble. When he got to the end, he dropped the paper to the ground, big globs of tears rolling down his cheeks as he clambered into his father’s lap.

“I don’t want him to leave,” he wailed, burying his face into Eddie’s chest. “I don’t want him to leave.”

“Hey, hey.” Eddie wrapped his arms around him, rocking him slowly as he cried harder and harder. He felt his phone vibrate in his pocket, but couldn’t dig it out in that moment to check. “He isn’t going to leave. He doesn’t want to leave.”

Shannon pulled out her own phone, and he could see the relief on her face at whatever she saw on the screen.

“He’s going to be okay, Chris,” she said, holding up her phone so he could see it. “See? He’s going to be okay.”

But all that seemed to do was make him cry harder, and Eddie could feel his heart breaking with each heaving sob his son let out.

How was it better this way?

Buck was so very still when Eddie stepped into his ICU room, nodding at the officer standing watch by the door. The only motion was the rise and fall of his chest as the ventilator pushed air into his lungs. For someone so big and tall, he always looked so small in hospital beds. And Eddie hated that he had seen him in this setting enough to know that.

“Anything new?” he asked Maddie, who was curled up in the only chair available. She looked tired, with her hair up in a quick ponytail and bags starting to form under her eyes. She had her own letter from Buck in her hand, still in its envelope, and was tapping it against her knee.

“The nurse said his vitals were good,” she said, looking up at him.

“That’s good,” he said, stepping up to the bed and taking Buck’s hand in his. He nodded at the envelope Maddie was holding. “Have you read it yet?”

“No,” she said, shaking her head. “At first, it felt like admitting that he wouldn’t… Now, whatever he had to say that was so important, he can tell me when he wakes up.”

Eddie nodded, understanding what she meant. He could only bring himself to read his own letter after they all got the confirmation that Buck had made it out of surgery okay. In his bed, long after Chris had finished crying himself to sleep and Shannon had gone home, Eddie had read the words and felt… Anger. Pain. Deep seated loathing for anyone and everyone who had hurt Buck before that point and made him think that he was merely spare parts or in any way expendable. Bull-fucking-shit.

“Did you just get off work?” Maddie asked.

“Yeah,” he said, glancing down at the uniform he was still wearing. He hadn’t even bothered changing at the station, just grabbed his bag and rushed to the hospital to see Buck. “Chimney said he was going to pick up Jee from the Lees.”

“I didn’t think having her here would be the best,” she said, and there was something odd about her tone. Something that sounded like relief. “The ICU is no place for an infant, especially not now…”

“Is she still colicky?”

“She’s been crying all the time,” Maddie whispered.

“It’ll pass,” he told her, trying to sound reassuring. “Chris was like that, too. I wasn’t there much for it, but I remember how much he cried when I was, and how nothing I could do could make it better. I felt like the worst father.”

“One of the very first things Buck told me about you was how wonderful of a father you are,” Maddie said, and for a moment a smile threatened to take over her frown. “I teased him about having a boy crush. Oh, how little I knew…”

“He was in love with a version of me since long before I met him,” Eddie said, gazing down at Buck. His face was starting to get scruffy, the blond stubble making it look dirty rather than rugged. Buck hated having scruff, he knew. He’d have to ask a nurse to give him a shave, or do it himself. “I still have trouble with it, sometimes. Like I’m competing with a ghost of myself. Fucking Edmundo.”

“Edmundo?”

“It’s easier, for me,” he explained. “It was Buck’s idea.”

“You don’t like the other you, do you?” she asked, tilted her head as she looked at him. “Edmundo, I mean.”

“Some of the things Buck’s told me about him, I just… I just can’t see myself doing. Ever,” Eddie told her. But while he didn’t particularly like Edmundo, he couldn’t truly say that he hated him. Whatever events led up to his announcement that fateful Christmas, it brought Buck to Eddie. Whatever reasons Edmundo had for leaving, whatever caused that Chris to be so frightened for him, Eddie was reaping the benefits of it. Shannon was alive and well, and he could hold Buck in his arms whenever he wanted.

Well, almost whenever.

“Every May,” he said, squeezing Buck’s hand, hoping he’d squeeze back. “Every May, this idiot ends up back in a hospital room.”

“Next May, maybe we just keep him locked up somewhere,” Maddie suggested, leaning forward to rest a hand on her brother’s arm. “Hear that, Buck? We’re going to wrap you up in bubble wrap and put you in one of those giant plastic ball things. Like a hamster.”

Whether or not she was seriously hoping her brother would be so offended he’d open his eyes, they remained stubbornly closed. The only noise was the beeping of his monitor and the pumping of the ventilator. She sat back, looking so very disappointed at the lack of response.

“He’ll wake up, he just needs time,” Eddie told her. “Getting shot takes a lot out of you.”

“How long are you staying today?”

“I don’t know, a little while,” he said. “Carla’s watching Chris. He’s been asking every morning when he’ll get to see Buck.”

“How has he been handling it?” she asked.

“Not well.”

“And his father?”

He looked up and gave her a wobbly smile.

“Not well.”

She nodded, as if she’d been expecting that answer. She probably had been. Everyone at work had been walking on eggshells around him, as if waiting for him to snap at any moment. He almost had, a few times. Poor Ravi was now refusing to step anywhere near him, after the last time.

“Do you want to take a break from watching him?” Eddie asked her. “Go home, take a shower, change your clothes? Maybe eat something.”

“I probably should,” Maddie said, and made no move to get up. She just kept sitting there, watching the rise and fall of Buck’s chest.

How was it better this way?

It was actually very easy to get lost on purpose, Eddie found. On a night that Shannon was keeping Chris, he got in his truck and started driving. He picked a direction at random and left the city, and from there started taking turns without a thought or care for where they took him. Not being one to go on long, aimless drives outside of Los Angeles, he quickly found roads he was unfamiliar with.

A question had been burning in him ever since the shooting, and there were only two people that could possibly answer it. And one of them was still unconscious in his hospital bed.

Eddie wasn’t really certain if this would work. He wasn’t really certain how, precisely, Buck had found Ichabod to begin with. But he had made multiple mentions of how lost he was, how lost he had felt, and so Eddie did his best to be just as lost. 

He took a turn here, and another there, and focused on how he had no idea what to do. He focused on how his boyfriend needed help and he didn’t know where to begin to give it. He focused on how his son had sobbed for an entire night and he could do nothing except hold him. He focused on how there was something so very wrong with Maddie and he had no idea what it could be. 

Eddie took a left, and then he took the next right.

He thought back to how adrift and alone he had felt after he had come home with new scars on his body, and Shannon expecting him to somehow be whole and ready to step into a role he had never prepared for. He thought back to that night Buck was confessing his love to him, and how he had felt when he thought Buck had been talking to Edmundo and not him. He thought back to the early days in the city, back before Buck brought Carla into their lives, when he was trying to juggle Christopher and the academy and the bills and had no idea how he was going to manage it all.

He took a right, and then a left, and the truck quietly rolled to a halt just as it reached a four-way stop, the engine suddenly dying. Taking a breath, he opened his door and hopped out. There were so many stars in the sky, he noticed, far more than he could have ever seen while still in the city.

In the middle of the road, stood a figure. Tall, looming, with a coat that fell to his ankles and a wide-brimmed hat perched on his head. 

“Howdy, stran-”

“Don’t have time for that,” Eddie said, marching towards him. The response seemed to have flummoxed Ichabod, the person or entity or whatever the hell he was. “How does this work?”

“Did you manage to find your way here on purpose?” Ichabod asked, sounding and looking delighted. Honestly, Eddie had never seen a more disturbing look of glee. “To talk to me?”

“Buck let himself get shot and said it was better that way,” Eddie said, balling his fists at his side and glaring at the… Man? Thing? At Ichabod. He glared at Ichabod. “And it’s utter bullshit, because there’s nothing I can think of that would ever make that true. But I can’t ask him until he wakes up, and even then, he probably wouldn’t tell me.”

“So you came here to ask a question.”

“I came here to tell you what I wanted. Now stop fucking around and ask.”

Ichabod tilted his - Its? Their? - head to the side, clearly contemplating. Finally, with a nod, he asked,

“What do you want, Eddie?”

It was the weirdest of feelings, like someone reaching down his throat and pulling the words out. There was nothing he could have done to stop them from coming up, to stop himself from answering the question. It was the worst, most violating thing he had ever experienced.

But it was for Buck, and so it was worth it.

“I want to know what happened in that other timeline,” he answered. “I want to know how he could ever possibly believe it was better that he got shot. I- I need to know what led to him ending up here, that Christmas.”

“Need?”

“Need.”

Ichabod’s eyes were black, inky pits of darkness from which light had no chance of escaping. He smiled - if one could call it a smile - and stepped to the side.

And Eddie was suddenly face-to-face with himself.

Conversations in Liminal Spaces

He looked tired, Eddie noticed. The bags beneath his eyes looked big enough to carry both his phone and wallet, and then maybe one of Chris’ crutches, and his skin was starting to look ashen. Honestly, the version of him he was looking at now resembled far too much the reflection he used to see in the mirror, right after he got home from Afghanistan. The absolute terror that was plain as day on his face was a new addition, however.

He was also holding a baseball bat, looking ready to take a swing with it.

“What the fuck is going on!?” he demanded, eyes flitting around. “Where did that demon go?”

“He’s not a demon,” Eddie corrected him - himself? - almost automatically. Looking around, he noticed that Ichabod had indeed vanished entirely. Buck had never mentioned being left alone at the crossroads before, what did he do from here?

“Wh- Who are you?” the other him asked, the bat still at the ready.

“I’m… Eddie.”

“No, de ningún modo. You’re not me.”

“Well, at least we’re in agreement there,” Eddie said, raising his hands and trying to seem non-threatening. This other version of himself looked as if he had been in fight-or-flight mode for a while now, and this whole situation was no doubt only making it worse. “He asked you a question. What was your answer?”

“Que?”

“He asked you what you wanted. What did you tell him?”

“I… I’m looking for someone,” the other him said, slowly lowering the bat. His entire body still looked tense, however. Like a bear trap waiting to take out the leg of the first person to step in it. “Evan Buckley. Do you… Do you have a…? Dios, what the fuck am I asking?”

“He’s the second most important person in my life,” Eddie said.

“Mine, too,” the other him said. “After-”

“After Chris.”

“He’s missing,” the other him said, and Eddie felt his heart skip a beat at the words. “Buck, I mean. He ran away and never came back. It’s been a month, and he hasn’t… I don’t know where he is. Anything could have happened to him.”

“Did he… Did he leave on Christmas?” Eddie asked, and prayed the answer was no.

“Yes. I- I said I was leaving the One-Eighteen, and he just… He just ran away.”

“Madre de Dios, you’re Edmundo,” Eddie breathed out, horrified for so many reasons. Because this was the him he could have been, if Buck hadn’t begun his crusade to fix everything. Because he had just said that his Buck had been missing for a month, meaning that Buck hadn’t merely gone back in time. Or if that had been the case originally, it hadn’t stayed that way. Because Buck had, in a way, abandoned his family. Entirely unwillingly, but Eddie knew that wouldn’t make a difference in his mind.

He decided then and there that his boyfriend could never know.

“He didn’t even say goodbye to Chris,” Edmundo continued on, oblivious to the world-altering revelation he had just dropped at Eddie’s feet. “He just ran away like the selfish prick that-”

“Shut up!” Eddie snapped, surprising Edmundo into silence. “That is the love of my life you are talking about. I don’t know what the hell happened to turn you into… This. And honestly? I don’t think I care. But you will not talk about Buck that way.”

“He ran away and never looked back!” Edmundo shouted at him. “He abandoned Chris! He abandoned me! I- I needed him. He was supposed to have my back, and he just… Left.”

Edmundo had no earthly idea, did he? Not a clue at all.

“You have his back, he has yours. It’s the two of you against anything and everything the world can throw at you,” Eddie said, the words coming easily to him. They had haunted him for years now, for almost as long as he had known Buck. They had been the spark to the burning question that had led him here, to these crossroads. To Ichabod. “And then, on Christmas, he tells you that he’s leaving, just like everyone else leaves, and you realize that you’re going to end up all alone. Again. Just like before, just like always.”

“But Buck didn’t tell me he was leaving, he just-”

“I didn’t know who he was talking about, when he said that,” Eddie said, interrupting this could-have-been version of himself. “I thought, I was so certain, that he was talking about an ex. That he was talking about someone he loved and who broke his heart. And I guess that he was, really. Even if you apparently never got your head out of your ass.”

“What are you saying?” Edmundo asked, voice turning hard and eyes taking on a dangerous glint.

“That he was talking about you,” Eddie said. “For so fucking long, I’ve felt like he was looking through me and only seeing you. Because you say that he ran away and never looked back, but he’s been looking back at you the entire time I’ve known him.”

“Where is he?” Edmundo demanded, and Eddie saw him adjust his grip on the bat.

“Right at this moment? In a hospital bed, recovering from a gunshot wound. Because a sniper shot him, after we went to help a kid being poisoned with eye drops by his own mother.” It was pure devastation that he saw on his own face, reflected back at him through a funhouse mirror. “He said it was better that way. He was smiling as he said it, as he pushed me towards the safety of the truck. I felt his blood on my face, Eddie. It got in my mouth. I had to scrub it out from between my fingers. And he said it was better that way! Tell me, damn it! How the fuck was that better!?”

“It was meant for us,” Edmundo said, voice almost a whisper. But it was so quiet at those crossroads that Eddie heard it just fine. “It was- I was the one who got shot, and Buck was the one who…”

“Oh, Buck…”

It was better for Buck. Whether or not he meant it that way, that was the answer, that’s how it was better. It was better for Buck, because it was less painful to be shot than to watch it happen to someone you loved, than to live through the aftermath and try to keep everything from crumbling beneath you.

And, oh, the guilt he had to have been carrying this entire time, because of course Buck would feel like he let him down by not protecting him. But for how long? For how many years? Edmundo looked worn down and tired and constantly on edge, but beneath all that, he didn’t look that much older than Eddie…

“He came into my hospital room after I woke up, and told me that he thought it would have been better if he’d been the one who was shot. He talked and acted like he was-”

“Expendable,” Eddie finished for him, remembering those awful words in that awful letter. The one that read too much like a goodbye. “Like he was nothing but spare parts.”

“Exactly.”

Eddie looked at the other him, at Edmundo, and things were starting to make more sense. Being under enemy fire again in downtown LA, when he hadn’t been expecting it and when they were supposed to be safe, had been a frightening enough experience for Eddie. But to be the one who suddenly got shot? To be the one who almost lost their life in circumstances so very similar to Afghanistan? No wonder Edmundo started having panic attacks, no wonder he seemed so afraid, no wonder he-

“Oh,” he said, the syllable punched out of him with the realization. That made sense. That made so much sense. “You’re running away, too.”

“What? No I’m not.”

“You are,” Eddie said, sure of it now. “You’re panicking. You’ve been-”

“I don’t panic.”

“Lie to your therapist, lie to Buck, but don’t lie to me. Don’t lie to yourself,” Eddie scolded. “It’s why you decided to leave the One-Eighteen. Because you’re afraid.”

“No, I’m leaving because-”

“Because of Chris, right? That’s the lie you gave everyone?” he interrupted, cutting him off without a care. “The same lie we gave Shannon when we reenlisted. That we were doing it for Chris, to help pay for the bills and to help with the insurance. That we were doing it because we had to. And sure, that was technically true, but that wasn’t the actual reason.”

Edmundo was glaring at him, his temper clearly rising, but Eddie didn’t care. He wasn’t frightened or intimidated by this broken version of himself.

“And how did that go? Do you remember?” Eddie asked, almost mockingly. “How did it go when, instead of actually talking to Shannon like she was our partner, we just made a decision and ran out on her? How did she react? How did she take it?”

“It’s not the same,” Edmundo ground out.

“You’re right, because when we did it then, we were young and stupid. Now you’re just stupid. And panicking.” Eddie couldn’t help but scoff  “Did you even talk about what happened, afterwards? Did you even let him know how much you were struggling? You didn’t, did you? You just, what? Sucked it up and moved on? Like dad taught us?”

“I was fine. It happened, I moved on. There wasn’t any need to talk about it afterwards, because I was fine.”

“No you weren’t. We weren’t fine after Afghanistan, and you aren’t fine now.” Eddie felt his patience beginning to fray. Did Buck find talking to him to be so frustrating? “Did you learn nothing from Shannon? How was Buck supposed to have your back when you didn’t even talk to him? How was he supposed to help when you didn’t even let him know that you needed help? Because he would. You know that he would. He loves you too much not to.”

“He loves me so much that he left me,” Edmundo said, jaw jutting out stubbornly. Now that he was looking for it, Eddie could see through the anger for the front it really was. Now that he was looking for it, Eddie could see the hurt and the fear that lingered behind it. But it wasn’t something he could help with, not if Edmundo was so unwilling to admit to even himself that he needed help. 

“And we’re back to this again,” Eddie sighed. He dragged a hand down his face, the whole conversation taking a toll on what little energy he had left after everything. “Talking to you is just… Exhausting. You’re exhausting.”

The face Edmundo made at hearing that would probably have been the same one he’d make if Eddie had taken his baseball bat and slugged him with it. There was a story there, one that probably involved his temper and bad decisions, but Eddie didn’t really have the energy or the interest to drag it out of the other man. He had gotten the answer he wanted. And maybe he didn’t know the full story of what led up to that Christmas, he at least knew the part Edmundo had played.

“Okay, I’m done here,” Eddie said. And then, louder, “How the hell do I leave?”

The sound of his truck coming to life had both versions of himself jumping out of their skin.

“You leave the same way you got here,” Ichabod said, suddenly appearing beside them. Well, beside him. The other version of himself had disappeared, his purpose apparently served.

“Where did Edmundo go?”

“Where he needed to go,” the entity answered. “You should probably stop asking questions and start driving. I believe someone is about to wake up.”

Eddie had never ran for his truck faster. He pulled a u-turn, and drove back the way he came. And suddenly, unexplainably, he was just outside the city when he knew that he had ended up miles and miles away before he managed to stumble upon Ichabod. But it was a gift horse he wasn’t willing to look too closely at.

“I thought it would hurt more than it did,” Buck said, looking up into the night sky above him. If he focused, he could start to see that infinite river curling and curving around the twinkling stars. And if he really, truly strained his eyes, he could almost see something that looked an awful lot like Bobby and Athena’s backyard, all decked out for a wedding. But then he had to blink, and was back to staring at nothing more than a star-filled sky. He shook his head to clear it. “Being shot, I mean.”

“And how much did you expect it to hurt?” Ichabod asked.

“I don’t know, about like my leg?” Buck shrugged, looking away from the sky to face the entity. “I mean, don’t get me wrong, getting shot hurt like a bitch. But only for like, a few moments? Before the shock, I guess. I s’pose I won’t really know until I wake up. Which will hopefully be soon.”

“In such a hurry to leave me?”

“I want to make sure Eddie is okay,” he said. “I mean, I know you told me that he didn’t get hurt, but I still want to see it for myself.”

“Were you okay?” Ichabod asked, cocking his head to the side. “When you watched the other Eddie get shot?”

“I was less okay after seeing him shot than he was after being shot,” Buck said. “But he was always made of tougher stuff than me.”

For some reason, this seemed to amuse the entity. But then again, many things he had said or done seemed to amuse Ichabod.

“It’s almost Christmas, again,” the entity said.

“It is.” He let out a sigh. “And I still don’t know what to do about Maddie. How the hell do I help someone that is so insistent on not telling anyone they need help?”

“Or perhaps what you needed to do, you’ve already done,” Ichabod suggested. “But Buck, it’s almost Christmas again.”

“Yeah, you said that,” Buck said, frowning at him. “What about it, though?”

“Do you remember what you said you wanted?” Ichabod asked, peering at him with eyes that were so very black. “That very first night?”

“Of course. I said… I said I wanted to fix whatever broke everything.”

“Buck?”

That voice, that painfully familiar voice, had him turning around on instinct. The sight that greeted him was not one he ever wanted to see here, in this place. On the other side of the crossroads stood Eddie, but he looked so much worse than he had when Buck had last seen him, out on that street. He wasn’t covered in blood, no, but even at this distance Buck could tell that he looked… Tired. Exhausted. Worn-down and threadbare and about to collapse under the weight of everything.

He was also holding a baseball bat, held loosely in his hand.

“Eddie? What the hell are you-? Ichabod, what the hell is he-?” But when Buck looked around, the black-eyed entity was nowhere to be seen.

“Buck, is that really you?”

“Yeah, love, it’s really me,” he answered. “What are you doing here?”

“I was looking for you,” Eddie said, his voice practically dripping with relief. Hell, the other man looked like he might even start to cry. “I- I’ve been… We’ve been looking for you for so long. Why did you leave?”

“Leave? What?” That didn’t make sense. Buck had been shot, Eddie had seen him get shot. Why would he think that he left? “Eds, I got shot, I didn’t leave.”

“On Christmas,” the other man said, and Buck’s heart stopped. No, no, no, no… “You just… You left me. You left us. I- We needed you and you just… Left.”

“Eddie?” This couldn’t be- No, no, it couldn’t-

“Buck,” Edmundo said, stepping closer to him, heedless of the way the bat slipped out of his grip to clatter on the dusty pavement.

“Eddie, what… What happened to you?” Those bags under his eyes. Had the man even slept since he’d last seen him? Oh God, how long had it been for him?

“You left,” the other man said again. “I needed you to have my back and you just… Left.”

“And I am so sorry for that,” Buck said, practically begging for him to believe it. “I regretted it and I’ve been regretting it, but by the time… I thought, I’d hoped…”

He had hoped that the other timeline had simply been rewritten, that he was actually retreading and fixing where things went wrong, but clearly… Clearly, multiverse theory was a bitch. 

(Oh God, all those times he tried preventing the truck bombing and died for it. Oh God, oh God, the tsunami…)

“Why did you leave?” Edmundo asked him, so close now they could almost touch. “Why? Why did you run away?”

“I was afraid,” Buck whispered, and he itched to reach out and touch him. But that distance between them had been uncrossable long before he ever found his way to these crossroads. “Because everyone I care about ends up leaving me. Maddie and Chimney left, and Abby and Ali left. I just… I couldn’t handle you leaving me, too.”

“But I wasn’t leaving you!”

“But I didn’t know that,” he whispered, and Edmundo’s face blurred with tears. “How could I trust that? That won’t happen to us, Buck. You won’t be left behind, Buck. You’re stuck with us, Buck. So many promises that were nothing but words. Why would I think that you weren’t leaving me, too?”

“It doesn’t matter. You know now, right? You know now, so you… You can come back with me.” Edmundo reached out to grab him, but Buck felt nothing. They both looked down, and saw the oddest, most disturbing of sights. They both watched as Edmundo’s hand went straight through Buck’s arm, as if it were a reflection in a pond.

“I don’t think I can,” Buck said.

“No, no, we can… You can… “ Edmundo kept grabbing for him, and his hands kept finding nothing but air. “No, no. We can… Tell that demon you want to leave. That’s what he does, right? You tell him what you want and he gives it to you? Tell him you want to leave.”

“He’s not a demon,” Buck said, smiling sadly at him. “And I don’t think I do. I don’t think I want to leave.”

“Why!?”

“Because when I left before, I didn’t mean to abandon everyone,” he said. “But if I leave now, if I choose to abandon them now…”

“He said you were going to wake up soon…”

“What do you have in that other place that you didn’t have with me?” Edmundo demanded. “What is so special about that other Eddie?”

“He loves me,” Buck answered. “And he tells me that he loves me.”

“I love you!”

“I love you, too. I’ve always loved you. But I’m happy with him. I’m happy where I am,” he said, and felt something within him break a little more at the sight of tears starting to fall down Edmundo’s face. “Can’t I be selfish? Just this one time, can’t I do something for me? Because it makes me happy?”

“Hey, what’s with the tears?”

“You could be happy with me, with us,” Edmundo said, practically begging. “Please.”

“But I’m happy now, with Eddie.”

“He’s me!”

“No, no he’s not,” Buck said, shaking his head. “And even if that were the case, I’m not going to abandon my family again.”

“Evan, please…”

“I’m sorry.”

“What are you sorry for?” Eddie asked, and Buck’s eyes fluttered open. Eddie - his Eddie - was staring down at him in concern. He looked tired, but not nearly like Edmundo had. “There’s those pretty blues.”

“Eds?” he croaked out, and his boyfriend smiled at him. It looked a little wobbly, and maybe a bit cracked.

“It wasn’t better,” Eddie said. “Just so you know. It wasn’t better, and I am absolutely furious with you.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You said that, but what were you apologizing for?”

“For…” For abandoning his other family, for leaving so many different Eddies behind and not even knowing it. “For putting you through that.”

“As you damn well should be,” the other man said. “And as soon as the nurses and doctors are all done checking you over, and after I call and let Chris talk to you, we are going to have a very long discussion. Starting with, ‘you are not expendable, you fucking idiot.’”

“Looking forward to it,” Buck said. And the damndest thing is, it wasn’t a lie.

Woops

True to his word, the moment they were done talking with Chris and Shannon, the moment they hung up the phone, Eddie turned to Buck and said,

“You are not expendable, you fucking idiot,” Eddie said, low and firm, finger poking at Buck’s uninjured shoulder. “You’re not just spare parts, you’re not worth less than anyone else. It was not better that it was you and not me, you self-sacrificing jackass. It hurt me seeing you get shot and then having to tell Chris about it as much as it no doubt hurt you when you had to do it.”

“Okay, I get it, I get it,” Buck said, smiling up at him. He was just a little bit high off the morphine drip, just a little bit, and the lovely fuzzy feeling was almost dangerously too lovely.

“I don’t think you do,” Eddie told him. His boyfriend was frowning down at him, and had been frowning from the moment he opened his eyes in that hospital room. “And I don’t know if I need to yell at your parents for this, or- I don’t know. I don’t know what I need to do to make you understand just how not better it was that you were the one shot. I don’t know what I need to say to make you understand that you mean just as much to everyone as we all mean to you.”

“I do know-”

“Chris cried, after reading your letter.”

“What?” That knocked him right off his high. “I- I didn’t mean to-”

“You wrote him a goodbye letter, Buck. What were you expecting?” Eddie asked, apparently done attempting to poke a bruise into his skin and instead reaching up to run his thumb over Buck’s birthmark. “And fuck you very much for that. It was not better this way.”

“I’m sorry…”

“I know you are, I’m just not sure I trust which part you’re actually sorry about,” Eddie said. “Because this? This has become a trend, Buck. You’re so certain that losing you wouldn’t hurt us as much as losing us would hurt you, and you’re so intent on taking on, or… Or physically shielding everyone else from being hurt. I don’t think you understand what it does to us, every time we see you get hurt.”

“I do, I promise I do.”

“And I don’t think you can even comprehend what it would do to me, to Chris, to us, if you weren’t… If you…” Some of Eddie’s anger leached out of his voice, and Buck wished he could reach up to wipe away the tears gathering in his boyfriend’s eyes. But his arm felt so heavy at that moment.

“I do,” Buck said again, remembering Edmundo, remembering the man he had left behind and who was so desperate to have him back.

“I don’t believe you,” his boyfriend declared. “So I’m making a unilateral decision. You’re going to therapy.”

“What.” Maybe he was on something stronger than morphine, because there was no way he heard that correctly. “You’re making me go to therapy? You?”

“I am,” Eddie declared, sitting back in the uncomfortable looking hospital chair. His arms were crossed and his jaw was set, an immovable object after making up his mind. “You are going to see a therapist. Maybe more than one, if that’s what it takes.”

“But Eds-”

“No buts,” he interrupted, shaking his head. “I’ve understood your concerns about going to therapy again for anything more than the department’s mandated counseling, and I stood by and let you keep using that excuse, but this… No more. Do you hear me? No more.”

“What am I supposed to tell them, huh? ‘Hey, I’m from the future, please don’t lock me up?’”

“I was thinking we start with ‘he said it was better this way, right before letting himself get shot’ and go from there.”

“We?”

“We,” Eddie said, nodding. “I watched someone I love very much get shot, right in front of me, and I couldn’t do anything to stop it. What was it you said, after the truck bombing? When you conspired with Alonzo to force all of us into therapy?”

“I didn’t conspire…” Buck tried protesting.

“It was something about how you knew how you’d feel, if things were reversed, right? Something about how the bombing happened to all of us, too, even if the truck was only on your leg?” He uncrossed his arms and reached over, taking Buck’s face in both his hands. “We are going to therapy. Because I refuse to let this fester until one of us breaks.”

There was something a little too close to knowing, a little too close to certainty, in his voice. And Buck wanted to ask about it, wanted to know what that was about, but he was exhausted, and his eyes were starting to droop.

“Go back to sleep, querido,” Eddie told him. “We’ll talk more about it later.”

“Yeah, okay,” Buck yawned. “But, before I do… There was a call, right? Guy stuck at the top of a crane with his arm pinned?”

“Yeah, what about it?”

“How did you…?”

“Cap climbed up and had us walk him through it over the radio,” Eddie said, and if he had the energy, Buck would have laughed.

“What a hypocrite…”

Eddie wasn’t quite as good at the grand gestures as Buck was, but then again, he didn’t have the money to dole out on things like a brand new truck. What he did have, however, was a large family willing to help set things up for him as he waited for his boyfriend to be discharged. The - non-opioid - pain meds they had prescribed to him were in Eddie’s pocket, having gone in there automatically and without question.

Two years on, and Buck still didn’t trust himself with it, not that Eddie thought any less of him.

After they had everything settled, Eddie helped him into the truck and then took them directly home, not even bothering to go by Buck’s apartment for anything. By this point, the man had enough of his things at the Diaz residence, he could theoretically spend at least a month there and be fine. Anything he needed but didn’t have, Eddie was perfectly willing to go fetch himself. Perhaps watching Buck get shot, and then being faced with the concept of him going missing from his life entirely, was taking its toll in regards to his willingness to let his boyfriend out of his sight. But that’s what their future therapy appointments were for.

It was always a heady feeling, to be able to surprise his boyfriend with something nice. He unlocked his front door and opened it, letting Buck go in first, and they were greeted by a loud cry of “SURPRISE” from everyone gathered. 

“Is this all for me?” Buck asked, looking around in awe. There were balloons and a banner, and the entire LA branch of the Diaz clan was gathered, along with Maddie and Chimney, and Albert.

“You matter,” Eddie whispered into his ear, gently urging him forward.

Buck was ushered to the couch, where Chris commandeered the seat next to him, gluing himself to his side. He tried to get up, once, to get his own food, but Abuela and Pepa shot that down with cold efficiency, volunteering Eddie to get it for him. Not that he minded, obviously.

For a while, Eddie stood by and watched as Buck basked in being the center of attention for a while. But there was something that was bothering him.

“Does she look tired to you?” he asked Shannon, pulling her to the side and nodding at Maddie. She was sitting on her brother’s other side, holding Jee so her uncle could coo at her. And he’d been right, those many, many weeks ago: seeing Buck with his niece was not healthy for his heart.

“She quit her job at the dispatch center,” Shannon said, surprising him.

“Why?”

“She didn’t really give me a reason. Something about wanting to spend more time with Jee.”

That sounded like a fairly good reason. God knew Eddie wished he had spent more time with Chris at that age, when he had the chance. But there was something about it that gnawed at him, something that cried out for him to pay attention. She had looked tired every time he saw her at the hospital, when their times visiting Buck overlapped, and that made sense. An infant at home with colic and a brother unconscious in the ICU were not conducive to restful nights.

What really bothered him, however, was how those bags beneath her eyes and the new lines on her face reminded him of Edmundo at the crossroads.

Eventually, most of the guests cleared out. Maddie and Chimney left first and rather early, saying they needed to get Jee home for her nap, and it left Eddie feeling even more certain that something was wrong. Buck’s face as he watched them leave only furthered it. Abuela and Pepa left a couple hours later, leaving him with a fridge filled with leftovers and ready-to-go meals waiting to be heated, and Shannon followed them shortly after with a hug for Chris.

Albert was the last one to leave. Albert, who had mostly stuck to the periphery of the party, constantly looking to be on the verge of asking something. Albert, who was currently dragging his feet.

“Spit it out, Albert,” Buck demanded, accepting a cup of water and his next dose of pain meds from Eddie. “What have you been wanting to say? Or ask?”

“Why did you two decide to become firefighters?” the young man asked.

“It was a way to help people and be a badass while doing it,” was Buck’s immediate answer.

“Wait, that’s why?” Eddie asked, glancing at him in surprise.

“I was not a very complicated person at that point of my life,” he said. He would have shrugged, but his uninjured shoulder currently had a sleeping Chris on it. “But it was the best impulsive decision I ever made. What about you, love?”

“Better pay, hours, and insurance than what I had in Texas,” he answered. “And it wasn’t much different from being in the army.”

“Why do you ask, Albert?” 

“I don’t know what I want to do with my life,” he said. “I came here on an impulse to get away from my father, to figure out what I wanted. And all I’m doing now is delivering food while sleeping in your guest room.”

“Pretty sure by this point, it’s your room,” Buck said. “And it took me several years, a lot of jobs, and two continents to figure out what I wanted to do. And many, many bad decisions.”

“So is becoming a firefighter something you’re considering?” Eddie asked, shelving his curiosity about Buck’s bad decisions for later. The man was shameless at the best of times, surely he could get another dozen embarrassing stories out of him while he was mildly high on pain meds.

“I’ve seen what you all do, and I respect it,” Albert said. “And I think I would like to try.”

“Then you should,” Buck said, nodding decisively. “I think you’d be just fine at it.”

Buck lay in bed, unable to sleep. More precisely, he lay in Eddie’s bed. The man was curled around him, resting his head on his chest and snoring softly. Buck would be running his fingers through his hair, which looked so fluffy in its sleep-tousled state, but he had one arm trapped under his boyfriend and his other stuck in a sling. So instead, he just contented himself with watching him, like a creep.

It was better than closing his eyes and seeing Edmundo’s tear-stained face again.

He was stuck in that moment of realization, tied to it with guilt and horror. Buck had abandoned his family. He had run away in a moment of panic and didn’t stop running until he met Ichabod, and then… He had abandoned his family. There was no other way to look at it. He had abandoned Edmundo, and he had abandoned Chris, when they both needed him. It was his worst fears realized, and he could no longer simply avoid thinking about it or delude himself into believing otherwise.

And he didn’t know what to do about that.

Edmundo had asked for Buck to go back with him, and he was, perversely, thankful that it was extremely evident that he could not have physically gone with the man even if he wanted to. But it did nothing to change the fact that he had abandoned his family before, and was still abandoning them. If actually given the chance, he didn’t know what he’d do, because he’d be damned either way.

He didn’t want to leave Eddie and Chris.

He felt so guilty for leaving Edmundo and that Chris, for not going back with Edmundo.

Ichabod had implied that he was running out of time, and Buck had the uncomfortable feeling that he’d either have to make the choice, or let the choice be made for him.

Ichabod stood there and debated on what, exactly, he could do about this. When Buck had arrived in his little domain that fateful night, with his want worded in just the right way to leave it ripe for interpretation, the entity hadn’t truly considered what he was doing beyond how it could provide much needed entertainment. When he scooped the mortal up - mind and soul - and poured him into his younger self, he hadn’t really given much thought to the consequences.

He hadn’t even known what the consequences were going to be, or if there even would be any.

The entity had never done something like that before, had never been given the chance. Ichabod had not realized that his actions would create a whole new branch in that infinite river. Not until it happened. And when it did, he was too busy being overjoyed with this brand new source of entertainment. Even the branches that sprouted off of it every time he undid Buck’s many deaths were a joy to observe, until they grew boring and he trimmed them like the limbs of a bonsai tree.

He definitely hadn’t paid any mind to the branch Buck had originally come from, beyond assuming that it would simply unravel itself or be replaced, and that was his mistake. He couldn’t even unweave it himself, because it was beyond his purview, much unlike the branch he accidentally created.

And now, certain other powers were nagging at him for making a mess of things.

“If you have any ideas for what to do, I’m perfectly willing to listen,” he told the butterfly, which was resting silently on the roof of the jeep.

His guest’s answer was judgmental silence, but its meaning was as clear to him as it ever was.

“If you were actually concerned, you’d be doing more than complaining to me, wouldn’t you? There’s nothing stopping you from fixing it,” he told it. He nudged the body at his feet, blue eyes open and unseeing, chest rising shallowly. “I don’t know what you’re worried about. Nothing’s imploding or exploding or doing any sort of -ploding at all. This is a minor problem, with absolutely minor consequences.”

More silence.

“I am limited in what I can do, you know that. I can’t just heave-hoe it out the door, like trash,” Ichabod reminded the other entity. But then he thought about it for a moment. “Can I? Would that work?”

The butterfly stared at him.

“Of course, even if it did, it wouldn’t actually solve my problem. In trying to give him an opportunity to fix things, I just broke everything in new and interesting ways.” He looked down at Buck, where his empty little head had been laying on the dusty pavement ever since that very first night. “Woops.”

Healing

Chapter Notes

Well that episode was disappointing in many ways. To heal, I'm giving you an update a couple hours early.

Buck was finding that being shot in the shoulder was a lot like getting his leg crushed, but far more inconvenient. Like with his leg, it came with the constant ache of bone and muscle knitting back together, barely dulled by the painkillers he was on. There was some minor nerve damage, too, which was to be expected when having a large caliber bullet explode through him. Honestly, it was a miracle he could even use his hand. Not that he was supposed to.

That was the most inconvenient part of this injury, compared to his leg. If someone gave him the choice of suffering either one of these injuries again, he’d lay down beside the truck and tell them to get on with it. Because this? This was unbearable. At least with his leg, after he hopped and limped and shuffled to where he needed to go, he had the use of both his hands for whatever he needed to do.

And to make matters even worse, it was his dominant hand! He was stuck trying to fumble through everything with his left hand, and only his left hand, which meant that he really couldn’t do anything at first. Sure, when he was a kid he was stuck in situations very similar to this, but an arm in a cast was still far more mobile than an arm in a sling. His lone attempt at cooking breakfast one morning ended with five eggs on the floor and him irritably tossing the mixing bowl into the sink.

At least he could still wipe his own ass. He thought he might just throw in the towel if he couldn’t even do that.

A lot of things he needed help with were just embarrassing, too. Like, leagues above what he needed help with concerning his leg. With that, once he got the cast covered up and was settled in the tub, he could wash everything just fine. But since he was down to one arm, he needed help with everything. Washing his hair was the least of it, and having someone else’s fingers going through it was relaxing, but beyond that? If Eddie hadn’t already seen, felt, and tasted everywhere he now needed help reaching, Buck would have combusted in embarrassment that very first shower.

He couldn’t help but wonder, sometimes, who helped Edmundo with all these things that Buck hadn’t even thought about beforehand. Had it been Carla, with her no-nonsense nurse training? Or had it been Ana?

(Buck tried to crush any and all feelings of jealousy at the thought of Ana doing these things for Edmundo. That man wasn’t his, not then and not now. Especially not now, not when he had abandoned him.)

And Eddie, blessed Eddie, was just so very patient with him through it all. He was patient with him when ‘I can make dinner’ turned into mopping up the floor and ‘maybe we should just order something.’ He was patient when ‘I can shave myself’ became ‘Jesus Christ just get this off my face, Eds.’ He was patient when Buck’s insistence that he could wash his own back turned into him just handing Eddie the loofa with a sigh and turning around.

Pepa hadn’t been wrong, that very first time he met her, when she called her nephew a saint.

Sometimes, a lot of times, the insecurities that lurked in his thoughts tried to come out and tear into everything. The insecurities tried to point out how his parents had done this very same thing, before worry became exasperation became anger became disinterest. They tried to point out that, once again, he had hurt himself and was being shown love and care, because the only times he was shown love and care was when he was hurt. Except it was all complete and utter bullshit, and Buck didn’t need a therapist to point it out to him.

He knew, he knew, he knew that Eddie wouldn’t stop showing him how much he cared after he healed. He knew, he knew, he knew that Eddie wasn’t showering him with adoration just because he was hurt.

With his parents, everything they’d done when he was hurt was tainted by guilt and their own pain. In those moments when he was bloodied or bruised or bleeding, they weren’t really caring for him, or at least his mother wasn’t. He was just a stand-in for Daniel, and they were soothing their own guilt for what they couldn’t do for their wanted son by soothing the hurts of the son they had gotten stuck with.

With Eddie, the only guilt that was there was the guilt one would always have, if they watched someone they loved get hurt and could do nothing to stop it. But he wasn’t doing it because he felt guilty. He wasn’t doing it because he felt obligated. He was doing it because he could, because he cared, because Buck needed him.

But just because Buck didn’t need a therapist to keep his insecurities at bay, didn’t mean he wasn’t being forced into seeing one, anyway.

A month after being discharged at the hospital, when healing was no longer leaving him feeling constantly exhausted, Eddie came home from work and told him,

“We have an appointment at Three on Monday, with Dr. Underwood.”

“Do I get a say in-?”

“No.”

Underwood - quite unlike what Buck imagined, based on the name - was an older gentleman of Southeast Asian descent. That first day, at 3pm exactly, Eddie herded him into the office and practically shoved him onto the couch. And then, after introductions were over, pointed at Buck and said,

“This motherfucker-”

“Eds!”

“This motherfucker got shot and told me it was ‘better this way.’”

Underwood turned kind, gentle eyes to him and said,

“Buck?”

“Yes…?”

“Why would you think that?”

“Because it’s true.”

That was not an acceptable answer, judging from the strangled noise Eddie let out.

Therapy this go around was not going to be an enjoyable experience, Buck could already tell.

In between appointments with Underwood and his rehab to get his arm back in working order, trips to the zoo with Chris became their own form of therapy. Sometimes Eddie would go with them, sometimes it was Shannon, or Carla, or Pepa and Abuela, but often Buck and Chris would take an uber on their own. When it was just the two of them, they never saw much of the zoo at any one time. With an arm out of commission, Buck couldn’t pick him up and carry him when he got tired or his legs began to hurt. So, as a compromise, they would spend most of the trip sitting on a bench and watching one group of animals for hours at a stretch.

And a lot of that time was spent talking.

This Chris wasn’t the other Chris. This Chris still had all of his parental figures, alive and mostly intact. But that didn’t mean that he was okay. Just because Shannon was still alive, just because Eddie hadn’t been the one shot, didn’t mean that the anxieties that haunted the other Chris weren’t starting to plague this one. Because they were.

While Eddie wasn’t quite - wasn’t nearly - as bad as Edmundo had been, when it came to compartmentalizing and pretending everything was okay, he still did it. Yes, he had done a complete one-eighty about things and was opening up in therapy about everything like he was being paid to do it, which Buck would love to know what led to that sudden development. But Chris had spent years in Texas soaking up Ramon’s particular ideas on manliness, and then years after trying to emulate his father, and that wasn’t undone in a single month.

Chris, the other Chris, had comforted him when Edmundo had been shot. The other Chris had taken everything that happened to him, everything he was afraid of, and compacted it down until it reached nuclear fission and exploded. And then he did it again. While they had, through some miracle, managed to avoid the blow-ups this time around, Buck didn’t trust it.

So, in between looking up facts on his phone about cassowaries or alpacas or tortoises, they would sit and they would talk. They would talk about how happy he was, to be able to see his Abuela and Carla again. They would talk about how scary it had been, to have the world suddenly upended and their lives so isolated for so long. They would talk about the nightmares they both still had of the tsunami.

They would talk about how angry Chris had been with him, after the letter.

“It felt like you were leaving me, too,” he said, and Buck’s heart broke. 

“Like your mom did, when she moved away?”

“Yeah. And Carla, and Abuela.”

“But they came back, and I didn’t go away, see?” Buck said. He reached out with his good arm and dragged him in for a sideways hug. “You’re my kid, Chris, and I love you so much. I’m never going to leave you, not if I can help it.”

“Promise?”

(“Don’t make promises you can’t keep, Mads.”)

“Promise,” he whispered, and prayed he could keep it.

“I wasn’t really expecting anyone,” Maddie said, awkwardly bouncing Jee-Yun on her knee.

“Well, Buck and Chris are having one of their days at the zoo, and Eddie’s working,” Shannon said, looking around the apartment. “I just decided to stop by, see how you were doing.”

“We’re doing fine,” Maddie said, smiling at her. Or, Shannon assumed it was supposed to be a smile. It looked more like a grimace, honestly.

“Are you sure?” she asked. “You look… Tired.”

That was an understatement. Maddie looked worn down. She could recognize, she thought, from that awful time with Chris, when she was stuck trying to raise him on her own with her in-laws circling like sharks. She imagined that if she looked at the other woman close enough, she could see the fractures starting to form beneath the surface.

Shannon had known she was breaking, had asked and begged and shouted for support, only to get nothing. In hindsight, she could see how Eddie had been breaking just the same, but at the time…

“Oh, no, we’re just… Still getting adjusted,” Maddie said, the smile remaining fixed. Shannon hummed in acknowledgement. This many months on, she thought things should be settling into a routine, but she supposed she really only had Chris to base her preconceptions on, and he had not been routine. Looking around, she noticed a familiar envelope sitting out on one of the end tables, still unopened.

“Is this the letter Buck wrote for you?” Shannon asked, pointing at it.

“Yeah, I haven’t gotten around to reading it yet,” Maddie said, glancing at it.

“Why not? It’s been weeks now.”

“At first, it felt like admitting it was goodbye, y’know? And then I figured, if it was important enough, he’d tell me.”

“Chris keeps his under his pillow,” Shannon told her, smiling fondly as she thought about it. “I don’t know if he reads it every night, but he quotes part of it. Whenever Eddie and Buck come back from therapy upset.”

“Eddie and Buck are going to therapy?”

“Yeah, apparently Eddie pretty much bullied him into going,” she said, giggling to herself about it. “But whenever they come back upset, he tells them… It’s okay to not be okay.”

She picked up the letter and held it out to Maddie.

“Read it,” Shannon told her. “Sometimes, it’s easier to put the really important words to print. I don’t know what he could have put in this letter, but the ones he wrote for Chris and Eddie were very, very important to him.”

Maddie took it and frowned at it silently, still not making any move to open it.

“And Maddie? It’s okay to not be okay.”

Surprises

Sometime in the weeks between getting the sling off and going through the steps to go back to work, Buck realized that he had basically moved in with the Diazes. He had more clothes in Eddie’s closet by this point than he probably had left at the apartment, though he didn’t really remember bringing so many of them over. Obviously he must have, because they were right there, clear as day. And both pairs of his sneakers had migrated to be next to the Diazes’, along with his work boots. And his hiking boots, which he could have sworn he saw by the door of the apartment when leaving the morning of the shooting.

Hadn’t he?

Obviously not, because they were mocking him from next to Eddie’s own hiking boots.

The idea of moving in with Eddie wasn’t exactly an appalling one. Hell, even before getting shot, he spent more nights at Casa de Diaz than his own place, and hadn’t stepped foot inside the apartment since he got shot. It was just that, he hadn’t meant to. Just like he hadn’t meant to basically move in with Abby, either, or for Taylor to basically move in with him.

Was he, perhaps, repeating the same mistakes?

This wasn’t the same, right? Those two, he’d done it too quickly, over a matter of months, if not mere weeks. This, with Eddie, had taken actual years. So no, he wasn’t repeating the exact same mistakes. But he did need to talk with him, and make sure he was okay with it, make sure they were both on the same page.

(The importance of communicating with each other had become a prominent theme in their sessions with Dr. Underwood. Buck personally hadn’t thought they had a problem with talking, but Edie had been insistent upon it.)

Eventually, after thinking it over, he realized he also had to talk to Albert. On a day while Eddie was still at work, and Chris was with his mother, he decided to surprise the younger man after he was done with his course at the fire academy. Grabbing his keys off the hook by the door, and putting on his shoes - no, seriously, hadn’t he left this pair at his place? - he headed for his jeep, which he could now blessedly drive himself. On the way, he stopped for pizzas, because he remembered how hungry he was after some of the courses.

“I brought food!” Buck announced himself, walking through the door with his eyes closed. “Is it safe to open my eyes?”

“Why would it not be safe to open your eyes?” Albert asked from the direction of his couch, sounding tired.

“Hey, I was young once,” he joked, cautiously peeking. The living room was honestly cleaner than he was expecting, which wasn’t to say it was clean. Albert, even now, had difficulties staying on the ball when it came to chores. He’d gotten better, though.

Albert himself was sprawled across the couch, looking wiped out. He moaned and made grabby hands for the pizza.

“Please tell me one of those is just for me,” he said, causing Buck to snort in amusement as he cleared a spot on the coffee table to set the boxes down. Immediately, Albert found a new well of energy to lunge for the top one like a starving animal, practically inhaling a whole slice, and then another.

“So, academy courses kicking your ass?”

“I ache, Buck,” Albert whined between mouthfuls. “Everywhere.”

“I always liked those days more than the ones sitting in a classroom,” Buck said, carefully reaching for his own slice and hoping he didn’t lose a hand. He was only just starting to be able to use it again, damn it. “But it’ll pass.”

They sat in silence, Buck watching in amusement as Albert finished off the first pizza and started on the second. Eventually, he started to wane, sitting back against the couch again in contentment.

“Marry me,” he said, and then burped in a way that Buck was certain would be very attractive to someone, somewhere, statistically speaking.

“Yeah, no,” he said, shaking his head. “You’re pretty, but Eddie’s prettier.”

“Damn.” The other man sighed in mock disappointment.

“So, I wanted to talk to you about something, since it affects you,” Buck said, trying to decide how best to approach the topic. He needed to do it quickly, too, because Albert didn’t seem like he would be staying awake for much longer. “I know I haven’t really been here in the last couple of months…”

“You’re officially moving in with Eddie.”

“Well… Yeah. I was thinking about it, but I haven't talked to him about it yet.”

“You haven’t?” Albert sat up, blinking in confusion. “He’s been coming here every week to grab your things.”

“I’m sorry, my boyfriend’s been doing what?”

“Yeah, he came over after he got off work the other day, I think? Grabbed some of your clothes and whatever, and left again.”

Buck was flabbergasted, and could feel his jaw literally hanging open. How long, precisely, had his boyfriend been doing this behind his back? How had he been doing it, without him noticing?

“I was at the zoo with Chris the other day,” he realized. “Que care-chimba. I knew I left these shoes and my boots here!”

“Did… Did you not know?”

“No! Here I was, worrying that I was practically moving in with him without talking to him about it first, and he was going behind my back to do it for me.” He could not believe this. “He spends every other session with Underwood preaching about communication, and here he is, not even talking to me about this. Jesus Christ, I love the idiot.”

“How did you manage to make that sound so…” Albert trailed off.

“So?”

“So heartfelt and frustrated at the same time.”

“Eddie. Eddie is how.” He let out a sigh. “So, clearly you’re okay with this. You are, right?”

“I am worried about the rent,” the younger man admitted.

“Don’t worry about it,” Buck said, waving off the concern. “I’ll keep covering it until you have a station and start getting that paycheck. I know for a fact you can afford this place on a first-year salary.”

“Are you certain?” Albert asked, looking unsure.

“Positive.” He wasn’t exactly hurting for money, after the treasure hunt. He wondered how Harcourt’s assistant was doing with his cut, after absconding with it to the Maldives. “We’ll see about switching the lease over to you after then. In the meanwhile… I guess we’ll talk about which of the kitchen appliances I’m taking with me.”

“I’m keeping the coffee maker,” Albert immediately declared.

Buck only stayed for another hour or so, divvying up what he wanted to move to Eddie’s and what Albert could keep. Honestly, he was only taking what was in his room and most of the kitchenware, along with everything he had panic-bought after he realized ghosts could very well be a thing.

A few hours later, as Eddie stumbled through the door and into the darkened living room of the house, Buck flicked on the lamp as dramatically as possible. His boyfriend screeched, and then clutched at his chest, because he was equally as dramatic.

“Hostia puta,” he swore. “What the hell, Buck?”

“I went over to the apartment today. Had a very lovely chat with Albert,” he said, steepling his fingers. If they had a cat, he would absolutely be stroking its fur, like a villain in one of those over-hyped spy movies that Chimney kept trying to get him to watch. “He told me something… Very interesting.’

“Oh?” His boyfriend tried to sound disinterested as he took off his shoes, but by the stiffness of his shoulders, Buck could tell he knew that he knew.

“You know, you could have just asked me.”

“I have no idea what you’re talking about.”

“Communication is important, Buck,” he mocked. “We should talk about things before they fester, Buck.”

“Okay, there’s no need for that tone,” Eddie scolded, turning on his Dad Voice. “And I was going to talk to you…”

“When? Before or after I woke up to you trying to switch the mattresses out from beneath me?”

“Dios, you’re dramatic,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes, but he was smiling. “I think I see where Chris gets it from, now.”

“Oh, no, that boy’s flare for drama is all Diaz,” he refuted. “I just helped him refine it. So, are you going to ask?”

“Do I really ne-?”

“Damn it, Eddie.”

His boyfriend huffed.

“Will you move in with me?” he asked dutifully.

“Mmmm, say please.”

“What?”

“Say please.”

Eddie rolled his eyes again.

“Please move in with me.”

“Now say pretty please.”

“Dios mío, eres un niño,” his boyfriend muttered. “Will you pretty please move in with me?”

“With a cherry on top.”

“With a-? Buck, just say yes.”

“Fine, ruin my fun,” he sighed. “Yes, I’ll move in with you, you drama queen.”

“Jesucristo,” Eddie grumbled, flicking him in the ear as he walked past. “I’m brushing my teeth and going to bed.”

“Love you!” Buck called after him.

“Love you, too,” the other man said. “Don’t know why, sometimes…”

“Are we being pranked?” Chimney asked, cresting the stairs to the loft. “I feel like we’re being pranked.”

“You’re hilarious,” Eddie grumbled, keeping his back to him and ducking his head, staying focused on the pans in front of him.
