He wasn’t certain how, precisely, his boyfriend managed to convince him to do this. Alright, okay, that was a lie. There were a lot of puppy dog eyes involved, and pouting.

“Buckaroo!” Hen cried, joining them herself. “What are you doing here? You’re not back yet, are you?”

“Not yet,” Buck said, from where he was perched on a stool by the counter. “I decided to surprise you all.”

“His babysitter was busy today,” Eddie remarked, turning his head to smile at him.

“He’s ten, I watch him.”

“Do you, though? Do you really?”

“I don’t have to put up with this,” Buck sniffed. “Where’s probie? I’ll go bother him.”

“Ravi’s busy,” Bobby said, from where he’d been standing over Eddie’s shoulder, watching everything he was doing. “So no, you may not.”

“What, exactly, is going on here?” Chimney interrupted, reaching the end of his patience. “Is he really cooking?”

“Yes he is!” Buck said, sounding inordinately proud of that fact, and hearing it had Eddie trying to hide a pleased smile from the others. Based on Bobby’s own smile, he wasn’t entirely successful. “When I still had the sling on and couldn’t do anything, I got tired of take-out whenever we ran out of Abuela’s meals. So I made Eddie learn how to do more than whatever came out of a box.”

“And uh, how did that go?”

“Surprisingly well.”

“I am actually capable of cooking,” Eddie said, turning off the stove. “Chris and I were doing just fine before we met you.”

“It’s cute you think that,” Buck said, laughing as he dodged a swipe from his boyfriend. From where he stood beside them, Bobby let out a loud sigh.

“Go help set the table,” he ordered.

A few minutes later, Eddie found himself sitting next to a widely grinning Buck while everyone else was quickly clearing their plates, throwing compliments between mouthfuls. He felt good about what he managed to do, felt proud for exceeding their (very low) expectations. But he wasn’t going to actually admit to that.

“Put that face away,” he said, poking at Buck’s cheek.

“You like this face,” the other man said, grabbing at his finger and kissing the back of his hand. 

“I do.”

“Cap! They’re doing it again!” Chimney complained.

“Not at the dinner table,” Bobby said, and Buck rolled his eyes.

“Yes, Cap.”

Dreaming of Guilt

Chapter Notes

warning: unpleasant imagery ahead

See the end of the chapter for more notes

“I’m leaving the One-Eighteen,” Eddie announced, hands clasped behind his back and shoulders straight, like he was back in the army and giving a report to a superior officer. And Buck just… He couldn’t. He couldn’t handle this. He couldn’t handle Eddie leaving him like everyone else had left him. So he turned on his heel, dropping the Santa hat he’d been strangling to the ground, and headed for his jeep.

“Why did you leave?” Eddie’s voice stopped him in his tracks, like hooks catching and digging into his skin. “You left me. You left us. We needed you and you just left.”

It was the pain in the other man’s voice that had Buck turning. He didn’t want to look, didn’t want to see. But he couldn’t help it, couldn’t resist it. The love of his life was hurting, and it was his fault.

“You left,” Eddie said again. “I needed you to have my back, and you left.”

Everyone else was gone, and it was just the two of them.

“I- I’m sorry,” Buck said. “I was… I was afraid.”

“You can come back with me now,” the other man said, reaching out for him. And Buck, he tried to grab his hand, but his fingers went straight through. “If you wanted.”

“I can’t,” he cried.

“You could if you wanted to,” Eddie said, and suddenly he was in his uniform. Or had he always been in his uniform? There was a hole in his shoulder, like a blooming rose pinned to his uniform shirt, and he was falling to the ground. Buck ran to his side on instinct, dropping to his knees to put pressure on the wound.

But his hands kept going through.

“I’m sorry,” he kept saying, over and over and over, praying for Eddie to believe him. “I’m sorry.”

“You ran away.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I needed you to have my back.”

“I’m so sorry.”

“Evan, please…”

“Buck keeps having nightmares,” Eddie confessed to Bobby, the shift before Buck was scheduled to return to work.

“Are they about the shooting?” the captain asked, and he shook his head.

“Most of them are, yeah. We’ve been talking about those nightmares, together at home and with Dr. Underwood,” Eddie said. “We both have nightmares about it. But those aren’t the ones that worry me.”

More than once, Eddie had woken up to his boyfriend crying in his sleep, tears leaving wet trails down his cheeks to soak the pillow. Whenever he woke him up, he’d be gasping out apologies, and then refuse to explain what he was apologizing for if Eddie asked. And then, Buck would go through the day as if the nightmare, or whatever it was, had never happened.

That wasn’t to imply that Buck was okay during the day, far from it. Whatever was bothering his boyfriend at night was obviously haunting him in the sunlight. Several, several times Eddie had turned to find Buck watching him with an expression of guilt on his face, only to have it be wiped away a moment later.

Sometimes, he missed the nights he would wake up to Buck obsessively scrubbing his hands clean, because at least then he had known what he was dealing with.

“Do you have any idea what they could be about?” Bobby asked, drawing him back out of his thoughts.

“Not a damn clue. And that worries the hell out of me, because the last time something was bothering him and he refused to talk about it, he nearly died.”

“It is a concerning pattern of his,” his captain agreed.

“You might want to check the black tent,” the faceless volunteer suggested, sounding tired and apologetic. Beside him, Eddie let out a noise like he’d been punched in the stomach.

Buck didn’t want to check the black tent, he knew what he would find in the black tent. He wasn’t sure how he knew what he’d find there, but he did. He didn’t want to go in there, and he definitely didn’t want Eddie to go in there. Except the man was as stubborn as him, perhaps even more so, and refused to be sidelined now.

“I have to make sure,” he said, and Buck could do nothing but walk into that hell beside him.

Inside, as far the eye could see, were rows upon rows upon rows of bodies beneath white sheets.

“We- We should go look for him elsewhere,” Buck said, despite knowing they wouldn’t find him elsewhere.

“Are you running away again?” Eddie asked, not looking at him, eyes fixed on the motionless mounds of sheets before them. “I need you.”

“No, no, of course not,” he hurried to say, wincing as someone in that infinite space cried out in horror and loss. It sounded like Eddie. “I’m here, of course I’m here. I’ll always be here.”

“For now,” the other man said, before stepping to the first body and lifting the sheet off to uncover the person’s face. Buck gagged at the sight of it, their head smashed to pieces. Eddie didn’t even blink at it, simply moved to the next one and uncovered it, revealing an overly cooked face, red and covered in blisters.

The next one had Buck screaming.

It was his face, his skin pale with blue lips, staring up at him with glazed over eyes. The next one Eddie uncovered, the one that was clearly missing their leg beneath the sheet, was also him. And the next one, and the next, and the next. Each time Eddie pulled off the sheet and didn’t even blink, didn’t even react, didn’t even pause before moving to the next covered body.

The eighth body was so very small beneath its sheet, and Buck reached out and grabbed Eddie’s arm before he could uncover it.

“Don’t,” he begged. “Please.”

“I have to,” Eddie said, reaching down and pulling the cover off, before collapsing to his knees like a puppet with its strings cut.

Chris stared blankly up at them, chest still and skin pale. His glasses were missing, and his shirt was torn. There were cuts and scrapes all over his face, wounds that would never bleed and never heal.

“I wish I could forget,” the boy said, sitting up.

“Forget what?” Buck asked the corpse.

“People go away,” Chris said, turning his empty gaze on him. “They leave and then I miss them. I don’t want to miss anyone else.”

“Yeah, people go away,” Buck said. “And it’s sad, and it hurts. But not everyone goes away forever. Sometimes they come back, and as much as we miss them, that’s how happy we are to see them again. Your grandma, your friends, Carla. You’re gonna see them all again.”

“Do you promise?”

“I do. And until that happens, you still got me. ‘Cause I’m not going anywhere.”

“But you did,” Chris’ corpse said. “You left and you didn’t come back.”

Buck felt something wet trailing down his arm, and he looked down to see he was bleeding. He pushed back the sleeve of his uniform to reveal a long gash, from wrist to elbow, absolutely pouring with blood.

“I lost everything,” Eddie said, breaking his silence. “I lost everything and then you left, too.”

“I didn’t mean to,” Buck said, begging for them to understand. “I didn’t know. I was just- I was just trying to fix everything, I swear.”

“But you didn’t fix anything.”

“You left,” Chris said, empty eyes accusing. “I was scared and you left.”

“I didn’t mean to, I swear,” Buck cried. “I just wanted to fix everything, I just wanted to make everything better.”

“Maybe this isn’t something you can fix,” Eddie said. “But you didn’t even try, did you? You just ran away.”

“I- I panicked, I didn’t mean to…”

“But you did,” he said, grabbing and holding up Buck’s bleeding arm. “You meant to.”

“You promised you weren’t going anywhere,” Chris said. “But you left. Dad told you I was scared and you left.”

“It wasn’t better,” Eddie said.

“I’m sorry,” Buck said. “I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’m so sorry…”

Eddie frowned down at his boyfriend, who was once again crying in his sleep. It had been two weeks since Buck’s return to work, two weeks since his conversation with Bobby, and he still had absolutely no idea what to do. Things were not getting better, and were indeed perhaps getting worse, because these particular nightmares were becoming more and more common as time went on.

“I wish you’d tell me what was going on,” he whispered, wiping away the tears with his thumb.

“I’m sorry,” Buck gasped out, blinking his eyes open. “W- What? Eds?”

“I said I wish you’d tell me what was going on,” he repeated. “You were crying again.”

“Was I?” His boyfriend reached up, wiping away at his eyes. “I didn’t wake you, did I?”

“No, I was already awake,” he told him. He wasn’t getting much sleep himself, these days, constantly worried about whatever was going on with the other man. “You can tell me, y’know. Whatever this is, whatever’s going on. You can tell me.”

“I- I- Nothing, it’s nothing,” Buck said, shaking his head. “Seriously, Eds. Everything’s fine. Just… Nightmares.”

“These nightmares are new,” Eddie pointed out. “I’ve seen you have nightmares before, and none of them had you crying in your sleep.”

“Seriously, love, it’s fine, it’s nothing. Just… You know I’d never leave you, right? You and Chris? You know if I had the choice, I’d never leave you?”

“Of course I do,” Eddie said, because it was a fact of his life. The sun would rise in the morning, the ocean was salty and wet, and Buck would never leave them unless forced to leave. And even then, he would claw his way back. “Is that what the dreams are about? People leaving?”

“Sure,” his boyfriend hedged, swinging his legs over the edge of the bed and standing. “I’m gonna wash my face and then check on Chris. I’ll be right back, I promise.”

“Alright,” Eddie said, letting him go.

This was definitely getting worse, he was realizing. This could not be allowed to continue, except he had no idea how to get it to stop. The sessions with Underwood were helping them both, or at least he had thought they were. They had talked about the shooting, they had talked about Buck’s abysmal sense of self-worth, and they had talked about how Eddie had felt after it happened. And then, when they had run that topic to the ground, they talked about the things that had happened before. 

Eddie had done everything he could to keep from becoming that broken man he saw at Ichabod’s crossroads, no matter how unpleasant and violating it felt to open up about his emotions to anyone. He had been adamant in his refusal to let their traumas fester until they broke them, but clearly he had missed something.

If only he could figure out the right words to make Buck talk to him about it.

Chapter End Notes

So my computer is currently on its last leg, kept going with nothing but a hope and a prayer. So updates might stop, for a couple days or more, until I get a new one. Hopefully, this one will keep chugging on until its replacement is here, but...

Not All Butterfly Effects Are Bad

Two weeks after Buck returned to work, towards the end of the month, the ransomware attack began. It started, as before, with random alerts to their phones: a tsunami alert to Buck, an earthquake for Bobby, a mudslide for Eddie. To cap it off, Hen’s begun dialing 9-1-1 automatically.

“Okay, I realize you probably weren’t serious,” Eddie said, after the call to the conga line of cars all waiting their turn to drive into the canal. “But were you serious? About the, uh…” He glanced about the station, making sure no one was around to hear him. “The barcode thing?”

 “This isn’t how the robot revolution starts, Eds,” Buck said, patting him on the shoulder. “But this is only going to get worse.”

He seriously regretted not buying a generator for the house, but with recovering from being shot and the nightmares and his ever present worry about Maddie, it had entirely slipped his mind. It meant that, after their shift, he spent the evening going through all the perishables in the fridge while Eddie watched him, frowning.

“I’m not even going to ask,” his boyfriend said, shaking his head and walking away.

“Probably for the best,” he called after him, trying to decide what he could make out of everything before the power was cut and it all went bad. As he did so, he debated calling his sister. He had been calling her regularly, almost every other day now, the closer they got to October. And now he was worried that he was bothering her too much, that he was being overbearing and pushing her away.

What was he going to do, when the black out hit? He couldn’t call in just to stay with Maddie, not when it was going to be an all hands on deck situation. Obviously Chimney wasn’t even able to beg off, or else he would have been there to help Maddie in the first place.

Right? Right.

Ichabod had suggested that he had already done something to change things with Maddie, but Buck had no clue what that could be. Was it the letter he had written for her, prior to being shot? Because so far, that didn’t seem to have done anything. His sister still wasn’t talking to anyone except Chimney about her mental health, and Chimney himself wasn’t talking to anyone about it, either.

Just like when she was with Doug, he couldn’t force his sister to accept his help, or even admit that she needed help. Her wagons were circled, and his options were limited to telling her that was a safe space to land or barreling right through everything, perhaps risking sending her running even faster and farther.

He refused, he absolutely refused, to accept that this was a thing he could not change. But there wasn’t any bullet to jump in front of, any car to keep from hitting her. There was just her and her demons, and he knew exactly how dangerous those could be.

Buck was still struggling with what he could and should do through the call to the airport for the heart attack and subsequent panic attacks, and then to the hospital where they spent time helping out before things went fully out of control. When the lights went out in the city, he could almost hear the warning klaxon going off in his head, telling him that he was out of time.

And then, a couple hours later, he got a text that filled him with such relief he collapsed against his boyfriend.

“Oh, it’s okay baby, don’t cry,” Maddie was practically begging, bouncing an upset Jee-Yun in her arm as she searched the apartment for candles. She was stuck doing it all with a baby in one hand and a small flashlight in the other. Her phone was on power-save mode, because she didn’t know how long this black out would last. This flashlight had, so far, been the only thing she had managed to find. “Just bear with me, honey. Please? Just a little bit?”

She was in need of a diaper change, but that would have to wait until they had something a bit better than a cheap dollar store flashlight to see by. There was a lantern somewhere, and candles. She knew there was. So where was it?

The sound of knocking at her door startled her, and that in turn set off Jee-Yun into more crying.

“Hold on!” she yelled out, extracting herself from the cupboard and cursing as she bumped her head. “I’m coming!”

Carefully making her way through the dark with the weak light to guide her, she unlocked and opened the door one handed. She was still blinking around the spots in her eyes from when she accidentally blinded herself when she realized who was on the other side.

“Shannon, Chris, what are you…?”

“We were on the way back from getting McDonalds for Superman here - don’t tell his fathers,” Shannon raised a finger to her lips and winked, making Chris giggle. “When the black out hit.”

“Aunt Maddie, I could see so many stars,” Chris said, sounding awed. “Like when Buck took me and dad to the planetarium.”

“So many stars,” his mother agreed, stepping past Maddie and into the darkened apartment. “And then you didn’t text me back, when I asked if you were okay.”

“Sorry, I’ve been…”

“No, no, Maddie, it’s okay,” Shannon assured her. She reached out a finger to tickle Jee-Yun’s chin. The little girl had settled into wet hiccups, apparently more interested in the new guests than in letting everyone in the building know about her displeasure. “Did the dark scare our little princess?”

“She needs her diaper changed,” Maddie said, adjusting her daughter. “But I can’t see anything, and I can’t find our lantern or our candles. I think Buck might have thrown those out in his baby proofing crusade.”

“Did he think she was going to try lighting one herself and set the building on fire?”

“I don’t know. He put childproof locks on the top cabinets, too.”

“Okay, well. How can I help?” Shannon asked, looking at her expectantly. Or Maddie thought she was, it was hard to tell with the little light they had available.

“What?”

“I’m here, she needs a diaper change, and I am willing to help,” she said, like it was the most obvious thing in the world. “Do you want me to hold the light or…?”

“I- No, Shannon, you don’t need to-”

“Need has nothing to do with it, Maddie.”

She didn’t say anything for a moment, struggling with herself. She needed help, she knew she needed help, she just couldn’t quite get the words out. She felt like such a failure already, struggling with Jee-Yun like she had been. She felt like she was repeating her own mother’s mistakes, doomed to make her daughter resent her like Buck resented Margaret.

(There is no shame in asking for help…)

“Actually, could you… Could you hold the light for me? Her changing table is right over here, with diapers and wipes,” Maddie said, trying to quash the shame that threatened to overwhelm her. “I just need… I just need a little help, seeing what I’m doing.”

“Of course,” Shannon said, smiling gently as she took the flashlight from her.

It was quite easy after that, to get Jee-Yun in a clean diaper and in clean clothes. Remarkably easy, shockingly easy. But she shouldn’t have needed help, she should have been able to manage this on her own. God, she was such a-

“I was thinking,” Shannon said, interrupting her spiral. “We have no idea how long this is going to last, right? And something this chaotic, there’s no way Chimney will be able to come home anytime soon, right?”

“Right…” Maddie said, not quite seeing where the other woman was heading with this.

“And I remember how difficult it could be at times, taking care of an infant when your partner is away for ages at a time,” she continued, and Maddie immediately wanted to interrupt and say that this wasn’t the same. But it kinda was, wasn’t it? “So, why don’t you and Jee come stay with me and Chris?”

“W- What?”

“C’mon, it’ll be fun. A little vacation, almost. Except without the mimosas and the cabana boys, and with an infant and a pre-teen.” Shannon paused for a moment. “Alright, so not the most exciting vacation, but still. And even better, I’ll be there to watch her for you if you need to take a nap or, I don’t know. Go scream at the stars.”

“Scream at the stars?”

“Oh, it’s very cathartic when your kid won’t stop crying long enough for either of you to sleep, and you’re another hour from either hallucinating God or field-kicking them across the road,” she said, and the absurdity of the statement surprised a laugh out of Maddie. “If there was one good thing - and trust me, it is only one thing - that came out of my in-laws’ hovering while Eddie was away, it’s that they were very willing to take their darling nieto for a night, any night. I think those nights were the only things that kept me from being the star of one of those Lifetime made-for-TV movies.”

“What do you mean?” Maddie asked, curious.

“Listen, I love him, and I would give up everything and anything for him,” Shannon said, lowering her voice and glancing over to where Chris was playing with her phone on the couch. “But some days? I was not joking about the field-kicking. Going for so long without any sleep with a constantly screaming child is…” She shook her head. “Things were not good some days.”

Maddie stared at her, at a complete loss for what to say. She had thought- No, she had known, on a detached and clinical level, that it wasn’t just her, that she wasn’t alone. She had known that other women had struggled the same as her, but being in the middle of it… It was like Shannon had come in at the darkest of hours and given her a light.

“Could you hold her for a bit?” she asked, quickly wiping away a stray tear. “While I go pack a bag?”

“Take your time getting whatever you need,” the other woman said, taking Jee-Yun from her. “Hey, Chris? Text Buck and tell him we’re taking Aunt Maddie to theirs.”

“Why Eddie’s?”

“Gas stove,” Shannon said. “Mine’s electric. Unless you want to be eating cold beans out of a can?”

“Not especially,” Maddie said, laughing. It was a small laugh, a quiet laugh, more of a chuckle than anything else. But it was a laugh, and it was the first time she had laughed in… She wasn’t sure how long. She wasn’t alone. For the first time in so many weeks and months, she didn’t feel alone.

She felt seen.

The black-out was as exhausting as Buck had known it was going to be, but it did nothing to stop the slight skip in his step. Knowing that Maddie and Jee-Yun were with Shannon was such a weight off his shoulders. It was like he’d been laboring through the days with a giant boulder strapped to his back, and now it was gone. That worry was still there, and probably would be until he saw Maddie for himself when this was all over, but so much of it had been lifted.

Being the Power Czar again definitely helped, because being given a clipboard always made him feel important, even if it was merely an illusion.

“After a requisition form has been submitted, you will be issued a personal charging device,” Buck recited, looking Chimney dead in the eye. “Once it's dead, you return it to the probie charging pool and it will be recharged for you.”

“You can just say Ravi,” Probie said, barely even sounding put out by it. “Ravi will recharge it for you.”

“One charge per twenty-four hours is the limit,” Buck continued, trying to keep his face straight. God, he had missed the probie so much. “Do not attempt to bribe me or you will be docked two charges.”

“Give me a charger,” Chimney said, leaning in and trying to be intimidating. “Or Uncle Buck won’t get to see his niece again.”

“Fill out the form,” Buck said, pushing the paper towards him, refusing to fold to the threat this time. “And you’ll get the charger.”

“Buck…”

“Chimney,” he said, using the same tone. “You’re not the only one with a partner or a kid at home that they’re worrying about, you’re just the only one refusing to fill out the form. It’s one sheet, man. C’mon.”

“Damn it Buck, just give me a charger.”

“Once you fill out the form,” he said, pulling out his phone when he felt it buzz. Grinning at the message, he ignored how Chimney grumbled and glared as he finally filled out the form. He pulled out one of the portable chargers and held it out. “Thank you. Here you go.”

“Thank you,” Chimney snapped, yanking it out of his hand.

“C’mon Ravi, my kid’s here,” Buck said, standing up and slapping the probie on the shoulder. “Come say hi.”

“You have a kid?” the probie asked as he stood to follow.

“Yup! He’s here with my sister and niece,” he said, making sure the words were loud enough for the paramedic to hear. He heard a muffled curse behind him and then Chimney ran past.

The sight that greeted him as they came around the trucks was a very welcome one. Shannon was standing next to Maddie, the former carrying a stack of tupperware while the latter was holding Jee-Yun. Eddie was already there, hugging Chris.

“Ravi, this is Chris,” Buck said, bending over and pulling the boy into a bear hug. “This is my sister Maddie and Jee-Yun, and this is Shannon, Chris’ mother.”

“Wait…” The probie was frowning in confusion, clearly trying to figure out the math problem he’d just been handed.

“Eddie’s ex-wife,” Shannon said, solving it for him. “Buck, where the hell should I put all of this at?”

“What is it?” Buck asked, putting Chris down and grabbing some of the containers. 

“Sandwiches, muffins. Some cookies,” she said. “This one is fruit salad. Chris wanted to come say hi, and I figured we might as well bring food.”

“I helped,” Chris declared.

“Bet you baked half the cookies on your own, didn’t ya?” Eddie joked, reaching over to mess up his hair. “Come on, we’ll put all of this up in the kitchen. No doubt everyone will be thankful they’ll have something other than powdered eggs to eat.”

Behind them, as they helped Shannon carry her load to the loft, Buck heard Ravi mutter to himself,

“I need a flow chart for this place…”

Bobby had been worried about Buck for… Well, perhaps for as long as he had known the young man. Nothing, absolutely nothing, that had happened in the past four years had done anything to lessen that worry, either. But that worry had only gotten worse since the shooting - since he let himself be shot, according to Eddie, God help them all - and it had especially increased since Eddie had confided in him about Buck’s nightmares.

Something was clearly bothering him, had been bothering him for months now. And even though something had happened that first night of the black out to make him stand a bit straighter and smile a bit brighter, there was still a haunted look in the back of his eyes. A guilty look.

It wasn’t like the young man was ever very forthright with whatever was bothering him. For as much as Buck was so open, he could be just as closed off. So Bobby was completely expecting to continue not having a clue what was bothering the young man until the next disaster was rearing its head and he was coming in with either a warning or some new way to get himself hurt in place of them.

What he wasn’t expecting was to enter the captain’s office in the middle of night five and find him waiting for him.

“Buck, is everything alright?” he asked, easing around his desk to sit down. It was almost pitch black in the room, the lantern he’d commandeered turned off to save power, but he could see the shape of the other man well enough.

“Yeah,” the young man said, and then shook his head. “No. I… Can I ask you something? Something personal?”

“Of course,” Bobby said.

“If you could, if you were given the choice, would you…” Buck trailed off, shaking his head again. “No, sorry, that isn’t… I’ll leave you alone.”

“No, Buck. What is it? What did you want to ask?”

“Would you… If you could… If you had the chance to be with Marcy and the kids again, would you?”

“In a heartbeat,” Bobby said immediately, not even taking a second to think about it.

“Even if it meant abandoning Athena and them?”

“I…” That threw him for a loop. Would he leave Athena and Harry and May, if it meant he could be with Marcy and the kids again? Four years ago, it wouldn’t have even been a question. But now? “I don’t know. But I don’t have to know. They’re gone, and…”

“What if they weren’t, though?” Buck whispering. “What if it was you that was gone?”

“Buck, what is this about?” Bobby asked, reaching over and flicking on the lantern. In the light of it, he could see tear stains on the other man’s face, and he immediately stood to be by his side. “What’s going on?”

“They’re still there,” he whispered. “Eddie and Chris and the others, they’re still there.”

“Of course, Eddie is-”

“No, not him, the… Edmundo, and the others, they… I woke up here and I thought they were all gone. I thought I’d lost all of you, that I’d lost them, forever. I thought… I thought I was just right back at the start, but I… I wasn’t…”

“What are you talking about, Buck?” Bobby asked, grabbing him by the shoulders. The words weren’t quite making sense to his ears.

“They’re still there,” Buck said again. “I left them. I abandoned them. I told Chris I wouldn’t leave him, I told Eddie I’d have his back, but I… I left them… And then he… He asked me to come back with him, and I- I couldn’t, but I- I don’t know what to do.”

Buck looked up at him, fresh tears streaming.

“Cap, what do I do?”

The Morning After

Athena sighed with relief as she stepped into her house. After a week of black out inspired madness, power and light had finally been restored to the city, and she was finally able to come home and sleep for the next week. Thankfully, it looked as if her oaf of an ex-husband had cleaned up after the house party- sorry, the neighborly gathering that he’d held here. There was no need to contemplate maiming the man, then.

(She decided it was David’s good influence at work.)

“Bobby, baby, you still up?” she called out, tiredly stomping down the stairs. She had seen his car in the driveway, so she knew he was home.

“In the kitchen,” he called out to her, and she shuffled her way to him. Bobby was sitting at the dining table, a mug clutched in his hands. He was staring down at it, but wasn’t making any moves to drink it. When Athena made it to his side, she could see it was still full.

“What’s the damage?” she asked him, gesturing at the fridge and pantry. “Please tell me Michael didn’t grill those steaks.”

“I haven’t looked yet,” Bobby said, not looking up at her. Her instincts were ringing with alarm, and she pulled out a chair to sit next to him.

“Baby, what’s wrong?” Because there was clearly something bothering her husband, based entirely on how he was just staring at his coffee like it would reveal the world’s secrets at any moment.

“Were you still willing to go to an AA meeting with me?”

“Of course, but I’m not sure there’s any going right now,” she answered. “Though there might be, you’d know better than me. But Bobby, what’s going on?”

“I think we’re going to lose Buck.”

“What!?” What did that mean? Had something happened and she’d not been told? No, no, surely Bobby would have told her if Buck had gotten hurt again. It had to be something else, then. “Are he and Eddie moving somewhere? Did he talk about transferring?”

“He asked me if I would go be with Marcy and Brooke and Junior, if I had the choice,” he said, and just hearing that sent panic racing through her nerves. “Even if it meant leaving you and Harry and May, and…” He looked up at her, and his eyes were so full of pain. “Athena, that choice would destroy me. It would tear me in two.”

“Of course it would, baby,” she said, rubbing a hand up and down his arm. She knew he still loved the family he had lost, that he still missed them and held so much guilt for that awful night. Just like she knew, with utter certainty, that Bobby loved the family he had now. There were no happy outcomes in that hypothetical, and she was selfishly happy that it would always be a hypothetical. “But why would Buck ask you something like that? He knows how much it had to hurt you.”

“Do you remember what he told us, after the tsunami?” he asked, instead of answering.

“You mean when we were certain our oldest was having a mental break?” That managed to get a subdued chuckle out of the man. “Yes, I remember. Something about a stranger at some crossroads, and then waking up on his first day at the station.”

“Apparently that time he left, it… It’s still there,” he whispered. “He could go back, if he wanted to. Or he could stay.”

“Is that what he said?” Athena asked, trying to make sure.

“It was definitely implied. I think somehow the Eddie he left… Found him somehow? Asked him to come back?” Bobby shook his head. “I don’t know, it didn’t make sense to me. Still doesn’t. But he has the choice, Athena. That awful choice, and he asked me what to do.”

“What did you tell him?”

“That I didn’t know,” he confessed, self-loathing lacing the words. “I told him that I didn’t know. What kind of useless answer is that?”

“An honest one,” she said, resting her hand on his shoulder. “Do you think he will go back?”

“I think it doesn’t matter. Either way, it… I told you, having to choose between staying with you or being with Marcy again would kill me, Athena,” Bobby said, reaching up to place his hand on hers. “No matter what he chooses, I think we’re going to lose him.”

There were no happy outcomes in this non-hypothetical, Athena was realizing. Or at least not any she could see.

Eddie was yawning as he unlocked the front door, very much looking forward to getting some time in his own bed. He wasn’t sure how likely that was, considering that at the very least, Shannon was still here. Beside him, Buck was uncharacteristically silent, but he was blaming that on their mutual exhaustion, because he just did not have the mental capacity at the moment to try and figure out what was wrong with his boyfriend.

They both tried to keep the noise level down as they walked in, dropping their bags to the floor and toeing off their boots, and Eddie made sure the door closed gently behind them. He didn’t see anyone in the living room, which meant that he probably wasn’t going to get to see his bed for another hour or so.

“I’m going to check on Chris,” he whispered to Buck, who nodded and followed him down the hall. Peeking his head in, he saw his son’s mess of curls peeking out from under his covers, and couldn’t help but smile at the sight. It was remarkably similar to Buck on the rare mornings that Eddie woke up before him.

He heard the door to his bedroom open, and he leaned back into the hallway to see the other man peering through the gap, taking large shuddering gasps.

“Buck?” Eddie crossed the space between them, placing a hand on his boyfriend’s lower back and peering around to see what was wrong. In their bed he could see Maddie and Shannon sprawled out and snoring, Jee sleeping cozily in her travel cot beside the bed. There was absolutely nothing wrong that he could see, nothing that would explain how the man was acting. “Buck, what’s wrong?”

“She stayed,” he gasped out. When Eddie pulled him back to see his face, the other man looked on the verge of crying. He was also smiling. “She didn’t leave, she stayed.”

“Who?”

“Maddie,” Buck said, burying his face into his shoulder and letting out sobs of relief. “She didn’t leave. She didn’t leave.”

Had that been the source of everything bothering him these past few months? The fear that his sister was going to leave? Shit, had the other Maddie just up and left? Eddie couldn’t think of any reason why she would. She’d been looking tired every time he saw her, yes, but being tired wasn’t typically a cause for people to pack their bags and go.

In Eddie’s experience, tired people just wanted to stay and not move, ever. Or maybe that was just him.

Not knowing precisely what to do in this situation - why did his boyfriend continue to insist on keeping these things so close to the chest until the very last minute? - he settled on guiding the both of them back through the hallway and to the couch. Gently pushing the other man onto it, he stepped back and turned his head as the sound of soft, uneven footsteps reached his ears.

“Hey, kiddo,” he said, smiling at Chris, who was wiping away the sleep from his eyes

“You’re home?” the boy groggily asked.

“Yup, the power came back on and we got sent home,” he said, nodding. “Hey, come sit with your Bucky while I go see if we have anything for breakfast.”

“Okay,” Chris said, stumbling slightly as he made his way to the couch. He stopped when he got at a good enough angle to see Buck’s face, frowning at him. “Bucky? Are you okay?”

“I’m wonderful, Superman,” Buck said, reaching over and pulling the boy into his lap. He was almost getting too big for that, Eddie knew, but he hadn’t started complaining yet whenever they did it. “I’m just really, really happy.”

“You’re weird,” Chris said, patting Buck on the face, and Eddie managed to hold his laughter until he was in the kitchen. 

Thankfully, there wasn’t a mountain of dishes needing to be washed, because no one who was currently in the house were savages. Also thankfully, his time traveling partner had the foresight to go through the fridge before the black out, so hopefully there was nothing too rotten in there. He wasn’t about to open it and check, however. That was a task for Future Eddie, not Present Eddie. Present Eddie was more interested in the cereal he’d just found.

“Who wants dry fruit loops for breakfast?” Eddie asked, poking his head out of the kitchen and shaking the box at his boys. He could see the moment that Buck almost made a joke, before glancing down at their son and thinking better of it. It was for the best, the joke had already been made when they bought the cereal.

“One of us should probably text Chimney and let him know that Maddie and Jee are both here, still,” Buck said, helping Chris to his feet before getting to his own with an exaggerated stretch. “Y’know, before he-”

Down the hall, they could hear a phone going off, which in turn set off Jee-Yun.

“That, before he does that,” Buck finished with a sigh. “I’ll get the princess settled again, while you get breakfast sorted.”

“Even without a clipboard he’s bossy,” Eddie stage-whispered to Chris, causing the boy to giggle and Buck to blow a raspberry. He watched his boyfriend shuffle down the hall, and smiled when he heard the muffled sounds of him greeting his niece.

Getting breakfast sorted was easy, requiring merely some clean bowls and spoons. He set out extra, in case the women woke up and wanted any, though he wasn’t certain there would be enough cereal left over for both. Eddie was just setting down the box when Buck came in, bouncing a now giggling baby in his arm.

“Maddie just slept straight through her phone going off,” he said. “So we’re probably couch-surfing in our own house for a few hours more.”

“Oh well,” Eddie said, shrugging. He’d slept in more uncomfortable and cramped places. “What about Shannon?”

“I’m awake,” she announced, yawning as she joined them. “Oh look, Eddie cooked breakfast.”

“Oh look, we’re all out,” he retorted, grabbing the box of cereal before she could and holding it out her reach. “I guess you don’t get any.”

“I am hungry and I will stab you with this spoon,” she threatened, brandishing the one she had just picked up.

“There are children present, Shan,” Buck said, laughing.

“Jee won’t remember and Chris can close his eyes,” she said. To prove her point, their son dutifully reached up and covered them, grinning and giggling as he did so. “Give me the fruit loops, you fruit loop.”

“Violence is not the answer,” Eddie mock-scolded, setting the box down far enough away that she had to stretch to grab it. Shannon huffed as she poured herself a bowl. “So does Chimney know that they’re here still, or…?”

“I talked to him,” Buck said, looking unfairly attractive as he managed to hold Jee and eat one-handed. “When are we going through the fridge to make sure there’s nothing… Evolving?”

“Oh God, I need to do that with mine,” Shannon said, sounding just as excited by the prospect as Eddie felt, though their fridge should be better off than hers.

“After a nap,” Eddie answered. “Food, then nap, then potential fridge horrors and a grocery run.”

“Aye, aye, captain,” Buck said, saluting him with the spoon.

An hour later and Shannon had gone back to her own home, Chris was playing in his room, and Maddie was still asleep in their bed. Things with his sister weren’t magically fixed, Buck knew that. But something had kept her from her breaking point. Shannon had helped her, somehow, and he couldn’t think of any way he could ever repay the woman for that.

He just hoped that this wasn’t simply a postponement.

Adjusting a sleeping Jee-Yun in his arms, he shifted where he sat on the floor, smiling up at how Eddie’s face was smashed into the throw pillow. The man’s arm was dangling off the side, and he reached with his free hand to thread his fingers through Eddie’s.

“I need to tell you something,” he whispered to the sleeping man. “But I don’t know how to tell you. I don’t want to hurt you, and I don’t want to hurt Chris, and I don’t want to hurt Maddie or Bobby or Athena or any of the others. I don’t know what to do, love.” He brought Eddie’s hand to his lips, kissing the back of it. “I don’t want to leave, but I don’t know if I can stay.”

He sighed and settled his head against the couch.

“I want to stay,” Buck said, closing his own eyes as he spoke. “But I think I need to go. I just… I wish I could have it both ways. I regret leaving them so much, I regret hurting them so much. But I don’t want to leave you, I don’t want to hurt you, either. I’m hurting them by staying here, and I’ll hurt you if I leave.

“I don’t know what to do.”

He sighed again and opened his eyes to look at Eddie’s face, and felt his heart stop when he found him staring back.

“Eds, oh God…”

“Buck.” Eddie pushed himself up slowly, not taking his eyes off Buck or taking his hand away. “What the fuck?”

“Eds, I-”

The sound of their bedroom door opening, followed by Maddie’s footsteps coming towards them, was a blessed interruption.

“We will talk about this later,” Eddie promised, and the look in his eyes did not imply a good talk.

No Avoiding It

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Chimney didn’t come and pick up Maddie and Jee-Yun until well into the afternoon, and Buck took the advantage of the opportunity to take his sister on a grocery run with him. It served the dual-purpose of avoiding Eddie, while getting to spend time with her. After all, the last time around, she had already been running to Boston by this point.

There was something different about Maddie now, he was noticing. He wasn’t certain if it was just from his perspective, or if spending time with Shannon during the black out had really made such a difference. But she seemed less… Something. She was still tired, still had bags around her eyes and her smile was still wan and cracked around the edges, but she was smiling.

“I’ve been sick,” she said out of the blue, in the middle of the dairy aisle. In his surprise, Buck almost dropped the milk he was placing into the cart.  He didn’t reply, just turned and faced her as she looked everywhere else. “I’ve been seeing a doctor, Dr. Bolsaro. He put me on this medicine - duloxetine - that was supposed to help, but really it’s just been making me so tired all the time. And he… He said it would take a few weeks to really take effect. But this is the second medication they’ve put me on, and I’m still just so. Tired.”

“Did you talk to-” Buck started, and then bit his tongue. This was not his show, and he had no lines in this play.

“I told Howie I was going to talk to Bolsaro,” she said. “But then I… Didn’t. I don’t know why, maybe I thought it just didn’t matter. Maybe I thought if I just kept marching on that things would just magically get better. But then the black out happened, and Jee just would not stop crying and I was trying to juggle her and everything else in the dark.

“And then Shannon was there, just to check on me, because she was worried. And she started talking, and I- I was a nurse, I knew all about postpartum depression, I knew how many women went through it and that it wasn’t anything to be ashamed of, but until that moment I… I was. I was ashamed of it. Because I felt like I was failing this one thing that I was supposed to be able to do, this one thing I had spent months and months looking forward to.”

“It’s different, when it’s other people,” Buck whispered, remembering how reluctant he’d been to admit he needed help with the alcohol and then his fear with the pills. Even knowing about Bobby, even after helping pick the man up following his own fall off the wagon, he had still been so ashamed to admit that it was happening to him. Buck had been so reluctant to tell even Eddie and Carla that the pills were too tempting, until they sat him down and pried it out of him. 

And then they had helped, because he needed it and there had been no shame in that.

“It is,” Maddie agreed, and then finally met his gaze. “But you already knew I was sick, didn’t you?”

“Yeah,” he admitted quietly.

“Because of the other Maddie.”

“Yeah.”

“She ran, didn’t she?” she asked, though it didn’t really sound like a question. “Something happened, and she ran. In that letter you wrote - that god awful goodbye letter, fuck, Buck. But you talked about how I shouldn’t run away. And… And I remember, after Red, when you…”

The pinky promise, the one he hadn’t let her make to him.

“I didn’t know that you- That she was sick,” he said, wrapping his arms around his middle. “I thought everything was fine. I mean, I knew she quit the dispatch center, but… She and the other Chimney didn’t tell me anything was wrong. She was alone with Jee for all those days, and I didn’t know anything was wrong until she was calling me to say goodbye.”

“I’m sorry,” Maddie whispered, stepping close to wrap her own arms around him. “I’m sorry you got left behind again.”

“It wasn’t her fault,” he said. “She was sick. It wasn’t her fault.”

“That doesn’t change the fact that you got hurt,” she said.

“Talking with Shannon helped, though?” He hadn’t known that it would be Eddie’s ex-wife that would make the difference. He hadn’t even thought about what saving her would mean, beyond sparing Eddie and Chris the pain of losing her.

“Yeah, it did,” she said, nodding. “I guess I just needed someone to hold the light for me, for a bit. Someone who understood what I was going through. It’s still there, it hasn’t gone away, but… But I can talk to her and I feel like she understands and isn’t judging me.”

“I’d never judge you,” Buck immediately said.

“I know, but…”

“But it’s different, I get it.”

“Yeah,” she said, stepping back and wiping at her eyes. “So what’s next on the list?”

“Uhh…” He pulled out the grocery list he’d written while steadfastly avoiding Eddie. “Butter, then eggs.”

“Conveniently right over there,” she said, pointing the way. Then she frowned and yanked the list from his hand. “Oh my God, Buck, did you really organize this list based on where they were in the store?”

“Yes…?”

“Can’t do math to save your son’s grades, but you have the store aisles memorized…”

“I can do math!” Buck argued, huffing.

“On a calculator, sure, and even then I bet you get confused half-way and have to start over.” The audacity of this woman.

“I get enough of this at home from Eddie and Chris, I do not need this from you, too.”

“I just don’t understand, I taught you how to do math.”

“Maybe not something you should be bragging about…”

“Not that I’m complaining about the free pizza,” Albert said, taking one of the boxes from Buck’s arms as he  and Ravi stepped into the apartment. “But why are you here?”

“He’s avoiding his boyfriend,” Ravi said, setting down the drinks he was carrying.

“I am not avoiding anyone,” Buck lied. He was totally avoiding being alone with Eddie. Chris was with Shannon for the weekend, which meant the house would be empty except for him and Eddie. And while usually that meant Very Good things, this time… “Oh! Probie, this is Probie. Probie, meet Probie.”

“Ravi,” the probie sighed. “My name is Ravi Panikkar.”

“Albert Han,” the other man said, holding out his hand for the other to shake. “Howie’s- Chimney’s brother. And why are you avoiding Eddie?”

“I’m not!” Buck said, and got almost matching looks of disbelief. “Can’t I just spend some quality time with the best probies in the city?”

“I think they had a fight, but I’m not sure,” Ravi said. “So if you’re Chimney’s brother, that makes you his brother-in-law, right?”

“He’s making a flowchart,” Buck explained. “And we haven’t had a fight.” Yet.

“Oh man, that would have been so useful when I first got here,” Albert said. “I asked Hen if Bobby was Buck’s actual dad, and she spent twenty minutes laughing before I got an answer.”

“Wait, he’s not? I thought for sure they were and they were just using different names on the job. I mean, they even kinda look the same?”

“I know, right!?” He took the beer Ravi offered, and then waved him off when the other probie started to ask if Buck wanted one. “He has a thing. There’s juice in the fridge, still.”

“Thank you,” Buck said, moving to find a clean cup to drink out of. Sadly, there wasn’t any, so he ended up having to wash one that was in the sink. “Seriously, Al, this place used to be spotless.”

“Shut up, you’re not paying the rent anymore, you don’t get to be bossy.”

“Oh man, Cap has him training me,” Ravi groused. “It’s awful.”

“I’ve heard horror stories. Is he really that bad when he gets a clipboard?”

“Worse.”

“Well clearly introducing the two of you was a giant mistake,” Buck said, squeezing in on the couch. His recliner had migrated to the Diaz house, along with his bed and everything else he wanted to keep. “I have done nothing to deserve this.”

“You drilled me for two hours on how to disassemble a chainsaw,” Ravi said. He turned to Albert, “He had a stopwatch!”

“Where was Eddie? Usually he’s able to talk him down.”

“Busy helping restock the ambulance, and then Bobby was making him help with lunch,” Buck said, feeling proud that he managed to drag his boyfriend into that level of culinary skill. No more pre-made or boxed meals for him and Chris whenever Buck was laid up or… Gone. “And you never know when you need to be able to disassemble a chainsaw, and you need to be able to do it quickly.”

“Is this a psychic thing?” Albert asked, leaning forward so he could look at him past Ravi. “Did you have, like, a vision involving Ravi and a chainsaw?”

“Wait, so is he really psychic?” the other probie asked. “I thought it was just a joke.”

“Howie says he is. Bobby and Eddie say he isn’t.”

“So, are you?” Ravi asked, turning to face Buck.

“I’m not psychic.”

“Bullshit!” Albert shouted, causing them to jump. “You kept telling me to avoid going on the Seven-Ten, and what happened? There was that pile-up!”

“So which is it?” Ravi asked. “Are you or aren’t you?”

“I’m not,” Buck answered at the same time Albert said, “He is.”

Ravi looked between them, his head swiveling on his neck, before taking a large swallow of his beer and sighing.

“I miss B-shift. B-shift was normal.”

“But boring,” Buck said, pulling him in to give him a noogie. “The B in B-shift stands for Boring. We’re the Awesome Shift.”

Buck hung out with the probies for several hours, watching a trashy movie and then taking turns playing at one of the fighting games he had left behind. Eventually, however, he knew he couldn’t put off going home forever. If for no other reason than, based on Ravi’s level of inebriation, that the couch wouldn’t be available to crash on.

For once, he seriously regretted that the apartment was so close to the house. For all that he felt like he was walking to his own execution, the drive was over far too soon. He managed to postpone the inevitable by several more minutes, but then the porch light flickered on and off, and he knew that there was no point in it.

“Okay, you can do this,” he told himself, getting out of the jeep and dragging his feet to the door. “He isn’t going to hate you. He isn’t going to hate you. He’s just going to be angry and a bit heartbroken, but- Oh God, he’s going to hate me.”

Taking a breath, Buck opened the door and stepped into the darkened living room. When the door closed behind him, he was momentarily blinded by the sudden light of a lamp being flicked on. Eddie was sitting next to it, glaring at him.

“Did you seriously run to that chair after messing with the porch light, just to be dramatic?” Buck asked. God, he was so fond of this man.

“I might have,” Eddie said. “We need to talk.”

“Actually, you know, I just remembered-”

“No,” the other man said, getting up and walking over. He reached up and turned the latch on the door, the sound of it making Buck flinch. “We are going to talk.”

“We talk all the time, love, I have no idea what you-”

“Buck.”

He swallowed, and nodded.

“Fine, okay,” he said, giving in and heading for the couch. He collapsed into it, slumping against the back cushions. “How much did you hear that morning?”

“You don’t want to leave, but you don’t know if you can stay,” Eddie said, coming to stand in front of him with his arms crossed. It was remarkably similar to that day, so many years ago, when he confessed about Doug. “Which, I don’t understand, because… If you don’t want to leave, then you just don’t leave. Easy as that.”

“It’s not that easy, Eds.”

“Not doing something is really easy. For example, I chose not to go over to Albert’s and drag you back here, and that was very easy.”

“They’re still there!” Buck snapped. “Edmundo and the others, they’re all still there. I abandoned them, I left them. They didn’t just get erased or rewritten or- Or whatever the hell I thought happened. They’re still there.”

“How do you know?” Eddie demanded. “Huh? Tell me that, how do you know?”

“Because I talked to Edmundo,” he said, looking down at the floor. “When I was shot, I- I ended up back at the crossroads, with Ichabod. And then… Then Edmundo showed up, and he… He looked so awful, Eddie. So much worse than when I left. I have no clue how long it had been for him, but he looked so awful. So broken.”

Buck looked up, in time to see Eddie’s face go purposefully blank, which was not a good sign.

“And if Edmundo is still there, then that means all the others are still there. That means Christopher is still there, Eds. If nothing else, I became yet another person that Christopher ended up losing. Because I left,” he said. “I said I wanted to fix things, but I haven’t fixed anything at all.”

“That’s not true,” Eddie said, almost sounding like he was pleading. “You fixed things here. I mean, Shannon is-”

“I didn’t fix anything,” Buck repeated. “I just kept them from breaking to begin with. But everything I wanted to fix over there is still broken, and then I broke it some more. Because I left them.”

“You didn’t mean to leave them.”

“I ran away and didn’t look back until it was too late. I fucking abandoned them.”

“So, what, you’re going to abandon us now?” Eddie asked, the anger Buck had been expecting finally starting to show. “You’re going to leave me and Chris?”

“That’s not fair.”

“None of this is fair, Buck. You’re sitting here telling me you want to leave.”

“But I don’t want to-”

“Then don’t!” Eddie screamed. Immediately, he stepped back and turned away, taking in large breaths of air and pinching the bridge of his nose. His shoulders were tense, and his arms were shaking. After a moment he turned back around and said, in a quieter voice, “Then don’t. It’s not that difficult. You’ve been perfectly fine here the past four years.”

“I didn’t know then,” Buck said, shaking his head. “I didn’t know that they were still there, and now I do, and… Eddie, I left Christopher.”

“And you’re talking about leaving Chris,” Eddie said.

“I’m going to hurt one of them,” he said. “I’m already hurting one of them. It doesn’t matter what I do.”

“Then stay,” Eddie said, sitting down beside him, hands framing Buck’s face. “If it doesn’t matter, then stay. Please.”

“I- I want to stay…”

“Then stay,” he said again. “When do you have to choose?”

“I don’t know. Ichabod was very ominous when he was talking about Christmas, so maybe then?”

“So then on Christmas, you tell him you want to stay. And then you don’t leave.”

Closing his eyes, Buck let his head fall forward, letting his forehead rest against Eddie’s. It sounded so easy, the way his boyfriend said it. It sounded so very easy.

It sounded too easy.

Like Having Your Heart Outside Your Body

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

It seemed to Buck like time started to speed up after the near-fight with Eddie. He felt like he was on a steam-powered locomotive going full tilt down the rails, the engineer adding more and more coal to the fire. The worst part was that he should have been happy, he knew that. Maddie and Chimney were both still there, with the former actually opening up more about her mental health. Mostly with Shannon, but she was actually talking instead of doing her best to grit her teeth and march through it.

And! And! Because Hudson had been dead for over a year, he obviously never escaped during the black out and therefore never kidnapped Harry. 

Buck wanted to be able to sit and enjoy this. He wanted to be able to have dinner with his Maddie and Chimney and take solace in the fact that they were still there. He wanted to be able to train Ravi with Eddie and not worry about whether or not the probie was good enough to step into his absence. He wanted to be able to hug his kid without guilt, to kiss his boyfriend with fear.

But Buck felt like he was on a runaway train going faster and faster towards disaster.

“I’ve noticed that Buck has you driving the two of you to work now,” Bobby commented to Eddie one day, when it was his turn to help the captain with lunch. Ever since Buck practically forced him to show off his cooking skills, Bobby seemed to make a point to force him into helping in the kitchen at least once a week. He still wasn’t sure how he felt about it.

“Yeah, I don’t really remember when the last time was that he drove himself somewhere.” That was a lie, the last time was when he drove himself home from the apartment before their talk about what Eddie had heard. He wasn’t sure how that was connected.

“But he’s fine?”

“Perfectly fine.”

Bobby looked for him a moment, looking on the verge of saying something. But whatever it was, he seemed to think better of it. Instead he turned back to the stove and directed Eddie on what to do next.

The truth of the matter was, Buck was not fine. He put on a good show of it in front of him and Chris and all the others, but Eddie knew him far too well to believe it. Ever since their talk after the black out, ever since Buck had stopped driving himself anywhere, the smiles he wore were a little more fake. They were their normal face-splitting size, but they would always fall just short of reaching his eyes. And Eddie wasn’t sure how to help, because…

Well, because he was being selfish and didn’t want to lose Buck to another version of their family.

At some point, Buck had started using the GPS app on his phone for any and every drive they took, be it to Abuela’s or Maddie’s, or the station, or the supermarket. Chris thought it amusing, but for Eddie it was another sign of something being terribly, terribly wrong. Especially when he asked why, and got the answer of,

“I just don’t want to get lost.”

Eventually, even the others managed to clock on to something being wrong. Shannon would ask, whenever she was over to pick up or drop off Chris. Ravi had, of his own initiative, taken Eddie aside one shift and asked him about Buck. Even Albert had noticed something was up, and Eddie was pretty sure most of his interactions with Buck anymore were relegated to texts and phone calls.

Bobby and Athena must have scented something in the air, too, because they were suddenly getting a lot of invitations to dinner at the Grant-Nash house.

“Everything’s fine,” he told Hen during a playdate at the Wilson house.

“And that’s why he decided not to come over and hang out with the kids today?” she asked, obviously not believing him. Which was fair, because Buck never passed up an opportunity to hang out with the 118 kids. Or any kids, really.

“He‘s just tired. He was planning on taking a nap and then catching up on some chores around the house.” The man was getting more and more reluctant to leave the house unless he had to, nowadays. It was getting worrisome, not that Eddie was going to tell her that.

“Y’know, it’s the damnedest thing. You sounded exactly like Chimney talking about Maddie, just then.”

“And Maddie’s fine, too.”

“Maddie’s getting better,” Hen corrected him. “But it seems to me like Buck is just getting worse.”

“But he isn’t,” Eddie refuted. “Everything’s fine. Buck isn’t going anywhere.”

The paramedic stared at him, frowning quizzically and narrowing her eyes behind her glasses.

“Is that a concern? Buck going somewhere?”

“No,” he was quick to say. “Never.”

She didn’t believe him, he could tell, but he couldn’t exactly blame her. He wasn’t believing it, either.

He and Chris stuck around for another few hours, Eddie dodging more probing questions about his boyfriend’s wellbeing. Eventually, he managed to get himself and his kid out of there with an excuse about homework that was thankfully very real. It was with guilty relief that he drove away, because he wasn’t sure how much longer he could take without exploding.

Because things were not okay, and it was increasingly obvious just how obvious it was.

Buck was pacing in the living room, clearly agitated, when they got in. Eddie sent Chris to his room to start on his homework while he tried to figure out which bomb he was diffusing now. He hadn’t realized at the time just how appropriate of a start to their relationship that exploding ambulance would be.

“We need to talk about tomorrow,” his boyfriend said.

“What about tomorrow?”

“This is technically a question about morals, I think,” Buck said, scratching the back of his neck. “And… And it affects you directly, so, uh…”

“Buck, what’s going on?” Eddie asked, trying to be patient, but the last few days-weeks-months had just sapped it out of him.

“There’s going to be a prison riot tomorrow,” his boyfriend said, and that immediately snagged his attention. “I just saw the date and remembered. But uh, we’ll be called to respond. There’s a, uh. A prisoner who uses it as an opportunity to escape.”

“So tell Athena, and she’ll take care of it.”

“It’s more complicated than that. There’s a, uh. A thing that makes it way more complicated.”

Eddie rubbed at his face with a sigh, really wishing they still kept alcohol in the house. It would be very nice to have in these moments.

“Okay, explain.”

The details were as straightforward as they were distressing. Two prisoners use the riot as cover to steal guard uniforms and escape, hijacking the ambulance and taking him and Buck hostage. Except it turns out the escape attempt was itself just an excuse for one of them to get to the hospital his son was being kept, so the prisoner could give up his own heart for his kid to live.

“And I really don’t want to go through that again,” Buck said, pacing. “And I don’t want you to go through it. But…”

“Does it work?”

“He- He kills himself, and Athena and Maynard manage to find a way so his heart could be used for the transplant.”

“But it works?” Eddie asked again. “His kid gets a new heart and he’s fine afterwards? Neither of us get hurt?”

“Yeah.” Buck reached up to rub at a spot above his birthmark.

“Buck…”

Buck let out a shaky breath and nodded.

“Yeah, I kinda figured.”

They would both always choose to save the kid, regardless of the danger to themselves, if given the option.

Was this how Buck felt every time there was an imminent disaster that he knew about? Because if his boyfriend felt this level of anxiety that often, Eddie was suddenly understanding why he acted the way he did sometimes. He had to hold his tongue when Bobby ordered the two of them to hurry on to the ambulance, and nearly bit it off when the fake guards got into the ambulance with them.

Now, the ambulance was parked on some side road, the two of them herded behind it with guns in their faces. Just because Eddie knew it was going to happen, just because he knew that they obviously both got through this unharmed, didn’t mean he particularly appreciated having a weapon pointed at his boyfriend again. But there was a kid at the end of all of this, who needed a new heart and would be getting one soon, and that was what mattered.

“Okay, so you broke out,” Eddie said, trying to sound calm as the shorter prisoner searched through their pockets for their phones and wallets, and tossed their radios to the ground. “What now? Patient in there fighting for every breath. That your handiwork?”

The last part was directed at the taller prisoner, the one with a bloody hole in his uniform shirt. He seemed to be the one in charge, the shorter one bringing him their phones and wallets to look through. Carefully and slowly, Eddie reached over and hooked his pinky around a silent Buck’s.

“Cute kid,” the tall one said, pulling out the picture of Chris that Eddie kept in his wallet. “Yours? I’m guessing he lives with you at Four-Nine-Nine-Five South Bedford Street.”

Beside him, he felt Buck almost start to rush for them. Almost. The taller prisoner smirked in amusement at it, and then he tilted his head, like a bird examining a worm.

“I think I recognize you,” he said, pointing at Buck. “Have you been on TV?’

“We’re firefighters,” Eddie said, answering for him. “We’ve had to give interviews before.”

“That’s probably it…” the tall prisoner said, but didn’t seem like he believed in. “Alright, so here’s what’s gonna happen next.”

What happened next turned out that the short one got into the driver’s seat while Buck and Eddie were herded into the back of the ambulance by the tall one, who was suddenly very concerned about keeping the guard alive. The transponder was torn out and left behind as they drove away towards the hospital the tall one’s kid was at. Not that they said that’s where they were going, but that’s where Buck had said they’d be heading.

“Wait!” the tall one cried out as they were in the process of intubating the real guard. Buck jumped and froze like a rabbit, while Eddie kept going. The guy was smiling, which did not make Eddie feel at ease. “I know where I recognize you from.”

“W- What?” Buck stuttered out, glancing between him and Eddie.

“You’re the firefighter who killed his brother-in-law.”

“I, uh. I have no idea what you’re-”

“Oh, c’mon kid, this is a safe space,” the guy said. “You can talk to me.”

“You have a gun pointed at us,” Eddie said. “Not feeling very safe.”

The guy glanced down at the gun in his hand and then shrugged.

“C”mon kid, tell me how ya did it.”

“Look man, I told you, I have no idea what you’re-”

“Yes you do. You flinched when I mentioned it, and you keep glancing at…” The guy trailed off, shifting his gaze to where Eddie was still working to keep the patient stable. “Oh, I get it, you’re shy in front of the pretty one.”

“Or maybe he isn’t like you,” Eddie snapped at him.

“Doesn’t look like we have any company,” the short one said, throwing open the doors to the ambulance. At some point, they had pulled into the bay of the hospital, though Eddie hadn’t really noticed them coming to a stop.

“All right then. Dom, take the pretty boy and our friend inside. Hand him off, then you know what to do,” the tall one said. “The kid stays here.”

“What? No!” Eddie said, getting up to put himself between Buck and the murderers threatening them. His boyfriend was staring wide-eyed at them, obviously not expecting to be kept behind. “He is not staying here with-”

“Go or I’ll shoot you,” the tall one said. “Or I’ll shoot him and then go to your house and shoot your kid. Or I’ll shoot all three of you.”

“Eds,” Buck said. “Love…”

“Love?” the tall one laughed. “Oh, that’s adorable. C’mon, out you go or I start shooting.”

Eddie turned his head to meet Buck’s fear-filled eyes. This was not how it was supposed to go. The guy was supposed to keep Eddie in the ambulance while Buck went inside and was safe.

But this was about more than the two of them.

“Fine,” he ground out. “Come on, Dom. Let’s go.”

At the very least, Eddie got to see the guy get tackled to the hospital floor by half a dozen cops within moments of entering the building.

“So, the pretty boy and the kid, huh?” the murderer laughed. “I had noticed that you both lived at the same address.”

“Shut up,” Buck said, not really putting any feeling to it. As terrifying as it was to be left here with the guy, he could take comfort that Eddie was far away. The chance of things suddenly taking a turn was always there, as this was helpfully reminding him, so knowing that Eddie was most definitely safe helped a lot.

“Alright, it’s just us girls here now,” the guy said, leaning forward. “So tell me, how’d you do it?”

“I told you, I-”

“Oh, c’mon, kid. I remember what that lady reporter said last year. I mean, the guy was hurting your sister. I’ve killed for less.”

“Please, stop comparing me to yourself,” Buck practically begged. He wasn’t anything like the other man. He wasn’t. He wasn’t.

“You’re right, we’re really not the same. I at least own up to what I am,” the guy said. “Murderer.”

“We’re not the same because I actually feel guilty for what I did,” Buck snapped. Then he realized what he said and started cursing himself. “Damn it.”

The guy grinned like Christmas had come early, and looked about ready to start asking more, but was thankfully interrupted by the sound of sirens and someone shouting over a megaphone.

“Mitchell Trent, this is LAPD. We have the area surrounded. Put your weapons down and come out with your hands up.”

Mitchell ducked down and opened the ambulance doors to shout back.

“I got a hostage! Don’t come any closer!” He slammed the doors closed again and sat down, looking much more agitated than he had before. “How did they find us so fast?”

“It’s called detective work,” Buck said, rolling his eyes. “You brought us to the hospital your kid is at.”

“How do you…?”

“If I told you the truth, you wouldn’t believe me,” he sighed. “Really, what was the plan here? You and the other guy - Dom? - force a bunch of doctors to do a heart transplant at gunpoint?”

“You wouldn’t understand,” Mitchell scoffed.

“My captain once said that having a kid is like having your heart outside your body. I guess you’re just gonna make it a bit more literal.”

“You are incredibly well-informed.”

“The joke at the station is that I’m psychic,” Buck said, clasping his hands together tightly to keep them from shaking. The way Mitchell was pacing the ambulance was not helping his nerves, and his legs were starting to get jittery themselves. “Listen, I get it, I do. I would do, and have done, so many things for my kid. I would give up, have given up, so much for him. Anything and everything. So I get it, I really, really, do. But your plan was never going to work, and now we’re stuck here until someone gets shot. Probably me. Again.”

“So what now, psychic guy?” Mitchell asked. The gun hadn’t been pointed at him for a whole now, but Buck still kept track of it where it was. “How does this end, then?”

What the hell was he supposed to say? It seemed so easy yesterday. Let it happen and ride it out to the messy, sorta happy ending. But now he was here, in the middle of it, and what was he supposed to do? Gently coax the guy into killing himself so the kid could get his heart? That wasn’t Buck.

And he almost let Eddie be stuck here, making this same decision. He really wasn’t all that different from Mitchell, was he?

“I don’t know,” he said instead. Because he was a coward. “If I knew how you could have it both ways, I would tell you. But I don’t know.”

“I’m not like him, am I?” Buck asked, hours and hours later, when they were back home. Mitchell had shot himself, and Eddie had the minor heart stopping moment of running out to the ambulance bay in fear that he would find the love of his life bleeding out again. He hadn’t, though. Everything had been fine, and Mitchell’s kid got a slightly used heart.

Now they were back home, standing outside the door to Christopher’s room, and Buck seemed to be coming undone in the aftermath.

“No, you’re nothing like him,” Eddie said.

“Eds, I went in there perfectly ready to let a man kill himself so they could give his heart to someone else,” he said. “That’s… I feel like that makes me at least as bad as him. Even without the whole…”

“We were ready to let it happen.”

“I’m a corrupting influence, even better,” Buck said. “God, what do you even see in me?”

“Someone who was willing to put themselves through a traumatic event just to save a kid they didn’t even know,” Eddie said, reaching across the distance between them to rub against Buck’s birthmark. “You’re not him. You could never be him.”

Buck reached up to hold his hand, but he didn’t look convinced. Eddie sighed and let it go for the moment, too tired and stressed and entirely unsure how to navigate this. He’d bring it up with Underwood, if the topic wasn’t so intertwined with things that the doctor was absolutely required to report.

“C’mon, let’s go squeeze ourselves into Chris’ bed for cuddles,” he said, nudging him into the room.

“I don’t think that bed can hold both of us and him, Eds,” Buck said, not really fighting against it.

“You’ve got money. You can buy him a new bed if it breaks.”

One Year and Several Months Late

“How are you and Karen doing?” Eddie asked Hen, sitting down in the chair across from her and Chimney, a couple shifts after Hurricane Eva made landfall again. He hadn’t been there for it, having asked for that day off to take Chris to a doctor’s appointment, so he hadn’t actually met the woman. But Buck had spoken about her in non-flattering terms, and he himself had seen the damage she had wrought on the Wilsons in his first few months at the station, so his opinion of the woman was not very high.

Honestly, if he had been in Hen’s shoes, he would have barred the woman from his life entirely and did his best to forget she existed. He definitely wouldn’t have agreed to speak to her again and then told his partner about it. But he wasn’t Hen and his ex was helping co-parent their kid, so his circumstances were so different that his opinion wasn’t really worth much.

“We’re doing good,” Hen said, setting down the medical textbook she had been reading through. “Well, better. We’ve talked. A lot.”

“Talking is good,” Eddie said, nodding.

“What about you and Buck?” Chimney asked, looking up from his phone. “Maddie’s concerned about him.”

Everyone was concerned about Buck. Since the prison riot, since whatever had happened in the time between Eddie being forced to leave him behind in the ambulance and Mitchell shooting himself, Buck had seemed to shrink in on himself. While before he had been able to fake being fine - and he had been faking it a lot for the others, Eddie knew - now he wasn’t even bothering to put on a smile half the time. From where he was sitting, he could see Buck in the kitchen area with Bobby, not nearly as animated as he usually was while cooking.

Eddie hadn’t been recruited to help Bobby in the kitchen for two whole weeks, because the captain had been using cooking together as an opportunity to try and get Buck to open up. He hadn’t a clue how successful Bobby had been, though, considering some of the content Buck was keeping to himself.

“I want to say he’s getting better, but…” But that would be an abject lie. “Underwood’s talked about getting him on antidepressants.”

“They switched Maddie’s again,” Chimney said. Eddie already knew that because Shannon and Buck both mentioned it to him independently. “This one seems to be helping, though. She isn’t sleeping as much, at least.”

“Is he still staying at home a lot?” Hen asked. “When was the last time you two went out somewhere?”

“We went to the zoo just the other week.”

“But that was with Chris, wasn’t it?”

“And Shannon,” he said.

“Yeah, no, I meant when was the last time you and Buck went out and did something? Just the two of you?”

“I…” Eddie closed his mouth, gnawing on his lip as he tried to think. Just the two of them? They went hiking together a few times, but that wasn’t nearly as often as it used to be. If they went out somewhere, they almost always took Chris. Usually they just stayed in, however. “Dios perdoname, I am an awful boyfriend.”

“Has it been that long?” Chimney asked.

“It’s been never,” Eddie said, covering his face so he couldn’t see the appalled looks his coworkers were giving him. “He had that skull fracture and the stab wound when we got together, and then the pandemic hit, and then he got shot, and we just… We’ve never gone on an actual date.”

“Never?” The incredulity was obvious in Hen’s tone.

“How the hell did that happen, Diaz?” Chimney demanded.

“Buck automatically plans everything with Chris in mind!” Eddie said, trying to defend himself. “And if it’s just the two of us, we stay in.”

“You have been together for almost a year and a half.” Hen’s textbook was on the table, utterly forgotten. “And you have never, not once, gone out somewhere on an actual date?”

“That is what I said.” Eddie kept his eyes on the table, tracing the grains in the wood. “I am an awful boyfriend, I know.”

The two paramedics fell silent, long enough for him to look up in curiosity and concern. They were looking at each other, clearly having their own mindmeld conversation. It was a very different silent language from his and Buck’s, and he was stuck watching it from the outside with absolutely no idea what was being communicated.

“When’s the next time Shannon has Chris?” Chimney asked, the telepathic talking over with.

“The weekend after next.”

“Much too long,” Hen said, shaking her head. “I’ll have to talk to Karen and Athena, but one of us can have a sleepover this week at some point.”

“I think, between the two of us, we can make a list of nice enough places for them to go,” Chimney said. “Definitely not the one with the spinning floor, though. Maddie and I went there once, and it was nice, but a lady nearly got crushed. With Buck’s luck, that would happen to him.”

“Yeah, no, we don’t want something to happen and their first date to be postponed until Bobby retires,” Hen said, nodding. “Where did you take Shannon that one time? We definitely don’t want that one, either.”

“What is going on here?” Eddie asked, bewildered. “Are you two planning the date for me?”

“Obviously. Keep up,” Chimney said. “Clearly if we left it to you, Chris’s grandkids will be on their own first dates before you get around to it.”

“I can plan my own date, thank you.”

“Oh really? Come on then, Eddie. Prove it.”

“Um, uh…” Shit, he hadn’t actually- Wait! “A picnic on the beach.”

“He’d probably like it,” Chimney said, shrugging at Hen.
