“Eddie could take him to a garbage dump to search through the trash and Buck would brag about it afterwards, just because it was Eddie that took him,” Hen said, shaking her head. “No, no, this is a first date over a year into the relationship-”

“Yeah, thanks, I know,” Eddie grumbled.

“It needs to be fancy,” she continued. “But not too fancy. Dress shirt fancy. Does Buck own a tie? Do you own a tie?”

“I have one,” Eddie said. “I don’t think Buck does, though.”

“We’ll talk to Bobby, he can lend him one,” Chimney said.

“We still haven’t decided where they’re going, though,” Hen reminded him, having pulled out her phone at some point and started typing. “Karen has suggestions. Do either of you have any allergies we don’t know about?”

“If you don’t know, then we don’t know,” Eddie said, slumping back into his chair and surrendering to his fate as the other two planned the date for him.

“We really don’t need to do this,” Buck said, standing in their bedroom and watching Eddie finish doing up the buttons of his shirt.

“I don’t think we’re really getting a choice here, corazon,” the other man said, moving on to his tie. “If we don’t go willingly, they might drag us to a date by force.”

“I just- You know I don’t need this, right?” he asked, wanting to make sure. Needing to make sure. “I’m perfectly happy with spending our nights on the couch watching bad movies.”

“I know,” Eddie said, pausing what he was doing to lean in and kiss him. “But they’re… They’re worried about you. And they decided that their best way to help was to arrange a fancy date for us.”

“Well, at least I get to see you dressed up,” Buck said, taking in the view. His boyfriend did look very good in his black button up. Then again, he was convinced that Eddie Diaz was beautiful wearing anything. Or nothing. He wasn’t picky. Someone knocking on their front door interrupted his enjoyment, and he went to answer it with a sigh.

Bobby was on the other side, waiting patiently. He’d volunteered to pick-up Chris for his sleepover, and to bring over the tie that people were insisting that Buck needed to wear.

“You’re looking very nice,” the captain said, smiling at him as he stepped into the house.

“Thanks,” Buck said, rubbing at the back of his neck. “Uh, Chris should be ready to go.”

“You’re not, though,” Bobby noted. He lifted his hand, a solid black tie dangling from it. “I’ve been told you need this?”

“Yeah. I never got around to getting one this time,” he said, reaching for it, but Bobby shook his head.

“I seem to remember a conversation we had a while ago,” Bobby said, draping the tie around Buck’s neck himself. He kept talking as his hands worked. “Where I offered to help you get ready for your next date.”

“Cap…”

“Now, I wasn’t expecting it to take so long,” the older man continued. “Or for your first date to happen after a year of you two being together-”

“I get it, okay, I dropped the ball!” Eddie shouted from down the hall, causing Buck to snicker. His boyfriend came around the corner with Chris in tow, keys in one hand and his son’s bag in the other.

“You got there,” Bobby told him. He finished tying the tie and smoothed down the collar of Buck’s shirt. “There, perfect.”

Buck reached up to fiddle with the tie. He hadn’t thought he’d get to have a moment like this with this version of the man, was quite convinced that he had torched the chances of it when he friendzoned Abby and therefore didn’t have that Valentine’s Day date with her. That moment with the other Bobby, with the closest thing he had to a loving father helping him get ready for his first actual date, had been precious to him.

He surged forward, wrapping his arms around Bobby and squeezing him tightly. The other man grunted with the suddenness of it, but settled into the hug, patting his back.

“Thank you,” he whispered.

“Of course, kid,” Bobby said. “But shouldn’t the two of you be heading off now?”

“Probably,” Buck said, stepping back and wiping at his eyes. “C’mon, love, let’s get to our date that our family is so lovingly forcing us to go on.”

“Don’t sound too excited,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes. To Chris, he said,“Be good for Bobby and them.”

“Yes, dad,” the boy said.

They locked up behind themselves, waving off their kid as he and Bobby drove away, before getting into Eddie’s truck and leaving in the opposite direction. They were half-way to their destination - a restaurant that was fancy enough to be considered ‘acceptable dating locale’ but not so fancy to require a reservation - when Eddie turned to him at a stoplight and asked,

“Do you actually want to go to this place?”

“I mean, I assume that you-”

“Buck.”

“God, no. I googled it earlier, and everything sounded way too damn fancy.”

“Want to get McDonalds instead?”

“Oh my God, please.”

So they went through the drive thru of the nearest McDonalds and went to the beach instead. They sat in the bed of the truck, stealing each other’s fries while they watched the sunset over the ocean. Afterwards, they slipped off their shoes and socks and rolled up their pants legs and walked down the beach with the tide hitting their ankles.

“See, I was going to do this from the beginning,” Eddie told him, swinging their joined hands. “A picnic on the beach.”

“Man, I would have loved that,” Buck said.

“Hen said it needed to be fancy, because it was our first date since getting together. A year ago.”

“Yeah, we really dropped the ball there,” he said, nodding. “How did we get so far without actually going on a date?”

“I think it’s your fault,” Eddie said, nodding decisively.

“What?” Buck squawked in outrage. “How the hell was it my fault?”

“Well, first you went and got your head bashed in-”

“Not my fault!”

“And then you went and let yourself get shot.”

“...Okay, that one was partially my fault,” Buck said, giving him that. “But only partially.”

“Try entirely- Hey!”

Buck had shoved him, sending him sprawling into the sand and water. His boyfriend looked so disgruntled when he pushed himself up, wet sand sticking to his face, that he couldn’t help it. He burst into laughter, bent double and clinging to his sides.

“Your face!” he gasped out between peals of laughter.

Eddie blinked up at him, looking awed for a moment, before his mouth curved into a smirk. He collected a handful of wet sand before standing, raising it threateningly.

“Don’t do it,” Buck said, stepping back and raising a hand in warning. “Don’t!”

“I’mma do it.”

“Don’t- Hey!” The sand smacked him right in the cheek, and he wiped it off with a glower. He knelt down and collected his own handfuls of sand. “That is it!”

Eddie took off at a sprint down the beach, and Buck chased after him, both of them laughing.

Hen was waiting eagerly at the table in the station loft, Chimney impatiently tapping his fingers on the wood beside her. She had seen Twiddle-Dee and Twiddle-Dum enter the bay a few minutes ago and head for the locker room to change, and now she was just waiting for them to come up so she could bombard them with questions.

They had both been smiling, when she saw them. Actual, genuine smiles, so she had a good feeling about everything.

“Good morning,” Eddie greeted them, heading straight for the coffee maker.

“Morning, Eddie,” Hen said. “Where’s your worse half?”

“Off pestering Ravi about something,” he said, shrugging. “I’m not sure what.”

“How did the date go?” Chimney asked, cutting to the chase.

“He stuffed sand down my pants.”

Neither of the paramedics really had a response to that. They turned to each other, blinking in dumbfounded silence. Hen was about to open her mouth to ask for context, when the sound of Buck’s laughter from the bottom of the stairs interrupted her. It startled her, because it had been weeks since she had heard him laugh like that.

Suddenly, the context didn’t matter as much as the results.

“Well, just as long as you both had a good time,” she said, nodding to herself.

“We did,” he said, smiling warmly as Buck and Ravi finally climbed the stairs to join them, the former animatedly waving his arms as he told the probie something. “We really, really did.”

Start the Final Countdown

The hospital was ablaze, fire devouring it from the inside out with an appetite that would never be satisfied. They had been tasked with evacuating everyone that couldn’t make it out themselves, resulting in a human chain carrying infants down the truck ladder to the parking lot. Buck and Eddie had just finished handing off the last of the babies from the nursery and were about to climb off the ladder when Bobby came hurrying over.

“I need you on the third floor,” he told them. “We’ve got an eight-year old boy, Parker. He’s trapped up there with his baby sister.”

“I thought that floor was cleared,” Buck said. There was something about this conversation, something he knew he needed to remember, something he knew he did remember. He just needed something to jog his memory.

“We must’ve missed him in all the chaos,” Bobby said. “He dialed from a patient’s room, Three-One-Eight.”

“Back up the ladder,” Eddie said, turning to go, but Buck stopped them with a raised hand.

“No, the fire’s right outside the nursery, but… Did you say Three-One-Eight, Cap?”

“Yes. What about it?”

Buck banged his fist against the ladder’s handrail in excitement.

“He gave the wrong room number!” That’s what was bugging him about this conversation. He remembered this. He remembered Edmundo being on the verge of a panic attack when they thought they had lost the kids and being the one to talk him down, and he remembered the other man having an epiphany while looking into the truck’s side view mirror. “It’s Eighty-one E! Three-One-Eight is fully engulfed, there’s no one left there. Edmundo figured it out, though. The kid was looking at a reflection and told them what he saw, but not where he actually was!”

“Okay, so where the hell is that room then?” Eddie asked, looking at him expectantly.

“I… I don’t remember,” Buck said, rubbing his mouth. His first instinct would be the eighth floor, since the room number started with eight, but the hospital didn’t have one. Plus, he didn’t remember climbing that many stairs with Edmundo. “Definitely not the third floor. But they can’t be that far from the nursery, right? The kid’s sister is a newborn, I remember that.”

“Dispatch, this is Captain Nash,” Bobby said, grabbing his radio. “Is there a room Eighty-One E?”

“Yes,” the dispatcher - a woman whose voice Buck didn’t recognize - answered, sounding hesitant and confused. “On the fifth floor. But why…?”

“Tell the kid we’re on the way,” the captain said, dismissing her question entirely. “Hurry up and go, you two.”

“On it, Cap,” Eddie said, jumping off the ladder, Buck right behind him.

“Oh wait!” Buck stopped and turned, grabbing Bobby's arm. “If you see Michael, tell him that David is okay. He’s just… Being one of us.”

“Now I’m concerned.”

“He’s just doing what any of us would do in his situation, Cap,” he said, hurrying after his boyfriend.

“Definitely concerned,” he heard Bobby say behind them.

The two of them rushed to and up the smoke-filled stairwell as fast as they could, panting a bit with the exertion. Midway up, the woman from dispatch radioed them again.

“Unit One-Eighteen, this is Dispatcher Collins.” That name sounded familiar to Buck, though he couldn’t quite place why. Probably dispatcher gossip from Josh or May or Maddie. “We’ve lost connection with a minor caller in room Three-One-Eight. Line is dead.”

“Copy that, Dispatch, we’re almost there,” Eddie answered her, voice muffled by his oxygen mask. He paused in front of the doors to the third floor, his hand dropping from his radio as he stared aghast at the flames on the other side. “That is…”

“They’re not there,” Buck told him, grabbing his arm and pulling him forward. “We have to go up two more. They’re fine, Eddie.”

“But you didn’t know that, the first time,” he said, sounding horrified as he followed along. “You and Edmundo, you got here to that and…”

“There was no room Three-One-Eight anymore.”

They double-timed it to the fifth floor, the sight of the inferno they had just passed giving extra urgency to their steps. Buck didn’t remember just how much of the hospital would be gone by morning, but he knew it was going to be a large portion of it. Come to think of it, he wasn’t sure he even knew what had started it, or what the blaze was feeding on to go through fire-resisting doors like plywood on a film set.

“Y’know, I think someone cheated on the fire inspection for this place,” Buck told Eddie as they made it to the fifth-floor landing. “It should not be spreading this easily.”

“Is this really the time?” his boyfriend asked, sounding exasperated and fond in equal measure. “Where to now?”

“There was something about elevators,” he said, leading the way. “Yeah, here we go! Odds on the left. Sixty-nine, seventy-one. But seriously, Eds. They spend a lot of money on fire safety at hospitals. It should not have spread this much, this fast. Someone messed up somewhere. Probably more than one someone.”

“Dispatch said something about an explosion, and Cap said the sprinklers were knocked out,” Eddie reminded him as they burst through another set of swinging doors. “Is this Fire Marshall Buckley making an appearance? Room Eighty-two, right here.”

“And there’s our room,” Buck said, pointing at the door across from Eight-two. “Three-One-Eight, backwards.”

“LAFD!” Eddie called out as they opened the door. “Anyone in there? Parker, you here?”

“Yeah!” the little boy shouted back, coughing as the smoke started to get to him. He was crouched down in the corner, holding a wailing infant to his chest. The two men hurried to get oxygen masks on them both, Buck taking the baby from her brother so his boyfriend could pick up Parker. “Dad said I had to protect her.”

“And you did,” Eddie told him. With his freehand, he thumbed his radio. “Dispatch, this is Firefighter Diaz. We have both kids and are evacuating now.”

“Good to hear, Firefighter Diaz.”

“Oh this was an exciting first day for you, huh?” Buck told the baby girl in his arms, trying to sound calm for both frightened children. He kept the infant close to his chest, his long legs quickly carrying him to the stairwell. Eddie was right on his heels, Parker secured in his arm. “You went from somewhere warm and dark and cozy, and now it’s all fire and mayhem. But we’ll get you and your big brother outside, where it’ll be nice and safe.”

“Don’t run down the stairs, Buck. Precious cargo,” Eddie reminded him.

“Yes, love,” Buck said, rolling his eyes as he held himself back from taking the steps two at a time. To the baby, he complained, “He’s so bossy all the time. He’s lucky he’s cute.”

“I’m bossy?” The faux-offense in Eddie’s voice had him smiling. “Parker, did he just say that I was bossy?”

“Y- Yes?” Parker answered. Buck glanced over his shoulder to see the boy was glancing between them, no longer looking nearly as frightened as he had when they first found him and his sister.

“That’s what I thought he said, but that couldn’t be right, because he’s the bossy one.”

“You got bi- Er, fussy with me for how I put away your socks!”

“You didn’t even bother trying to match them up, Buck.”

“They were all black! You have two-dozen pairs of the exact same socks. There was no point in matching!”

“That doesn’t mean you just throw them all into the drawer and call it a day,” Eddie said, and Buck didn’t need to look at him to know he was shaking his head in a show of disappointment. “He didn’t even ball them up or fold them, Parker. He just stuffed them all into the drawer and said he was done.”

“I was done, it’s not my fault you didn’t like how it was done,” Buck told him. At some point during their played-up banter, the baby had ceased crying and was just looking up at him. “Remember this, baby girl. Don’t date anyone who gets uppity about their socks, no matter how cute they are.”

“Her name is Sofia,” Parker told him, sounding almost scolding even while muffled by his oxygen mask. “Not baby girl.”

“My apologies,” Buck said, thankful the kid couldn’t see his smile. “Names are important.”

“You excited to be a big brother?” Eddie asked. “You’ve done a very good job at it, so far.”

“Dad told me I had to love and protect her,” the kid said.

“And he was exactly right.”

They got to the bottom of the stairs and hurried to the exit, rushing to the triage tents. After that it was a matter of finding someone to hand off the kids, making sure their names were known and that their parents were located in the chaos. Parker grabbed little Sofia from Buck’s arms the moment he had the chance, clinging to her as tightly as he had been when they first found him.

“If you don’t like how I put away your socks,” Buck said, taking off his helmet and mask. “Then you can do it yourself.”

“I didn’t make you do it that time, you volunteered,” Eddie said, running his fingers through his now fluffed-up hair. “And don’t think I didn’t notice how all of your socks were matched and balled up, you lazy ass.”

“Nag, nag, nag,” Buck mocked. “C’mon, let’s go see if we’re needed elsewhere.”

“Lead the way. And not all of my socks are black. Some are navy blue.”

“So, Cap, did anything happen the other night?” Hen asked over the comms on their way to a scene, and from the way she sounded, she obviously already knew the answer. Buck was the one driving the truck this time, with Bobby in the captain’s seat and the others in the back. “Something embarrassing perhaps?”

“I have no idea what you’re talking about,” the captain said, keeping his eyes forward. Buck glanced at him and could see the hint of a blush forming on his face.

“Uh-huh. From what I hear, May walked in on you and Athena connecting in the kitchen.”

“Oh, God,” Eddie said, laughing. “Parental nightmare.”

“Apparently my wife has been oversharing,” Bobby grumbled.

“I just wasn’t aware that we were able to bring our gear home for recreational purposes,” she said. 

If Buck wasn’t the one driving, he’d take a rolling dive straight out the door. For four and a half years, he had managed to forget this mental image. He did not need to be reminded of it. God, he couldn’t even drink it away, either. Life just wasn’t fair at the moment.

“You’ve been playing sexy firefighter, Cap?” Ravi asked, and perhaps he had intentionally provoked the EMS Gods with the Q-word his first day. The probie clearly reveled in chaos and did not deserve the mercy Buck had been bestowing upon him.

“What makes you think I was the firefighter?” the captain asked, smugness creeping into his voice.

“Cap!” Chimney sounded simultaneously disgusted and impressed. “Was she, uh, in the midst of putting out any fires when May walked in or…?”

“Oh God, kill me now,” Buck groaned, causing the others to laugh. “If you do not drop this conversation, I will drive us off the road.”

“What’s wrong, Buck? Don’t want to think about your mom and dad doing it?” Ravi asked.

“You know what, Probie? When we get back to the station, I’m getting out the stopwatch and we’re going to work on how fast you can take apart that chainsaw.”

“I’ll shut up now.”

“That’s what I thought.”

“Does Athena ever bring home anything from her work for… Connecting purposes?” Chimney asked, and Buck really was tempted to jackknife them into the first thing he saw.

“Eddie, please kick him for me.”

“Don’t you- Ow!”

“Thank you, love.”

“You’re welcome, dear,” Eddie said.

“From the neighborhood?” Eddie quoted. They were gathered around the firetruck, waiting for Ravi to return with their drinks. Hen was telling them about Clive, her mother’s old flame, whom Buck had totally forgotten about. The man was barely around for a month before Christmas came and Buck was running away from Edmundo and them, so he didn’t think he could be blamed for his lapse in memory.

“That’s all she said. Like he was just some guy she used to see on the corner or something,” Hen said.

“She used to definitely see him, all right.”

“Right? I wasn’t just imagining that.”

“Clive and Toni were definitely a thing,” Eddie said. “And I mean, like, big time, long-lost-love kind of thing. My abuela would eat this up. She loves a good telenovela.”

“Just her?” Buck asked, grinning at him. He always did get enjoyment from watching his boyfriend enjoy himself. “No one else? Not you, maybe?”

“I watch ‘em with Christopher,” Eddie said, nose in the air. “It’s how we practice our Spanish.”

“Now explain the times I’ve found you watching them by yourself.”

“Oh, is our Eddie a fan of Spanish melodrama?” Chimney asked, leaning against the side of the truck.

“He’s a fan of all drama,” he said.

“Explains why he’s with you.”

“The real question is,” Eddie said, side-stepping the issue. Buck just smirked at him. “What happens next in the story?”

“I do have his number,” Hen said. “I could call him, just to see how he’s doing after his fall.”

“Of course,” Eddie said, always eager to encourage drama, as long as it was other people’s. Chimney nodded along, because none of them were above it, really.

“You might want to find out why they broke up first. I mean, for all you know, one of them ran away and broke the other’s heart, and trying to get them back together could just lead to disaster and pain,” Buck said, and he suddenly had three pairs of eyes staring up at him. “What?”

“Do you know something we don’t?” Chimney asked.

“Many things,” he answered. “I’m just saying, you need context.”

“Nah,” Eddie said, shaking his head. “I say you go for it, Hen. I mean, what’s the worst that could happen? They stay broken up?”

“He has a point, but just for funsies.” Chimney reached up and grabbed the sides of Buck’s head, shaking it lightly. “Should Hen meddle in her mother’s affairs?”

“Reply hazy,” Buck said, glaring at him. “Try again.”

“Okay,” the paramedic said, shaking his head like a magic 8-ball again.

“Are you going to stop this?” Hen asked Eddie.

“Nah, it’s fine,” his boyfriend said, waving it away. “Oh hey! Ravi’s back.”

“How did you manage to shave almost three minutes off of Buck’s best coffee run time?” Hen asked the probie, getting up to get her drink.

“It’s called a mobile order,” Ravi said, waiting patiently while everyone descended upon the carriers in his hand. “Walk in and the drinks were waiting.”

“This better be oat milk,” she said, taking a sip. She shook her head. “Damn it, he even got the order right.”

“Chimney, stop shaking my head and get your drink,” Buck complained, batting away the paramedic’s hands. “You’re making me dizzy.”

“You’re cleaning it up if he pukes,” Eddie said, handing his boyfriend the coffee he ordered.

“That’s what we have probies for,” the paramedic pointed out.

“Ravi suffers enough under Buck’s tutelage, he doesn’t need to do that, too.”

The first thing Eddie noticed when he woke up was that the other side of the bed was empty, the sheets and pillows cold to the touch. This immediately had him scrambling to his feet, tugging on a pair of cut-off sweatpants and hurrying down the hall. Buck wasn’t in the bathroom or Chris’ room, nor was he in the living room.

He was, however, in the kitchen.

“There you are,” Eddie said, shoulders slumping in relief. “I woke up and you were gone.”

“Oh, sorry, love,” Buck said. He was standing by the fridge, fiddling with a marker in his hand and staring at the wall-calendar that had migrated over from the apartment when he moved in. “Woke up, couldn’t go back to sleep.”

“Is everything okay?” he asked, shuffling over and wrapping his arms around his boyfriend.

“Everything’s fine,” the other man said, uncapping the marker and putting a giant red X through Wednesday, December 1st. “Everything’s fine.”

Christmas Time is Here

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Christmas was fast approaching, and Buck was suddenly understanding why Chris had been so insistent on everything needing to be perfect. Ichabod’s ominous remarks the last time he saw him was echoing in his head, and while he was going out of his way to ensure he didn’t get lost or grievously injured - and thus not end up back at the crossroads - he still wasn’t quite sure he trusted, well. Anything.

He didn’t want to leave, he really, really did not want to leave. And Eddie had been right, that day after the black out. If it didn’t matter what he did, if someone was going to be hurt no matter what choice he made, then he might as well stay. Did that make him an awful, cowardly person? Yes. Did he care? Also yes. Was he going to continue the course and feel guilty about it the entire time? Hell yes.

None of this changed the fact that the looming holiday filled him with dread. Every red X on the wall-calendar back home was another day closer to… He didn’t know. He just knew it was another day closer to something that wasn’t good. Was this how dogs and cats felt right before an earthquake?

“Remind me again why I agreed to go Christmas shopping with you?” Maddie asked, sounding very long suffering. The two of them - well, three if they counted little Jee-Yun in her stroller - were going through the mall. Rather, Buck was dragging his sister through the mall, while he bounced in and out of storefronts.

“Because you love me,” Buck said, adjusting the bags on his arms. “And also I said I’d buy you food afterwards.”

“At least one of those was a convincing argument,” she said. “I cannot believe you put this off until the last minute.”

“What? No, these are all additional Santa gifts and stocking stuffers,” Buck said, shaking his head. “Well, a couple things I wanted because they looked neat. We’re mostly here for Eddie’s.”

“You haven’t gotten Eddie a gift yet?” She sounded rightfully appalled, and so he hurried to correct her.

“I did! His was the first one, I swear! But I have to pick it up now.” He looked around. “Right there!”

He led - well, dragged - his sister into the jewelry store. Maddie edged around the displays with the stroller cautiously, as if afraid she’d breathe too hard and send them all tumbling down, and then be responsible for the damages. He couldn’t really blame her, because there were absolutely no price tags to be seen, which was never a good sign for one’s wallet. The clerk’s smile, when he told her what he was there for, went from fake customer service to real in a matter of seconds, and she hurried off to the back.

“What exactly are you getting him from here?” Maddie asked. “Is it a ring? Oh my God, are you proposing?”

“What? No,” he said, shaking his head. “We haven’t even talked about that. I mean, obviously if one of us asked, we’d say yes, but no.”

“You sound very confident about that.”

“Only an idiot would say no to a marriage proposal from Eddie Diaz,” he said, sniffing imperiously. “And I am a catch.”

“So’s rotten fish, technically,” his sister said, popping his bubble. 

“Just for that, I’m going back to that toy store we passed and buying the loudest toy I can find for Jee.”

The clerk finally came back at that moment, carrying a black box. At Maddie’s raised eyebrow, he rolled his eyes and opened the lid for her, showing the fancy Rolex he had bought his boyfriend.

“I didn’t want to get anything too crazy, because it’s Eddie. It’s waterproof up to a hundred meters, and really durable. And uh, it was made with cave exploring in mind. Y’know, in case he gets stuck underground again? It’s, uh, Oystersteel, which only Rolex makes and- Maddie?”

She was glancing between the watch and him, jaw hanging loose enough that he was honestly a little worried it might literally hit the floor. At the sound of her name, she blinked several times and shook her head.

“How much did this cost?”

“The newest Explorer Two model typically goes for eight and half grand,” the clerk helpfully told her.

“Eight and- Buck! Did you spend eight and half grand on a fancy watch for your boyfriend!?”

“Well, uh. A bit more than that, because I got it engraved…”

“Buck!”

The first thing that hit her when Shannon entered the house was just how… Festive, everything looked. It was as if the spirit of Christmas Itself had vomited all over the inside of Eddie’s living room. There was tinsel tacked onto the walls with strings of lights that were twinkling incessantly, along with an actual neighborhood of gingerbread houses with little gingerbread people that had taken over a table to the side of everything. And the Christmas tree…

Shannon was honestly amazed they had managed to get it through the front door, because it was nearly brushing the ceiling. The star on top was actually bent forward a little, because of it. There were so many lights and ornaments on its branches that someone had anchored it to the wall with twine to keep it from falling over.

“Kill me now,” Eddie begged the moment he walked into the living room and saw her. “I cannot take this anymore, Shannon.”

“What happened here?”

“Buck has corrupted our sweet baby boy,” he told her. “I thought it was bad enough dealing with him at work whenever he got his hands on a clipboard. I mean, it was cute, y’know? The bossiness, I mean. But I have spent the past week being ordered around by both him and Chris, and this is- Do you know how many times I got sent back to the store for more decorations? And that was after I had to move the tree and spin it around until they were both satisfied. By myself!”

“Dad! The popcorn’s ready!”

“And now we’re making homemade popcorn and cranberry garland,” Eddie said, eyes focusing on something in the middle-distance, looking like some prisoner of war that had just returned home. “Because Buck saw it on pinterest and thought it would be nice, and Chris agreed with him.”

“You could have said no,” Shannon pointed out.

“No I couldn’t!” he denied, ironically proving that yes, he could. “They ganged up on me, Shan! The eyes! The eyes!”

“Uh-huh, okay. Well I’m just here to drop this off,” she said, lifting up the gift bag to bring it to Eddie’s attention. “Where should it go?”

“I’ll put it in the bedroom closet,” he said, taking it from her. “Along with the rest of the hoard that both Santa and Buck have gotten him.”

“Where is Buck?”

“He was out with Maddie,” Eddie said. “He should be- Never mind, here he is.”

Buck came bursting through the front door, bags dangling from his arms and carrying a-

“Do not tell me that you got a Santa Claus lawn ornament.”

“He lights up!” his boyfriend said, grinning as he set it down. “Chris! Come look!”

Chris shuffled into the living room, smiling widely at the sight of his parents there. His eyes landed on the new lawn ornament and he looked up at Buck.

“We should get a Rudolph one, too,” he said. Buck gasped.

“You are absolutely right!”

“Okay, so this is a madhouse and I am leaving,” Shannon said, raising her hands and backing away towards the door. “I’ll see you all on Christmas.”

“No, no, Shan, please don’t go!” Eddie begged. “Don’t abandon me to these monsters!”

“Dad,” Chris whined. “We still need to do the popcorn garland.”

“You haven’t gotten around to that yet?” Buck asked, shaking his head in disapproval.

“Shannon!”

She felt absolutely no remorse when she closed the door behind her.

When Christmas finally arrived, Eddie could not be happier. It meant that the holiday insanity that had overtaken his loved ones would, hopefully, ease off and go away. He was not looking forward to taking down all the decorations, nor in finding places to put them. But the day was here, and he was going to get to see his son smiling so happily at the sight of the small mountain of presents that Buck-as-Santa had gotten him.

Eddie had started to get the dreadful suspicion that his son absolutely knew the truth about Santa and was just pretending to not break their hearts. But he wouldn’t ask, because ignorance was bliss. And then that ignorance was obliterated when Chris thanked Buck for a present from Santa.

After the moderate crisis of “oh God, our baby boy is growing up,” Buck and he exchanged their own gifts. The Rolex he got was unexpected, but not surprising. At least it wasn’t another truck. After making sure the kid was distracted, he said,

“Am I your sugar baby?”

His boyfriend choked on air, wheezing as his face turned red.

“W- What?”

“It’s just, y’know. The truck, then the HILDY, and now this? People are going to start asking questions.”

“Well, who else am I going to spend my money on if not you and Chris?”

“I don’t know, yourself? I mean, you can’t tell me your jeep doesn’t need replacing.”

“That jeep is my baby!” Buck cried, with the expression he’d probably wear if someone suggested replacing Chris. “I’ve had it ever since I left Hershey.”

“It’s like that riddle about the ax, no part of that jeep has ever been in Hershey.”

“I’ll have you know that I have taken very good care of that thing, and I haven’t had to replace nearly as much as you’re implying.”

“Whatever, just open your present.”

Buck blew a raspberry at him, but did as he was told. The present Eddie got for him was a small box in blue wrapping paper, a small red bow placed on top. He waited eagerly as his boyfriend opened it, and smiled at the face he made when he took out the necklace within.

“Eds, is this-?”

“A St. Christopher medal,” he confirmed, nodding. “The patron saint of travelers. So you don’t get lost again.”

Buck clutched it to his chest, reaching over to drag Eddie into a kiss that eventually had Chris making disgusted noises. Afterwards, when everyone was changed out of their pajamas, they piled into Eddie’s truck and made their way to where Athena and Bobby were holding the Christmas party this year. Originally, it was going to be at the Grant-Nash house, but with so many people saying they were going to be a no-show - each one making Buck pout more and more - they opted to host a celebration of the residents who had been forced out of their condemned apartment building and stuck in a hotel for the holiday.

Buck had gotten more and more agitated the closer they got to the place, his body tensing like a spring the moment they pulled into the parking lot.

“Are you okay?" Eddie asked him after they watched Chris run-off to the festivities. Shannon was already here, as were Maddie and Chimney, with Jee-Yun.

“I’m fine, love.” The lie was given away by the tremble in his voice and the way he squeezed Eddie’s hand. “All of my family’s here, or is about to be. Let’s go see if Bobby needs any help.”

Eddie let it go. Christmas, for as long as he had known Buck, had always been a touchy day for the man. Originally, no one had understood why, not until he had started confiding in others about that awful day where he had felt so alone and abandoned he had fled in a panic and lost everything. So instead of pressuring or asking questions he knew he wasn’t going to get the answer to, Eddie followed him to where their captain was cooking up a storm fit to feed an army.

Buck’s smile became less and less forced, turning more real with every passing moment spent celebrating the day with his family. At some point, he ended up holding Jee-Yun and refused to set her down, even as he continued to help Bobby cook. Eddie managed to slip away from grill duties, sitting with Shannon and Maddie as they gossiped like old hens. Ravi arrived at one point, followed by Albert, and then Hen and Karen.

Eventually, they all sat around the table, enjoying Bobby and Buck’s cooking while the kids made new friends.

“God, I thought Twenty-Twenty was bad,” Hen complained. “But this year felt like it was worse? Like, how was that possible?”

“It wasn’t all bad,” Shannon said.

“My boyfriend got shot,” Eddie pointed out. “It sucked.”

“I didn’t say it was all good, either.”

“Maybe next year will be better?” Ravi offered, only to cower in his seat when everyone glared at him.

“Stop provoking fate,” Buck said, throwing a roll at him.

“Stop throwing food,” Athena scolded.

“Wait, hey, maybe the psychic can tell us,” Chimney chimed in, leading forward across the table. “Hey Buck, how bad is next year going to be?”

“Hell if I know, I wasn’t here for it,” Buck said, shrugging. The odd remark got him several confused looks, and several that were perhaps too knowing.

“What does that mean?” Shannon asked.

“Okay, I have a confession to make,” Buck said, sitting up straight and drawing in a breath. “I’m not psychic.”

“Bullshit!” Albert and Chimney cried out together.

“I’m not! I’m, uh. I’m actually from the future. Uh…” He pulled out his phone and squinted at the screen. “Uh, eleven- Ten hours? No- Tonight. I’m from tonight.”

“Tonight!?” four people shouted together. The others all looked between Bobby, Athena, Eddie and Maddie, confusion evident on their faces.

“It’s today? This Christmas is that Christmas?” Eddie asked. Buck nodded. He had known that Edmundo hadn’t looked much older than him, but to find out that he had been so much closer to being that person than he had even realized. It felt very much like dodging a bullet.

“I’m sorry, I’m very confused,” Ravi said, interrupting his thoughts. “Everyone thought you were psychic, but you’re saying that you’re actually a time traveler?”

“Yes,” Buck said, nodding again.

“How?” Chimney demanded.

“Why?” Hen demanded.

“What?” Albert added.

“I miss B-shift,” Ravi moaned, Karen reaching over to pat him on the shoulder.

Buck glanced at Eddie, who squeezed his hand comfortingly, and then at Maddie and Bobby and Athena, who all nodded in turn. He let out a sigh and said,

“I want to start by saying that I’m not crazy…”

Buck opened his eyes and saw stars, which made no sense. After the Christmas party, where he finally explained to everyone else the true reasons for why he sometimes knew things he shouldn’t, they had gone home. Eddie and he had clung to each other for a bit, and then gone to bed, where Buck had stayed awake for as long as he could, watching the numbers on the alarm clock ticking forward.

And now he was waking up, standing in the crossroads with a blanket of stars above him.

“Howdy, friend,” Ichabod said behind him.

“How did I get here?” he demanded. “I didn’t get lost, I didn’t get hurt, I- Oh God, nothing happened while I was asleep, did it? Eddie and Chris, they’re-?”

“They’re fine. Well, for now.”

“What the hell does that mean?”

“It’s Christmas time,” the entity said. “The exact same Christmas, in fact. The exact same time!”

“So, what, I have to make the choice now?” Buck asked. He had been going out of his way to avoid having to make the choice, but he hadn’t expected to be kidnapped in his sleep for it. “Well, okay, fine, my choice is-”

“Choice?” Ichabod sounded amused. “At what point did I give the impression that I was giving you a choice about anything?”

“I- I- What?” Had he been so afraid for nothing? Had he been tearing himself up with guilt over nothing?

“You came here that very first night, remember? All ‘oh no my friend is leaving me’ and ‘I’m all alone.’ You remember that?”

“I do…”

“And then I asked you what you wanted, and you said you wanted to fix whatever broke your family, but that you didn’t know what it was, or when it was. Remember that?”

“Yes.”

“I want you to understand, Buck, that I don’t choose to ask and give people what they want. I am, by my very nature, compelled to do it,” Ichabod said, pacing a circle around him. “A lost soul finds their way here and I have to ask them what they want, and then they have to tell me what they want. Their truest desire at that moment, dragged out from the deepest parts of themselves.

“That’s not to say that I can’t have a little fun with it. I have gotten very, very good over my time stuck here, finding ways to twist things to be as entertaining for myself as possible while still giving them what they wanted. How they phrase it is very helpful for that, sometimes. So when you said you didn’t know when things broke…”

“You sent me back in time,” Buck finished the thought for him, twisting around to keep his eyes on the entity.

“I scooped out your mind and your soul and stuffed them into your younger self, the morning of your first day on the job,” the entity said, sounding proud of himself. That would explain that massive headache Buck had suffered when he woke up, and the way he had muscle memories he really shouldn’t have. “Like… Like pouring one glass of water into another glass of water.”

“Okay, but that doesn’t explain what-”

“The problem with pouring one glass of water into another,” Ichabod interrupted, grabbing him by the shoulders and turning him around. “Is that there is always an empty glass left behind…”

Buck gasped in horror at what he saw. Automatically, without thought, he ran to the body slumped onto the ground right next to the jeep. He reached down to feel for a pulse, but his fingers just went straight through their neck. His neck. It was him laying there, blue eyes wide open and seeing nothing. The chest - his chest - was rising and falling, so at least they - he? - wasn’t dead.

Just… Not all there.

“I- I don’t… Ichabod, what the hell?”

“An example of just how… Not fixed anything is,” the entity said, coming to stand over them. “I’ll admit, I wasn’t really thinking ahead. I was more interested in the chance to have some fun. But then Eddie - the other Eddie, the one you left behind, showed up looking for you and I realized… Well, I realized that I had really messed up.”

“You messed up?” Buck repeated. It was overwhelming. He was staring down at himself, the version of himself who had come here on that awful Christmas day and abandoned everyone. It was a shell, a- a- an empty glass. “What do you mean, you messed up?”

“You told me you wanted to fix things, but-”

“But I haven’t been,” he said. “I’ve just been… Keeping them from breaking.”

“Exactly. Which means I haven’t actually given you what you wanted.”

“B- But, what does that…?”

“I would simply… Erase that timeline, make it a non-issue, but-”

“I’m sorry, erase? You can erase timelines?”

“Well, not just any timeline, which is the problem. I can only erase the ones I helped make. Like all those branches that formed from you dying.”

Buck stared up at him in horror. He had assumed that if Edmundo and his timeline were still there that there was the chance that the ones where he had died - the one where he had killed himself - were also still around, but to hear Ichabod just casually talk about erasing them from reality, was just… There were no appropriate words.

“So, the solution to both our problems is obvious, I think,” Ichabod continued. “I stuff you back into that body and send you on your merry way to Eddie- Well, you call him Edmundo now, right? I send you back to Edmundo and all the others you left behind, let you try again at actually fixing things.”

“And- And Eddie? Chris? The ones I’d be abandoning if I did that?”

“I erase them, obviously. Trim the branch like all the others. You can’t abandon them if they no longer exist.”

“W- What? No!” He got to his feet, and got into Ichabod’s space, finger in his face. “No! I- I will not do it! I refuse! And I refuse to let you just… Just… Erase Eddie and Chris and the rest of my family from existence!”

“You’re not really understanding how this works, are you?” the entity said, entirely unfazed by his outburst. “You don’t have a choice, I don’t have a choice. You came here and told me what you wanted-”

“This isn’t what I wanted!”

“And that is exactly the problem!” Ichabod shouted, and the suddenness of him raising his voice had Buck nearly tripping backwards. “You wanted to fix things and all we did was break it some more! And now we’re both stuck cleaning up the mess!”

“A mess that you made!” Buck shouted back.

“And I have acknowledged my fault in the matter,” the entity said. “But fault doesn’t matter. All that matters is that you told me a want, and I have left it unfulfilled.”

No, no, no. Buck couldn’t let this happen. He couldn’t let an entire version of his family be erased - again! - and he couldn’t just abandon them and he- No, no, no. This wasn’t what he wanted.

He didn’t want this.

He didn’t want this.

He didn’t-

“Want,” he whispered aloud. “Ichabod, you have to give me what I want, right? You have to?”

“That is exactly what I’ve been saying. It’s the entire problem here.”

“Then I’m telling you my deepest desire, right now. The thing I want most in the world at this moment,” Buck said, excitement bubbling in his stomach. “I want you to find a way that I- That I can be with both Eddies, with both Chrises. I want you to find a way that I can fix things over there, without abandoning anyone over here.”

Ichabod’s face twisted into something ugly, something mean. His eyes turned black- No, they became actual pits in his face, filled with crawling shadows. There was suddenly wind in the crossroads, where every time before it had been calm and still like tranquil water. It tore at Buck’s clothes and at his hair, threatening to bowl him over.

“That is not how this works, Buck,” the entity snarled, looming over him. Had he gotten taller in the past few seconds? His hat seemed to be brushing against the sky. “I ask you what you want, you tell me what you want, I give you what you want.”

“And I told you-!”

“No!” Ichabod roared, and there was thunder in the distance to go with it. “You do not get to come here and twist the rules to your fancy! You do not get to-!”

“I don’t care!” Buck shouted back, refusing to be cowed. This was too damn important. “I told you what I wanted! Now you have to give it to me!”

“No!”

“Yes!”

The entity glared at him, thunder clapping in the distance and wind tearing at Buck’s clothes. For long, long moments, he was certain he was about to be smote from existence, to go wherever the erased timelines had gone. And then, finally, the wind calmed down and the thunder stopped, and Ichabod’s eyes returned to normal.

“Fine,” he said, sounding stiff. “Fine, you’ll get what you want. Though I can’t give it to you myself.”

“Who then?” Buck demanded. In response, the entity raised his hand and from the sky came… A butterfly? It was large and blue, and Buck was certain he recognized it from somewhere. “I- I think that’s the same butterfly that was there every time I stopped the truck bombing.”

“It does love chaos and drama,” Ichabod said, sounding almost fond. The butterfly landed on his finger and he tilted his ear at it for a moment, as if listening. “Well don’t complain too much, you’re the one who’s been nagging at me about this mess.”

"I’m sorry,” Buck said, not wanting to interrupt but needing to know. “Are you talking to it?”

“Yes,” the entity said.

“Does it… Talk back?”

“Yes,” he said again, and then to the butterfly, “I don’t want to do it myself, that’s why I-... The faster you do it, the faster you can go back to… Thank you.”

The butterfly flapped its wings and lifted off from his finger, fluttering across the space to land on Buck’s nose. His eyes went cross trying to focus on it, and it had far more weight to it than he thought any butterfly should.

“So, uh, what now?”

“Now you just let it happen,” Ichabod said, dark amusement in his words. “And scream, if you need to.”

“W- What?”

And suddenly, all Buck could see was blue.

And all he could feel was pain.

Chapter End Notes

Jiminy Cricket, this was a long one. Uh... Tomorrow will be fun. For some people.

The Present is a Gift

Buck awoke with a jerk, gasping for breath. His eyes - his incredibly dry eyes - were burning, and he rubbed at them and blinked until his vision blurred with tears. And his head, God, did it ache. It was like someone had stuffed an entire orchestra in there, and they were now playing that overture that came complete with a cannon section.

“He does flop like a fish,” he heard Ichabod say, and he pushed himself up to a sitting position. Immediately, his vision momentarily blacked out as the blood started flowing elsewhere. His limbs all tingled, and one of his legs was asleep. Shaking his head to clear it, which was the absolute worst decision, he realized there was something wet on his face.

“Is my nose bleeding?” he asked, reaching up to wipe at it and finding that yes, it indeed was. “Why is my nose bleeding?”

“We’ll worry about that later,” the entity said. “What do you remember?”

“Everything,” he said. “Up to and including getting brainfucked by what I am assuming is the literal embodiment of the Butterfly Effect.”

Said butterfly was perched on his knee, and Buck had the feeling that it was silently judging him for something. The language he used? The way he phrased it? He didn’t know and didn’t care.

“Good, good.”

“It worked then?” he asked. “There’s, uh. Two of me now?”

“Yes,” the entity grumbled.

“Then… Where’s the other me?”

“He’s waking up in his bed,” Ichabod said, and the smile he wore was concerningly pleased. “Best not to be concerned about him, or any of them. They’re all out of your reach now.”

“But it worked, though? They aren’t going to be erased, they’re not going to wake up to find me missing?”

“I assure you, Buck, that there will be a version of you in both branches. It’s what you wanted, after all.”

“Good,” he said, nodding to himself. “That’s… That’s good.”

It didn’t taste like victory, or if it did, then victory tasted an awful lot like the blood that had gotten into his mouth when he licked his dry lips. It felt like he was leaving everyone without saying goodbye again, although he supposed that wasn’t really the case. There was another Buck there, a Buck that wasn’t leaving them.

A Buck that would get to stay with Eddie and Chris, that would get to stay with his family.

“So what now?” he asked Ichabod, using the jeep to pull himself to his feet. The butterfly took flight, fluttering over to land on the entity’s hat. Buck himself swayed for a moment, leaning heavily against the door, because these legs had not been used for a very long time. “I seem to remember my jeep being out of-”

The vehicle rumbled to life behind him, startling him enough that he nearly tripped over himself to get away.

“Never mind,” he said, shaking his head. “I forgot who I was talking to.”

“That does so often seem to be a running theme with you,” Ichabod said. “Now, you should probably get in and go.”

“What, you’re that eager to get rid of me?”

“Yes.”

Buck snickered to himself as he opened the door and climbed into the driver’s seat. Digging into the glove compartment, he found a paper napkin to wipe away the remnants of the nosebleed. As he did so, an awful, horrible thought occurred to him.

“Oh my God,” he said.

“What?” the entity asked, cocking his head to the side. The butterfly didn’t even move, sticking to its spot on the brim of his hat.

“I have to break up with Taylor.”

“Good luck with that.”

“Do I just… Tell her that I don’t want to be with her anymore or…?”

“I don’t know,” Ichabod said, shrugging. “And I don’t care.”

 “You are of no help,” he said, slamming the door closed. Pulling the jeep around, he awkwardly waved before leaving the way he had come so long ago. Eventually, much like that Halloween night many years before, the crossroads faded from his rearview mirror, along with the black-eyed not-demon and the blue butterfly. He didn’t remember how far he had driven in those twelve hours before ending up with Ichabod, but he knew that he should have been farther away from the city than he currently found himself.

For the briefest of moments as he drove into the city, he debated on where to go first. His phone was dead, as it had been long before he had gotten lost, and so he wasn’t actually sure what time it was, or the date. He should probably go to his loft, change and shower and charge his phone, but that place had never really been anything more than a place to hide from the world and hang his hat. It was even less than that, now.

So he went to one of the two places that had always been home, long before any time-travel shenanigans.

The journey to the Diaz residence was still the same, even now. The drive took him past what was his apartment, and he resisted the urge to pull over and see Albert, because Albert did not live there. Instead he continued on, taking the turn that placed him on Eddie’s street.

The first obvious difference he saw was the truck. It was the stupid truck that Eddie had impulse-bought years before, during his fight clubbing days. For a moment after he parked next to it, Buck could only sit there and stare as the enormity of what he had done hit him. This was not the Eddie he had woken up so many times with kisses, not the one he had chased down on the beach and thrown sand at, not the one he had bullied into learning how to cook.

That Eddie was out of his reach, now. Along with that Chris, and that Maddie, and everyone else. But he took solace in the knowledge that they weren’t alone. He was with him, sort of, even if he himself felt so alone at that moment. He spent several minutes letting himself mourn what he had lost before stepping out and making his way up the path to the front door.

There wasn’t even a question in his mind about whether or not he should knock. He flipped through his keys - pausing to stare at the loft key, having not seen it in years - until he found the right one and let himself in. The inside was dark, and quiet, with not a single Christmas decoration hanging on the walls. His hand automatically found the light switch and he flicked it on, letting out a shuddering breath at the changes that he saw.

Gone was everything that had been his, gone was every sign that he had lived here. Because he had never lived here, because all of his things were at the loft, just as they had been for the past two or three years.

Letting his feet guide him, he went down the hall and immediately checked Chris’ room. The bed was empty, he noticed, so he assumed he was with- No, not Shannon. This Shannon was dead. Probably Abuela, then. Continuing on, he went to Eddie’s room to find that the bed in there was empty, too.

Frowning, he turned to go back to the living room, and then had to duck the bat swinging for his head.

“Who the fuck are you!?” Edmundo shouted, swinging again.

“Eddie!” Buck cried, raising his arms to protect his head. “It’s me!”

“B- Buck?” The other man lowered the bat, peering at him in disbelief. God, he looked somehow even worse than he had at the crossroads. Not only were the bags under his eyes still there, and even more evident in proper lighting, but there were tear stains all over his face. It looked like he had cried himself to sleep, and not too long ago, either. “Evan?”

“Yeah, lo- Eds. It’s me.”

The bat clattered to the ground, and he suddenly had his arms filled with the other man. He grunted with the impacted, stumbling back a bit. There was something soaking into the fabric of his shirt, and it took him a moment to realize that the other man was crying. Crying so hard that he was shaking with it.

“You came back,” he sobbed. “You came back.”

“I did, I did,” Buck said, wrapping his arms around the other man and letting his head thump against the wall. “I’m sorry for leaving that day. I’m sorry, I’m so sorry, for not being here, for- For abandoning everyone.”

It took a while for Edmundo to calm down, a long, long while. Eventually, however, he stopped crying and clinging enough that Buck could maneuver them into the living room and onto the couch. The entire time, though, the other man kept touching him. Like he was afraid Buck would disappear if he wasn’t.

“How long has it been?” he asked. “Since…?”

“A month,” the other man said. He was pressed into his side, gripping tightly to his hand. “A month since you- Since Christmas. A few hours since I talked to myself and then your ghost at that… Wherever the fuck that place was.”

“You talked to Eddie?” That would explain the man’s sudden crusade for therapy and communication and all of that, if he had seen the state of Edmundo. But what the hell was he even doing there to begin with?

A question Buck would never be able to ask him, now.

“He was a dick,” Edmundo said.

“We’re never very kind to ourselves, I’ve learned.”

“He also wasn’t wrong. I’m not fine. I haven’t been fine for a very long time, and I was lying to myself, and… And I pushed you away.”

“I ran away, Eds,” Buck said, shaking his head. “Don’t take credit for my stupid decisions.”

“Did you mean it, what you said there?” Edmundo asked. “You love me?”

“I do,” he whispered, closing his eyes.

“But you love that other Eddie, too.”

“Yes.”

“Why did you come back?”

“Because you needed me,” Buck said, opening his eyes and turning his head to look at him. “I promised to have your back, and I promised that I wouldn’t leave Christopher. And I was breaking those promises.”

“We should probably talk,” Edmundo said. “About what this means, about what we’re going to do. Because… Because I’m not okay, and I don’t know how to be okay.”

“It’s okay to not be okay. But yeah, we probably should.”

“Later, though. Right now I just… I just want to sit here with my best friend again.”

“Okay,” he said, squeezing his hand. “Then that’s what we’ll do. I was looking for an excuse to put off talking to Taylor, anyways.”

“Oh?”

“Yeah. I’ve never broken up with anyone before.”

The statement got a burst of wet laughter from Edmundo, and the sound of it settled something in Buck’s heart. This place had been his home once, and while it wasn’t quite his home now, it could be again.

It could be again.

Buck blinked awake, his head feeling strangely… Light. He’d had the weirdest, strangest dream. There was a man in it, creepy and dressed all in black, with eyes that were just as dark. There was a butterfly in it, wings so blue they seemed to glow. And… And there was himself. He had seen himself, laying there as he talked to the man in black.

But what had they been talking about?

“Shit!”

He bolted upright, horrified that he had forgotten. It was his first day at the station! His first day as an actual firefighter after getting through the academy. He had been so excited yesterday, how the hell could he have forgotten?

Actually, more importantly, where the hell was he? This was not his bedroom at the apartment he shared with Felix and them. He had never even seen this room before. On the bedside table was someone’s necklace, and a picture of a kid in glasses. Someone’s phone was beside it, but he didn’t recognize it so he assumed it belonged to whoever’s room this was.

“What the hell?” he asked aloud, before shaking his head. Pants, he needed his pants, where were- There were no pants. His clothes were nowhere to be seen, along with his phone and his wallet and his keys. Maybe they were in one of the other rooms? Yeah, that could be it, that would make sense. He didn’t remember stripping on his way to the bed, but then again, he didn’t remember ending up in this bed.

There was obviously at least one kid here, or so he could assume, so he wrapped the sheet around himself before leaving the bedroom. He was immediately struck by the way it looked like Christmas had vomited all over the place. Don’t get him wrong, he loved the festive season, but it was a few months early for this. It wasn’t even Halloween, yet.

Buck crept down the hall, peeking curiously into rooms. He bypassed what looked like the kid’s room, based on the decorations on the closed door, and the bathroom. There were no signs of his clothes anywhere, not even in the living room that was almost overwhelmingly Christmas, with lights and tinsel tacked to the wall. He appreciated the tree, though. Whoever picked it out and decorated it had good taste.

Noise, and the smell of food, drew him into the kitchen where the most beautiful man he had ever seen was standing at the stove. He was in cut-off sweatpants and wearing a t-shirt that was at least a size too big, which was impressive since the man was very much not small looking.

“Oh, hey! You’re awake!” the man said, smiling brightly at him. “I was going to bring you breakfast in bed. The bacon should be done in a bit.”

“I- Thanks?” Buck wasn’t ever quite sure what the etiquette was for mornings after. He typically managed to avoid those, not wanting to overstay his welcome. “You didn’t need to. Uh, I’ll just… I’m just trying to find my keys and phone and everything?”

“Your keys are in the bowl by the door,” the other man said, frowning at him. “And your phone’s by the bed.”

“And my pants?”

“In the hamper…”

“Okay, then I’ll get them and go.”

“Buck.” The other man knew his name, and he couldn’t even remember his. God, he couldn’t even do this right. “Go where?”

“To work,” he explained, shifting on his feet and clutching the sheet closer to himself. “It’s uh, my first day at my new job? I- I didn’t really intend to do something like this the night before- I don’t even remember doing it. Like, I’m sure it was wonderful, but uh… I should really get going? Because it’s my first day and I don’t want to be late and-”

“Buck.” His name again, this time with a level of concern that he wasn’t used to hearing from anyone except his sister. The man turned off the burners on the stove and turned to face him completely. The way he was staring had dread coiling in his stomach. “What year is it?”

“Uh, Twenty Seventeen?” What the hell kind of question was that?

“It’s Twenty Twenty-Two next week,” the other man said, and, oh. That was… That was. “Stay there, don’t move, I- I’m going to, uh. Fuck, uh. I need to call Bobby, and- And Maddie…”

“Maddie? My sister? You know her? Y- You’ve talked to her?”

“Yeah, she- Fuck, just- Fuck.”

Buck watched him rush out, feeling so very lost. That couldn’t be the right year, obviously the very, very beautiful man was wrong. Or crazy. Right? Right. There was no way he had lost four years of his life. But the man, whose name he still didn’t know, had obviously known him. He had recognized him, and had not been surprised or annoyed by having him in his home.

Letting his curiosity get the better of him, and trying to distract himself from the panic threatening to well up inside, he looked around. It was a cozy looking kitchen, he thought, with some kind of fancy coffee maker on the counter. There were already a pair of mugs sitting by it, one that said #1 Dad and the other with the LAFD emblem on it. On the wall was a calendar, flipped open to December, the days marked out with giant red Xs. There were pictures stuck to the fridge, a child’s drawings, and he shuffled closer to look at them.

The first one his eyes landed on stole his breath, and did not give it back.

It was a family of stick figures drawn in crayon, three tall and one short. Each figure was labeled: Mom, for the one on the left, followed by Dad. The short one was labeled Me, and the last one was labeled Bucky. It even had a little pink splotch on the head, where his birthmark would be. 

He felt so much love for this little stick figure family, he was realizing. He felt so much love for the man that had just been in here, so much that it was nearly all-consuming, and he didn’t even know who he was.

“No, I don’t know what happened!” the other man suddenly shouted from down the hall, causing Buck to jump. He crept out of the kitchen and back down the hall, where he found the stranger pacing in front of the bed. “He just- He doesn’t remember, okay? I don’t know what happened, but he just doesn’t-... Okay, okay, yeah. We’ll meet you there, and-... You’ll call her for me? Thanks.”

The man ended the call and sat on the bed, holding his head in his hands. He looked scared, and troubled, and so Buck followed his instincts. He sat next to him and awkwardly patted his arm.

“It’s, uh. It’s going to be okay?” he tried. It at least got the man to bark out a laugh, even if it was edging towards hysteria.

“Yeah, sure,” the man said. He let out a sigh. “We’ll get dressed and then meet Bobby and your sister at the hospital. You have clothes in the closet, and in the drawers.”

“Okay. Okay. So… I live with you?”

“Yeah, Buck, you do.”

“And you have a kid!” he said, gesturing at the picture beside the bed. “I, uh. I love kids.”

“I know,” the other man said, a hint of a smile appearing on his face despite everything. It brought to mind images of the sun peeking out from behind clouds. “His name is Christopher.”

“Christopher,” he repeated. “And, uh. Who’s Bobby?”

“Our captain at the station.”

“Oh! He’s Captain Nash?” He knew that at least, that was something. Now for the question he kept putting off, because he knew how much it was going to hurt hearing it. “And, uh… Who are you?”

“Eddie,” the other man said, closing his eyes.

“Is that short for Eduardo?”

“No. No it is not.”

A Stranger in a Familiar Land

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

When Buck finally charged and turned on his phone for the first time in a month - or over four years, depending on your perspective - he was greeted by an influx of messages, both text and voice. They kept coming, each one more frantic than the last, and he finally threw his phone back down and opted to leave it be until it was done chiming. All of that could wait, even the ones from Taylor.

Especially the ones from Taylor.

He had spent the hours before on the couch with Edmundo, simply sitting there. Eventually the other man had fallen back asleep, perhaps the first restful sleep he’d had since Buck had run away, judging from appearances. Buck himself hadn’t been very tired, though, and so spent the time until sunrise trying to figure out his next steps and trying not to think about Eddie.

Once, he had looked at Eddie and the sight of him had made him think of Edmundo with painful longing. Now, he looked at the sleeping Edmundo, and he could only wish that Eddie was there with him. That wasn’t fair to either of them, however, so he did his best to push those thoughts away when they cropped up.

When the sun had fully risen, Buck carefully slithered out from beneath Edmundo, doing his best not to wake the man. Afterwards, he borrowed a charger for his phone and set about making breakfast while it charged. Now, he was doing his best to ignore his phone as yet another notification finally came through, focusing on flipping the pancakes he had made.

“You’re here,” Edmundo said, sounding relieved as he shuffled into the kitchen, rubbing the sleep from his eyes. And maybe, one day, he’ll be able to think of him as just Eddie again. But that day wasn’t today, and it probably wasn’t going to be any time soon. “I woke up and I thought I dreamt it.”

“I needed to charge my phone,” Buck said, pointing his spatula at it as it chimed with yet another missed call or new text or what-the-fuck-ever. “And I figured, y’know. You probably haven’t had a proper breakfast since…”

“I, uh. I’ve actually been learning to cook?” he said, looking sheepish. “Better, I mean. Learning to cook better. I’ve had time now, since I’m working a nine-to-five at the dispatch center.”

“Dispatch?” He could see it, actually. Edmundo could absolutely be the dependable voice on the other side of the line, keeping a person calm until help arrived.

“I’m the department’s liaison, or whatever. Answer phones, file reports, post traffic and safety updates.”

“Wait. To Twitter?” He wasn’t actually a dispatcher, then. “You’re a social media manager. Edmundo Diaz is a social media manager.”

“Shut up.”

“You, Mr. Technophobe, transferred to be a social media manager?” That was hilarious, but also concerning, because, “Did I end up back in the wrong timeline?”

“Shut up,” the other man said again. “We should probably tell the others that you’re back. I should definitely let Chris know.”

“He’s going to hate me.”

“He didn’t hate me,” Edmundo said. “He didn’t hate Shannon.”

“That’s… Yeah.” It was a good point, it was a very good point. “Fuck, what am I even going to tell the others? The truth is definitely not an option.”

“They’re going to notice something happened while you were gone. You’re… Different.”

“Time does that to a person.”

“How long was it for you?” Edmundo asked. “You asked how long it was for me, but you never said how long it had been for you.”

Buck didn’t answer right away. Instead, he turned off the burner and plated the pancakes, before making the other man grab everything else they needed. It wasn’t until they were sitting at the dining table, Edmundo starting to eat, that he finally answered.

“Four years, and change,” he said, poking at his food with a fork. He had been starving just a moment ago, but now his appetite was gone.

Edmundo had been about to take a bite, but now he let the fork drop to his plate as he stared bug-eyed at Buck.

“Four years?” he repeated. “It’s been four years for you?”

“And change.” Four years, three months, and a couple weeks, technically.

“That’s… That’s longer than I’ve even known you.”

“I know,” Buck said, trying not to think about it. Trying very, very hard not to focus on what he had lost. He hadn’t abandoned them, hadn’t left them, because this time there was a version of him back home. Knowing that didn’t do anything for the hollow pit in his stomach, however.

“What changed?” Edmundo asked. “What made you decide to come back now, when you wouldn’t before?”

“You and Chris need me.”

“We needed you before. So why did you choose to come back now?” When no answer was forthcoming, he asked again, more agitated, “Why did you choose to come back?”

Buck didn’t look at him, didn’t look anywhere other than at his food, which he was slowly tearing apart with his fork.

“You didn’t choose to come back, did you?” The words were coated with hoarfrost.

“...No.”

“Something forced you to come back, didn’t it?” Edmundo pushed his chair back and stood, leaning onto the table as he glared at him. “Would you have chosen to come back, if actually given the choice? Or were you going to stay with that other Eddie? With your other family?”

Buck didn’t answer, and that was answer enough for them both.

After breakfast, which had turned into a cold enough affair that Buck could have been convinced he was spending another winter in Hershey with his parents, they started the process of letting everyone else know of his return. Edmundo called Athena and asked her to come over, while Buck sat on the couch and looked everywhere but him. The half hour that it took the sargeant to arrive was tense, Edmundo once again angry and Buck once again guilty, and neither of them talking to the other.

It didn’t mean that Edmundo wasn’t in his space, however. Because even while rightfully pissed, he seemed reluctant to test his fear that Buck could disappear again at any time if he wasn’t touching him somehow.

Frantic banging on the door broke the silence, and when Edmundo answered it, a uniformed Athena Grant came rushing through. She didn’t seem at all different from the other Athena. She looked the exact same, in fact, and that part was startling to realize.

“I saw his jeep out front,” she was saying. “Is he here? Did he-? Buck!”

He was bull rushed by the shorter woman the moment her eyes landed on him, her arms wrapping around him and squeezing him as tight as she could. It brought tears to his eyes, the evidence that someone here other than Edmundo and Chris had missed him.

“Hi, ‘Thena,” he said, awkwardly patting her back.

“Where the hell have you been!?” she demanded, stepping back to glare at him. After everything, an angry Athena Grant still scared him more than a raging not-demon.

“I… I don’t remember,” he lied, glancing over her head at Edmundo, who had shut the door and was now watching with his arms crossed over his chest.

“You don’t remember?” she repeated, hands going to her hips.

“Nope!” he said, doing his best to smile believably. “I remember, uh, Christmas… I remember getting into the jeep on Christmas, and then, uh… Then I was here.”

“I’m assuming you haven’t gotten checked out at the hospital yet?”

“No,” Buck said. “Do I have to?”

“Yes!” the officer snapped at him. “You have been missing for a month! A month that you just said you didn’t remember. There’s no telling what could have happened to you in that time.”

“I’ll take him,” Edmundo volunteered.

“No, we’ll take him,” Athena said. “Get to the damn car.”

“Yes, ma’am,” Buck said.

The days that followed were more painful than not for Buck. The parade of familiar faces, of people that had once been his family, only served to ram home just how much he had actually lost with this plan. Knowing that it was definitely worth it, that he would have lost everyone in the other timeline anyway, did not help the hurt at all. There were times, even, that he felt irrationally jealous of the Buck who got to wake up next to Eddie, and then felt stupid because he was being jealous of himself and this had been his choice.

Even if it hadn’t really been a choice at all.

A glimmer of brightness in everything was the discovery that Maddie and Chimney had come back in his absence. He wasn’t sure how that had happened - there was something about Hen having told Chimney he was missing, who had in turn managed to somehow let Maddie know - but he wasn’t looking that gift horse in the mouth. His sister was looking better than she had in that farewell video, or at least he thought she was. It had been so long since he had seen this version of her that it was hard to be sure.

The first interaction with Chimney at the hospital Athena dragged him to, where everyone had flocked after the news of his return spread, was awkward. The man seemed simultaneously happy to see him, and also extremely anxious about him being there. It wasn’t until the paramedic had managed to get him alone that Buck understood why.

“Listen, man, I am so sorry for how I acted,” he said. “I am so sorry for- For everything, really.”

“For how you-? Oh!” Right, the punch. Buck had honestly not given it much thought for a while now. Sure, it had taken him a bit to get over it, and it had him flinching away from the other Chimney for those first few weeks, but now? “Don’t worry about it, man. Water under the bridge.”

“Are… Are you sure?”

“Positive!” he said, giving the man a friendly slap on the shoulder that turned into a bruising grip. “But if you ever lay a hand like that on Maddie, or anyone else I care about? While they might manage to find your body, they’ll never be able to prove what happened.” He smiled brightly at the man. “Got it?”

Chimney nodded frantically, and Buck left him alone to dwell on the threat.

The most painful part of it all had been seeing Christopher again. Edmundo had gone and picked him up while Buck was being poked and prodded and pestered, and the boy just about ran over five nurses, two doctors, and an underpaid janitor to get to his side.

“You came back,” the boy said, clinging to him, and Buck felt such guilt for having ever gone away, for becoming yet another person who left him. 

“I did,” he said, and ignored the way his voice broke with the words.

“Where did you go?”

“I, uh… I don’t remember. The doctors think it was something called a fugue state,” he explained. “It’s uh, it’s where something happens and your brain just decides it’s time for a vacation. And so I got a bit lost.”

“But dad found you?”

“Yes he did,” Buck said, glancing at Edmundo over Chris’ head. It was even true, technically, and so for the boy’s sake - and everyone else’s - it’s what they’d go with.

“Good. I didn’t want you to be alone somewhere.”

One day, he’ll figure out what he had done to deserve the treasure that was Christopher in his life.

Buck took three days before finally talking to Taylor. It was a combination of just absolutely dreading the imminent conversation and being so busy with literally everyone else demanding his time. Most of those three days were spent at the Diazes’ house, where both Christopher and Edmundo pulled out every tool in their arsenal to convince him to spend just one more night on their couch. And he didn’t fight very hard against it, because he didn’t want to leave, either.

Spending the nights on the couch were agony enough, and he was not looking forward to trying to sleep alone in his old bed.

But on the third day, he finally went and met Taylor at his loft. Taylor, who had apparently not been informed of his return. Taylor, who had said she loved him just a month before Christmas. Taylor, who in another timeline had done her best to convict him in the court of public opinion for what he had done to Doug.

“I think you should have kept the bracelet,” she told him when she arrived. She came with wine, because of course she did, and looked at him oddly when he didn’t want any. “Where did you go?”

“I, uh. Don’t remember,” he said, continuing with the lie. “The doctors called it a fugue state.”

“I’ve heard of those. I think Agatha Christie had one,” she said.

“Yeah, I think so, too. Listen, Taylor…”

“Yeah?” The look on his face must have told her everything she needed to know, because she slammed the wine down. “No.”

“Taylor…”

“No! Don’t even- Are you kidding me? You disappear for a month without a word, and now that you’re back you’re…”

“I think the fact that I disappeared for a month should really have been a clue that things weren’t working,” he pointed out. “Because they weren’t. I don’t think they ever did.”

“You said you loved me.”

“I lied,” he said, and felt awful for it, even if it was the truth. “I lied to you, I lied to myself. Just like we have spent our entire relationship lying to each other. I wasn’t in a good place when this relationship started, and I wasn’t in a good place a month ago, and I’m not in a good place now.”

“So, what? It’s you, not me?”

“It’s us,” he said. “It’s always been us, because this? The two of us? It’s toxic. I was so afraid of everyone leaving me that I was clinging to anyone that was willing to stay, and that’s no basis for a healthy relationship. And I’ve ignored everything you’ve said about me, everything you’ve done, because I thought this was the best I was going to get. But I deserve better than this, even if it just means being alone.”

“I thought we were happy together,” she bit out.

“I’ve never really been happy when I’m with you.”

“If this is how you were like with your other relationships, no wonder you’ve always been left behind,” Taylor practically snarled, grabbing her purse and her bottle of wine. “Good luck finding someone else willing to tolerate your needy ass!”

The door slammed shut behind her, leaving him alone in the loft. The first thing he thought of doing, the very first thing, was tell Eddie all about it. And then he remembered that the Eddie he wanted to tell was out of his reach, and Edmundo deserved more than to be treated as a stand-in. So instead he got up and went about the motions of turning the loft livable again, starting with getting rid of all the dust that had built up.

And then he tried to settle in for his first night truly alone in years.

“I’m thinking of going back to Frank,” Edmundo told him, while they watched Christopher run around the playground. The ease with which the boy made friends would always amaze Buck, and he would always be envious of him for it.

“That’s good,” he said, turning on the park bench to face the other man. “May I ask what brought this on?”

“It’s like I said when you came back,” he answered. “That other me was right, I’m not fine. I haven’t been fine. I- I’ve been panicking for months, if not longer. And I was running away, too, when I said I was leaving because of Christopher. I was doing the exact same thing I did when I reenlisted after his diagnosis, and just like then, I pushed someone away that I loved.”

“Eds…”

“I’m scared,” he admitted. “I’ve been so scared of leaving Christopher. Of him losing another parent. I’m scared of dying and leaving him behind. Because I got shot in the middle of the street helping a kid, and people get hurt pulling into their driveway or get killed crossing the street, and I- I’m scared, Evan.”
