“There’s no shame in fear,” Buck told him. “And there’s no shame in needing help.”

“Well, I- I need help.”

“Okay, so then, what can I do?” he asked, reaching over to take Edmundo’s hand in his own. “Because I promised to have your back, and I know I’ve really dropped the ball there in the past few months, but I- Whatever you need, Eds.”

“I need to feel safe,” he whispered. “But uh, go with me? When I go to see Frank?”

“Of course,” Buck promised. After a moment’s thought, he raised his hand up between them, pinky out.

“Seriously?” the other man asked, staring at it with a smile.

“Don’t mock it.”

“I wouldn’t dare,” Edmundo said, reaching up with his own pinky and hooking them together.

“So when are you planning on coming back to the station?” Hen asked, during one of her by now regular visits to the loft. It had been three weeks since his return from the crossroads, time fast approaching the end of February, and Buck had managed to clear the psych eval required of him after going missing for a month. He just... Hadn't gone back, yet.

“I don’t know,” he answered truthfully.

“You don’t know?”

“Nope.”

Trying to reinsert himself back into his old life had been difficult and painful, and Buck wasn’t really certain if he had it in him some days. The first time he laid eyes on Jee-Yun - this version of her - since October, she had hidden her face from him and cried, because he had been an utter stranger to the little girl. And there were times he caught himself almost picking up the phone to gossip with Shannon, only to be reminded that she was dead here. 

To add going back to this version of the station without even Edmundo there by his side would probably be his actual breaking point.

“Maybe when Eddie decides he’s ready to come back,” he offered.

“Buck, we have no idea when or if he’s going to come back.”

“Then we have no idea when or if I’m going to. I’ve accrued a lot of leave time, I don’t have to decide now,” he said. “Hen, nothing I said back in October has really changed. And obviously, I was right, because you’ve all managed to get along without me so far.”

“Buckaroo,” she said, reaching up to cup his cheek with her hand, forcing him to look at her. “Are you okay? Because you look…”

“I’m getting there,” he told her, and it was almost the truth. “Just been having some trouble sleeping.”

“A lot of trouble, from the looks of it,” she said. 

And he had been having a lot of trouble sleeping. He still wasn’t used to having the bed to himself, and the most restful nights he got anymore were spent on Edmundo’s couch. The absence of Eddie - the other Eddie, the one he had started thinking of as his - was like a missing limb, filling him with such a deep ache that it kept him awake. 

It both did and didn’t help when Edmundo did something that was so very him - that was so very them - and Buck couldn’t see the difference between the two any more.

“I’ll be fine,” he assured her. “Seriously. I- I might not be fine now, but I will be. I promise.”

“Just as long as you keep that promise.”

The nights spent at the Diaz residence always had been, and always would be, his favorite nights. Maybe it was because of how familiar they were, no matter the timeline. Maybe it was because he was spending it with family, his family, no matter how altered or changed. Either way, for either reason, he spent far more nights there than he did at the loft.

Not that either Diaz boy was complaining. Chris would practically beg him to stay, and Edmundo would make a point of locking the doors, and Buck would just settle back into the couch for another movie. And then, when Chris inevitably passed out on his shoulder, he’d help carry him to bed and get his own bedding out for the couch.

On the thirty-first night since Buck came back, Edmundo decided to change the script a little.

“Why do you keep sleeping on the couch?” he asked.

“Because you keep locking the doors on me so I can’t leave,” Buck said, arms filled with sheets and a pillow.

“That’s not what I meant,” Edmundo said, looking torn about the conversation. “I meant… I know you can’t be sleeping very well-”

“Better than you’d think.”

“Uh-huh. But, I mean… Buck, there’s room in the bed with-”

“No.” The sharpness of his voice had Edmundo blinking at him in surprise.

“No?”

“No,” he repeated, shaking his head. “I- I can’t…”

“Buck, it doesn’t have to mean anything.”

“I just can’t, Eddie, okay? I’m perfectly fine on the couch, I swear.”

Edmundo fell silent, crossing his arms and leaning against the wall to watch him set up his make-shift bed. Buck felt him staring the entire time, felt his eyes burning into the side of his face as he knelt by the couch and tucked in the sheet.

“It’s because of him, isn’t it?” he finally asked.

“Yes,” Buck answered, voice barely more than a whisper.

“Because you still love him.”

“I still love you, too,” he said, pausing in his task to face the other man. “I’ve loved you for longer than I even knew him. It’s just… I’m trying, okay? I’m trying not to- To- I’m trying not to just replace him with you. You deserve better than that, and he deserves better than that, and I deserve better than that. Because you aren’t him, and he wasn’t you, and… I just need time.”

“Why did you come back?” Edmundo asked, voice as quiet as Buck’s had been.

“I told you, you two-”

“No, Buck. The truth.”

“It is the truth,” he said, standing up. His left knee popped with it, and he grimaced at the sound. “You needed me, and Chris needed me, and it killed me a little every day that you two were hurting because I wasn’t here. But they needed me, too, and while I didn’t choose to abandon the two of you like that, if I chose to come back then I’d be choosing to abandon them.”

“But you did come back.”

“Because you were right,” Buck said, crossing the space to frame Edmundo’s face with his palms. “I just had to tell Ichabod what I wanted. Because I did want to be here, I swear. Not a day went by that I didn’t regret running away like I did. So I told Ichabod what I wanted, and now there’s a me there, and there’s a me here, and no one’s being left behind.”

“Just like that?”

“Just like that.”

“But you, this you… You did lose them,” Edmundo said.

“I did,” he said, blinking away the tears that fact brought out. “So I just… I just need some time. I’m not going anywhere, I’m not leaving again. I just need time.”

“Alright,” the other man said, letting out a sigh. He reached up to take one of Buck’s hands in his, turning it so he could place a chaste kiss to the knuckles there before letting it go and stepping back. “Then… Then I guess I’ll wait.”

“Thank you,” Buck whispered.

“And the offer is still open, you know. If you can’t sleep.”

“Thank you. I’ll keep that in mind, just not-”

“Not now, I get it,” Edmundo said. “Are you… Are you still driving me to Frank’s tomorrow?”

“It was a pinky promise,” Buck said. “And then we’ll get something greasy afterwards, as a reward for being so brave about it.”

“Thanks,” Edmundo said, rolling his eyes, but the irritation was obviously put upon. “Then, I guess… Good night.”

“Good night, Eds,” he said, and stood there long enough to watch the other man close the bedroom door behind him. When the latch clicked shut, he let himself lean onto the wall for support. He wasn’t quite okay, and this place wasn’t quite home again, yet.

But they’d both get there.

Chapter End Notes

Deep breaths.

Lost and Found

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The trip to the hospital to get his brain checked out was an awkward one. Apparently Christopher was with his mother, and so it was just Eddie and Buck. The latter spent the car ride looking through his phone, the one that had been on the bedside table with the necklace which was currently in his pocket. He wasn’t sure why he grabbed it, but it had felt important and he hadn’t wanted to leave it behind.

“Who’s Fire Dad?” Buck asked, frowning at his contacts list. It was listed right below “EdDILF,” which he was assuming was Eddie.

“That’s probably Bobby.”

“Captain Nash.”

“Yes.”

“And Police Mom is…?”

“Athena, she’s Bobby’s wife.”

“God, I need a flow chart,” he groused.

“I think Ravi made one.”

Buck frowned at the name and started scrolling through his contact list. He saw Weird Al Hankovic and It’s Gonna Be May and Literal Rocket Scientist, but no Ravi or even anything to hint at him. He looked up at Eddie, who apparently noticed his confusion, because he said,

“I think you have him under Probie-ly Jinxed.”

“Oh, there he is. Okay, so who’s Baby Mama? Wait, do I have a kid?” And then, the moment it was out of his mouth, felt compelled to add, “Another kid besides Chris, I mean.”

“No, just Chris,” Eddie said, glancing at him curiously before turning back to the traffic ahead. “And it’s probably Shannon. That’s his mom, my ex-wife.”

“Well I would hope she’s your ex. Wait, I’m not a homewrecker, am I?”

“No!” the other man exclaimed, shaking his head. “The marriage was dead long before me and you were a thing.”

“Good, that’s good,” he said, nodding. “So I can’t help but notice that uh, the captain and his wife are the only Mom and Dad I have on my phone. Did mine finally give up on me entirely or…?”

“Fuck your parents.” The vehemence in Eddie’s words took him aback.

“Have you met them?”

“They came down to see Maddie. It was a dumpster fire.”

“At least they’re talking to her again, I guess. They cut her off when she married Doug.” Eddie’s face did something funny at the mention of the man’s name. Buck couldn’t really label what kind of expression it was, but it was a complicated twist of muscles that told a story he wasn’t privy to anymore. “Please tell me she left him.”

“She did,” the other man confirmed, a strange tone to his voice.

“About time. He was such a dick when I knew him, Eds. A massive, raging asshole. Not liking him was one of the only things my parents and I ever agreed fully on.”

Eddie fell silent, and Buck spent the rest of the car ride looking through the pictures on his phone. There seemed to be hundreds of them, each one filled with scenes and faces he couldn’t remember. The majority were of Chris and Eddie, together and separately. Occasionally they were joined by a woman he assumed was Shannon, or a pair of boys that were Chris’ age, or with a pair of older women that he could assume were related to Eddie based entirely on appearance.

But the best picture he found had also been the one set as his lock screen, the one of Eddie sleeping on the couch with a snoozing Chris practically on top of him, neither of them in a position that looked comfortable. It made Buck’s heart ache, and it made him jealous of the version of him who had managed to find this little family.

They pulled into a spot not far from the entrance to the ER - and Buck could agree that suddenly losing entire years worth of memories was an emergency - and Eddie checked his phone before getting out.

“They’re waiting for us just inside,” he said, slipping it back into his pocket.

“Maddie?” Buck asked, feeling excitement at the prospect of seeing his sister again. Screw it if he had seen her just the day before, he didn’t remember that. The last time he remembered seeing her was right after his motorcycle crash, when she was giving him the keys to the jeep and telling him to go.

“Yeah. Bobby and Athena’s here, too.”

“Why?” he asked, and the question had Eddie stopping to frown at him.

“Because something’s happened to you and they’re worried,” he said, as if it was an obvious reason and Buck really should have known that.

“Okay, but that doesn’t really explain why they’re here…?”

The other man stared at him for a moment, before shaking his head and continuing to lead them into the building.

“Fuck your parents,” he said again as they stepped into the controlled chaos of the ER waiting room. 

“Eddie! Buck!” someone called, and Buck turned to look at them. The man making his way towards them was about as tall as he was and frowning in concern. There was a woman on his heels, dark-skinned and frowning just as much.

“Hi, uh… Captain Nash?” Buck assumed that was who this was. The greeting had the two of them stuttering to a stop.

“He doesn’t remember,” Eddie said. “Like I said.”

“I had hoped- Never mind,” the captain said, shaking his head. “And just call me Bobby, kid.”

“Bobby,” he repeated. To the woman, he held out an awkward hand and said, “And you’re Mrs. Nash?”

Bobby and Eddie both drew sharp breaths at that, and it left Buck wondering what he said wrong.

“It’s Grant-Nash, actually,” she said, crossing her arms.

“Oh, I- I’m sorry, Mrs-”

“Sergeant.”

“Sergeant Grant-Nash, uh-”

“Just call me Athena, baby,” she said, uncrossing her arms and dragging him into a hug. It was unexpected, and he stiffened at first before letting himself melt into it. It was a nice hug, the kind he had imagined other kids would get from their mothers.

“It’s uh, nice to meet you both? Again?” he said, feeling extremely awkward about this.

“Well, it’s certainly a better first meeting than the first time I actually met you,” Athena said, letting him go and stepping back.

“Why, what happened?”

“You pissed me off and I yelled at you.”

“Oh. I’m sorry?”

“Evan?” His sister’s voice cut through the conversation, and Buck perked up. He spotted her a few steps away.

“Maddie!” he cried, face breaking into a grin as he ran forward to hug her. “You’re here!”

“I’m here,” she said, returning the hug.

“I’ve missed you so much,” he said, stepping back to smile at her. “And you’re looking so good, too!”

“So he remembers his sister, at least,” he heard Bobby say.

“He woke up thinking it was the morning of his first day at the station,” Eddie told them, and Buck turned around to see them all sharing a loaded glance. Much like with Doug, there was a story there that he was sure he once knew. 

“Well, let’s go see what the doctors have to say,” Maddie urged. “C’mon.”

It turns out what the doctors had to say amounted to a shrug, just with a bunch of fancy words attached. They put him through MRI and CT scans, took vial after vial of blood, ran tests for seizures. None of it pointed to a probable cause. Buck just woke up one day with years taken from his brain, and no one could say why or how.

“Has he had any emotional shock recently?” the doctor asked, after the tests failed to show any cause. Buck was fairly certain they didn’t normally let four people stay with a patient, but the nurses had simply met them with a knowing look and let them go.

“I woke up thinking it was four years ago, does that count?”

“There’s been nothing in the past month,” Eddie said, shaking his head.

“Well, he has no signs of trauma to the brain, no physical causes for the memory loss,” the doctor said. “The only thing we can think of is that it’s psychogenic.”

“So I’m crazy,” Buck said, only for Athena to smack him on the back of the head.

“The good news is that it’s typically temporary.”

“Typically,” Eddie repeated. “It’s typically temporary. So it could also not be? It could be permanent?”

“A lot of the ways the mind works is still a mystery,” the doctor said, shrugging. “It’s really hard to say.”

Eddie drew in a breath, let it out. He drew in another, let it out. And then he turned on his heel and walked out the door into the hall. Bobby went after him, and the doctor excused himself as well, leaving only Maddie and Athena in the room with Buck.

“I feel like I should apologize to him,” he said, frowning at the doorway.

“For what? This isn’t your fault,” Athena said, patting him on the arm.

“For not being the Buck he wants.”

He ignored the way the sergeant and his sister frowned at each other.

“He’s so different,” Eddie told Bobby between calls one shift. It had been days since a Buck he sometimes could only barely recognize woke up in their bed. A Buck who had actually wanted to go out to the bars and drink on New Years Eve, a Buck who didn’t know how to cook breakfast, a Buck that was brash and loud and so very insecure about everything. A couple nights after the trip to the hospital, Buck had tried seducing him. And Eddie had shut it down, because he felt so uncomfortable with the idea of having sex with a version of his boyfriend that was practically a stranger.

The way the man had acted afterwards, like a kicked dog waiting to be thrown out the door, was very concerning for all its implications.

“He is missing years of his life,” the captain said. “A decade, almost.”

They hadn’t told this version of Buck about the time-traveling and had kept their theories about its connection to his memory loss to themselves. They weren’t sure if it would help, or if the man would even believe them.

“How have you been?”

“I miss him,” Eddie confessed. “He’s right there, but he’s also not. And then he does something that is so very him and I forget for a moment what’s changed.”

“And Chris?”

“Chris is… Handling it,” he said. “Honestly, when he’s with Chris is one of the times I forget that he’s not my- That he’s not the Buck I knew.”

“Things will get better,” Bobby said, and he sounded so confident about it that Eddie almost believed him.

Almost.

Christopher was the coolest kid Buck had ever met, and was absolutely his favorite person. He was funny and smart and a goddamn ball of sunshine, and the fact that Buck was a dad to this kid, had been helping raise this kid, was just so mind blowing at times that he had difficulties wrapping his head around it. From the moment he had laid eyes on that drawing of the stick figure family, Buck knew that he would die a thousand times over for both him and Eddie.

And he couldn’t even remember his first time meeting the boy.

It was overwhelming at times. He had fallen asleep one night in a crowded apartment he shared with people that were little better than strangers, and woke up to a family that actually cared about him, a family that would actually show up if something was wrong. The only problem, really, was the ghost that was haunting him. Or, perhaps he was the ghost that was haunting everyone else.

He saw it in the way everyone looked at him when he said or did something that was obviously not what they were expecting, or when he didn’t say or do something that they were expecting. He felt it in the way there would be a joke made that he was obviously supposed to be in on, but which just flew right over his head. He knew it in the way Eddie had refused to fuck him just because Buck couldn’t remember little things like their anniversary or how they first met.

Okay, so they weren’t little things, but Buck had been feeling anything but generous afterwards. Sex was what he was good at, sex was what all of his previous partners had wanted from him, and if Eddie didn’t want it, then… Then Buck had no idea what Eddie wanted him around for.

He had almost ran to Maddie’s that night, but something in the back of his mind recoiled violently at the thought of leaving Eddie and Chris like that. So instead he settled for sleeping on the couch. It was where he had been spending every night since.

The only person who looked at him and made him think they were actually seeing him was Chris. Chris who was, somehow, his son. Not by blood, but still. The fact that someone, the fact that Eddie had looked at him and thought him a functional enough adult to be trusted with a living, breathing child was…

It was so far outside his point of reference that he didn’t really have a way to describe it.

But Chris was at school now, and Buck was left to his own devices, since they weren’t really comfortable letting a firefighter with unexplained memory loss back on rotation right away. And being left to his own devices often went poorly for him, especially if given time to think. Because now he was trying to figure out how he could make Eddie want to keep him around. He couldn’t really cook, and Eddie clearly didn’t want him for sex, and literally no one in history had ever wanted him around for his personality, so… What did that leave?

Cleaning was what he decided to try.

He started in the kitchen, mopping the floor and wiping the counter and running the dishes. He vacuumed and swept the living room and the hall. He picked up the floor in Chris’ room, careful not to really disturb anything, before starting to strip the bed to run through the washer. And there, under the pillows, was a letter.

Now, curiosity had always been his fatal flaw, and it was made worse when he recognized his own handwriting. So he read it, the ink smeared in places where someone’s tears had fallen on the paper, fiddling with the necklace that had been next to his phone that first day and which he had taken to wearing. The words left him confused, because this was a goodbye letter, or at least it read that way. A goodbye letter that he had written.

Frowning, he set it aside and finished stripping the bed, before moving on to their- to Eddie’s room to collect the laundry in there. But he walked away from that letter with the ghost-like feeling of a small hand on his cheek, and the echo of someone saying,

“You’re gonna be okay, kid.”

“So this is the Buck we almost had,” Hen said, watching him with Ravi. It was Buck’s first day back to work since being cleared again, and no one was quite sure how to handle it. It had been weird the entire day, with Buck needing to be shown the ropes again like a run of the mill probie. The man had to often be held back from just running headlong into danger and was even more impulsive than the one they’d gotten used to.

Currently, the actual probie was showing him the flow chart he had made to make sense of the interpersonal dynamics of the station. The two of them had formed a dynamic that was almost the reverse of what it had been, with Ravi taking the older man under his wing.

“I wasn’t sure if I believed the time travel story on Christmas,” she continued. “But this is…”

“He’s different.” Eddie had said and thought that phrase so much in the past few weeks that it was automatic now.  “I am very thankful he made me learn how to cook over the summer, or we’d all be screwed right now.”

“Oh God, did you see his face when Bobby asked him to help with breakfast this morning?” she asked. “Before Cap remembered himself and things got awkward, I mean.”

“Did you see Bobby’s face when Buck called him pops?”

“He called it Buck One-point-Oh once, when he was telling me about the other timeline,” Bobby said, joining them. “Along with a Two-point-Oh, and a Three-point-Oh.”

“Like software updates?” Eddie asked. God, his boyfriend was so weird, and he missed him so much.

“Apparently so,” the captain said. “He warned me that this one couldn’t cook, couldn’t tie a tie, and apparently stole fire trucks for hookups.”

“Well, this Buck One-point-Oh is giving Underwood fits.”

“You’re still dragging him to therapy?” Hen asked.

“With the way he’s acted since Christmas? I am definitely still dragging him with me to therapy.” This version of Buck needed it just as much as the older one, if in different ways and for different reasons. “And there’s also… Daniel.”

Both Bobby and Hen winced at the name.

“I had forgotten about that particular family trauma,” the paramedic said.

“And he hasn’t learned about it yet,” the captain said. “Has he?”

“Nope,” Eddie said, shaking his head. “As far as this Buck knows, it was always just him and Maddie. I’m going to talk to Underwood about it, because I’m not comfortable keeping it a secret, but I also have no idea how to go about telling him. But even besides all that, he’s been having nightmares.”

It was hard to tell most nights, because Buck was still sleeping on the couch, even after Eddie had offered to let him take the bed. But he was certain the man had been having nightmares because there were nights he woke up to him moving about in the hallway, like he was checking on him and Chris. The night before, even, he had been woken up by Buck poking his head through the door and then letting out a sigh of relief when he saw Eddie was okay.

“Nightmares? Do you know what they’re about?” Hen asked.

“He hasn’t actually said.”

“Do you think…?” Bobby trailed off, but he heard the question regardless.

“I don’t-”

He was interrupted by a startled shout and the sound of a chair being knocked over. They turned to find Buck with his back pressed against the wall, while Ravi looked on in confusion and Chimney stood with his hand still in the air.

“I- I’m sorry,” Chimney said. “I didn’t mean to…”

“It’s fine,” Buck said, plastic smile firmly in place. “I- I’m gonna…”

He practically ran away from the situation, leaving confusion and concern in his wake.

“What happened?” the captain asked, walking over to the table Ravi had been sitting at with Buck.

“I don’t know,” the probie said, getting up and picking up the chair Buck must have knocked over. “We were sitting here going over the flowchart when…”

“I reached for his shoulder,” Chimney said, sounding almost hopeful. “I reached for him and he got startled.”

The dreams had been a nightly occurrence for weeks, now. They started with that first one, the one with the man in black and the bright blue butterfly, and then increased with intensity after reading that letter he found under Chris’ pillow. Buck hadn’t really paid the dreams much mind, honestly didn’t remember them much after waking up. The details of some of them clung to his waking world like wet sand, however, even as he forgot the broad strokes of them.

He had dreamt, so far, of an exploding ambulance and of a piece of rebar in someone’s head. He had dreamt of that blue butterfly dancing in the air beneath a streetlamp, and of being surrounded by a bunch of tiny women he was terrified of stepping on. There was the dream of running through a snow-covered forest, and the dream of someone in a car that always had him scrubbing his hands red and raw when he woke up, even though he couldn’t remember why. He had dreamt, also, of having his leg trapped in a multitude of situations and scenarios.

But the worst dreams were the ones he couldn’t forget, no matter how hard he tried, and which kept repeating themselves. Those dreams involved Eddie and Chris, and the constant fear of losing them. But they were also the most confusing, because details would switch part way through.

There was the one with Chris on the pier, for example, which started with the boy asking where the water went. One moment it would just be the two of them, running for their lives before the water yanked them apart, and then it would change so Shannon was there with them. Or it would involve Buck searching through wreckage alone, repeatedly calling out for the boy, and then suddenly Eddie would be there searching with him, and they would both be in their LAFD uniforms.

And how it ended would change, too, sometimes melting together in the same dream. Buck would either be telling Eddie that he had lost their kid, only for a complete stranger to suddenly appear with him like a miracle from God, or Buck would be with Shannon and Chris as Eddie found them. Or… Or the one, where Eddie and Buck found Chris in a tent…

Then there was the dream which Buck was certain was a memory, because he had the scar to prove it. But even then the details changed and rearranged themselves, because half the time he was watching Eddie get shot, when it was his chest marred by the circle of puckered skin. And sometimes it would start out as another dream, one where Buck would hear a gunshot and start running out of a hospital calling Eddie’s name, and then find himself back on that street with Eddie on the pavement, bleeding out.

It was after weeks, and weeks, and weeks of these dreams, of dreaming of a too-still Chris surrounded by equally still sheet-covered mounds, of dreaming about Eddie bleeding out on a pavement while telling him he was leaving, that Buck finally broke. He peeled himself off the couch and pulled the sheet around him, trailing it down the hall in an imitation of that first morning after Christmas. 

There was a light on in the room, and he didn’t bother knocking before opening the door. A startled Eddie looked up from where he was reading a crumpled looking letter.

“I know I’m not him,” he said, feeling so very small and vulnerable. “I know I’m not the Buck that you actually want. I know you want the other Buck, the- The one who can cook, the one who isn’t an idiot, the one who you keep looking for whenever you look at me. And I get it, okay? This me is a disappointment to literally everyone and I’m sorry that you lost the improved version.”

“Buck…”

“But can we just… Can we just pretend for a night?” he asked, wiping away the tears before he could fall. “Because I- I am tired of being alone, and I just want you to hold me, and… Please? Just for a night?”

“It’s not pretend,” Eddie said, placing the letter onto the bedside table and patting the space beside him. Buck sniffled and climbed into the bed, immediately grabbing and clutching a pillow to his chest. “I do want you. I always want you. I’m sorry I’ve made you feel like I didn’t.”

“Why the hell would anyone want me, Eds?” he asked, closing his eyes. “I’m just spare, defective parts.”

The other man fell silent, long enough that Buck almost fell asleep. The bed was far more comfier than the couch, but honestly, it was probably the way Eddie had started running his fingers through his hair that was doing it.

“You’re not defective,” Eddie finally said, the words coming out like a sigh. “And you’re still you. In all the ways that count, you are still you, even if you don’t remember everything. I love you so very much that it aches, and I’m sorry that I- That I haven’t been seeing you for you.”

“I knew I loved you before I even knew your name,” Buck said, smiling sleepily up at him. “And I forgive you. It’s what it means to be part of a team, right?”

“Right…”

Seeing Buck with a baby was always, and would always, be one Eddie’s biggest weaknesses. Seeing Buck with his baby niece was even worse. Even now, seeing him playing with the one year old was enough to make Eddie melt. Add Chris to the mix - as he was now - and someone might as well stick a fork in him, because Eddie was done.

“Take a picture, it lasts longer,” Maddie said, smirking at him. The meds they had switched her to after the black out were helping her a lot, as was being able to talk to Shannon about things she couldn’t talk to the rest of them about. 

“He’s taken ten,” Chimney said, sounding equally amused. They - Eddie and Buck and Chris - had been invited to theirs for dinner, and now Eddie had been abandoned in favor of a toddler that couldn’t even say his name.

“Shut up, the both of you,” Eddie groused, tearing his eyes away and setting his phone down.

“So, you two are… Adjusting?” Maddie asked, sounding like she was trying to be delicate.

“That’s a term for it.” Things were better, but he was still having trouble looking past the differences between this Buck and the other. “I’ve been feeling newfound sympathy for how Buck must have struggled with everything. It’s… It’s been hard to look at him and not see the other Buck, and then…”

“That was why you were so adamant that he didn’t love you, at the beginning,” Chimney said. “Right? Because you already knew about the time travel by then, and so…”

“I accused him of loving a ghost,” Eddie said. “And now here I am, loving a ghost.”

“So then, get to know this one,” Maddie suggested. “Fall in love with this one.”

“That’s half the problem. I’m already in love with him,” he said, resting his head in his palm. “I mean, it’s Buck. Who wouldn’t fall in love with him if given half the chance? I just… No, it’s stupid.”

“Whatever it is, I’m sure it’s not stupid.”

“I feel like I’m cheating on him,” he confessed in a whisper. “It’s stupid, because I’m not. It’s still Buck, in all the ways that count, it’s still him. But…”

“But it’s also not,” Chimney said.

“Yeah. We’re sleeping together again - not like that, just sleeping - and it’s nice, but I still feel so stupidly guilty.”

“Just take your time,” Maddie suggested. “He still loves you, anyone could see that, so just take your time.”

Eddie let out a sigh and nodded, because that was all he could do. Forcing it would only hurt them both, especially with the way this Buck viewed his self-worth in a relationship. He didn’t want Buck to start thinking that sex was the only thing he wanted out of the man, when all he really wanted was Buck. So he would give it time, and pray that time gave them what they needed.

Buck was cleaning again, because despite everything, he still didn’t trust his place in this house, in this family the other him had made and which he had woken up to. While they were sharing a bed again, Eddie still didn’t want to do anything more than cuddle, which was… Actually, it was nice. The cuddling. Curling up in someone else’s arms, or having them curl up in his. Waking up to someone else in the bed with him and not having to sneak out. But it still left Buck feeling like he needed to prove to the man he was worth keeping around. Bobby might have been teaching him to cook - which sometimes felt like he was relearning things, and sometimes felt like he was being handed a book written in Latin and expected to already understand it - but he was barely able to do more than scramble eggs. 

So, he was cleaning again. He washed the dishes, he did the laundry. He mopped, he vacuumed, he swept, he dusted. Hell, he even cleaned the toilet and scrubbed the sides of the shower. He made sure the place was as spotless as it damn well could be. And then he put away the laundry, even matching and balling up all of Eddie’s black socks so he couldn’t complain again.

He was about done when his eyes fell on something sticking out of the table drawer on Eddie’s side of the bed. When he pulled it out, he saw that it was once again a letter in his handwriting, the same letter he remembered Eddie was reading when he burst into the room the other night. Curiosity winning out, he sat down and started reading it himself.

And then, when he was done, he started to remember.

He remembered a grenade in a man’s leg, and he remembered promising to have each other’s backs. He remembered a day spent at the station with the best kid in the world, and he remembered pushing him on a skateboard made just for him. He remembered going to a concert with a man that he wished so very much was his real father, and he remembered hearing the woman he wished was his mother fighting for her life. He remembered the joy he felt when he first saw his sister again, both times. 

He remembered the tsunami, each tsunami. He remembered Eddie being shot, and he remembered being shot in his stead. He remembered the truck bombing, and he remembered stopping the truck bombing, and he remembered letting the truck bombing happen.

He remembered his family breaking apart around him, and he remembered running away in a panic from everything he loved.

He remembered eyes of black, and he remembered a blue that encompassed everything.

He remembered Eddie saying, “You are not expendable,” and he remembered Eddie saying, “It felt like you weren’t seeing me.”

But mostly, he remembered each and every time that Eddie said, “I love you.”

When Eddie opened the front door, he knew right away that something was different. Perhaps it was the smell of food that alerted him to the change, or the sound of singing in the kitchen. He glanced down at Chris, whom he’d just picked up from Shannon's, and shrugged at his questioning gaze.

“Go put your things away, mijo,” he said, taking off his coat and hanging it on the hook on the wall. “I’ll go see what Buck’s up to.”

“Okay, Dad,” Chris said, agreeing readily and going off to do just that.

Eddie slipped off his shoes, leaving them with the others by the door, and crept towards the kitchen. Poking his head in, he saw the other man at the stove, swinging his hips as he sang along to the music playing on his phone.

“Too high, can’t come down!” Buck belted out, loudly and horribly off key, as he practically bounced in place. “It’s in the air and it’s all around-”

“Am I interrupting something?” Eddie asked, and was instantly greeted by the other man spinning around and smiling brightly at him, the St. Christopher medal he’d gotten him for Christmas swinging around his neck.

“Not at all, love,” he said. The pet name had Eddie’s heart skipping a beat. “I was just about done with dinner.”

“Dinner that you cooked.”

“Yup. It’s a, uh, recipe that Bobby taught me forever ago.”

“Buck?” Eddie took a cautious step forward, unwilling to trust it, unwilling to hope. All the signs pointed towards it, but if it wasn’t…

“It’s me, love,” Buck said, his bright smile turning into something softer and cozier. Eddie let out a breath that was more of a sob and practically ran to him, wrapping his arms around him and squeezing him as tightly as he could.

“I missed you,” he said. “I- I tried not to, because you were right there, but I- I still missed you so much…”

“I know, and I’m so sorry about that,” his boyfriend said, hugging him back.

“What happened?”

“I chose to stay,” Buck said with a helpless shrug. “And then I… I got a bit lost?”

“But you found your way home,” Eddie said, burying his face into the other man’s shoulder.

“Eventually,” the other man said, rubbing his back. “I love you.”

“I love you, too.”

“So much you ache with it, apparently,” Buck said, and then snickered when he got smacked for it. “Should we go tell Chris?”

“Probably,” Eddie agreed, not moving a muscle to let go of the other man. “Just give me a minute.”

“I’ll give you forever,” Buck said. “I’m not planning on going anywhere anytime soon…”

Vanessa did not know where she was. The young woman had been driving - fleeing, really - for hours, now. The sun had set sometime ago, although the clock in her used car hadn’t been working for at least two presidential administrations, so she wasn’t really certain how long ago that was. It was an old car, and an ugly one, but it had served her well up to this point.

So it was heartbreaking, when it suddenly came to a rolling stop.

“Fuck!” she shouted, banging a fist on the steering wheel. It had died just short of a four-way intersection, no other cars in sight. Not even a road sign, to point her in the direction of civilization. “Great, just… Great!”

She threw the door open and stepped out onto the dusty pavement, throwing her head back to glare up into the starry sky above. There wasn’t time for this, she had to keep moving. She had to-

“Howdy, stranger.”

The young woman swirled around, eyes landing on a man standing in the middle of the road. He hadn’t been there before, she was certain of it. He was tall and looming, wearing a wide brimmed hat and a long black coat. The man wasn’t making any moves to come closer, and that fact helped settle her nerves a little. Only a little though.

“Who are you?” she demanded.

“My name’s Ichabod,” the man said. “And you?”

“Vanessa,” she said, and was not certain why she said it. 

“It’s a bit late for a drive, isn’t it?” the man - Ichabod - asked, taking slow, measured steps towards her.

“I- I was trying to get away,” she told him. “My husband, he… He’s not a very good one.”

“That is always a shame,” Ichabod said, voice laced with sympathy. Now he was closer, the moonlight helped her see just how thin his face looked, with sunken eyes and jutting cheekbones. Like a skull, she thought.

“My father always adored him, he wouldn’t listen when I-” She shook her head. “I just couldn’t stay there any longer.”

“And so you ran away.”

“I- Yeah, I guess I did.”

“Tell me, Vanessa,” the man said, holding his hand out for her to take. “What do you want?”

Had his eyes always been black?

 

Fin.
